title: Heavy-Tailed Memory Traces in Long-Horizon Language Agents
summary: Long-horizon language agents increasingly rely on external memory as a frozen world model, yet current memory systems are usually judged only by task success or token cost. We argue that the missing object is the shape of memory use: under finite context and repeated retrieval, agent memory can concentrate on a small core while leaving rare states in a long tail where prediction errors accumulate. We study this effect through a conservative tail audit and find that concentration is reproducible but policy-dependent. Random-walk agents produce log-normal-compatible retrieval artifacts, whereas semantic LLM policies yield the strongest truncated-power-law-compatible core--tail traces. Motivated by this audit, we propose Core--Tail World Model (CTWM), a rank-based memory controller that allocates prompt budget with a single exponent $τ$ while retaining a summarized tail. On Synthetic Graph World, CTWM preserves full state and transition coverage, reduces prompt tokens by 5.9%, and lowers bottom-half tail prediction error by 13.6% relative to a graph-memory baseline. The same paired comparison gives consistent token savings on ALFWorld and a 24.48% token reduction on LongMemEval with aggregate accuracy parity. These results suggest that heavy-tailed memory traces are not only a diagnostic of finite retrieval, but also a practical control signal for token-efficient agent world models.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how long-horizon language agents actually use external memory, finds that memory access patterns form a heavy-tailed core–tail distribution, and introduces a rank-based controller (CTWM) that exploits this structure to reduce token usage while preserving performance.
AI.motivation: Most work on external memory for language agents evaluates memory systems only by overall task success or token cost, ignoring how memory usage is distributed across states. Under finite context windows and repeated retrieval, this can cause agents to over-focus on a small core of frequently retrieved states while neglecting rare but important states, where prediction errors can accumulate. The authors aim to characterize this core–tail effect, understand how policies influence it, and turn these observations into a more principled and efficient memory controller.
AI.method: The authors perform a “tail audit” of memory use in long-horizon language agents, characterizing the distribution of memory retrievals under different policies (random-walk vs. semantic LLM policies) and fitting these distributions to heavy-tailed families (log-normal vs. truncated power law). Based on the insight that memory retrievals are heavy-tailed, they introduce Core–Tail World Model (CTWM), a rank-based memory controller parameterized by a single exponent τ. CTWM allocates more of the prompt budget to a frequently used core while maintaining a summarized representation of the long tail, and they evaluate CTWM against a graph-memory baseline in Synthetic Graph World, ALFWorld, and LongMemEval.
AI.result: In Synthetic Graph World, CTWM maintains full coverage of states and transitions, reduces prompt tokens by 5.9%, and lowers prediction error on the bottom-half of tail states by 13.6% compared with a graph-memory baseline. In ALFWorld, CTWM again yields consistent token savings while preserving performance. On LongMemEval, it achieves a 24.48% reduction in token usage with no drop in aggregate accuracy. The tail audit also shows that random-walk agents yield log-normal-like retrieval distributions, while semantic LLM policies produce stronger truncated-power-law-like core–tail patterns.
AI.conclusion: Agent memory usage naturally exhibits heavy-tailed, core–tail patterns under finite-context retrieval, and these patterns depend on the agent’s policy. Rather than treating this as merely a pathology, the heavy-tailed structure can be used as a control signal. The proposed CTWM controller leverages a simple rank-based scheme with a single exponent to allocate prompt budget efficiently, achieving significant token savings and reduced tail prediction errors while maintaining state coverage and task performance. Heavy-tailed memory traces thus provide both diagnostic insight and a practical design principle for token-efficient world models in long-horizon language agents.

title: When Do Causal World Models Help Modular LLM Agents
summary: LLM agents increasingly act through modular systems, such as order, payment, inventory, and shipment services, where actions in one module change which transitions are valid in another. Standard world models usually fit observational traces, but this is not the quantity needed for intervention-time planning: a trace may show that payment precedes shipment without identifying whether payment authorizes shipment, inventory mediates the effect, or a hidden trigger explains both. We study this gap through FedCausalCompose, a causal world-model framework for modular LLM agents in which local actions provide intervention-response evidence for cross-module interfaces. We first show that observational world models incur an irreducible interventional error under unblocked back-door paths, that interface recovery improves with intervention-response coverage, and that an oracle causal composition can beat the non-causal lower bound when coverage and local mechanism errors are controlled. We then test the resulting prediction in diagnostic agent settings. Causal interfaces help most in structured tool environments, where API signatures expose preconditions and downstream effects. In contrast, dialogue and narrative environments often ignore raw edge lists unless a short attention anchor makes the causal information decision-relevant. These results identify a concrete condition for causal world models in LLM agents: causal structure helps when cross-module interfaces are both statistically identifiable and presented in a form the agent can use at action time.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces FedCausalCompose, a causal world-model framework for modular LLM agents, showing when and how causal interfaces across modules improve planning over purely observational world models.
AI.motivation: LLM agents increasingly operate via multiple tools and services (order, payment, inventory, shipment), where actions in one module constrain and enable actions in others. Existing observational world models learn from passive traces but fail to capture the interventional structure needed for planning: observing that event A precedes B does not reveal whether A causes B, whether another variable mediates the effect, or whether both share a hidden cause. This mismatch between observational fitting and interventional decision-making motivates a framework that explicitly models causal interfaces between modules using intervention data from local actions.
AI.method: The authors formalize FedCausalCompose, a framework for causal world models where each module’s local actions provide intervention-response data that inform cross-module interfaces. They analyze the theoretical gap between observational and interventional world models, showing conditions under which observational models incur irreducible interventional error via unblocked back-door paths. They study how interface recovery quality depends on intervention-response coverage and local mechanism accuracy, and derive that an oracle causal composition can surpass a non-causal lower bound under these conditions. They then implement diagnostic LLM-agent environments (structured API tools vs dialogue/narrative settings) to empirically test when causal interfaces actually benefit decision-making.
AI.result: Theoretical results show that purely observational world models suffer unavoidable intervention-time errors when there are unblocked back-door paths between modules, while causal composition can mitigate this if there is sufficient intervention coverage and limited local error. Empirically, in structured tool environments—where APIs surface clear preconditions and downstream effects—causal interfaces yield substantial performance gains for LLM agents. However, in dialogue and narrative environments, simply adding causal edge lists brings little benefit unless causal information is made locally salient at decision time (e.g., via short attention anchors).
AI.conclusion: Causal world models are not universally beneficial for LLM agents; they help specifically when cross-module interfaces are (1) statistically identifiable from intervention data and (2) exposed in a representation that the agent can readily exploit at action time. FedCausalCompose provides a framework for building such causal interfaces, clarifying when causal modeling can outperform observational world models in modular tool-using agents.

title: From Proposal to Verified Effect: Praxa, an Evidence-Bound Harness for Governed AI Agent Execution
comment: 30 pages, 8 figures. Engineering validation and descriptive pilot. Public artifacts: https://github.com/praxa-labs/praxa-benchmarks/releases/tag/preprint-v1.4.0
summary: Large-language-model agents can propose and execute actions, but proposal, authority, dispatch, verified external effect, and serving promotion are different claims. We present Praxa, an agent harness that represents these states explicitly through deterministic admission, brokered execution, external read-back, reconciliation, and reviewed promotion. We report four evidence lanes. First, an author-run repository-local audit at a pinned revision passed 1,027/1,027 unit tests and 89/89 Workerd tests, instrumented all 363 expected source files, and met four coverage floors; raw per-test transcripts and independent reproduction are unavailable. Second, in a provider-backed Terminal-Bench Core 0.1.1 pilot across 12 curated tasks, baseline and reliability-layer arms each passed 17/36 strict trials. The reliability layer used 37.49% more input and 50.73% more output tokens, so the pilot does not support superiority. Third, in a post-debug, two-order coordination-proxy development comparison, baseline and a source-authored candidate each completed 180/180 trials with equal measured accuracy, full hermetic crash recovery, and zero protected violations. The candidate used 37.11% fewer tokens, 33.84% lower estimated endpoint cost, and 11.63% fewer steps; this does not establish improved quality, latency, or production behavior. Fourth, deployed source/configuration evidence shows bounded reflection, recall accounting, memory compilation, and tool-health paths, but no production outcome lift. Praxa's supported contribution is an evidence-bound architecture that makes authority-to-effect transitions explicit and testable. Current evidence does not establish adversarial security, production safety, general specialist superiority, autonomous recursive optimization, or user benefit.

AI.tldr: Praxa is an agent architecture that makes each step from model suggestion to real-world effect explicit and testable, with current evidence focusing on correctness and observability rather than performance or safety gains.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agents often blur the distinction between proposing actions, having authority to act, actually executing, verifying external impact, and promoting results to users or systems. This opacity makes it hard to reason about reliability, safety, and accountability. The paper aims to introduce an architecture that explicitly models and tests these transitions so that behavior can be better audited and controlled.
AI.method: The authors define Praxa, an 'agent harness' that decomposes agent operation into explicit states: deterministic admission (what proposals are allowed in), brokered execution (controlled tool calls), external read-back (verifying external side effects), reconciliation (aligning internal state with external outcomes), and reviewed promotion (deciding what is exposed or committed). They then provide four empirical evidence lanes: (1) an internal audit of the codebase via unit and integration tests with coverage checks; (2) a small-scale pilot on Terminal-Bench Core comparing a baseline to a reliability-layer variant; (3) a post-debug controlled comparison on a coordination-proxy development task between a baseline and a source-authored Praxa-based candidate; and (4) evidence from real deployment configurations showing how the architecture supports bounded reflection, accounting, memory compilation, and monitoring of tool health.
AI.result: (1) The internal audit shows the system passes all listed tests with complete instrumentation and specified coverage floors, but raw logs and independent reproduction are unavailable. (2) On Terminal-Bench Core, both baseline and reliability-layer arms pass the same number of strict trials (17/36), with the reliability layer consuming substantially more tokens, so there is no demonstrated performance advantage. (3) In the coordination-proxy comparison, baseline and Praxa-based candidate both achieve perfect completion and equal measured accuracy, but the candidate uses fewer tokens, reduces estimated cost, and takes fewer steps, without proving better quality or latency. (4) Production evidence confirms certain architectural behaviors (bounded reflection, recall accounting, memory compilation, tool-health paths) but shows no measurable lift in production outcomes.
AI.conclusion: Praxa is presented as an architecture that makes the chain from model authority to external effect explicit, observable, and testable. The current evidence supports that the architecture can be implemented with strong internal testing and that it does not obviously degrade task success, sometimes improving efficiency. However, the paper explicitly states that it does not yet demonstrate stronger claims such as improved adversarial robustness, safety, specialist performance, autonomous optimization, or end-user benefit; the contribution is primarily architectural and evidence-bounded rather than outcome-based.

title: What Do Rationales Communicate? A Message-Intervention Study in Role-Specialized QA
summary: Role-specialized QA pipelines increasingly pass rationales from a reasoner to a verifier, but it is unclear what this message actually buys: better answers, stronger support assessment, or a new failure surface. We introduce a message-intervention diagnostic that fixes the evidence and candidate answer while varying only the rationale passed across the reasoner-to-verifier boundary. On 400 MuSiQue, HotpotQA, and 2WikiMultiHopQA examples with DeepSeek as generator and verifier, faithful rationales add almost no answer accuracy over no rationale, while corrupted rationales strongly alter support judgments. Under a blind verifier prompt, harmless paraphrases shift support by only 0--2.5%, whereas corrupted rationales shift support by 10--22%; an explicit rationale-checking prompt amplifies the same pattern to 34--55%. Final answers move less (2--30%), and only 2.9--35.3% of corrupted support flips co-occur with answer changes. Human audits show why this matters: 16/42 valid corruptions are corruption-overtrust cases, and blind humans reject or mark unclear 9/10 audited corrupted rationales that the model accepts. Cross-model and task-boundary checks show when the channel is active, amplified, inert, or folded into the task label. Rationale sharing should be evaluated as a verification-message mechanism, not merely as a route to higher answer accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates what is actually gained or risked by passing rationales from a reasoning model to a verification model in QA pipelines, using controlled message interventions.
AI.motivation: Many QA systems now use pipelines where a 'reasoner' model generates an explanation or rationale that is passed to a 'verifier' model, but it is unclear whether this improves answer accuracy, better enables verification, or instead introduces new vulnerabilities when the rationale is misleading or corrupted.
AI.method: They design a message-intervention diagnostic that holds fixed the evidence and candidate answer while systematically varying only the rationale passed from the reasoner to the verifier. Using DeepSeek as both generator and verifier, they test on 400 examples from multi-hop QA datasets (MuSiQue, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA), comparing conditions: no rationale, faithful rationale, paraphrased rationale, and intentionally corrupted rationale. They prompt verifiers in both a 'blind' way and with explicit rationale-checking instructions, and analyze how support judgments and final answers change. Human audits examine how humans react to the same corrupted rationales that models accept.
AI.result: Faithful rationales bring almost no improvement in answer accuracy over having no rationale at all. However, corrupted rationales significantly change support judgments: under a blind verifier prompt, benign paraphrases only slightly affect support (0–2.5% shift), but corrupted rationales cause a large shift (10–22%). When the verifier is explicitly prompted to check rationales, these effects are amplified (34–55% shift). Final answer changes are smaller (2–30%), and only 2.9–35.3% of instances where support flips due to corruption are accompanied by answer changes. Human evaluators largely reject or flag as unclear the corrupted rationales that models still accept, and they identify multiple corruption-overtrust cases. Additional experiments across models and tasks map when the rationale channel is influential, amplified, negligible, or conflated with the task label itself.
AI.conclusion: Passing rationales from a reasoner to a verifier in QA pipelines should be treated and evaluated primarily as a communication and verification-message channel rather than as a simple way to improve answer accuracy. Faithful rationales offer little accuracy gain, while corrupted ones substantially distort support judgments and can induce overtrust, indicating that rationale-sharing introduces a new and important failure surface that must be carefully analyzed and controlled.

title: On-Device Named-Entity Recognition: A Deployability Study of Accuracy, Cost, Reliability, and Confidence
comment: 7 pages, 5 figures, 12 tables. Code and per-span records reproduce all reported numbers offline
summary: Named-entity recognition (NER) is increasingly wanted on-device (no API, low latency, data kept local). The practitioner's question is not the leaderboard but which model is deployable, how to evaluate it without human annotation, and whether its confidence can be trusted. We answer these jointly. We place nine systems across three paradigms and 13 M to 8 B parameters: a classical tagger (spaCy), bidirectional-encoder specialists (GLiNER, 166 to 460 M), and generative LLMs run locally (Qwen3-0.6B/1.7B/4B-Instruct, DeepSeek-R1-1.5B/8B), on three datasets of differing character, and report accuracy plus two axes the literature omits: latency and output validity. Because our corpus (RSS-News) had no gold, we built silver gold from a cross-family LLM judge panel, then measured its fidelity against benchmark gold and a full human re-validation of the corpus (strict F1 0.95, an upper bound since the human gold was silver-seeded); gold provenance flips the paradigm ranking, moving from LLM-authored silver to human gold raises every encoder and lowers every generative model. On accuracy alone a 4 B instruct LLM is competitive (it leads on clean newswire), so the encoder's case is deployability: it matches or slightly trails at one-ninth to one-twenty-fourth the size, at millisecond-to-second latency, with zero malformed output, while the smallest generative models emit up to 27% invalid output on long inputs, a failure fixed by scale, not output budget. We then characterize GLiNER's per-span confidence: it ranks correctness well (AUROC 0.76 to 0.86) but is overconfident (ECE 0.24 to 0.47, halved by temperature scaling); thresholding gives a small honest out-of-sample F1 gain; an all-local small-to-large cascade gives a modest, corpus-dependent gain over cost-matched random routing; and confidence tracks correctness but not novelty. Every number recomputes offline from per-span records.

AI.tldr: The paper compares classical NER taggers, encoder-based NER models, and small-to-medium local LLMs for on-device NER, evaluating not just accuracy but also latency, output validity, and confidence calibration, using both LLM-generated and human-validated gold labels.
AI.motivation: On-device NER is needed for privacy, low latency, and no-API scenarios, but practitioners lack guidance on which models are actually deployable, how to evaluate them without manual labels, and whether their confidence scores are trustworthy. Existing work focuses on accuracy leaderboards and largely ignores latency, robustness of outputs, and calibration.
AI.method: The authors benchmark nine NER systems spanning three paradigms—(1) a classical tagger (spaCy), (2) encoder-based NER specialists (GLiNER variants, 166–460M params), and (3) local instruction-tuned LLMs (Qwen3 0.6B/1.7B/4B, DeepSeek-R1 1.5B/8B)—on three datasets. For an unlabeled RSS-News corpus, they build silver labels via a cross-family LLM judge panel, then validate these against both standard benchmarks and a fully human-revalidated version of the corpus. They measure accuracy, latency, proportion of malformed/invalid outputs, and perform a detailed analysis of GLiNER’s per-span confidence, including AUROC, ECE, temperature scaling, thresholding strategies, and small-to-large routing cascades.
AI.result: Using LLM-authored silver labels, generative LLMs appear competitive or superior; however, when evaluated against human gold labels, encoder models consistently improve while generative models drop, flipping the ranking. A 4B instruct LLM can match or slightly beat encoders on accuracy (especially on clean newswire), but encoders achieve similar performance at 1/9–1/24 the size, with much lower latency and no malformed outputs. Small generative models produce up to 27% invalid outputs on long inputs, an issue alleviated only by scaling up the model, not by constraining output length. GLiNER’s span-level confidence is discriminative (AUROC 0.76–0.86) but miscalibrated (ECE 0.24–0.47); temperature scaling halves the calibration error. Confidence-based thresholding yields small but real F1 gains out of sample; routing in a small-to-large cascade offers modest, dataset-dependent gains over random routing. Confidence correlates with correctness but not with the novelty of entities.
AI.conclusion: For on-device NER, encoder-based specialists are generally the most deployable option: they provide near-LLM accuracy at a fraction of the size and latency and with robustly well-formed outputs. Apparent superiority of generative LLMs under LLM-authored silver labels can be misleading, as human gold reverses the ranking. Confidence estimates from models like GLiNER are useful but overconfident and require calibration; calibrated confidence can modestly improve F1 and enable simple cascaded systems, though it does not reliably detect novel entities. The authors release per-span records so all reported metrics can be recomputed offline.

title: Measuring the Microtask Eligibility Gap: When Is an Off-the-Shelf SLM Enough for an Agent Harness?
comment: Preprint. under review at a NeurIPS 2026 workshop. 15 pages, 8 figures, 14 tables
summary: Agent harnesses increasingly want to run small language models (SLMs) on the microtasks around a frontier large language model (LLM) planner: auto-approving shell commands, writing memory, selecting tools, ranking past turns. We ask whether off-the-shelf SLMs meet practitioner-defined thresholds and, when they fail, why, and whether quantization changes the answer. We build a benchmark of 4 such microtasks with fixed prompts and automatic metrics, each with a pre-specified threshold $τ$ anchored to a cheap non-LLM baseline and a CI-aware eligibility rule (a configuration passes only if its confidence bound clears $τ$). Sweeping Qwen3 0.6/1.7/4/8B at their best (FP16, greedy, one frozen prompt, no tuning), we find an eligibility gap: 0 of 16 (4 tasks $\times$ 4 models) configurations pass (verified by checking the raw outputs and parser behavior). A logprob decision-threshold diagnostic (T1/T3/T4; T2 via a context-length/cascade probe) separates the failures into capability deficits and failures that can be addressed by changing the decoding threshold (4 regimes). Quantization to 4-bit (RTN/GPTQ/AWQ) does damage that depends on model size and moves no configuration into eligibility (certified on the reconstructable hard-label tasks T1/T3, diagnostic/windowed robustness on T2/T4), so the gap tracks model size more than precision; it replicates on Llama-3.x (12/12 ineligible) and is robust to the anchor choice (a $τ$-sweep) and to prompt wording (0/112 eligible across the original plus 3 neutral paraphrases per cell). The practical implication: place SLMs behind a baseline that meets the CI-backed threshold, and use the SLM only where the baseline fails to meet the threshold; e.g. a 4B re-ranker over a BM25 shortlist beats BM25 ($+0.047$ [0.020, 0.073], without itself certifying eligibility).

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates whether small language models (SLMs) are reliable enough to handle specific agent microtasks around a strong LLM planner and finds that, under strict confidence-interval-based thresholds, none of the tested SLM configurations qualify, even after quantization, though SLMs can still add value when used behind a strong baseline.
AI.motivation: As LLM-based agents become more complex, practitioners want to offload simple, frequent microtasks (like approving shell commands or ranking past turns) to cheaper small language models to reduce cost and latency. However, it is unclear whether off-the-shelf SLMs are reliable enough to meet production-level accuracy and robustness requirements when used in these roles. There is also uncertainty about how quantization, commonly used to deploy SLMs efficiently, affects their reliability. The paper aims to provide an empirical, thresholded evaluation of SLM suitability for such microtasks, using practitioner-like pass/fail criteria instead of only aggregate scores.
AI.method: The authors construct a benchmark of four representative agent microtasks, each with fixed prompts and automatic evaluation metrics. For each task they define a practitioner-style eligibility threshold τ, anchored to a cheap non-LLM baseline, and require that model configurations meet this threshold with confidence intervals (a model only passes if its CI lower bound exceeds τ). They systematically sweep four Qwen3 models (0.6B, 1.7B, 4B, 8B) in their best straightforward setting (FP16, greedy decoding, one fixed prompt, no fine-tuning) across these tasks. They then analyze failures using a log-probability decision-threshold diagnostic to distinguish capability limitations from errors that could be fixed by adjusting decision thresholds, and they apply a context-length/cascade probe for one task. They further evaluate 4-bit quantization variants (RTN, GPTQ, AWQ) to see how precision reduction affects performance and eligibility. Robustness checks include verifying results on reconstructable hard-label tasks, running diagnostics on the others, replicating on Llama-3.x models, sweeping τ, and testing paraphrased prompts.
AI.result: None of the 16 Qwen3 configurations (4 tasks × 4 model sizes) satisfied the CI-backed eligibility thresholds, even under their most favorable straightforward settings. Analysis with the logprob decision-threshold diagnostic reveals four regimes of failure, separating true capability deficits from cases where performance is limited by suboptimal decoding/decision thresholds. Quantizing models to 4-bit precision (RTN, GPTQ, AWQ) degrades performance in a model-size-dependent way but does not move any configuration into eligibility; the eligibility gap is thus more closely tied to model size than to precision. The same ineligibility pattern appears for Llama-3.x models (12/12 ineligible). These findings are robust to the choice of baseline anchor (τ-sweep) and to prompt wording (0/112 eligible when using the original prompts plus three neutral paraphrases per cell).
AI.conclusion: Off-the-shelf small language models, even when run in reasonably strong but simple configurations and under various quantization schemes, do not currently meet stringent, confidence-interval-aware reliability thresholds for key agent microtasks. The primary limiting factor is model capacity, not just precision or decoding choices, though some errors could be mitigated via better decision thresholds. In practice, systems designers should deploy SLMs behind stronger, non-LLM baselines that already satisfy the required thresholds and use SLMs only as secondary modules where the baseline fails. Under this pattern, SLMs can still offer incremental gains—for example, a 4B SLM re-ranking a BM25 shortlist improves over BM25 alone—without being solely responsible for meeting reliability criteria.

title: SCM-based Fairness and Faithful Explainability for Legal Document Classification
summary: Transformer models such as LegalBERT are increasingly used in legal decision support, raising concerns about both fairness and the transparency of model explanations. These properties are usually evaluated separately, leaving open whether a debiasing intervention that changes fairness also changes how faithfully explanations reflect model reasoning. This study investigates that relationship on the ECtHR alleged-violations corpus from LexGLUE. It compares a LegalBERT baseline with a fairness-regularized variant that penalizes stereotypical warmth and competence representations during fine-tuning. The evaluation covers predictive performance, demographic fairness, and SHAP explanation faithfulness across five random seeds. At the performance-optimal regularization strength, the intervention does not reduce demographic disparity. This null result holds across two fairness definitions and a conventional word-pair control on the gender axis. Classification performance is largely unchanged. However, the intervention consistently degrades explanation sufficiency across all five seeds and three thresholds. A shuffled-pair control reproduces this degradation while leaving performance and fairness unchanged, indicating that the effect arises from contrastive representational regularization rather than specifically from the warmth and competence structure. The results demonstrate a dissociation between fairness and explanation faithfulness: changes in explanation behavior do not necessarily indicate changes in fairness, and fairness must therefore be evaluated directly.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether making a legal NLP model ‘fairer’ via representational regularization also affects how faithful its explanations are, and finds that explanation behavior changes even when fairness does not.
AI.motivation: Legal transformer models like LegalBERT are used in decision support, where both demographic fairness and the transparency of model explanations are critical. Prior work usually studies fairness and explanation quality separately, so it is unclear whether interventions intended to improve fairness also alter explanation faithfulness, or whether changes in explanations imply changes in fairness. This gap is especially important in law, where explanations may be scrutinized by courts and stakeholders.
AI.method: Using the ECtHR alleged-violations dataset from LexGLUE, the authors compare a baseline LegalBERT model to a variant fine-tuned with a fairness regularizer. The regularizer penalizes stereotypical representations along psychological ‘warmth’ and ‘competence’ dimensions during contrastive representation learning. They evaluate (1) predictive performance, (2) demographic fairness using two different fairness definitions and a classic gender word-pair axis control, and (3) explanation faithfulness using SHAP-based sufficiency metrics, across five random seeds and multiple thresholds. They also introduce a shuffled-word-pair control to test whether any observed effects are due to the specific warmth/competence structure or to contrastive representational regularization more generally.
AI.result: At the regularization strength that best preserves predictive performance, the fairness-regularized model does not reduce demographic disparities relative to the baseline, under either fairness definition or the gender word-pair control. Classification performance remains roughly the same. However, across all seeds and thresholds, explanation sufficiency systematically worsens: SHAP explanations become less faithful to the model’s internal decision process. A shuffled-pair control yields a similar degradation in explanation sufficiency while leaving performance and fairness unchanged, showing that the negative impact on explanation faithfulness stems from the contrastive representational regularization rather than the specific warmth–competence stereotype structure.
AI.conclusion: The study reveals a clear dissociation between fairness and explanation faithfulness in legal NLP: a debiasing-style representational intervention can significantly change explanation behavior without improving fairness or harming accuracy. Therefore, changes in explanations cannot be taken as evidence of improved or worsened fairness, and fairness must be measured directly rather than inferred from explanation metrics. This warns against over-relying on explanation behavior as a proxy for fairness in high-stakes applications like legal decision support.

title: Characterizing a Configuration Where Inference-Time PRM-Pruned Fragment Grafting Is Inert: Evidence from Three Reasoning LMs
summary: Diversity collapse in parallel chain-of-thought has motivated inference-time interventions built on a natural design: when a process reward model (PRM) prunes a chain, its high-PRM prefix is extracted and grafted verbatim as an in-context demonstration into a still-decoding sibling. We isolate this mechanism, PRM-Pruned Fragment Grafting (PPFG), as the most cost-minimal operationalization of cross-trajectory step-level transfer, and test it at the operating point where prior fragment-grafting work reports gains only under additional compensating ingredients. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with Math-Shepherd on full MATH500 (n=500, three seeds), PPFG in both stagnation- and random-targeting variants is statistically indistinguishable from an independent parallel-CoT baseline on every measured axis. We characterize why: a four-bucket classification of 322 stagnation-rule injection events shows only 14% targeted a genuinely struggling chain; the rest landed on chains that had already succeeded, were near completion, or sat on a flat PRM plateau, states a rescue graft cannot change. No compound-gate refinement jointly achieves well-targeted firing and adequate density, and a random control matches the same parity at 2.4x the firing rate, so the inertness is not heuristic-specific. The finding replicates across three base LMs, six benchmarks, a second PRM, and a compatibility-gate sweep; two-one-sided-tests analysis promotes the parity to positive equivalence on all twelve Qwen/LLaMA cells. A per-event spot-check finds injected chains prune at 2.75x the matched-step rate, but a surviving-sibling counterfactual finds no population-level compensation. A hindsight oracle bounds any per-problem gain from choosing PPFG over independent at +0.13 pp. We contribute an equivalence-testing template for establishing inference-time mechanism nulls, with every claim scoped to its tested operating point.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates a specific inference-time mechanism, PRM-Pruned Fragment Grafting (PPFG), for sharing partial solutions between parallel chains of thought, and finds it provides no measurable benefit over a simple independent parallel chain-of-thought baseline across models and benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Parallel chain-of-thought decoding often suffers from diversity collapse and inefficiency, leading to proposals that let stronger partial solutions guide weaker chains. A natural and widely used idea is to take high-scoring prefixes (per a process reward model, PRM) from one chain and inject them as in-context demonstrations into other chains. Prior work reported improvements but only when combined with extra components, leaving open whether the core fragment-grafting mechanism itself actually helps. The paper aims to isolate and rigorously test this bare mechanism at a realistic operating point, and to determine whether it yields real performance gains or is effectively inert.
AI.method: The authors formalize and isolate PRM-Pruned Fragment Grafting (PPFG): when a chain is pruned by a process reward model, its high-PRM prefix is copied and grafted verbatim into another still-decoding chain as an in-context demonstration. They implement PPFG variants (stagnation-targeted and random-targeted) on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct using the Math-Shepherd PRM and evaluate on the full MATH500 benchmark with multiple random seeds. They compare PPFG against an independent parallel chain-of-thought baseline across multiple metrics. To understand why PPFG might fail or succeed, they categorize hundreds of actual injection events into four buckets (truly struggling chains vs already-solved vs near-complete vs PRM-plateau). They also test refined gating strategies, run random-control comparisons, replicate across multiple base LMs, benchmarks, and a second PRM, and use two-one-sided tests (TOST) to perform equivalence testing rather than just non-significance. Additional analyses look at pruning rates after injection and a hindsight oracle that computes an upper bound on possible gains from PPFG versus independence.
AI.result: Empirically, across MATH500 on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, both stagnation-targeted and random-targeted PPFG perform statistically indistinguishably from a standard independent parallel chain-of-thought baseline on all measured metrics. Event-level analysis shows that only 14% of PPFG injections actually hit chains that are genuinely struggling and in need of rescue; most injections fall on chains that are already successful, nearly done, or in regions where the PRM score offers no useful gradient. Attempts to refine the triggering gate cannot simultaneously achieve good targeting and sufficient firing frequency. A random injection strategy matches PPFG’s performance parity despite firing about 2.4 times more often, suggesting the lack of effect is not tied to a particular heuristic. These null results replicate across three base language models, six benchmarks, a second PRM, and a sweep over compatibility gates. Injected chains are pruned 2.75x more often at matched steps, but surviving siblings do not show compensating gains at the population level. A hindsight oracle analysis bounds any per-problem advantage of PPFG over an independent baseline to at most +0.13 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that, at the tested operating points, PRM-Pruned Fragment Grafting (PPFG) provides no practical benefit over simply running independent parallel chain-of-thought decoding. The core fragment-grafting mechanism is effectively inert: injections rarely reach chains where they could help, and refinements to the gating logic cannot fix this without causing other issues. This null result is robust across models, benchmarks, PRMs, and gating variations. Methodologically, the authors contribute an equivalence-testing framework (using TOST and related analyses) as a template for rigorously showing that an inference-time mechanism is not just statistically non-significant but positively equivalent to a simpler baseline within tight bounds, with all claims carefully scoped to the specific operating conditions they study.

title: The First Token Is Not the Verdict: Hidden Costs of Reading LLM Judges Without Generating
summary: Reading an LLM judge's verdict from the logits of its first generated token is cheap, requires no generation, and is exactly what constrained decoding and likelihood-scoring evaluation harnesses produce. We show that this readout distorts position bias in one direction: it overstates it in every condition we test, so figures obtained this way behave as upper bounds. The mechanism is that judges do not always lead with a verdict token, on 12% to 49% of pairs for three Qwen3 judges and under 3% for Llama-3.1-8B and Phi-3.5-mini, and forcing a read on those pairs returns whichever response was shown first rather than a judgment. Pooled over the 924 pairs where a judge did not commit, the forced read flips on 89.7% of them when the responses are swapped, against 47.5% read after generation (paired difference +0.422, 95% CI [+0.365, +0.467]). The distortion is specific to what is measured: it moves position bias by 42 points while moving judge accuracy by under one point in seven of ten conditions, so it misleads whoever audits a judge rather than whoever uses one. A second, smaller failure occurs even when the judge does lead with a verdict token, since it sometimes opens with one letter and reasons its way to the other, on 0 to 5.5% of pairs at a rate uncorrelated with compliance. We recommend reporting the rate at which a judge leads with a verdict token, which costs one forward pass and no labels, alongside any position-bias figure.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that using only the first-token logits of an LLM judge to infer its verdict strongly overestimates position bias, because judges do not always immediately output a verdict token and sometimes change verdict mid-generation.
AI.motivation: Many evaluations of LLM judges or constrained decoding methods infer judgments from the model’s first-token logits, assuming this is a cheap and faithful proxy for the judge’s final verdict. This is widely used for measuring position bias and accuracy, but it has not been carefully validated. The authors want to test whether this shortcut introduces systematic distortions, especially in estimates of position bias, which could mislead audits of LLM judges.
AI.method: They compare two ways of reading a judge model’s decision on pairs of responses: (1) a forced read from the first-token logits (as in constrained decoding and likelihood scoring), and (2) reading the explicit verdict after the model is allowed to generate its full answer. They run this comparison across multiple judge models (three Qwen3 variants, Llama-3.1-8B, Phi-3.5-mini) and many response pairs, including conditions where the order of the responses is swapped. They measure how often the model begins with a clear verdict token, how often forced reads disagree with post-generation verdicts, and how these differences affect measured position bias and accuracy, with confidence intervals.
AI.result: They find that judges fail to lead with a verdict token on 12–49% of pairs for Qwen3 judges and under 3% for Llama-3.1-8B and Phi-3.5-mini. On the 924 pairs where the judge does not commit immediately, the forced first-token read flips on 89.7% of pairs when the responses are swapped, compared to 47.5% flips when reading the verdict after full generation, indicating a large artificial increase in measured position sensitivity (paired difference +0.422, 95% CI [+0.365, +0.467]). This distortion drastically inflates position-bias estimates (by about 42 percentage points) while barely affecting measured accuracy (less than one point in seven of ten tested conditions). They also find a smaller issue even when the judge starts with a verdict token: in up to 5.5% of cases the model begins with one verdict letter but later reasons itself to the opposite verdict, and this rate does not correlate with compliance.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating LLM judges via first-token logits is systematically misleading for position-bias measurement because models often do not immediately commit to a verdict and can even change verdict mid-generation. Forced first-token reads therefore act as upper bounds on position bias and are unreliable for auditing judges, even though they minimally affect accuracy estimates. The authors recommend that any reported position-bias figure be accompanied by the rate at which the judge starts with a verdict token, a statistic that is inexpensive to compute and requires no labels, so that users can judge how trustworthy first-token-based bias measurements are.

title: Gradient-Aligned Pair Selection for Personalized Preference Optimization
summary: Personalizing large language models (LLMs) requires aligning generation behavior with user-specific preferences rather than aggregate quality. While Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) provides a stable framework for preference learning, its effectiveness in personalized settings critically depends on how preference pairs are selected. Existing approaches typically rely on heuristic criteria, such as likelihood-based extremes, which decouple optimization from explicit user utility and can lead to degraded personalization. We formalize personalized preference learning as a geometry-aligned optimization problem by analyzing the first-order interaction between gradients of expected user utility and DPO update directions. Our analysis reveals that, under off-policy sampling, the DPO update transitions from a purely error-corrective signal to a reinforcement-like update when preference margins are directionally aligned with utility gradients. This perspective exposes pair selection as a geometric decision that governs whether preference optimization advances or hinders personalization. Motivated by this insight, we propose GAP-DPO (Geometry-Aligned Preference DPO), an iterative algorithm that performs utility-aware, geometry-aligned pair selection while controlling distribution shift via epoch-wise regeneration. Experiments on personalized text generation benchmarks show that GAP-DPO consistently improves stylistic fidelity, preference alignment, and generation quality compared to standard DPO variants. Together, our results establish gradient alignment as a unifying principle for personalized preference optimization and demonstrate that pair selection is an intrinsic component of the optimization geometry rather than a heuristic preprocessing step.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces GAP-DPO, a geometry-aligned extension of Direct Preference Optimization for personalizing LLMs, showing that utility-aware pair selection based on gradient alignment significantly improves user-specific preference alignment.
AI.motivation: Standard preference optimization methods like DPO focus on aggregate quality and use heuristic pair selection (e.g., extreme likelihood differences), which fails to reflect individual user utilities and can even harm personalization. The authors aim to ground personalization in a principled optimization framework that directly connects user utility with the learning signal, particularly under off-policy sampling where naive DPO updates may not improve user-specific behavior.
AI.method: They analyze personalized preference learning as a geometry-aligned optimization problem by studying first-order interactions between gradients of expected user utility and DPO update directions. Through this analysis, they show that DPO’s behavior under off-policy data depends on the directional alignment between preference margins and utility gradients, turning the update from error-correction into a reinforcement-like signal when aligned. Building on this, they propose GAP-DPO, an iterative algorithm that selects preference pairs in a utility-aware way to ensure gradient alignment, while mitigating distribution shift via epoch-wise data regeneration.
AI.result: On personalized text generation benchmarks, GAP-DPO outperforms standard DPO variants, achieving higher stylistic fidelity to users, better alignment with user preferences, and improved overall generation quality. These improvements are consistent across evaluated tasks, indicating that geometry-aligned pair selection is practically beneficial.
AI.conclusion: Gradient alignment between user utility and preference updates is a central principle for effective personalized preference optimization. Pair selection is not just a heuristic preprocessing choice but a core part of the optimization geometry. By explicitly enforcing geometry-aligned, utility-aware pair selection and controlling distribution shift, GAP-DPO offers a more principled and empirically superior approach to personalizing LLMs compared to conventional DPO-based methods.

title: Measuring Human-Like Bias in LLMs? A Critique of Human-Derived Bias Constructs in LLM Evaluation
summary: Researchers increasingly use human-derived bias constructs to study Large Language Models (LLMs), including social-cognitive constructs such as implicit bias and stereotype activation, and cognitive biases such as anchoring, framing effects, and confirmation bias. Such approaches offer alternatives to overt bias probes, particularly when direct questioning may obscure bias or when model behaviour appears normatively acceptable. However, adapting human bias constructs to LLMs introduces an inferential gap. Psychological instruments were developed to study human cognition and social behaviour, whereas LLM evaluations rely on probabilities, text completions, rankings, or simulated decisions. This paper critiques human-centered bias evaluation in LLMs. We show how this gap arises from mismatches pertaining to human-derived constructs, human-model differences, and evaluation contexts, which can blur distinct interpretations of model bias. We then introduce a framework providing an analytical lens for relating these elements to warranted interpretations, with attention to target constructs, operationalizations, scope of inference, and limits of human analogy.

AI.tldr: The paper critiques using human psychological bias constructs to evaluate LLMs and proposes a framework to better align constructs, methods, and interpretations.
AI.motivation: Researchers want to understand and measure bias in LLMs, and many have begun importing established human psychological constructs (implicit bias, stereotypes, anchoring, framing, confirmation bias) as ready-made tools. However, these constructs and their measurement tools were originally developed for human cognition and behavior, not for probabilistic text-generation systems. This raises concerns that inferences about model bias may be unwarranted or misleading. The authors are motivated to clarify where and why these human-centered approaches break down and how to reason more carefully about what LLM bias evaluations actually show.
AI.method: Conceptual and methodological analysis rather than experiments: (1) Survey and characterize current practices that adapt human psychological bias measures for LLMs. (2) Analyze the "inferential gap" generated when human-oriented constructs and instruments are mapped onto LLM behavior, focusing on mismatches in constructs, human–model differences, and evaluation contexts. (3) Develop a structured framework that specifies how to connect target constructs, their operationalization in LLMs, and the scope of valid inference, as well as constraints on drawing analogies between human and model biases.
AI.result: They identify several systematic mismatches between human-based psychological constructs and LLM evaluations: constructs may not translate directly; LLMs lack human cognition, embodiment, and social experience; and evaluation settings for models differ sharply from human experimental contexts. These mismatches can lead to ambiguous or overextended claims about what constitutes "bias" in LLMs. In response, they formulate a framework that organizes the relationship between (a) the bias construct of interest, (b) how it is operationalized for LLMs, (c) what claims are warranted about the model, and (d) explicit limits of analogy to human psychology.
AI.conclusion: Human-derived psychological bias constructs cannot be straightforwardly applied to LLMs without risking misinterpretation. Evaluating LLM bias requires carefully specifying the target construct, the operationalization in model outputs, and the justified scope of inference, while openly acknowledging where human–model analogies break down. The proposed framework is intended to guide more precise, theoretically grounded, and cautious interpretations of bias evaluations in LLM research.

title: K-Dense BYOK: An Open-Source AI Research Assistant That Runs Locally and Keeps a Hash-Chained Lab Notebook
comment: 38 pages, 8 figures plus a graphical abstract; includes benchmark prompts, scoring rubric, and per-prompt scores. Code: https://github.com/K-Dense-AI/k-dense-byok
summary: K-Dense BYOK (bring your own keys) is a free, open-source AI research assistant for scientists in any field that runs on the researcher's own computer. The researcher supplies access to a model of their choice, hosted or running locally, and the application supplies everything else: a place for the work to run, a layer of scientific scaffolding, and a complete record. Each project is an ordinary folder, so the data, the code, the results, and the record stay on a machine the researcher administers and can be read years later without the application. Three things separate it from a chat assistant or a general-purpose coding agent. It ships a library of written scientific procedures, guided workflow templates, catalogs of where research data can be found, and reviewer and writer roles the agent can hand work to. It keeps a Living Lab Notebook whose entries link into an argument and are added to but never erased. And it records what happened by watching what the agent does rather than by taking the agent's word for it, in a log the agent has no tool that can write to. That choice targets the most common failure, model overclaiming, in our earlier benchmark of nine frontier models, by making claims checkable rather than preventing them. On twenty interdisciplinary research prompts, scored under a rubric fixed in advance, K-Dense BYOK led two managed platforms on both scientific quality and research execution. Its deliverables were the only ones that recorded the software they ran in, and the only ones that usually arrived with a command that regenerates the results. One of the managed platforms ran the same frontier model and supplied neither. Those environment records were files the agent wrote, not part of the observed log, which does not yet capture the software environment itself. The code is available under the MIT license at https://github.com/K-Dense-AI/k-dense-byok.

AI.tldr: K-Dense BYOK is an open-source, local-first AI research assistant that wraps any LLM in a structured scientific workflow, with verifiable logs and reproducible outputs, outperforming managed platforms on research quality and execution.
AI.motivation: Many AI assistants and coding agents are not tailored to scientific work, often lack reproducibility, and rely on unverifiable self-reporting by the model. The authors previously benchmarked frontier models and found overclaiming and poor record-keeping to be major problems for serious research use. They aim to create an AI assistant that supports rigorous, auditable, and long-lived scientific projects while letting researchers keep full control of data and compute.
AI.method: They design K-Dense BYOK as a local or self-hosted application that connects to any model the researcher chooses. The system uses: (1) a library of written scientific procedures, workflow templates, data-source catalogs, and specialized roles (reviewer, writer) to guide the agent; (2) a "Living Lab Notebook" where entries are append-only and linked into a structured argument; and (3) an observation-based logging mechanism that records the agent’s actions via an external logger the agent cannot modify. They then evaluate K-Dense BYOK on 20 interdisciplinary research prompts against two managed platforms, using a pre-fixed rubric that assesses scientific quality and research execution.
AI.result: On the 20 research prompts, K-Dense BYOK outperforms both managed platforms on scientific quality and research execution. Its outputs uniquely include explicit records of the software environment and, in most cases, a command to regenerate results. One managed platform using the same frontier model does not provide either environment metadata or reproducible commands. The current observed log still does not automatically capture the full software environment; environment records are produced by the agent itself as files.
AI.conclusion: K-Dense BYOK demonstrates that wrapping general-purpose models in a structured, local-first research environment with append-only notebooks and external logging can improve scientific quality, traceability, and reproducibility compared to managed AI platforms. While environment capture is not yet fully automatic, the tool already produces richer records and more reproducible outputs, suggesting that this approach can make AI more suitable for serious, long-term scientific research. The system is openly available under the MIT license for others to adopt and extend.

title: Legal text classification in Korean sexual offense cases: from traditional machine learning to large language models with XAI insights
comment: 22 pages, 3 figures. Published in Artificial Intelligence and Law
summary: The advancement of natural language processing (NLP) has expanded AI-based text classification in the legal domain. However, accurately classifying legal documents remains challenging due to the complexity of legal texts and subtle differences between legal categories. This study evaluates legal text classification models ranging from traditional machine learning techniques to large language models (LLMs) using ten categories of Korean sexual offense precedents. The results show that fine-tuning small-scale models such as KLUE-BERT on legal data outperforms general-purpose models such as GPT-3.5 and GPT-4.0, as well as traditional machine learning models. KLUE-BERT achieved the highest accuracy of 99.3%, indicating that domain adaptation and fine-tuning can be more important than model size for legal document classification. We further employ explainable AI (XAI) techniques to analyze model predictions and misclassification cases. XAI analysis identifies linguistic features influencing model decisions and limitations in capturing subtle textual cues. Using KICS data, which closely resembles real-world legal case records, we further evaluate the model's generalization capabilities and find that it struggles to interpret implicit contextual cues. These findings highlight the importance of both performance and interpretability in legal AI and demonstrate how XAI can improve transparency in legal text classification. AI-assisted tools can support legal professionals in tasks including document classification, legal information retrieval, and case assessment.

AI.tldr: The paper compares various legal text classification models on Korean sexual offense precedents and finds that a domain‑fine‑tuned small model (KLUE‑BERT) outperforms larger general LLMs, while XAI reveals strengths, weaknesses, and interpretability aspects important for legal AI tools.
AI.motivation: Legal document classification is difficult due to complex language, subtle category differences, and the need for high reliability and transparency. Existing work often focuses on general-purpose models or non‑legal data, leaving open whether large LLMs or smaller, domain‑adapted models are better suited for real legal precedents and how to interpret their decisions.
AI.method: The authors benchmark multiple approaches—traditional machine learning methods, small transformer models fine‑tuned on legal data (especially KLUE‑BERT), and general‑purpose LLMs like GPT‑3.5 and GPT‑4—on a dataset of Korean sexual offense precedents with ten categories. They additionally apply explainable AI (XAI) techniques to understand feature importance, analyze misclassifications, and study model behavior on KICS data that more closely reflects real case records.
AI.result: Fine‑tuned KLUE‑BERT achieves the best performance with 99.3% accuracy, outperforming both traditional machine learning baselines and larger general LLMs (GPT‑3.5/4). XAI analyses show which linguistic features drive predictions, reveal failures to capture subtle cues, and demonstrate reduced generalization on more realistic KICS data where implicit contextual information is harder to interpret.
AI.conclusion: Domain adaptation and fine‑tuning on legal texts can be more critical than scaling to large general LLMs for accurate legal document classification. At the same time, explainability is essential: XAI helps uncover decision rationales and limitations, especially in handling implicit context. Together, these insights support the design of AI tools that are both accurate and transparent for legal tasks such as document classification, information retrieval, and case assessment.

title: Scientific Agents: Evaluating Profession-Specific System Prompts on Scientific Tasks
comment: 46 pages (11 pages main text, references, 33-page appendix); 10 figures, 29 tables. Evaluated corpus: https://github.com/K-Dense-AI/scientific-agents (commit 48dedd2); evaluation code and item-level records are not released
summary: Detailed profession-specific system prompts raise token use and estimated cost per response without a consistent accuracy gain. We evaluate Scientific Agents, an open-source corpus of 503 profession-specific AGENTS.md profiles, with Gemini 3.8 Flash via OpenRouter in the Pi agent harness. We compare matched profiles with four controls: a minimal baseline ("You are a helpful assistant"), the profile's opening role sentence, a generic scientific rigor guide, and a profile from an unrelated domain. Across nine text-based science benchmarks (4,531 sampled questions, 100 matched profiles), 4,488 items completed all five conditions after API-error retries, scored with automated, rule-based grading. The average profile-baseline accuracy difference is -0.6 percentage points (95% bootstrap interval [-1.5, +0.2] across fixed tasks), and no benchmark shows a statistically clear improvement. Matched profiles produced 1.5-2.3 times as many output tokens and cost 2.2-4.5 times more per successful call. On 60 tool-using BioMysteryBench bioinformatics problems (three runs each for baseline and profile), mean solve rates were 46.7% with the profile and 56.7% at baseline, a difference of -10.0 percentage points (95% interval [-16.7, -3.3]) driven by more frequent token- and time-limit stops under the profile. Longer prompts had one unexpected operational advantage: on SuperGPQA, frequent provider API drops left the short baseline with a correct first-pass answer on only 54.0% of items, against 71.6% with the profile. Generic and mismatched prompts were about as reliable, so this gain comes from prompt length or formatting rather than domain expertise. For the tested model and tasks, loading full profession profiles by default does not improve accuracy and costs considerably more; whether selective retrieval of profile sections or open-ended scientific tasks would change this remains to be tested.

AI.tldr: The paper finds that long, profession-specific system prompts substantially increase token usage and cost without yielding consistent accuracy gains on scientific benchmarks for the tested LLM and setup.
AI.motivation: Many practitioners use long, detailed profession-specific system prompts (e.g., AGENTS.md-style profiles) assuming they improve LLM performance, but this adds prompt length, latency, and cost. There is little systematic, controlled evidence on whether these heavy system prompts actually help accuracy in realistic scientific tasks.
AI.method: The authors evaluate 503 profession-specific AGENTS.md-style profiles (Scientific Agents corpus) using Gemini 3.8 Flash via OpenRouter in the Pi agent harness. They select 100 matched profession profiles and compare them against four prompt baselines: a minimal generic system prompt, the profile’s first role sentence only, a generic scientific rigor guide, and an unrelated-domain profile. They run nine text-based science benchmarks (4,531 sampled questions; 4,488 completed across all five prompt conditions after API retries) with automated rule-based grading, and a 60-item tool-using BioMysteryBench bioinformatics benchmark (three runs per condition). They use bootstrap confidence intervals to compare accuracy and analyze token usage, cost, timeouts, and provider API drop behavior across conditions.
AI.result: Across the nine text benchmarks, the profession-specific profiles slightly underperform the minimal baseline: the mean accuracy difference is -0.6 percentage points with a 95% bootstrap interval of [-1.5, +0.2], and no benchmark shows a clear statistical improvement for profiles. Profession profiles generate 1.5–2.3× more output tokens and make each successful call 2.2–4.5× more expensive. On the tool-using BioMysteryBench tasks, the profiles significantly hurt performance: solve rates are 46.7% with profiles vs. 56.7% at baseline, a -10.0 percentage point difference (95% interval [-16.7, -3.3]), mainly because longer prompts trigger token and time limits more often. However, on SuperGPQA under unreliable API conditions, longer prompts have an operational advantage: the profile condition yields a correct first-pass answer on 71.6% of items vs. 54.0% for the short baseline, likely because longer messages reduce the chance of dropped calls succeeding with an empty or truncated response. Generic rigor prompts and mismatched profiles behave similarly to matched profiles, suggesting the advantage is due to prompt length/formatting rather than encoding profession expertise.
AI.conclusion: For Gemini 3.8 Flash on the tested scientific benchmarks and agent harness, loading full profession-specific profiles by default does not improve and may slightly worsen accuracy, while substantially increasing token usage and monetary cost; in tool-using bioinformatics tasks it clearly hurts performance due to more timeouts and token-limit failures. Longer prompts can offer robustness benefits under unstable API conditions, but this seems tied to length/structure rather than genuine domain conditioning. The authors conclude that practitioners should avoid indiscriminate use of long AGENTS.md-style prompts for routine scientific QA, and instead investigate more selective retrieval of relevant profile sections or test on open-ended, more realistic scientific workflows where rich profiles might still provide value.

title: BudgetSchemaBench: A Budget-Swept Diagnostic for Schema Context in Text-to-SQL
summary: Data agents over structured sources must fit database schema into the model's context window. Large catalogs can span many databases and thousands of columns, so cost constraints may require choosing between table coverage and serialization detail well before the context window is full. We introduce BudgetSchemaBench, an execution-grounded diagnostic for this setting. Its construction derives relevance labels mechanically from gold SQL, without human- or LLM-authored ground truth. Using a pooled 80-database catalog, we sweep four schema-context budgets and compare three representations while keeping each retriever's table ranking fixed. A source-namespace check rejects queries that obtain the correct result from the wrong database. The evaluation covers three conditions: end-to-end retrieval; frozen-gold, in which the required tables are guaranteed; and a probe that removes those tables. For the primary solver with raw serialization, raising the budget from 2.5% to 50% of the catalog improves execution accuracy on 1,279 held-out questions by 18 percentage points under lexical retrieval but only 3 under dense retrieval; the dense retriever already finds most required tables at the smallest budget. When the required tables are removed, 94.6% of correct predictions name one of them exactly, consistent with reconstruction of absent schema from parametric knowledge. For the two main solvers in the frozen-gold condition, the three representations differ by at most 2 percentage points, and the widest paired 95% confidence interval bounds the difference within +/-4 points. We observe the same qualitative patterns with one reasoning model from a different family. When retrieval is coverage-limited, execution accuracy is more sensitive to the schema budget than to the tested serializations. The diagnostic and the code used to construct and evaluate it are publicly available.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces BudgetSchemaBench, a benchmark to test how schema size and representation affect database question answering by LLM-based agents under tight context budgets.
AI.motivation: LLM-based data agents must load database schemas into a limited context window. Large enterprise catalogs include many databases and thousands of columns, forcing trade-offs between how many tables to include and how much detail to serialize for each table. Existing evaluations don’t systematically analyze this budgeted setting or provide scalable, execution-grounded labels without human annotation. The authors want a way to precisely measure how different schema budgets and representations impact end-to-end SQL execution accuracy for data agents.
AI.method: They build BudgetSchemaBench from a pooled catalog of 80 databases. For each question with gold SQL, they mechanically infer which tables and databases are relevant and use the execution result as ground truth, avoiding human or LLM labeling. They test four schema-context budgets (from 2.5% to 50% of the catalog) and three schema representations, while holding each retriever’s table ranking fixed. They add a source-namespace check to discard cases where a model answers correctly but from the wrong database. They design three evaluation conditions: (1) end-to-end retrieval with the actual retriever, (2) frozen-gold where all required tables are guaranteed in context, and (3) a probe where those required tables are removed to test reconstruction from parametric knowledge. They then compare lexical versus dense retrieval and multiple solvers / model families using raw serialization and other representations, computing accuracy and confidence intervals.
AI.result: For the primary solver with raw serialization, increasing the schema budget from 2.5% to 50% of the catalog improves execution accuracy on 1,279 held-out questions by 18 percentage points under lexical retrieval but only 3 points under dense retrieval, because the dense retriever already retrieves most required tables even at the smallest budget. When the required tables are artificially removed, 94.6% of correct model predictions still name one of those missing tables exactly, indicating that models often reconstruct absent schema elements from parametric knowledge. In the frozen-gold setting (required tables always present), the three schema representations differ by at most 2 percentage points in accuracy, with the widest 95% paired confidence interval limiting differences to within +/-4 points. Similar qualitative trends appear with another reasoning model from a different family. Overall, accuracy is more sensitive to how much schema coverage (budget) is provided than to the particular serialization tested.
AI.conclusion: BudgetSchemaBench shows that, under coverage-limited retrieval, the main driver of execution accuracy for LLM-based data agents is the schema budget—how much of the catalog can be included—rather than the fine details of schema serialization, at least across the tested formats. Dense retrieval mitigates the harm of low schema budgets better than lexical retrieval by finding needed tables even with minimal context. Models can often reconstruct missing schema based on prior (parametric) knowledge, as evidenced by their naming of removed tables. The benchmark and its construction/evaluation code are released to support future research on schema representation, retrieval, and context budgeting for LLM database agents.

title: Comedic Fool's Gold: Reward Exploits and Countermeasures in Conversational Humor
summary: We investigate automated rewards for training language models in conversational humor, focusing on reward exploits and countermeasures. Two approaches aim to capture understandable surprise and predicted audience amusement. Controlled tests show that an embedding-based surprise reward accepts word-shuffled replies as readily as witty ones. A fluency filter detects the shuffles, but the combined reward also rejects some witty replies and fails further validation. An audience model's predicted laughter is instead vulnerable to laughter cues in either speaker's messages. Normalizing these cues across speakers blocks the covered attacks, although unmatched expressions remain exploitable. Three reinforcement-learning runs evaluate training with successive reward revisions. The final run improves the combined evaluation score by 0.0903 and reduces zero-score sessions by 40%, but its humor-specific improvement remains below our preregistered target. These findings illustrate a broader challenge for automated reward design: countermeasures must block exploitable shortcuts while preserving the behavior the reward was intended to encourage.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to automatically reward conversational humor in language model training, showing that naive reward designs are easily exploited and proposing partial countermeasures, though humor gains remain limited.
AI.motivation: As language models are increasingly used in conversational settings, there is interest in making them funnier and more engaging. Reinforcement learning from automated rewards could scale humor training, but designing reliable humor rewards is hard because models can exploit shortcuts that fool the reward system without actually being funny. The paper aims to understand these exploits and develop more robust automated rewards for conversational humor.
AI.method: The authors design and test two automated reward signals: (1) an embedding-based surprise reward intended to capture understandable, witty surprise, optionally combined with a fluency filter; and (2) an audience model reward based on predicted laughter from conversation transcripts. They run controlled experiments to probe failure modes: testing whether the surprise reward accepts word-shuffled responses, and whether the audience model is gamed by explicit laughter cues from either speaker. They then iteratively revise the reward (e.g., adding fluency filtering, normalizing laughter cues between speakers) and conduct three reinforcement-learning runs using successive reward versions, comparing evaluation scores and zero-score session rates to preregistered targets.
AI.result: The embedding-based surprise reward by itself fails: it rates word-shuffled responses as favorably as genuinely witty ones. Adding a fluency filter helps catch shuffled responses, but the combined reward begins to reject some genuinely witty replies and still fails later validation checks. The audience laughter model is shown to be highly sensitive to superficial laughter cues (e.g., “lol”, “haha”) anywhere in the dialog, allowing easy gaming. Normalizing laughter features across speakers blocks those specific attacks, but leaves other exploitable mismatches. In RL experiments, the final, revised reward yields a 0.0903 increase in combined evaluation score and a 40% reduction in zero-score sessions, but the humor-specific performance improvement does not meet the preregistered success threshold.
AI.conclusion: Automated rewards for conversational humor are highly vulnerable to reward hacking via superficial shortcuts such as word shuffling and injecting laughter tokens. Simple countermeasures like fluency filtering and cue normalization can close some exploits but risk suppressing genuinely humorous behavior and still leave other vulnerabilities. The study underscores a general difficulty in reward design for alignment: robust rewards must simultaneously resist exploitation and faithfully capture the nuanced behaviors—here, humor—that we actually want to encourage. Overall, the work offers incremental improvements and diagnostic methodology rather than a fully satisfactory solution for training funnier language models via automated rewards.

title: FACET at WMT 2026 Automated Translation Quality Evaluation Task
comment: Accepted at WMT 2026 (shared task system paper)
summary: Different error types in machine translation require different evidence. Whether meaning is preserved can be judged only against the source, while whether the target is well-formed, or whether it names one entity consistently, can be judged from the target alone. We present FACET, our reference-free submission to the WMT26 Automated Translation Quality Evaluation Task, which decomposes evaluation into Fluency, Accuracy, and Consistency passes and gives each pass only the context its error type requires. A single fixed model is prompted three times, and the merged error spans yield the three task outputs, error spans, quality scores, and error-free labels, with no trained components. We also submit FACET-C, which omits the Consistency pass. Without gold labels, we characterize the predictions of FACET. Its system rankings place post-edited human translation first, and the Consistency pass changes about a tenth of segment scores while leaving the ranking nearly unchanged.

AI.tldr: FACET is a reference-free MT evaluation method that runs three separate passes—Fluency, Accuracy, and Consistency—using only the information needed for each error type, and merges their error spans into final scores and labels without training.
AI.motivation: Existing automatic MT evaluation often treats all error types together and may rely on references or unnecessary context. However, different errors (meaning preservation vs. target well-formedness vs. consistent entity naming) require different evidence. The authors want a principled, reference-free way to evaluate MT that respects these differences while remaining simple and model-agnostic.
AI.method: They build FACET, a reference-free evaluation pipeline that decomposes evaluation into three passes: Fluency (checks target well-formedness using only the target), Accuracy (checks meaning preservation requiring the source), and Consistency (checks consistent naming of entities using only target-level information and context). A single fixed language model is prompted three times with the appropriate context for each pass. The error spans from all passes are merged to produce (1) error spans, (2) segment-level quality scores, and (3) error-free labels. FACET-C is a variant that removes the Consistency pass. No components are trained; the method relies entirely on prompting.
AI.result: FACET produces system rankings in which post-edited human translations are ranked highest, aligning with expectations about translation quality. The Consistency pass modifies roughly 10% of segment-level scores, meaning it has a noticeable but not dominant impact on segment assessments, while aggregate system rankings remain largely unchanged compared to the version without Consistency. The authors also analyze FACET’s predictions despite not having gold labels, focusing on ranking behavior and the effect of the Consistency pass.
