AI.conclusion: Decomposing MT evaluation into targeted Fluency, Accuracy, and Consistency passes using a single prompted model is a viable, fully reference-free approach that can generate error spans, quality scores, and error-free labels without training. FACET yields plausible system rankings (with post-edited human translations on top), and adding a dedicated Consistency pass produces local changes in segment scores without substantially altering overall system rankings. This suggests that structured, error-type-specific prompting can be an effective design for MT quality evaluation.

title: EviGraph: Proof-Carrying Selective Recommendation over Temporal Public-Service Knowledge Graphs
summary: Public-service recommendations require evidence that matches the requested service, scope, and date. Yet treating every missing detail as decisive can withhold useful recommendations. We introduce EviGraph, which distinguishes critical decision requirements from information that can remain unresolved. A language agent links these requirements to evidence in a temporal knowledge graph, while a deterministic checker establishes whether a recommendation is supported. Evaluation on a bilingual Hong Kong public-service benchmark with executable policy references shows that this distinction reduces unnecessary abstention. Additional verification, however, can withdraw supported recommendations without improving decision quality. These findings suggest that reliable evidence-based navigation depends on specifying what must be established for a decision, rather than simply adding more verification.

AI.tldr: The paper presents EviGraph, a system for making public-service recommendations by distinguishing which information is truly required for a decision and which can be left unresolved.
AI.motivation: In public-service settings, recommendation systems often abstain from giving advice whenever requested details are missing, even if these details are not truly critical for the decision. This over-cautiousness can prevent users from receiving helpful guidance. The authors aim to solve the problem of distinguishing essential decision requirements from nonessential information to reduce unnecessary abstentions while retaining reliability.
AI.method: The authors design EviGraph, which decomposes a decision into explicit critical requirements versus optional information. A language agent identifies and links these requirements to evidence stored in a temporal knowledge graph that reflects policy and service rules over time. A deterministic checker then verifies whether the gathered evidence is sufficient to support a recommendation. The system is evaluated on a bilingual Hong Kong public-service benchmark that includes executable policy references.
AI.result: EviGraph’s approach of separating critical requirements from noncritical details leads to fewer unnecessary abstentions in public-service recommendations. However, when they add extra verification steps, some valid recommendations are incorrectly withdrawn, and this added checking does not improve the overall quality of decisions.
AI.conclusion: Reliable evidence-based public-service recommendation depends more on carefully specifying what must be proven for a decision than on adding layers of verification. Explicitly modeling decision requirements and linking them to time-aware evidence enables more helpful recommendations without sacrificing reliability.

title: Metric-Construction Coupling Inflates Measured Synthetic Dialect Recovery
summary: Korean dialect corpora are available but not redistributable: weights may be released, while reproducing training and evaluation from the underlying data cannot be. We ask how much of that supervision synthetic data recovers, and whether that recovery can be measured independently of the synthesis pipeline. We contribute KoDialectBench, 1,000 items across five regions on three axes, released as identifier hashes and scoring code so users reconstruct the items from their own licensed copy. Recovery is strongly axis-dependent: our best synthetic arm reaches 91.2% of the real-data gain on region identification but 63.7% on comprehension. On generation the answer depends on the metric: the deployed marker lexicon reports 92.3% on dialectness and 119.3% on region match, the latter exceeding the real-data reference, whereas reference-based generation reaches 72.4%. We find the marker metrics' scoring inventory is entirely contained in the inventory our transformation rules can emit. We test the effect of construction access directly with an exact-form construction-disjoint arm that withholds 20% of marker types from the rules. At exactly matched training size (8,600 examples) it reduces dialectness recovery from 91.8% to 8.1% and region-match recovery from 101.9% to 25.6% on the held-out marker inventory, while the three pipeline-independent measurements do not fall at all. A complementary evaluator sweep defines metric-construction coverage (MCC) and finds measured dialectness recovery increasing monotonically as overlap rises from MCC=0 to MCC=1. Shared construction and evaluation inventories can therefore substantially inflate estimates of synthetic-data recovery.

AI.tldr: Study of how well synthetic data can recover supervision from non-redistributable Korean dialect corpora, and how evaluation metrics can overestimate this recovery when they share constructions with the data generator.
AI.motivation: Because Korean dialect corpora are legally non-redistributable, researchers often resort to synthetic data generated from transformation rules or models. However, it is unclear how much of the original supervision signal this synthetic data actually recovers, and whether existing evaluation metrics provide an unbiased estimate of that recovery, especially when the generator and evaluator share the same dialectal constructions.
AI.method: The authors build KoDialectBench, a benchmark of 1,000 items across five Korean regions and three task axes (region identification, comprehension, and generation). They release it via identifier hashes plus scoring code so users reconstruct the items from their own licensed data. They create several synthetic-data “arms” using transformation rules with controlled access to dialect constructions, including a special construction-disjoint arm that withholds 20% of dialectal marker types from the rule inventory. They then measure performance on multiple metrics: classification performance on region ID and comprehension, a marker-lexicon-based metric for dialectness and region match in generation, and reference-based generation metrics. They also vary the overlap between the generator’s construction inventory and the evaluation metric’s inventory, defining a measure called metric-construction coverage (MCC).
AI.result: Synthetic data recovers different amounts of supervision depending on the task axis: the best synthetic arm recovers 91.2% of the real-data gain for region identification but only 63.7% for comprehension. For generation, the marker-lexicon metric reports 92.3% dialectness recovery and 119.3% region-match recovery, suggesting synthetic data can appear to outperform real data under this metric, while reference-based metrics show only 72.4% recovery. The marker-based metric’s inventory is fully contained in the constructions that the transformation rules can generate, revealing a strong overlap. When the authors withhold 20% of marker types from the generation rules in an exact-form construction-disjoint arm, and keep training size fixed (8,600 examples), recovery on the held-out markers collapses: dialectness recovery falls from 91.8% to 8.1% and region-match from 101.9% to 25.6%. However, three pipeline-independent measurements do not decline. A sweep over evaluator designs shows measured dialectness recovery increases monotonically with metric-construction coverage (MCC) from 0 to 1.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic data can partially recover supervision from non-redistributable Korean dialect corpora, but the apparent level of recovery is highly axis- and metric-dependent. When evaluation metrics share construction inventories with the data-generation pipeline, they can substantially overestimate recovery, even to the point of synthetic data appearing to surpass real-data training. Controlling or minimizing overlap between generator and evaluator constructions (low MCC) yields more reliable, pipeline-independent estimates. The work provides KoDialectBench and MCC as tools to more rigorously assess synthetic-data-based dialect modeling under data-sharing constraints.

title: Build2SPARQL: A Large-Scale Text-to-SPARQL Benchmark Dataset for Building Knowledge Graph Querying
comment: 26 pages, 2 figures, 16 tables. Data paper. Dataset openly available at https://zenodo.org/records/20451474. Under review at the ASCE Journal of Computing in Civil Engineering
summary: Building automation systems are increasingly represented as semantic knowledge graphs (KGs) using ontologies such as Brick and ASHRAE 223P, creating a machine-readable substrate for artificial-intelligence applications. One promising application is translating natural-language questions into SPARQL (text-to-SPARQL), which would let building operators query these graphs through language agents, but progress is limited by the scarcity of large natural-language/SPARQL benchmarks. This paper presents Build2SPARQL, a large-scale benchmark for building KGs generated by a KG-grounded pipeline: SPARQL queries are produced and validated entirely by graph-traversal code, while large language models generate only the natural-language questions, keeping query correctness independent of model behavior. The pipeline mines six query-pattern families -- linear chains, branching, UNION, aggregation, OPTIONAL, and attribute-filtered -- and phrases each query across five vocabulary registers. Applied to 201 building KGs (180 Brick, 21 ASHRAE 223P), it yields 6,136 executable SPARQL queries and 30,680 questions. A two-rater human validation of 300 questions found 98.8% semantic fidelity, 98.8% naturalness, and 84.0% operational plausibility. A retrieval-augmented evaluation across three open-weight language models raised exact-match accuracy from 0.2-20% (zero-shot) to 56-65% (three-shot retrieved).

AI.tldr: Build2SPARQL is a large benchmark that pairs natural-language questions with SPARQL queries for building-automation knowledge graphs, enabling robust training and evaluation of text-to-SPARQL models.
AI.motivation: Text-to-SPARQL over building automation knowledge graphs could let operators query complex building data using natural language. However, progress is limited by the lack of large, high-quality benchmarks that pair natural-language questions with correct SPARQL queries, especially for ontologies like Brick and ASHRAE 223P. Existing datasets are small, not domain-specific, or entangle query correctness with language-model behavior during generation.
AI.method: The authors design a KG-grounded pipeline in which SPARQL queries are generated and validated solely via graph-traversal code on real building KGs, ensuring correctness independent of language models. They define six families of query patterns (linear chains, branching, UNION, aggregation, OPTIONAL, and attribute-filtered) and systematically mine these patterns from 201 building KGs (180 Brick, 21 ASHRAE 223P). Large language models are then used only to paraphrase each query into natural-language questions across five vocabulary registers, giving multiple ways of asking for the same information. Human evaluators assess semantic fidelity, naturalness, and operational plausibility of a sample of questions. Finally, they evaluate several open-weight LLMs on the benchmark, including a retrieval-augmented three-shot setting.
AI.result: The pipeline yields 6,136 executable SPARQL queries and 30,680 associated natural-language questions over 201 real building KGs. Human validation of 300 sampled questions reports 98.8% semantic fidelity, 98.8% naturalness, and 84.0% operational plausibility, indicating that the questions closely match the queries, read naturally, and are mostly realistic from an operator’s standpoint. Baseline text-to-SPARQL experiments on three open-weight language models show low zero-shot exact-match accuracy (0.2–20%), but retrieval-augmented three-shot prompting improves accuracy substantially to 56–65%.
AI.conclusion: KG-grounded generation can produce a large, high-quality text-to-SPARQL benchmark for building automation KGs while decoupling query correctness from language-model errors. Build2SPARQL covers diverse query patterns and linguistic variations and is validated to be semantically accurate and natural. The strong performance gains from retrieval-augmented prompting suggest that the dataset is challenging yet tractable and that language agents querying building KGs can be significantly improved with appropriate training and retrieval strategies.

title: When a Data Artifact Isn't a Shortcut: Causal Auditing of Synthetic RLVR Corpora
summary: Several recent pipelines build RLVR training data by masking a span of real corpus text and asking a language model to invent plausible wrong answers around it. The correct option is therefore genuine human prose; every distractor is synthetic. Correctness and provenance become entangled, and a policy could in principle learn the second instead of the first. We audit that possibility in GooseReason-0.7M. First we ask whether the asymmetry is visible at all: a classifier reading only five surface statistics (never the meaning) reaches AUROC 0.562 over 315,499 options, barely above chance. The aggregate hides something, though. Code sits at 0.416, below chance, and manual inspection explains why: code distractors turn out to be single-operator mutations of the gold answer rather than freely written alternatives, so the two classes are nearly identical by construction. Detecting a signal is not the same as showing a model uses it, so we then run an intervention. We build a paraphrase-matched control corpus, hold training-set size identical across arms, and train two policies under one fixed budget. The exploitation gap does not favour the unmodified-data arm: 0.021 against 0.027 for the control. Under our budget, in other words, a detectable artifact went unexploited. We think that dissociation, along with the domain-specific construction finding, is worth knowing for anyone curating corpora of this kind, and we release the audit as a mostly CPU-only protocol.

AI.tldr: The paper audits whether RLVR training data that mixes real correct answers with synthetic distractors leads models to exploit superficial provenance artifacts rather than true correctness signals.
AI.motivation: RLVR datasets are often constructed so that the correct answer is real human-written text while the distractors are LM-generated, potentially letting models distinguish options by human-vs-synthetic artifacts instead of genuine correctness, which could harm robustness and evaluation validity.
AI.method: The authors analyze the GooseReason-0.7M dataset in two stages: (1) they train a simple classifier that only uses five shallow surface statistics to see if it can distinguish real from synthetic options, and examine performance across domains like code; (2) they perform an intervention by constructing a paraphrase-matched control corpus, keeping training set size and compute budget fixed, and then comparing two policies trained on original vs control data to measure whether any detectable artifact is actually exploited.
AI.result: The surface-statistics classifier achieves a modest AUROC of 0.562 overall, showing a weak but real distinguishability signal, but for code it falls below chance (0.416) because code distractors are constructed as near-identical single-operator mutations of the gold answer. In the intervention, the policy trained on unmodified data does not show higher exploitation of artifacts: its exploitation gap is 0.021 versus 0.027 for the control, indicating no advantage from potential provenance artifacts under the given budget.
AI.conclusion: Although some detectable artifacts distinguish human-written answers from synthetic distractors in RLVR-style data, the authors find that under their training conditions these signals are not actually exploited by policies, and that domain-specific construction choices (especially in code) can erase or invert such signals. They conclude that dataset curators should be aware of these subtleties and provide their audit protocol, which is largely CPU-only, as a practical tool for checking similar corpora.

title: Robust Is Salient: An Informed Adversary Moves the Optimal Signal onto the Salience Pole
summary: When an informed adversary shares the audience of a constrained signalling channel, the signal that best protects the truth is the signal that best describes it. On 108 confirmatory items, the adversary-robust optimum aligns exactly with the salience pole from prior work. Across a 200,000-item pool, the two differ on only 2,748 items --- lying exactly where the prior salience-to-Bayes coordinate is undefined. Where defined, robustness is achieved by moving from Bayesian discrimination entirely to salience. We show this by introducing an adversary to a forced-choice task (abstracted from Deception: Murder in Hong Kong). The adversary knows the target, observes the signal, and argues for the strongest wrong answer using a persuasion budget, $β$. As $β$ grows, the optimal signal shifts from the posterior-maximizing option to the margin-maximizing one; at $β= 0$, the game reproduces the original oracle model with a listener temperature of $τ= 1$. This effect is real: 18.2 percent of the pool has an optimum that shifts under a finite budget, and each item's critical budget is exact. This coincidence structurally limits empirical evaluation. Two adversary framings change the chosen option of seven language models on 30 to 77 of 108 items against an exact no-effect rate. Yet, no measurement can determine whether this movement is toward the adversary-aware optimum or toward salience, because the two options are identical. This is a structural limit, not a null result. The diagnostic check is cheap: before evaluating adversary-awareness, verify whether the robust target coincides with a heuristic target on the evaluation items.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to choose signals that remain truthful when an informed adversary shares the same audience, showing that in a common forced-choice setting the adversary-robust signal coincides almost exactly with a simple salience heuristic rather than a full Bayesian criterion.
AI.motivation: Benchmarks and models are increasingly evaluated with adversarial framings or corruption, but it is unclear what the truly adversary-robust signalling strategy is and how it relates to simpler heuristics like salience. The authors want to understand, in a principled game-theoretic way, how an informed adversary affects optimal communication and whether robust behaviour can really be distinguished from heuristic shortcuts in empirical tests.
AI.method: They formalize a forced-choice question-answering game inspired by the board game Deception: Murder in Hong Kong. A sender picks a signal for a known target; an adversary who also knows the target observes the signal and uses a persuasion budget β to argue for an incorrect option; a listener then chooses among options. They analytically characterize the optimal sender strategy as β varies, compare it with a prior salience measure and with Bayesian posterior maximization, and compute these quantities over a large item pool of 200,000 items and a set of 108 confirmatory items. They also probe seven language models under different adversarial framings to see how their choices shift.
AI.result: Analytically, as the adversary’s persuasion budget β increases from 0, the sender’s optimal signal transitions from the option that maximizes the listener’s posterior (Bayesian discrimination) to the option that maximizes the margin relative to the adversary (a salience-like criterion). On the 108-item benchmark, the adversary-robust optimum coincides exactly with the previously defined salience pole. In a 200,000-item pool, the two differ on only 2,748 items, precisely those where the prior salience-to-Bayes coordinate is undefined. About 18.2% of items have an optimal signal that changes at some finite β, and each such critical β can be computed exactly. Experiments with seven language models show that adversarial framings frequently change their chosen options, but observed movements cannot be interpreted as evidence for or against genuine adversary-awareness because the robust and heuristic (salience) targets are almost always identical on the test set.
AI.conclusion: In this forced-choice signalling game, protecting truth against an informed adversary effectively reduces to choosing the same signal as a simple salience heuristic, not a distinct adversary-aware policy. This structural coincidence means that common adversarial evaluations cannot empirically distinguish robust optimization from heuristic salience when the two targets align. Therefore, before claiming to measure adversary-aware behaviour, one must first check whether the theoretically robust target differs from heuristic targets on the chosen items; otherwise, the evaluation is structurally uninformative rather than merely inconclusive.

title: A Holistic Assessment of the Carbon Footprint of Noor, a Very Large Arabic Language Model
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Published in Proceedings of BigScience Episode #5 -- Workshop on Challenges & Perspectives in Creating Large Language Models (ACL 2022)
summary: As ever larger language models grow more ubiquitous, it is crucial to consider their environmental impact. Characterised by extreme size and resource use, recent generations of models have been criticised for their voracious appetite for compute, and thus significant carbon footprint. Although reporting of carbon impact has grown more common in machine learning papers, this reporting is usually limited to compute resources used strictly for training. In this work, we propose a holistic assessment of the footprint of an extreme-scale language model, Noor. Noor is an ongoing project aiming to develop the largest multi-task Arabic language models -- with up to 13B parameters -- leveraging zero-shot generalisation to enable a wide range of downstream tasks via natural language instructions. We assess the total carbon bill of the entire project: starting with data collection and storage costs, including research and development budgets, pretraining costs, future serving estimates, and other exogenous costs necessary for this international cooperation. Notably, we find that inference costs and exogenous factors can have a significant impact on total budget. Finally, we discuss pathways to reduce the carbon footprint of extreme-scale models.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a holistic carbon-footprint assessment of Noor, a large Arabic language model, going beyond training to include data, R&D, pretraining, inference, and exogenous project costs, and discusses ways to reduce emissions.
AI.motivation: Existing work on large language models mostly reports carbon emissions only for training compute, overlooking other life-cycle stages such as data collection, R&D experimentation, storage, and long-term inference/serving. As extreme-scale models grow in size and deployment, this narrow view underestimates their true environmental impact. The authors aim to provide a more complete, realistic picture for Noor, a very large Arabic LLM, to better inform sustainable model development and deployment.
AI.method: They perform a life-cycle style accounting of Noor’s carbon footprint, cataloging and estimating emissions from multiple stages: data collection and storage, research and development compute, pretraining runs, planned future inference/serving loads, and additional exogenous costs specific to the international collaboration context. They then compare the relative contribution of each component to the total carbon budget.
AI.result: The analysis shows that the carbon budget of Noor is not dominated solely by pretraining; inference/serving and exogenous factors can contribute a substantial, possibly comparable or greater, share of total emissions. This indicates that focusing only on training compute underestimates the environmental impact of large models.
AI.conclusion: A holistic, project-wide assessment is necessary to understand and manage the environmental footprint of extreme-scale language models. Since inference and other non-training components can significantly affect total emissions, mitigation strategies must target the entire model lifecycle. The authors outline pathways—such as more efficient serving, better infrastructure choices, and careful design of collaboration workflows—to reduce the overall carbon footprint of such models.

title: Conflicting Supervision Moves Commitment, Not Capability: A 12.29σ arrangement effect that is exactly zero under a convention-agnostic score
summary: "Train a model on the same problems written under two incompatible conventions, both correct, and ask what the ordering of that data writes into the parameters. The learning-rate schedule is not a background condition for that question. It is the averaging operator, and it decides the answer. We prove a bound in which the arrangement and the schedule enter the ordering effect as separate multiplied factors: the arrangement only as a block period, the schedule only as how much weight the endpoint can place on any one moment of the run. A decaying schedule cannot put a large step size and an uncontracted remainder at the same moment; a constant one does exactly that at the last step. That decay moderates ordering effects has been reported in pretraining; the mechanism, the separation, and a controlled measurement of both halves are ours. Ten orderings of one corpus, one budget, everything but the path held fixed, run twice under families differing in lr_scheduler_type and nothing else: at a constant rate the interior spans 0.2221 in allocation, 11.63 contrast floors, monotone in how blocked the arrangement is. Under the single cosine every published arm uses, the same ten arms occupy two distinguishable states where their own resolution would allow about ten. "Order matters" and "order does not matter" are the two ends of one knob. What the path writes is which convention the model commits to, and no exact-match benchmark can see it. Across twelve arms acc_A+acc_B is constant to within 9.7% while the allocation share runs 0.04 to 0.87, so the 12.29-sigma arrangement switch this paper measures is exactly zero under a convention-agnostic metric. That conservation is quoted from the decayed family throughout, the constant-rate one being a noisier place to read it. Marking the convention in the prompt collapses the switch and reaches 87.5% of the union ceiling."

AI.tldr: The paper studies how the order of training examples, combined with the learning-rate schedule, imprints one of two equally correct conventions into a model, and quantifies how strongly this ordering effect depends on the schedule.
AI.motivation: When a dataset can be expressed under multiple incompatible yet correct conventions (e.g., two labelings or tokenizations), training order can push a model to favor one convention over the other. Prior work notes that decayed learning rates seem to reduce ordering effects, but lacks a clear theoretical mechanism or controlled empirical separation of the roles of data arrangement versus learning-rate schedule. The authors want to understand and precisely measure how these two factors interact to determine which convention a model adopts, especially since standard exact-match metrics may miss such differences.
AI.method: The authors analyze stochastic optimization where a model is trained on the same problems written in two incompatible conventions. They derive a bound in which data arrangement (how examples from each convention are blocked or interleaved) and the learning-rate schedule enter multiplicatively into the overall ordering effect. Empirically, they construct ten different orderings of a single corpus, keep total training budget and all other settings fixed, and train models twice under families of learning-rate schedules that differ only in lr_scheduler_type (constant vs cosine decay). They then measure how much of the model’s ‘allocation’ is committed to each convention, how this depends on data blocking, and compare results under constant and decaying schedules.
AI.result: The theory shows that arrangement affects ordering only through a block period, while the learning-rate schedule affects only how much weight can be placed on any training moment. A constant schedule allows a large step size at the last step and thus can preserve strong ordering effects; a decaying schedule cannot simultaneously have a large step size and a large uncontracted remainder, so it moderates ordering effects. Empirically, with a constant rate, the ten corpus orderings produce a wide spread in allocation (range 0.2221) and large differences in contrast floors (11.63), monotone in how strongly the data is blocked. Under a single cosine schedule (as commonly used in practice), the same ten orderings collapse into only two distinguishable states although, in principle, the resolution could separate about ten. Across twelve runs, the sum acc_A+acc_B remains nearly constant (within 9.7%) while the allocation share of conventions ranges from 0.04 to 0.87, indicating a large (12.29-sigma) ordering effect that is invisible to a convention-agnostic metric. Adding explicit convention markers to the prompt removes the hidden switch and recovers 87.5% of the performance achievable by treating both conventions jointly.
AI.conclusion: Ordering effects in training are jointly governed by data arrangement and learning-rate schedule, and these influences factorize: arrangement sets the structure of exposure, while the schedule sets how much any moment of exposure can influence the final parameters. Decaying schedules sharply reduce the observable impact of data ordering on which convention a model adopts, even though overall task accuracy (pooled across conventions) can remain nearly unchanged. As a result, standard exact-match benchmarks can report similar scores while models internally commit to very different conventions. Explicitly marking conventions in prompts largely resolves this ambiguity and recovers most of the attainable combined performance.

title: CAVE-Mem: Boundary-Aware Experience Validation for Memory Search
summary: Long-term memory agents increasingly rely on it- erative search and reusable experience to answer questions over large personal, factual, or narrative histories. However, current experience-memory systems largely optimize relevance: they re- trieve past search lessons that appear similar to the current state and inject them into the prompt. A relevant experience can still be harmful when the memory substrate, question intent, answer granularity, or evidence boundary changes. We propose CAVE- Mem, a training-free framework that represents experience as a typed intervention operator with applicability, boundary, and utility conditions. CAVE-Mem first obtains a base memory-search answer, then allows an operator to change it only if the oper- ator matches the current substrate, answer contract, evidence boundary, and cross-fitted utility; otherwise the system abstains. Experiments across long-term conversational memory, multi-hop question answering, and long-document narrative reasoning show consistent gains over relevance-only experience reuse.

AI.tldr: CAVE-Mem is a training-free framework that improves long-term memory agents by using typed intervention operators that decide when and how to reuse past experiences, going beyond simple relevance-based retrieval.
AI.motivation: Existing long-term memory agents mostly reuse past experiences based on surface relevance: they retrieve similar past queries or search traces and insert them into the prompt. However, “relevant” experiences can still hurt performance if the underlying memory structure, question intent, required answer granularity, or evidence boundaries differ from the past situation, leading to incorrect or overconfident answers. There is a need for a more principled way to decide when past experience should be applied and when the system should abstain.
AI.method: The paper introduces CAVE-Mem, which models each reusable experience as a typed intervention operator rather than just a piece of text to be stuffed into the prompt. Each operator is annotated with conditions: (1) applicability to a given memory substrate and answer contract, (2) boundary compatibility with the evidence scope, and (3) utility estimated via cross-fitting. At inference time, the system first runs a standard memory-search process to generate a base answer, then checks which operators are applicable to the current context. Only operators that match the substrate, answer type, evidence boundary, and pass a utility threshold are allowed to modify or override the base answer; otherwise, the system abstains from reusing the experience.
AI.result: Across three settings—long-term conversational memory, multi-hop question answering, and long-document narrative reasoning—CAVE-Mem yields consistent performance improvements over baselines that reuse experience solely on the basis of relevance. The gains demonstrate that enforcing applicability and boundary conditions plus utility checks reduces harmful experience transfer while preserving or enhancing benefits from reuse.
AI.conclusion: Naively reusing relevant past experiences in long-term memory agents is insufficient and can be harmful. Representing experiences as typed intervention operators with explicit applicability, boundary, and utility conditions enables safer and more effective reuse. CAVE-Mem, a training-free instantiation of this idea, improves performance across several long-context reasoning tasks and highlights the value of conservative, contract-aware experience application rather than relevance-only retrieval.

title: Knowing When to Yield: Grounded Arbitration of User Corrections in Text-Based Embodied Agents
summary: How should an embodied agent respond when a person's correction may be wrong? We formulate grounded correction arbitration as a choice among accepting, rejecting, inspecting the world, and asking the speaker. GAVA implements this interface with observation-bounded evidence, legal probes, and a one-step expected-loss rule. In text-only ALFWorld, 162 checkpoints produce 972 paired true and false interventions. Complete local inspections give GAVA and always verify 100 percent correction accuracy, establishing the evidence contract rather than a comparative advantage. In same-episode execution, GAVA reduces interaction cost against always verify but ties a cost threshold under a perfect speaker. An exploratory training-only object-location prior lowers interaction and declared joint cost on 340 unseen scenarios by 0.490 and 0.420 relative to uniform GAVA. After freezing the policy, costs, baselines, and multiplicity plan, the gains replicate on 77 non-overlapping seen checkpoints, covering 308 scenarios: 0.595 and 0.517, with both 95 percent checkpoint-bootstrap confidence intervals excluding zero. Joint cost also improves over an identical-prior fixed policy, while the matched calibrated no-VOI comparison remains inconclusive. Semantic GAVA makes four factual errors in each cohort, corresponding to 98.8 percent and 98.7 percent accuracy, and all methods complete every task. Results support selective information gathering with semantic priors under declared costs, but do not establish a general advantage of environmental value of information over clarification. The study uses normalized claims, complete symbolic observations, and controlled speakers; it evaluates neither human participants, visual input, nor physical robots.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how an embodied agent should handle possibly-wrong human corrections by arbitrating between verifying in the environment and asking clarifying questions, using a formal decision-theoretic framework and experiments in a text-based environment.
AI.motivation: Embodied agents often receive corrective feedback from users, but humans can be mistaken. Naively trusting or always verifying corrections can be costly or unsafe. The authors want a principled way for an agent to decide when to accept, reject, verify in the environment, or ask the human, under explicit costs and noisy, fallible feedback.
AI.method: They formalize "grounded correction arbitration" as a decision problem with four actions: accept, reject, inspect the world, and query the speaker. They introduce GAVA, an interface/algorithm that uses observation-bounded evidence, legally constrained probes of the environment, and a one-step expected-loss decision rule. They evaluate it in ALFWorld, a text-only environment, constructing many paired settings where an intervention is either correct or incorrect. They compare variants with and without priors, with always-verify baselines, and with/without environmental value-of-information (VOI) components, using normalized, symbolic observations and controlled (non-human) speakers.
AI.result: In settings where the agent can completely inspect local state, both GAVA and an always-verify strategy achieve 100% correction accuracy, eliminating any advantage from the arbitration mechanism under full evidence. In same-episode execution, GAVA reduces interaction cost versus always-verify, but its advantage disappears if the speaker is assumed perfect beyond a certain cost threshold. Introducing a training-only object-location prior decreases interaction and joint declared cost on 340 unseen scenarios by 0.490 and 0.420, respectively, versus uniform GAVA; these gains replicate on a separate set of 77 checkpoints (308 scenarios) with similar magnitudes (0.595 and 0.517) and 95% CI excluding zero. Joint cost also improves compared to a fixed policy using the same prior, while a no-VOI, calibrated baseline yields inconclusive differences. Semantic GAVA makes four factual errors in each cohort (≈98.7–98.8% accuracy), and all methods succeed on all tasks.
AI.conclusion: Selective information gathering guided by semantic priors, under explicit cost models, can reduce the interaction and joint costs of handling human-like corrections without sacrificing task completion or much factual accuracy. However, the results do not show a broad, consistent advantage for using environmental value of information over simply asking clarification questions. The conclusions are limited by the use of text-only, fully symbolic environments with controlled speakers and no human users, vision, or real robots, so the findings are more about a clean, formal testbed than directly about real-world deployment.

title: Signed Lexical Confidence for Risk-Calibrated Intent Routing
summary: Selective intent routing allows an assistant to act on reliable predictions while deferring uncertain requests. Standard confidence scores primarily reflect the base model's representation, leaving an opportunity to incorporate complementary evidence without changing its decisions. We introduce a signed lexical gate that combines a sentence classifier's logit margin with a sparse lexical model's support for the classifier's predicted intent. By assigning positive evidence to lexical agreement and negative evidence to a lexically favored competing intent, the gate retains more information than either unsigned lexical confidence or a hard agreement rule. An independent binomial calibration stage selects an operating threshold for a specified risk target. Across ten runs on BANKING77, CLINC150, and HWU64, the proposed score reduces area under the risk-coverage curve by 15.8%, 15.1%, and 11.8% relative to a learned semantic-only gate. At a nominal 5% error target, it increases accepted coverage by 1.83 and 5.14 percentage points on BANKING77 and HWU64, while CLINC150 is already near full coverage. At a stricter 2% target, the simultaneous binomial procedure yields a nonempty policy in all 30 dataset-run combinations at the available calibration budgets. Matched controls show that the proposed feature improves average error ranking over the tested unsigned lexical-confidence feature, with dataset-dependent gains over binary agreement. The resulting two-feature gate provides a compact, interpretable confidence enhancement for risk-calibrated intent routing while preserving the base classifier's predictions.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new, interpretable confidence-scoring mechanism for intent classification that combines semantic model confidence with signed lexical evidence, improving selective intent routing and risk calibration without changing the underlying classifier’s predictions.
AI.motivation: In intent classification systems, especially for conversational assistants, it is crucial to accept only those predictions that are reliable and to defer uncertain cases. Existing confidence estimates mostly reflect the base model’s semantic representation and do not effectively incorporate additional, complementary lexical evidence. Simple lexical agreement signals or unsigned lexical confidence fail to capture situations where lexical cues support an alternative intent, and existing methods may not be well calibrated to operate at strict error (risk) targets. There is therefore a need for a better, compact, and interpretable way to combine semantic and lexical signals for risk-calibrated selective intent routing.
AI.method: The authors introduce a “signed lexical gate,” a two-feature confidence score that combines (1) the logit margin of a sentence-level intent classifier (semantic model) and (2) a sparse lexical model’s evidence for the predicted intent versus competing intents. The lexical component is signed: it adds positive evidence when lexical features agree with the classifier’s predicted intent, and negative evidence when lexical evidence instead favors an alternative intent. This retains more information than treating lexical confidence as unsigned or using a hard agreement rule. They then apply an independent binomial calibration procedure to learn decision thresholds for given risk (error) targets, constructing risk-coverage curves and policies that specify when to accept or defer predictions. The method is evaluated through multiple runs on three benchmark intent datasets (BANKING77, CLINC150, HWU64) and compared to semantic-only and alternative lexical gating baselines, including unsigned lexical confidence and binary lexical agreement features.
AI.result: On BANKING77, CLINC150, and HWU64, the signed lexical gate consistently improves selective routing quality. Relative to a learned semantic-only gate, the new score reduces the area under the risk-coverage curve by 15.8%, 15.1%, and 11.8% respectively, indicating better trade-offs between error rate and coverage. At a 5% nominal error target, the method increases accepted coverage by 1.83 and 5.14 percentage points on BANKING77 and HWU64, with CLINC150 already near full coverage and thus showing little room for improvement. At a stricter 2% target, the simultaneous binomial calibration procedure yields a nonempty acceptance policy for all 30 combinations of dataset and random run, even with limited calibration data. Ablation-style controls show that the signed lexical feature improves average error ranking compared to an unsigned lexical-confidence feature and can outperform a binary agreement feature depending on the dataset.
AI.conclusion: The proposed signed lexical gate—combining a classifier’s logit margin with signed lexical support—offers a compact, interpretable enhancement to confidence estimation for intent classification. It improves risk-calibrated selective routing over semantic-only and simpler lexical baselines, especially under strict error constraints, while leaving the base classifier’s predictions unchanged. The two-feature gate thus provides a practical way to leverage lexical cues to refine confidence scores, yielding better coverage at fixed risk levels and more reliable intent acceptance policies in conversational systems.

title: Rules to Tools: Executable Checks for LLM Agents in Scientific Computing
summary: Scientific coding agents receive equations, boundary conditions, and output requirements in writing, then must assess the programs they revise. Rules to Tools (R2T) supplies prepared executable checks of public scientific requirements. Matched SciCode repair groups share written checks, starting programs, model, and budgets; the tool group receives a callable implementation. Across two task-ID cohorts, complete repair is 26/30 with text and 29/30 with the prepared checks. Three task IDs favor tools, one favors text, and eleven tie. The eight-ID cohort scores 13/16 versus 15/16, with a task-cluster bootstrap 95% interval of [-12.5, 43.75] percentage points for the difference. The larger shared-definition SciCode cohort ties at 13/24 per group. Five development-exposed tasks with alternate starting programs score 3/10 versus 7/10. The tool group favors tasks 17, 77, and 11; initial checks flag task 17 and report no violation for tasks 77 and 11. Task 37 favors text and has no initial reported violation. A fresh source-through-Python arm also reaches 15/16, matching the dedicated command's aggregate. In a matched PDE comparison, detailed text scores 23/24 and checks score 24/24, with 31.2% lower reported model output for checks. Agent-side output savings vary by cohort, while public CPU use rises in both task-ID cohorts. These results measure task-dependent repair outcomes and agent-side costs with prepared checks.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how providing scientific coding agents with pre-written executable checks (Rules to Tools, R2T) versus only textual descriptions affects code repair success and computational cost across multiple benchmark cohorts.
AI.motivation: Scientific coding agents must interpret written problem specifications—equations, boundary conditions, desired outputs—and then verify and repair code. Manually crafting tests or checks for every task is expensive and error-prone. The authors want to know whether converting public, textual requirements into reusable executable checks (R2T) can improve reliability, reduce agent-side effort, and better quantify performance across shared scientific coding benchmarks.
AI.method: They introduce Rules to Tools (R2T), which converts written scientific task requirements into prepared executable checks that can be reused across agents. They organize matched task groups (SciCode repair benchmarks) where one group (“text”) receives only written requirements and the other (“tools”) additionally receives callable implementations of the checks. Multiple cohorts are evaluated: two task-ID cohorts with 30 tasks, another with 8 tasks, a larger 24-task SciCode cohort, five development-exposed tasks with alternate starting programs, and a matched PDE subset. For each, they compare repair success rates, bootstrap confidence intervals, and computational metrics such as agent-side tokens or CPU usage and model output volume when using text vs. tools vs. a fresh source-through-Python setup.
AI.result: Across the main 30-task cohorts, the tool group achieves 29/30 complete repairs versus 26/30 for text, with tools favored on three task IDs, text on one, and eleven ties. In the 8-task cohort, performance is 15/16 vs. 13/16 (tools better), with a wide 95% bootstrap CI for the difference ([-12.5, 43.75] percentage points). In a 24-task shared-definition SciCode cohort, the performance ties at 13/24. For five development-exposed tasks with alternate starting programs, the tool group scores 7/10 vs. 3/10. A separate source-through-Python arm attains 15/16, matching the dedicated command approach. In a PDE-focused comparison, text achieves 23/24 and checks 24/24, with the check-based setup producing 31.2% less reported model output. Agent-side output savings differ by cohort, but in both 30-task ID cohorts, public CPU usage rises when using tools.
AI.conclusion: Providing prepared executable checks derived from public scientific requirements (R2T) generally improves or matches code repair success of scientific agents compared with relying on text descriptions alone, though benefits are task-dependent. Tools can significantly help on some tasks (e.g., 17, 77, 11) while having little effect or even a disadvantage on others (e.g., 37). The method also changes the computational cost profile: it can reduce model output on the agent side but increases public CPU use due to running checks. Overall, R2T offers a structured way to share and measure requirements, enabling more systematic evaluation of scientific coding agents and clarifying trade-offs between success rates and compute costs.

title: Certainty Is Not Just Correctness: Rethinking Token-Level Certainty in LLM Reasoning
summary: Token-level certainty is widely used as a proxy for correctness in LLM training and inference. However, the performance of certainty-based methods depends both on the information in certainty scores and on how those scores are used. We therefore directly assess certainty's predictive ability through controlled empirical evaluations across models and tasks. We distinguish two prediction targets: identifying questions a model is more likely to answer correctly and distinguishing correct from incorrect responses to the same question. In our experiments, certainty is generally better at identifying questions a model is likely to answer correctly than at distinguishing correct from incorrect responses to the same question. Certainty also varies systematically across token types and positions within words, reflecting local properties of words and text form. Information about question difficulty appears early in generation, while the weaker information about answer correctness is more concentrated near the end. These findings show that the information certainty provides for decisions depends on the prediction target, the model, the certainty metric, and which token positions in the response are included in aggregation. We further demonstrate the practical value of these findings for test-time compute. We allocate the number of responses using certainty early in generation and weight answer votes using certainty near the end of each response. Compared with a fixed-sampling majority-voting baseline, this approach increases overall accuracy from 78.71\% to 79.54\% while reducing generated-token cost by 82.4\%.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how well token-level certainty scores from LLMs predict correctness and shows that their usefulness depends on what, when, and how you aggregate them, enabling more efficient test-time compute.
AI.motivation: Certainty scores (e.g., probabilities, entropy) are widely used as proxies for correctness in LLM training, calibration, and inference strategies, yet it is unclear how predictive they actually are, and for which decisions they are most informative. The authors want to rigorously test the limits and structure of this information to better guide methods that rely on certainty.
AI.method: The authors conduct controlled empirical studies across multiple LLMs and tasks, defining two distinct prediction targets: (1) predicting which questions a model will answer correctly overall, and (2) distinguishing correct vs. incorrect candidate answers to the same question. They analyze token-level certainty across token types and positions within words and responses, and evaluate aggregation schemes over different segments of the generated text. Finally, they design a test-time compute allocation scheme that uses early-generation certainty to decide how many responses to sample and late-generation certainty to weight votes among responses.
AI.result: They find that certainty is more informative for identifying which questions are easy (i.e., likely to be answered correctly) than for discriminating between correct and incorrect answers to the same question. Certainty patterns vary by token type and intra-word position, and question difficulty information appears early in the generation, while (weaker) signal about final answer correctness appears closer to the end. Leveraging these patterns, their adaptive test-time compute strategy improves accuracy from 78.71% to 79.54% while cutting generated-token cost by 82.4% relative to fixed-sampling majority vote.
AI.conclusion: Token-level certainty contains structured but task- and position-dependent information: its value depends on the prediction target, model, metric, and aggregation window. By exploiting where in the sequence different kinds of information are concentrated, practitioners can design more efficient and accurate inference-time strategies, such as adaptive sampling and certainty-weighted voting, instead of relying on naive or uniform use of certainty signals.

title: Predictive Credit: Measuring What Scientific Explanations Add to Experimental Forecasts
summary: Research agents explain planned experiments. We measure predictive credit with paired forecasts sharing an intervention, forecaster, and outcome while varying description, matched explanation, and donor context. Five checks track commitment, delivery, predictive gain, alignment, and known-signal uptake. Across 336 prospective states in controlled learning, 12 Tox21 endpoints, and 24 OpenML tasks, v5's frozen credit decision was inconclusive. Tox21's preregistered ROC AUC interval-score harm test was unmet ($D-M=-.0026$, 95 percent interval [$-.0174$, .0104]); OpenML's joint formation, point-equivalence, and repeatability rule was unmet. Matched point-accuracy gains over description remained unconfirmed, and Tox21/OpenML seed-donor intervals spanned zero. Under requested DeepSeek V4 Pro, matched and donor cards reduced secondary Tox21 drift by 64.5 and 59.1 percent. A DeepSeek V4 Flash replay raised matched point MAE from .01823 to .02020 and missed matched-donor interval-score equivalence. OpenML full-card assignment widened nominal 80 percent intervals by 21 percent, with 49.3 percent coverage versus 51.4 percent for description and content in 66/144 cards. Direct-text Flash delivered all 144 notes without detectable matched point-accuracy gain. A researcher-authored mechanism positive control lowered point MAE by 2.60 percentage points versus description. The protocol measures predictive credit for research-agent benchmarks and scientific forecasting; natural-explanation credit remained unconfirmed at the tested donor resolutions.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how much predictive improvement (“predictive credit”) can be attributed to explanations and experimental plans produced by research agents, across several machine-learning benchmarks, using a structured testing protocol.
AI.motivation: As AI research agents increasingly propose experiments and provide explanations, we need a rigorous way to quantify whether these explanations genuinely improve predictive performance or scientific forecasting, rather than just sounding plausible. Existing benchmarks often lack a clear measure of how much value explanations add beyond baseline descriptions.
AI.method: The authors define “predictive credit” via paired forecasts that share the same intervention, forecaster, and outcome but differ in the information provided: description only, matched explanation cards, and donor explanation cards. They introduce five diagnostic checks: commitment, delivery, predictive gain, alignment, and known-signal uptake. They test these on 336 prospective states in controlled learning experiments, 12 toxicity prediction tasks from Tox21, and 24 supervised-learning tasks from OpenML. They analyze accuracy (e.g., ROC AUC and MAE), interval scores, interval widths and coverage, and drift, under different research-agent configurations (e.g., DeepSeek V4 Pro, DeepSeek V4 Flash) and a human-authored mechanism-based positive control.
AI.result: For the main frozen v5 credit decision, evidence for added predictive credit from natural explanations was inconclusive: preregistered criteria on Tox21 ROC AUC interval scores and OpenML joint rules were not met, and matched point-accuracy gains over description could not be confirmed, with confidence intervals including zero. DeepSeek V4 Pro explanations did reduce secondary drift on Tox21, but Flash replays worsened MAE and failed equivalence tests. On OpenML, full explanation cards broadened predicted intervals without improving coverage compared to bare descriptions, and many cards lacked scientific content. Direct-text Flash produced all notes but still showed no reliable point-accuracy gains. In contrast, a researcher-authored mechanistic explanation (positive control) produced clear MAE improvements over the description-only baseline.
AI.conclusion: The proposed protocol offers a systematic way to measure predictive credit from research-agent explanations in scientific and ML forecasting settings. In the tested setups and resolutions, “natural” agent-generated explanations did not reliably improve predictive performance beyond baseline descriptions, while a carefully designed human mechanistic explanation did. Thus, robust predictive credit for current research-agent explanations remains unconfirmed, underscoring the need for more informative explanation generation or refined evaluation conditions.

title: DuplexSpeechBench-Document Grounding: Benchmarking Document Grounding and Hallucinations in Voice Agents
summary: Voice agents enable low-latency, natural interaction, yet their ability to faithfully ground responses in external documents remains underexplored. We introduce DuplexSpeechBench-Document Grounding (DSB-DG), a benchmark for evaluating document grounding in voice agents across five professional domains. DSB-DG targets three failure modes: Context Saturation, which measures grounding under increasing document length; Grounding Decay, which measures retention of document facts across multi-turn dialogue; and Proactive Grounding, which evaluates whether context re-injection mitigates conversational drift. The benchmark contains 1,636 adversarially verified QA pairs from 50 documents covering five professional domains, and supports fully automatic evaluation of grounding accuracy, hallucination, and response latency. Across systems spanning cascaded, proprietary full-duplex and real-time, and open-weight speech2speech architectures, we find substantial differences in effective grounding capacity. While cascaded pipeline (ASR-LLM-TTS) achieves the highest grounding accuracy, Gemini-Live and GPT-Realtime closely trail behind. Open-weight systems exhibit distinct failure modes, most notably an abrupt context-capacity collapse and multi-turn grounding decay. More broadly, grounding fidelity degrades with context and conversational load, and failures frequently manifest as unsupported generations rather than abstention. We show that contextual grounding as a key unresolved challenge for reliable full-duplex voice agents.

AI.tldr: A new benchmark (DSB-DG) evaluates how well voice agents ground their answers in external documents across long contexts and multi-turn dialogue, revealing significant grounding limits and distinctive failure modes across architectures.
AI.motivation: Voice agents are increasingly used for interactive, low-latency tasks, but it is unclear how reliably they can base their responses on external documents rather than hallucinating or drifting off-grounding, especially in long or multi-turn conversations. Existing evaluations largely focus on text-only models or do not rigorously stress-test grounding under realistic conversational conditions, motivating a specialized benchmark for document grounding in speech-based systems.
AI.method: The authors build DuplexSpeechBench-Document Grounding (DSB-DG), a benchmark of 1,636 adversarially verified question–answer pairs derived from 50 documents spanning five professional domains. They design three stress-test regimes: (1) Context Saturation, where document length is increased to test grounding under larger contexts; (2) Grounding Decay, which measures how well systems retain and use document facts over multi-turn dialogues; and (3) Proactive Grounding, which checks if re-injecting context can prevent conversational drift. They then evaluate multiple voice-agent architectures—including cascaded ASR-LLM-TTS pipelines, proprietary full-duplex and real-time systems, and open-weight speech-to-speech models—using automatic metrics for grounding accuracy, hallucination rates, and response latency.
AI.result: The evaluation shows marked variation in grounding performance across architectures. Cascaded ASR-LLM-TTS pipelines achieve the highest grounding accuracy, with Gemini-Live and GPT-Realtime performing slightly worse but competitively. Open-weight speech-to-speech systems suffer from notable issues, including abrupt failures when context becomes too long (context-capacity collapse) and degradation of grounding quality over multi-turn interactions. Overall, as context length and conversational complexity increase, grounding fidelity declines and systems more often generate unsupported content instead of abstaining.
AI.conclusion: Document-grounded reasoning remains a major challenge for full-duplex voice agents. Even strong systems experience degraded grounding under long contexts and multi-turn dialogue, and they tend to hallucinate rather than explicitly decline to answer when uncertain. DSB-DG provides a focused benchmark that exposes these weaknesses and can guide the development and comparison of future voice-agent architectures aimed at improving robust, document-grounded speech interaction.

title: ContractRL: Shielded Group-Relative Policy Optimization for Auditable Tool-Call Repair
summary: Structured tool calls often fail after only a small number of fields violate a schema or an execution contract. Regenerating the complete object enlarges the action surface and makes repeated repair difficult to audit. We introduce ContractRL, a contract-constrained sequential repair protocol that models verifier-guided JSON repair as a bounded decision process. At each step the policy observes the candidate, typed verifier feedback, JSON Pointer, immutable repair history, and remaining budget; a contract-derived action mask filters malformed or prohibited RFC-6902 operations before a deterministic validator performs the transition. We specify a contract-constrained group-relative objective for patch, retry, and abstention decisions while keeping canonical targets and semantic labels outside the online state until trace freeze. Under identical verifier information, ContractRL attains 0.9362 semantic success with 34.4 generated tokens, compared with 0.9076 and 44.9 tokens for Patch-SFT and 0.9148 and 137.2 tokens for full regeneration over 192 cases per seed and five seeds. Policy optimization improves semantic success from 0.9186 for supervised ContractRL to 0.9375. A separate three-seed paired evaluation against Patch-SFT yields a semantic difference of +0.0396 (95% CI $[+0.0137,+0.0662], p=0.0039$). Feedback, action-mask, budget, and schema-shift analyses connect these gains to localized correction, while adversarial and multi-turn evaluations characterize the remaining failure modes.

AI.tldr: The paper presents ContractRL, a reinforcement-learning-based method for incrementally repairing structured tool outputs (JSON) under a contract, achieving higher semantic success with fewer tokens than baselines.
AI.motivation: Structured tool calls (like JSON outputs) often fail if only a few fields violate a schema; existing approaches regenerate the entire object, which increases the chance of new errors, wastes tokens, and makes repairs hard to inspect and audit. The authors want a principled, efficient, and auditable way to locally repair invalid tool outputs using verifier feedback and formal contracts.
AI.method: They formulate JSON repair as a bounded decision process and propose ContractRL, a contract-constrained sequential repair protocol. At each step, the policy observes the current JSON candidate, typed verifier feedback, a JSON Pointer indicating where the issue is, an immutable history of past repairs, and the remaining budget. A contract-derived action mask filters out malformed or prohibited RFC-6902 patch operations, and a deterministic validator applies the chosen edit. They define a group-relative objective over patch, retry, and abstain decisions while keeping canonical targets and semantic labels out of the online state until traces are frozen. They compare supervised and RL-optimized versions of this policy and analyze how feedback, action masks, budget, and schema shifts impact performance.
AI.result: On a benchmark with 192 cases per seed over five seeds, ContractRL achieves 0.9362 semantic success with 34.4 generated tokens, outperforming Patch-SFT (0.9076 success, 44.9 tokens) and full regeneration (0.9148 success, 137.2 tokens) under the same verifier information. Policy optimization further improves semantic success from 0.9186 (supervised ContractRL) to 0.9375. In a three-seed paired comparison versus Patch-SFT, ContractRL shows a semantic success improvement of +0.0396 with 95% confidence interval [+0.0137,+0.0662] and p=0.0039. Additional analyses show robustness benefits and characterize remaining failure modes.
AI.conclusion: ContractRL enables more efficient and reliable localized repair of structured tool outputs by framing JSON correction as a contract-constrained sequential decision process, outperforming both patch-only supervised baselines and full regeneration in semantic success and token usage. The gains are linked to the use of explicit contracts, action masking, and budget-aware policies, while remaining errors are studied through adversarial and multi-turn evaluations to guide future improvements.

title: Refusal Localizes, the Damage Relocates: Safety Layers Under Few-Sample Fine-Tuning
comment: 24 pages, 7 figures, 21 tables. Jungseob Lee and Dongyub Jude Lee contributed equally
summary: Fine-tuning adapts aligned large language models (LLMs) to downstream tasks, but a few dozen harmful examples can remove their refusal of harmful requests. Prior work localizes safety-related behavior to specific layers, directions, and tokens, suggesting targets for protection. We test whether successful localization and recovery support defenses that survive changes in the attack. Across six checkpoints from four model families, harmful and benign prompts remain linearly separable after attack, and patching full clean hidden states into the compromised model restores refusal at a reproducible transition depth. Building on a prior layer-freezing defense, we freeze every layer up to this depth and repeat the attack. At a hundred harmful examples, refusal remains near zero on all six checkpoints, with recovery transitions above the frozen boundary. In a second study, removing the update's top two singular directions restores refusal after short attention-only fine-tunes on four checkpoints. On Llama-3.1-8B, ordinary training changes weaken this repair and an attacker who spreads the update defeats it. A spectral detector calibrated on benign Llama fine-tunes misses most repair failures on that checkpoint. Localized freezing can nevertheless help preserve refusal when a few harmful examples enter training data unintentionally. These results show that an attacker can bypass a region identified by recovery and defeat a repair that works across multiple checkpoints, motivating five checks for defenses against adaptive fine-tuning. Code is available at https://github.com/js-lee-AI/refusal-relocates.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how robust safety defenses are in fine-tuned LLMs when an attacker adaptively changes the fine-tuning procedure. It finds that although safety behavior can be localized and temporarily repaired, attackers can move harmful behavior to other regions of the model, defeating these repairs.
AI.motivation: Safety-aligned LLMs can be compromised by fine-tuning on only a small number of harmful examples, causing them to stop refusing harmful requests. Prior work suggests that safety-related internal features can be localized and manipulated to restore refusal, raising hope that we can build robust defenses (like freezing layers or removing harmful directions). However, it is unclear whether these defenses remain effective when attackers adapt their strategies (e.g., change training setups, spread updates, or target other layers). The paper aims to test whether localization-based defenses actually hold up against such adaptive fine-tuning attacks across different models and checkpoints.
AI.method: The authors examine six checkpoints from four LLM families and perform several experiments: (1) They fine-tune models with harmful examples and analyze hidden representations of harmful vs. benign prompts, checking linear separability and where in depth the model’s refusal behavior changes. They then patch in clean hidden states at various layers to identify a stable “recovery transition depth.” (2) They build on a prior layer-freezing defense and freeze all layers up to this depth, re-running harmful fine-tuning to see if safety persists. (3) They perform short attention-only fine-tunes and apply a spectral repair: removing the top two singular directions of the fine-tuning update, observing whether refusal is restored across checkpoints. (4) On Llama-3.1-8B specifically, they explore how ordinary (benign) training changes and more diffuse attacker updates degrade this repair and test a spectral detector calibrated on benign fine-tunes to see if it can detect repair failures. They then synthesize their findings into a set of practical checks for designing and evaluating defenses against adaptive fine-tuning attacks.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Even after harmful fine-tuning, harmful and benign prompts remain linearly separable in representation space, and patching in full clean hidden states reliably restores refusal at a reproducible transition depth across six checkpoints. (2) Freezing all layers up to this transition depth significantly protects models: when fine-tuned with ~100 harmful examples, refusal stays near zero (i.e., strong refusal) on all six checkpoints, and the recovery transition moves to above the frozen layers. (3) Removing the top two singular directions of the update effectively restores refusal after short attention-only fine-tunes on four checkpoints, but this repair is fragile. (4) On Llama-3.1-8B, additional ordinary training erodes the effectiveness of this spectral repair, and attackers who distribute their update across directions can bypass it. (5) A spectral detector trained on benign Llama fine-tunes fails to catch most of these repair failures. Nonetheless, localized freezing still helps preserve refusal when only a few harmful examples are unintentionally included in training data.
AI.conclusion: Localization-based defenses (like freezing certain layers or removing dominant update directions) can temporarily preserve refusal behavior under some attack models and data conditions, but they are not robust to adaptive attackers who change where and how harmful information is encoded. Attackers can relocate the harmful behavior outside the previously identified protected region and spread their updates to evade spectral repairs and detectors. The paper concludes that safety defenses should be evaluated under adaptive fine-tuning scenarios and proposes five concrete checks for such evaluations. Localized freezing remains useful primarily as a partial safeguard against accidental inclusion of harmful data rather than as a comprehensive defense against deliberate adaptive attacks.

title: Mathematical Transfer in LLMs Follows Reasoning Approach More Than Topic
summary: When selecting mathematical training data for LLMs, a natural organizing principle is topic: probability examples for probability targets. An alternative is reasoning approach: worked solutions that share a solution method with the target, even when the mathematical domain differs. We ask which relation produces greater transfer after fine-tuning. We evaluate two counterbalanced $2\times2$ designs: probability and combinatorics crossed with invariant reasoning and double counting (2,000 problems), and number theory and geometry crossed with complement and pigeonhole reasoning (800 problems). In each design, every cell serves as the held-out target in turn: same-approach (SA) sources share the target's method but change the topic, while same-topic (ST) sources share the topic but change the method. Every source appears once in each role, so additive source-quality effects cancel from the equally weighted aggregate contrast. Across five base models and three training seeds per design, SA outperforms ST in all 40 seed-pooled model--target comparisons. Model-level advantages range from 8.2 to 16.2 percentage points in the primary design (mean: 10.8) and from 12.0 to 16.0 in the second design (mean: 14.3); all ten model-level 95% confidence intervals exclude zero. In both designs, ST sources are more similar to targets under embedding and lexical measures, so the SA advantage runs opposite to the measured ordering of statement-level resemblance. These findings identify reasoning approach as a more effective matching criterion than topic for mathematical transfer across the evaluated topic--approach combinations.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to best choose math training data for LLMs and finds that matching problems by reasoning method transfers better than matching by topic.
AI.motivation: LLMs often struggle with mathematical reasoning, and fine-tuning data is typically organized by topic (e.g., train on probability to improve probability). However, many math problems across different topics share similar solution strategies. The authors want to know whether it is more beneficial for transfer learning to match training and target data by mathematical topic or by underlying reasoning approach.
AI.method: The authors design two controlled, counterbalanced 2×2 experimental setups. In the first, they cross two topics (probability, combinatorics) with two reasoning approaches (invariant reasoning, double counting), yielding four topic–approach cells and 2,000 problems. In the second, they cross number theory and geometry with complement and pigeonhole reasoning (800 problems). For each setup, each cell is treated in turn as a held-out target set. Training sources are divided into same-approach (SA) sets that share reasoning method but differ in topic, and same-topic (ST) sets that share topic but use different reasoning methods. Each problem appears once in each role to neutralize quality differences via symmetric, equally weighted comparisons. They fine-tune five different base LLMs, with three random seeds per design, and compare performance gains for SA vs ST training. They also compute embedding and lexical similarity between source and target statements.
AI.result: Same-approach (SA) training consistently yields better transfer than same-topic (ST) training. Across five models and both designs, SA outperforms ST in all 40 model–target comparisons when pooling over seeds. In the primary design, model-level advantages range from 8.2 to 16.2 percentage points (mean 10.8); in the second design, from 12.0 to 16.0 points (mean 14.3). All ten model-level 95% confidence intervals exclude zero, indicating robust statistical significance. Interestingly, standard similarity metrics (embeddings and lexical overlap) rate ST sources as more similar to their targets than SA sources, so the performance advantage of SA goes against naive similarity measures.
AI.conclusion: For the investigated mathematical domains, aligning training data with target problems by reasoning approach is more effective than aligning by topic. This suggests that, in constructing math training curricula for LLMs, prioritizing shared solution methods across different topics can yield better generalization than focusing on topical similarity alone. It also indicates that common embedding or lexical similarity metrics may not capture the aspects of problem structure most relevant for reasoning transfer.

title: CAST: Cost-Aware Speculative Trees from One-Pass Block Drafters
summary: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by drafting future tokens cheaply and verifying them with the target model in parallel. Block drafters score a whole block of future tokens in one forward pass, yet standard decoding verifies only the top-scoring chain and discards the other candidates. Because these candidates are already scored, verifying more of them adds target computation but no extra drafting. We introduce CAST (Cost-Aware Speculative Trees), which packs these candidates into a tree and verifies it in a single target pass, leaving the target model, drafter weights, and decoding rule untouched. To decide how wide the tree should be, CAST adds candidates while the expected gain from the next one outweighs the verification time it adds. The width therefore adapts to each deployment from a latency measurement, without sweeping over widths. We evaluate CAST across five domains on three GPU generations and two model families. At its predicted width, CAST is faster than the standard chain in all eight settings, by up to 43%. We also find that the best width depends strongly on the deployment. Where verification cost jumps at a kernel boundary, a 128-token tree is only 2% faster than the standard chain, whereas the tree at the predicted width is 20% faster. Furthermore, we prove that CAST leaves the target output distribution unchanged under both greedy and sampled decoding. Code is available at https://github.com/js-lee-AI/CAST.

AI.tldr: Introduces CAST, a cost-aware speculative decoding method that verifies a tree of drafted token candidates in a single pass, adaptively choosing tree width to maximize speedup without changing model behavior.
AI.motivation: Standard speculative decoding with block drafters wastes computation by discarding many already-scored candidate continuations and uses a fixed, hand-tuned width that may not match hardware or deployment constraints. There is a need to better exploit drafted candidates and to automatically adapt speculative decoding to different hardware and latency characteristics while preserving the model’s output distribution.
AI.method: They propose CAST (Cost-Aware Speculative Trees), which organizes the multiple candidate continuations from a block drafter into a verification tree. Instead of verifying only the top-scoring chain, CAST verifies many candidates in a single forward pass of the target model, without changing the target model, drafter weights, or decoding rule. CAST uses a cost-aware criterion to grow the tree width: it incrementally adds candidates as long as the expected speed gain from adding another branch exceeds the additional verification time, which is estimated from actual latency measurements on the deployment hardware. This yields an automatically tuned tree width tailored to each deployment scenario.
