Additionally, probability averaging across the 32B and 72B models further improves Task 1a when the underlying models make complementary errors.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that explainable suicide-risk assessment on social media benefits from carefully aligning both training objectives and prediction aggregation strategies with the structure of each subtask, even when using a shared large language model backbone. Multi-task training is advantageous for closely related subtasks like risk classification and evidence extraction, whereas more distinct outputs like multi-label factor prediction benefit from separate, specialized training. Ensemble-style probability averaging and calibrated decision thresholds further enhance performance. Overall, the work demonstrates that a unified, parameter-efficient LLM framework can deliver strong, explainable performance across multiple dimensions of suicide-risk assessment.

title: Worse Together: How Performance Breaks Down in Multi-User Multi-Agent Teams
comment: 63 pages, 22 Figures, 10 Tables, Code: https://github.com/safety-research/MAMUBench (will be released after review)
summary: People are increasingly delegating tasks to AI agents, and those agents are increasingly encountering other people's agents over shared resources such as a codebase, a calendar, or a budget. When each agent acts for a different user with different goals, coordination often fails, and the group ends up worse off than if a single agent had acted for everyone. We study this multi-user, multi-agent setting across five frontier models and 77 scenarios in four environments: an API key environment in which agents share a compute budget, a clinic in which they share a calendar, a personal assistant environment in which they share a group order or booking, and a merge queue in which they share a release cutoff. In each scenario, we compare a single agent that serves every user (a coordinator) to a team in which each agent serves one user, with and without a communication channel between the agents. Teams deliver worse group outcomes than the coordinator in every environment: without a channel, they completely collapse in two environments, and even with one, coordination overhead creates substantial gaps. For example, in the personal assistant environment, the coordinator fulfills a targeted user request about twice as often as teams. We identify distinct behaviors associated with this poor group-level performance, including stalling as teams grow, overriding each other's actions, and fabricating claims. We find effective but environment-specific mitigations, such as a team lead, explicit procedural instructions, and a platform check that makes an agent read its peers' messages before committing. We will release the API key, clinic, and personal assistant environments as MAMUBench, comprising 74 scenarios for evaluating multi-user, multi-agent coordination.

AI.tldr: The paper benchmarks how well frontier AI models coordinate when acting as multiple agents for different users sharing resources, finding that multi-agent teams underperform a single coordinating agent and proposing mitigations plus a new benchmark suite (MAMUBench).
AI.motivation: As AI agents are increasingly used in real-world settings, they must operate alongside other agents working for different users over shared resources (e.g., codebases, calendars, budgets). Existing work often evaluates single-agent performance or cooperative settings with aligned goals, leaving a gap in understanding how current models behave in realistic, multi-user, multi-agent coordination problems where goals may differ and resources are shared. This paper aims to systematically study whether multiple agents acting for different users can coordinate effectively and how their performance compares to a single coordinating agent.
AI.method: The authors design 77 scenarios across four controlled environments that instantiate realistic shared-resource settings: (1) an API key environment with a shared compute budget, (2) a clinic with a shared calendar, (3) a personal assistant environment with shared group orders or bookings, and (4) a merge queue with a shared release cutoff. For each scenario, they compare three setups using five frontier LLMs as agents: (a) a single coordinator agent acting on behalf of all users, (b) a team of agents where each serves one user without inter-agent communication, and (c) a similar team but with a communication channel. They measure group-level success in fulfilling target user requests while respecting constraints and analyze qualitative behaviors of agents. They also test targeted mitigation strategies such as designating a team lead, giving explicit procedural instructions, and adding platform-level checks (e.g., forcing agents to read peers' messages before acting).
AI.result: Across all environments, teams of per-user agents achieve worse group outcomes than a single coordinating agent. In two environments, teams with no communication channel effectively fail entirely ("collapse"). Even when a communication channel exists, coordination overhead and misalignment lead to substantial performance gaps; for instance, in the personal assistant environment the single coordinator satisfies targeted user requests about twice as often as multi-agent teams. The authors observe problematic behaviors in multi-agent setups: agents stalling as team size grows, overriding each other's actions, and fabricating claims about what others have done. Mitigation interventions such as appointing a team lead, adding explicit procedural coordination instructions, or enforcing that agents read others' messages before committing improve performance but in environment-specific ways and do not close the gap universally.
AI.conclusion: Current frontier LLMs are poor at decentralized coordination when instantiated as multiple agents acting for different users over shared resources, and they systematically underperform a single coordinating agent on group-level metrics. Communication alone does not resolve coordination failures and can introduce overhead and new failure modes. While design interventions can partially mitigate issues, they are highly dependent on the environment and do not yet yield robust, general solutions. The paper contributes MAMUBench—a benchmark of 74 scenarios in three of the environments—to facilitate future work on multi-user, multi-agent coordination and underscores the need for better architectures, protocols, and safety mechanisms for AI agents operating in shared, multi-stakeholder settings.

title: Mixture of Decoders for Diverse Dialog Response Generation
summary: Mixture modeling is a long established machine learning technique for learning large sets of multi-modal data. While it is known that sequence-to-sequence models for dialog response generation suffer from the problem of low diversity, we hypothesize that it is because sequence-to-sequence models tend to learn a degenerate uni-modal distribution of responses. We then propose to incorporate a mixture of decoders into sequence-to-sequence models and try to make each decoder learn specialized topics in order to improve the diversity of generated responses. Our model is developed under the framework of conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE). We evaluate our approach on an open domain chat corpus and show improvement over strong baselines in quantitative measures and human evaluation.

AI.tldr: They improve dialog response diversity by using a mixture of specialized decoders within a CVAE framework, outperforming strong baselines on open-domain chat.
AI.motivation: Sequence-to-sequence dialog models often generate dull, generic, and low-diversity responses, likely because they effectively learn a single (uni-modal) distribution over possible replies, which cannot capture the naturally multi-modal nature of conversation where many valid, distinct responses may exist for a given input.
AI.method: Introduce a mixture-of-decoders architecture inside a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) for dialog. Each decoder in the mixture is encouraged to specialize on different response modes or topics, so that the overall model represents a multi-modal response distribution. Training is done on an open-domain chat corpus, and the model is compared with strong seq2seq and CVAE baselines using both automatic metrics and human judgments.
AI.result: On an open-domain chat dataset, the proposed mixture-of-decoders CVAE produces more diverse responses and shows better performance than strong baseline models according to quantitative diversity/quality metrics and human evaluation scores.
AI.conclusion: Modeling dialog responses as a mixture of specialized decoders within a CVAE better captures the inherent multi-modality of conversational data, leading to more diverse and improved responses compared to standard seq2seq and CVAE baselines.

title: Legal Research Bench: Measuring End-to-End Reliability in Long-Horizon Legal Research Agents
summary: Legal research is a core and time-consuming legal workflow. Lawyers must identify controlling authority, verify that it remains valid, reconcile statutes and cases, and synthesize a grounded answer. Language model agents are a natural fit for this retrieval-intensive workflow, and automating even part of it would be valuable. But that value depends on reliability: a single missing authority, stale citation, or wrong legal conclusion can make an otherwise plausible answer unusable. We introduce \textbf{Legal Research Bench} (LRB), a benchmark of 413 open-ended U.S. legal research questions written by experts, each paired with a gold answer, supporting authorities, and a binary grading rubric. We evaluate thirteen frontier models in a harness with web search, case-law search, page parsing, and retrieval tools. We score agent responses through all-pass grading with source verification, where a response is correct only if every required criterion is satisfied and its cited authorities verify. We also validate the LLM judge against expert attorneys ensuring that benchmark scores track attorney judgment. Agents remain far from reliable: among the models we tested, the strongest, Claude Opus 4.8, is fully correct on 42.9\% of questions. Performance also varies substantially by task setting: all-pass rates differ across areas of law and are lower on questions requiring reconciliation of conflicting authorities. Across models, more turns, tool calls, and inference cost do not predict higher accuracy.

AI.tldr: Introduces Legal Research Bench, a rigorous benchmark to measure how reliably LLM-based agents can perform end-to-end U.S. legal research using tools, showing current models are still far from dependable.
AI.motivation: Legal research is central to legal practice but is time-consuming and error-sensitive: missing a key authority, relying on overruled precedent, or drawing an incorrect legal conclusion can invalidate an entire analysis. While language model agents seem well-suited to retrieval-heavy workflows and could substantially reduce effort, any practical value hinges on high reliability, not just plausible-sounding answers. Existing benchmarks typically test isolated capabilities or do not reflect true end-to-end legal research with verification against primary authorities, leaving a gap in evaluating whether LLM agents can safely assist lawyers.
AI.method: The authors construct Legal Research Bench (LRB), a dataset of 413 open-ended U.S. legal research questions authored by legal experts. Each question is paired with (1) a gold reference answer, (2) supporting legal authorities (cases, statutes, etc.), and (3) a binary, all-or-nothing grading rubric specifying criteria that must all be satisfied. They build an evaluation harness in which LLM agents can access web search, case-law search, page parsing, and retrieval tools. Thirteen frontier models are tested under agentic settings. Responses are graded via an “all-pass” scheme: an answer is marked correct only if it meets every rubric criterion and the cited authorities substantively support the claims. They also use an LLM judge for grading and validate this judge by comparing its evaluations with expert attorneys’ judgments to ensure that benchmark scores correlate with human expert assessment.
AI.result: The benchmark shows that current LLM-based legal research agents are significantly unreliable for fully autonomous use. Among the thirteen evaluated models, the strongest (Claude Opus 4.8) attains full correctness on only 42.9% of questions under the stringent all-pass, source-verified grading. Accuracy varies meaningfully across legal domains and drops on questions that require reconciling conflicting authorities, suggesting that nuanced doctrinal synthesis remains challenging. Additionally, process metrics such as number of interaction turns, frequency of tool calls, and total inference cost do not correlate with, nor reliably improve, final answer accuracy, indicating that simply increasing agent complexity or spending more compute does not straightforwardly enhance reliability.
AI.conclusion: Legal Research Bench provides a realistic, high-precision benchmark for assessing end-to-end legal research capabilities of LLM agents, emphasizing strict correctness and source verification. The evaluation reveals that even state-of-the-art models fall well short of the reliability standards needed for unsupervised legal practice, especially on tasks involving conflict resolution between authorities. The weak relationship between agent complexity/cost and accuracy suggests that progress will require better reasoning and verification methods rather than just more tools or longer interactions. LRB can thus serve as a challenging testbed to drive and measure future advances in trustworthy AI assistance for legal research.

title: Self-Evolving Coding Rules for AI Coding Agents
summary: The performance of AI coding agents is highly dependent on their underlying coding rules. However, existing coding rules are typically hand-crafted and fixed, making the process labor-intensive and often suboptimal. In this work, we propose RuleEvolve, a self-evolving framework for coding rules. RuleEvolve maintains a pool of candidate coding rules and iteratively improves them. In each iteration, it employs an LLM-powered mutator module to generate variants from existing candidates, and then uses a judge module to evaluate these variants and update the pool with the best-performing ones. Extensive evaluations across two coding-agent frameworks, four backbone LLMs, and three benchmarks demonstrate that RuleEvolve outperforms both manual engineering and existing prompt optimization baselines in terms of functional correctness of the generated code, code length, and/or generation cost (e.g., tokens used).

AI.tldr: RuleEvolve is a framework that automatically evolves and optimizes coding rules for AI coding agents using LLM-based mutation and evaluation.
AI.motivation: Existing coding rules for AI coding agents are hand-crafted, fixed, and often suboptimal, requiring significant manual effort. There is a need for an automated way to discover and refine better coding rules that improve agent performance and efficiency.
AI.method: RuleEvolve maintains a pool of candidate coding rules and iteratively refines them. In each iteration, an LLM-based mutator generates new rule variants from existing ones. A judge module then evaluates these variants, selecting the best-performing rules based on metrics like functional correctness, code length, and generation cost, and updates the pool accordingly.
AI.result: Across two coding-agent frameworks, four backbone LLMs, and three benchmarks, RuleEvolve delivers better functional correctness of generated code and, in many settings, shorter code and/or reduced generation cost compared to manually engineered rules and prompt optimization baselines.
AI.conclusion: Automatically evolving coding rules with RuleEvolve leads to more effective and efficient AI coding agents than using manually designed or conventionally optimized prompts, showing that coding rules themselves can be treated as optimizable artifacts within an LLM-based system.

title: Spatial Strategies, Not Actions: Vector-Quantized Geodesics as Tools for LLM-Driven Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) based agents are often criticized for lacking spatial understanding and mainly exploiting statistical text patterns. We investigate their spatial comprehension through an architecture combining geometrical tools with a LLM serving as a high-level orchestrator in grid-world environments. The agent first collects geodesic trajectories, which are then vector-quantized to extract a representative subset. Offline, the LLM associates a natural language description of the underlying behavioral patterns to each selected trajectory, making it a tool. Online, the LLM chooses the appropriate tool conditioned on the current state and goal. Low-level control is handled by primitive actions that execute the trajectory associated with the tool. From an agentic AI perspective, this approach separates learning into two levels: tool discovery is handled through unsupervised quantization of trajectories, while reasoning and decision-making are handled by the LLM. We test the approach in a partially observable dynamic 2D grid environment with an open vision-language model (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B). Pairing the geometry-derived tool library with an agent-centered zoom tool and a collision detection tool lets a fast, non-reasoning configuration match the goal-reaching rate of a much more costly chain-of-thought version, while cutting the cost of a decision from minutes to seconds.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an LLM-based agent architecture that gains spatial competence in grid worlds by using vector-quantized trajectory "tools" plus an LLM orchestrator, achieving CoT-level performance with much lower cost.
AI.motivation: LLM agents are criticized for weak spatial understanding and over-reliance on text statistics. The authors want to give LLM agents robust spatial behavior in dynamic, partially observable grid environments without relying on expensive chain-of-thought reasoning at every step, and to separate low-level spatial skill acquisition from high-level reasoning.
AI.method: In a 2D partially observable grid-world, the agent first collects geodesic trajectories between states and goals. These trajectories are vector-quantized to form a discrete library of representative trajectory prototypes. Offline, an LLM is prompted to assign a natural language description and usage conditions to each prototype, treating each as a "tool." Online, given the current state and goal, the LLM acts as a high-level orchestrator that selects which tool to apply; the corresponding low-level action sequence (trajectory) is then executed by primitive controllers. Additional tools, such as an agent-centered zoom tool and collision detection tool, are integrated to support decision making. The system uses the open vision-language model Qwen3.6-35B-A3B as the LLM component.
AI.result: In the tested dynamic 2D grid environment, combining the geometry-derived trajectory tools with zoom and collision tools enables a "fast, non-reasoning" configuration that attains a goal-reaching rate comparable to a much more computationally expensive chain-of-thought setup. The decision latency is reduced from minutes to seconds while preserving task performance.
AI.conclusion: Separating spatial skill discovery from LLM-based high-level reasoning via trajectory quantization and tool abstraction can give LLM agents strong spatial competence at low inference cost. Geometry-driven tools, when paired with lightweight auxiliary tools and a non-CoT LLM policy, can match the success rate of expensive CoT reasoning while dramatically reducing decision time, indicating a promising path for more efficient agentic AI in spatial environments.

title: Lingtai: What Concept Geometry Reveals--and Does Not Reveal--About LLM Inference
comment: 15 pages, 4 figures, 7 tables. An earlier version was publicly released on Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23068698)
summary: Observing what a large language model computes during autoregressive inference--online and without training probes--remains difficult. We introduce Lingtai, a training-free concept telemetry layer: at each generation step, residual states are projected onto a domain-specific bank of named concept anchors, constructed without labeled concept examples, outcome labels, gradient fitting, or activation-space optimization, producing a structured per-step concept-coordinate signal. Across code generation and grade-school mathematical reasoning, this signal exhibits a robust association with predictive uncertainty: the association survives problem-identity and token-position controls and is not attributable to a single token type, is not explained by a simple correct/incorrect mixture on GSM8K, and is not reproduced by matched random anchors; it is markedly weaker or direction-inconsistent in K-means and PCA projections. Two structures emerge: a recurring uncertainty-linked activity signal whose functional geometry is task-conditioned (distinct activity-entropy shapes on HumanEval, MBPP, and GSM8K), and an execution-specific trajectory identity with strong local inertia but weak re-instantiation invariance--under completion-only elastic alignment, corruption at k=32 (approximately a median quarter of the completion) on the matched re-execution subset still retrieves the archived episode at 62.0%, while a fresh execution retrieves it only 11.7-16.0% of the time. Finally, a matched audit finds no evidence that the scalar concept-activity signal used here supplies a stable correctness coordinate under the tested protocol; we therefore treat correctness as externally supplied. Telemetry adds 0.7-1.6% per-token decode overhead for the 161-anchor code implementation, with unchanged generated tokens.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Lingtai, a training-free telemetry layer that projects a model’s residual states onto unlabeled concept anchors during generation, yielding concept-coordinate signals that track uncertainty and execution trajectories with low overhead but do not form a stable correctness signal.
AI.motivation: Understanding what large language models internally compute during autoregressive inference, in real time and without training external probes or using labeled concept data, is challenging. Existing interpretability methods often require supervision, gradient access, or offline analysis. The authors aim to develop a lightweight, training-free way to monitor interpretable concept-like activity and its relation to uncertainty and correctness during generation.
AI.method: They propose Lingtai, a concept telemetry layer that projects the model’s residual stream at each generation step onto a bank of named concept anchors. These anchors are domain-specific but are constructed without labeled examples, outcome labels, gradient fitting, or activation optimization. This produces a per-token vector of concept coordinates. They then empirically study how these coordinates relate to predictive uncertainty (entropy), compare against random anchors and unsupervised projections (K-means, PCA), and analyze trajectory identity and re-instantiation across re-executions and corrupted continuations in tasks like code generation (HumanEval, MBPP) and grade-school math (GSM8K).
AI.result: The concept-coordinate signal strongly correlates with predictive uncertainty across code and math tasks, even after controlling for problem identity and token position. The signal is not driven by specific token types, not explained by a simple correct/incorrect mixture on GSM8K, and does not emerge with matched random anchors. K-means and PCA projections show much weaker or inconsistent uncertainty associations. Two main structures appear: (1) a robust, task-conditioned uncertainty-linked activity pattern with distinct shapes per benchmark; and (2) execution-specific trajectories with strong local inertia but weak invariance across runs—corrupted continuations at k=32 still match archived executions 62.0% of the time, versus 11.7–16.0% for fresh re-executions. An audit indicates the scalar activity signal does not provide a stable correctness dimension under their protocol. Telemetry overhead is small (0.7–1.6% per-token) and leaves outputs unchanged.
AI.conclusion: Lingtai enables low-overhead, training-free telemetry of concept-like activity in large language models by projecting residual states onto domain-specific anchors. The resulting signals reliably track uncertainty and capture execution-specific trajectories but do not serve as stable correctness indicators in the tested setting. This suggests such telemetry is a promising tool for online interpretability and monitoring of model behavior, particularly for uncertainty-aware analysis, while correctness assessment likely requires external signals or additional structure.

title: CompMat-Bench: Benchmarking AI Agents for Computational Materials Science
summary: Evaluating AI agents on scientific research tasks is constrained by the time and resources required for the underlying experiments or calculations. In computational materials research, repeating the same expensive simulations across agents and trials can make evaluation impractical. We introduce CompMat-Bench, a benchmark of 94 tasks derived from recently published computational materials studies, each asking agents to complete a step toward achieving the study's scientific goal. We reproduce the research steps in advance and assess agents on preparing inputs and analyzing outputs for expensive simulations, so expensive simulations can be avoided during evaluation. The reproduced inputs and results serve as ground truth for grading agents with fixed rules, without an LLM judge. The benchmark supports four evaluation conditions: single tasks and workflows composed of related tasks, each with full or reduced methodological guidance. With full guidance on single tasks, agents based on three LLMs demonstrate the ability to complete individual materials research steps, with pass rates of 66.0-90.4% across 94 tasks. Both longer workflows and reduced guidance can limit agent performance, but in different ways for different agents: they lower the pass rates of the weaker agents, whereas the strongest agent falls only when a long workflow is combined with reduced guidance. Failure analysis attributes most failures to scientific errors rather than to errors in software usage. CompMat-Bench provides a basis for comparing agents on the steps of real materials research and for analyzing agent failure modes.

AI.tldr: CompMat-Bench is a benchmark of 94 pre-reproduced computational materials research tasks that evaluates AI agents on realistic research steps without rerunning expensive simulations, revealing different failure modes under varying guidance and workflow length.
AI.motivation: Evaluating AI agents on scientific and especially computational materials research tasks is difficult because underlying simulations are computationally expensive and must be repeated across agents, trials, and conditions. This makes large-scale, fair, and reproducible evaluation impractical and hinders progress on developing and comparing AI research assistants. The authors aim to create a benchmark that captures realistic research steps, avoids repeated costly simulations, and allows objective, scalable comparison of agents and analysis of their failure modes.
AI.method: The authors construct CompMat-Bench from recently published computational materials studies, extracting 94 concrete tasks that each represent a step toward the original study’s scientific goal (e.g., preparing inputs, analyzing outputs of simulations). They pre-run and reproduce the relevant simulations or calculations once, storing the inputs and outputs. During evaluation, AI agents are asked to generate inputs or perform analyses, and their outputs are graded automatically against this stored ground truth via fixed rule-based grading, removing the need for rerunning expensive simulations or using LLM judges. The benchmark defines four evaluation settings: single independent tasks vs. chained workflows of related tasks, and for each, conditions with full methodological guidance vs. reduced guidance, to probe robustness and reliance on instructions.
AI.result: Across the 94 tasks in the benchmark, agents built on three different LLMs can successfully complete many individual materials research steps when provided full methodological guidance, achieving pass rates between 66.0% and 90.4%. Performance degrades when tasks are arranged into longer workflows or when methodological guidance is reduced, but the degradation pattern depends on the agent: weaker agents show lowered pass rates under either longer workflows or reduced guidance, whereas the strongest agent’s performance only drops significantly when both conditions—long workflow and reduced guidance—are combined. An analysis of incorrect cases shows that most failures are due to scientific reasoning errors (e.g., misunderstanding materials science concepts or misinterpreting results) rather than mistakes in using the software tools themselves.
AI.conclusion: CompMat-Bench enables rigorous, scalable evaluation of AI agents on realistic computational materials research steps, eliminating the need for repeated expensive simulations and subjective LLM-based judging. The benchmark exposes nuanced differences in how agents handle workflow complexity and varying levels of guidance, and highlights that scientific reasoning, not just tool operation, is a primary bottleneck. It thus provides a foundation for comparing research agents, studying their failure modes, and guiding future improvements in AI systems intended to assist with real-world materials science research.

title: PhysicsMate: A Curriculum-Grounded Bengali Benchmark for Secondary Physics QA with Small-Model Adaptation
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. Accepted at 11th IEEE Asia-Pacific Conference on Computer Science and Data Engineering (IEEE CSDE 2026)
summary: Bengali secondary education lacks curriculum-grounded benchmarks for STEM question-solving, and general-purpose language models struggle with the precise terminology, unit conventions, and derivations that physics problems demand. We introduce PhysicsMate, a benchmark of 1834 question-answer pairs built from the National Curriculum and Textbook Board (NCTB) Grade 9-10 physics syllabus and grounded in a multi-relational knowledge graph of 1760 nodes and 2600 edges across ten ontological types. We Low-Rank Adapt at 0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B parameters, with a unified recipe and demonstrate a significant increase in closed-book accuracy in all scales (+5.5, +15.0, and +23.3 percentage points). A node-type analysis shows that the most benefited by adaptation is the structured curricular knowledge, which consists of physical quantities and named laws, while the least benefited is the loosely specified entity-level knowledge. The 4B model has been adapted and quantized to a small offline binary that can be used for local inference in resource constrained environments and offers a viable path to curriculum aligned physics support in environments with limited connectivity and hardware.

AI.tldr: They build a Bengali Grade 9–10 physics benchmark and show that domain adaptation of small LMs greatly improves closed-book physics question answering and can run offline.
AI.motivation: There is no standardized, curriculum-aligned benchmark for Bengali STEM problem solving, and general LMs struggle with physics-specific terminology, units, and derivations, especially in low-resource languages like Bengali. This gap hinders the development and evaluation of educational AI tools for Bengali secondary education.
AI.method: They construct PhysicsMate, a benchmark of 1834 Q&A pairs based on the official NCTB Grade 9–10 physics syllabus, and ground it in a multi-relational knowledge graph with 1760 nodes and 2600 edges of ten ontological types (e.g., quantities, laws, entities). They then apply Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to base language models of sizes 0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B parameters using a unified fine-tuning recipe on this curriculum-aligned dataset and knowledge graph. They evaluate closed-book question-answering accuracy and analyze performance by node type in the knowledge graph.
AI.result: All adapted models show substantial gains in closed-book accuracy over the base models: +5.5, +15.0, and +23.3 percentage points for the 0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B models respectively. Node-type analysis reveals that adaptation most improves structured curricular knowledge (physical quantities and named laws) and least improves loosely defined entity-level knowledge. The 4B model is further quantized into a compact binary suitable for offline, local inference under constrained hardware and connectivity.
AI.conclusion: Curriculum-grounded adaptation of small language models using a knowledge-graph-backed benchmark significantly improves Bengali secondary-school physics QA, especially for structured concepts like quantities and laws. The resulting 4B model can run offline as a small binary, making it practical for low-resource educational settings and suggesting a pathway toward scalable, curriculum-aligned STEM tutoring tools in under-resourced languages.

title: Incident-Arena: Getting agents to the last nine of reliability
summary: AI coding agents are ubiquitous in engineering workflows amongst industry and academia. Yet, despite their use in app coding, relatively less attention has been paid to their ability to execute on production incident response. This emerging field, termed agentic site-reliability-engineering (SRE) contains benchmarks limited by (1) unrealistic environments, typically toy repositories (2) non-standard framework implementations and (3) simple static verifiers. We introduce Incident-Arena, a human-built benchmark of 20 carefully selected tasks grounded in real-world deployed open source software. Each task deploys a production application to an ephemeral Kubernetes cluster, injecting a fault from the config layer through underlying images, and a sustained load profile given the task requirements. We also present a novel verification method, going beyond static checks to functional verifiers, holding systems level metrics stable, while ensuring repairs are done safely. Agent trials run an average of 2.81M tokens and 41 turns, going beyond existing benchmarks, demonstrating agentic long horizon reasoning. Across 20 tasks and 3 application substrates, frontier models score below 64.3%, with failures extending from diagnosis/localization errors, through incomplete repairs and unsafe regressions.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Incident-Arena, a realistic benchmark to evaluate AI coding agents on production incident response tasks in Kubernetes-based environments, showing that current frontier models still struggle, achieving under 64.3% success.
AI.motivation: While AI coding agents are widely used for application development, there is a gap in understanding and evaluating their effectiveness in handling real-world production incidents, a critical aspect of site reliability engineering. Existing benchmarks are limited by toy environments, inconsistent frameworks, and oversimplified verification, so a more realistic, standardized, and rigorous benchmark is needed.
AI.method: The authors construct Incident-Arena, a benchmark of 20 human-designed incident-response tasks based on real-world open-source applications. Each task deploys a production-grade app to an ephemeral Kubernetes cluster, injects realistic faults across the stack (from configuration to container images), and applies a sustained load. They also design a functional verification framework that assesses not only static properties but also end-to-end behavior and system-level metrics, including safety of the applied fixes. They then run multi-turn, long-horizon agent trials (on the order of millions of tokens and dozens of dialogue turns) across different application substrates.
AI.result: Agent runs in Incident-Arena average 2.81M tokens and 41 turns, indicating substantial long-horizon reasoning. Across 20 tasks and 3 different application substrates, frontier LLM-based agents achieve less than 64.3% task success. Failure modes include incorrect or incomplete diagnosis and localization of faults, partial or ineffective fixes, and repairs that introduce unsafe regressions or destabilize system metrics.
AI.conclusion: Incident-Arena provides a challenging, realistic benchmark for agentic site reliability engineering, exposing substantial limitations in current AI coding agents’ ability to handle production incidents safely and reliably. The results suggest that significant work remains to improve diagnostic reasoning, repair completeness, and safety-aware verification for agentic SRE systems.

title: Closing the Loop: Practical Training Recipes for Looped Language Models
summary: Looped language models increase effective depth by repeatedly applying a shared block of layers, but existing large-scale recipes require multi-stage training over trillions of tokens, while the benefits of recurrence remain difficult to separate from differences in data and training. In this work, we establish practical training recipes for looped language models, with three main results. (1) We develop a compute-efficient from-scratch pipeline that reduces the training budget from 7.7T tokens in Ouro to 310B tokens while retaining strong reasoning performance. Pretraining followed by high-quality mid-training, together with learning-rate warmup and stronger exit-gate regularization, enables stable recurrent training without prior multi-stage schedules. (2) Under controlled comparisons, our 1.4B LoopLM outperforms a parameter-matched dense model trained on the same data and token budget on all 12 evaluated benchmarks, including +14 points on GSM8K, +10 on MATH, and +22 on DROP. At matched inference compute, it approaches a 3.9B dense model on mathematical reasoning and reading comprehension while using only 36\% as many parameters. (3) We introduce a minimal recipe for converting pretrained dense models into looped ones: a single learned input-mixing scalar and a smoothed exit loss, with no step-specific parameters. Applied to Qwen3-1.7B-Base, Looped Qwen improves over an identically continued dense baseline on every evaluated benchmark across two data regimes, with statistically clear gains on GSM8K, MATH, and MMLU-Pro on the curated mixture. Together, these results make looped language models substantially cheaper to train from scratch and practical to introduce into existing pretrained checkpoints, while isolating the gains due to recurrence itself.

AI.tldr: This paper develops practical, compute-efficient training and conversion recipes for looped (recurrent-depth) language models, showing they can be trained from scratch or converted from dense models to achieve significantly better reasoning performance at similar or lower compute and parameter counts.
AI.motivation: Previous looped language models like Ouro showed strong reasoning but required extremely expensive multi-stage training over trillions of tokens, making them impractical and confounding the benefits of recurrence with differences in data and training setup. The authors want scalable, stable, and cheaper ways to train and deploy looped models, and to cleanly isolate how much performance gain truly comes from recurrence itself rather than from larger or more complex training recipes.
AI.method: The authors propose (1) a from-scratch, compute-efficient training pipeline that combines standard pretraining with a phase of high-quality mid-training, plus learning-rate warmup and stronger exit-gate regularization to stabilize recurrent training without elaborate multi-stage schedules; (2) controlled experimental comparisons between a 1.4B-parameter looped language model and a parameter-matched dense baseline using identical data and token budgets, as well as comparisons at matched inference compute with a 3.9B dense model; and (3) a minimal conversion procedure that turns an existing dense model into a looped one by adding only a learned input-mixing scalar and a smoothed exit loss, without introducing step-specific parameters, then evaluating this on the Qwen3-1.7B-Base model across multiple benchmarks and data regimes.
AI.result: Using their recipe, they reduce the training budget needed to reach strong reasoning performance from 7.7T tokens (in prior work Ouro) to 310B tokens. Their 1.4B LoopLM beats an equally sized dense model trained on the same data and tokens on all 12 tested benchmarks, with large gains on GSM8K (+14), MATH (+10), and DROP (+22). At matched inference compute, the 1.4B looped model approaches the performance of a 3.9B dense model on math and reading comprehension while using only 36% of the parameters. The minimal conversion recipe applied to Qwen3-1.7B-Base yields looped variants that consistently outperform dense baselines continued under identical conditions, with clear gains on GSM8K, MATH, and MMLU-Pro, in both standard and curated training mixtures.
AI.conclusion: Looped language models can be trained and deployed far more efficiently than previous recipes suggested, both from scratch and by converting existing dense checkpoints. With appropriate training techniques—high-quality mid-training, LR warmup, and exit-gate regularization—recurrence becomes stable and practical without expensive multi-stage schedules. The experiments demonstrate that recurrence itself yields substantial gains in reasoning and reading comprehension per parameter and per unit of inference compute, making looped architectures a cost-effective and scalable alternative to conventional dense transformers.

title: Agent Evaluation Reliability: More Tasks Won't (Always) Fix An Agent Leaderboard
summary: Agent evaluations are increasingly used to compare LLMs and inform deployment decisions, yet ranks can reflect not only the model but also the effects of the evaluation conditions such as the scaffolds or tasks. This makes reliability claim-dependent: an evaluation that reliably ranks deployed systems may not reliably rank underlying models. We ask which conclusions current agent evaluations reliably support and what additional evaluation would improve them. We develop a Bayesian variance-decomposition framework for sparse, imbalanced agent leaderboards and apply it to 22 benchmarks from the Holistic Agent Leaderboard and Harbor Index. The framework separates signal, performance differences relevant to the intended claim, from noise, irrelevant variation that can still change rankings. We find: (1) Reliability depends on the measurement goal. Fixed model-scaffold systems are ranked reliably (0.935-0.994), while underlying-model reliability is substantially lower (0.148-0.841). (2) Scaffold choice can change conclusions. Inter-scaffold reliability measures whether scaffolds preserve model rankings, showing that scaffold effects vary substantially across evaluations. (3) More tasks cannot resolve all uncertainty. Even infinitely many similarly constructed tasks improve model-ranking reliability of a benchmark by at most 0.097 when uncertainty is dominated by limited scaffold coverage. (4) Pooling diverse benchmarks can improve cross-task rankings at lower cost. For rankings across diverse agentic tasks, pooling benchmarks raises projected reliability from 0.44 to 0.75 at the same task budget and can reduce projected cost by up to 83\%. Evaluation design should follow the intended claim: identify what a score or ranking should mean, diagnose what limits its reliability, and spend evaluation budget on the sources of uncertainty that matter.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how reliable current LLM agent leaderboards are, showing that reliability strongly depends on what exactly is being ranked (full agent systems vs. underlying models) and on evaluation design choices such as scaffolds, tasks, and benchmark pooling.
AI.motivation: Agent-based evaluations are increasingly used to compare LLMs and guide deployment, but observed rankings may conflate true model quality with artifacts of scaffolds, task selection, and benchmark design. This raises concern about whether current leaderboards actually support the claims people infer from them—for example, about which base models are best. The authors aim to clarify what conclusions existing evaluations can legitimately support and how to redesign evaluations to be more claim-aligned and reliable.
AI.method: The authors introduce a Bayesian variance-decomposition framework tailored to sparse, imbalanced agent leaderboards, in which not all models, scaffolds, and tasks are fully crossed. Applying this to 22 benchmarks from the Holistic Agent Leaderboard and Harbor Index, they decompose observed performance into (i) signal components aligned with particular measurement goals (e.g., fixed model–scaffold system performance, underlying model performance across scaffolds, cross-task performance), and (ii) noise components (irrelevant variation that can still affect rank). They then compute reliability metrics under different claim definitions and simulate the effects of adding more tasks, varying scaffold coverage, and pooling benchmarks within a Bayesian projection setting.
AI.result: Across the 22 benchmarks, they find: (1) Rankings of fixed model–scaffold systems are highly reliable, with reliability between 0.935 and 0.994, but rankings intended to reflect underlying base models are much less reliable, with reliability from 0.148 to 0.841. (2) Scaffold choice can significantly shift model rankings; inter-scaffold reliability varies widely, indicating that some scaffolds preserve model ordering better than others. (3) Simply adding more tasks to a benchmark has limited returns when scaffold effects dominate; even an infinite number of similar tasks would increase model-ranking reliability by at most 0.097 under scaffold-limited conditions. (4) Pooling heterogeneous benchmarks yields more reliable cross-task rankings at the same task budget, with projected reliability improvements from 0.44 to 0.75 and potential cost reductions of up to 83%.
AI.conclusion: The reliability of agent evaluations is highly claim-dependent: leaderboards are trustworthy for ranking complete model–scaffold systems but often unreliable proxies for ranking underlying base models, especially when scaffold effects are large. Evaluation design must therefore start from the intended interpretation of scores and rankings, use variance decomposition to diagnose what drives uncertainty (tasks vs. scaffolds vs. other factors), and allocate evaluation budget to better cover the dominant sources of variance. Pooling diverse benchmarks and expanding scaffold coverage can substantially improve reliability for cross-task, cross-scaffold claims, whereas naively adding more similar tasks cannot fully resolve uncertainty when scaffold-induced variation is the main limitation.

title: Bayesian Fine-tuning Yields Language Models that are as Bayesian as their Beliefs Allow
summary: Language models (LMs) are increasingly used for tasks that require reasoning about hidden variables from a few observations, for which Bayesian inference is the normatively correct solution. While supervised fine-tuning of an LM on the outputs of an optimal $\textit{Bayesian}$ model leads to near-Bayesian behavior, standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on the true answers for the task falls short of it. But behavior alone does not tell us $\textit{why}$ tuning on a $\textit{Bayesian}$ or an $\textit{oracle}$ (true answers) signal differs: whether the resulting LM represents Bayesian beliefs, acts on them, or turns them into a choice the way Bayes' rule does. To compare them, we formulate increasingly demanding requirements for an LM to count as a Bayesian decision maker, spanning its behavior, representations, and computations, and test them on a flight recommendation task. The Bayes-trained LM acts Bayesian, encodes quantities of Bayes' rule in its middle layers, and uses the encoded belief for the recommendation to a certain extent. The oracle-trained LM differs from it both in the beliefs it holds and whether it reads beliefs out into recommendations. Exchanging beliefs between the LMs transfers a part of the Bayesian advantage. Bayes fine-tuning thus installs usable Bayesian beliefs in an LM for reasoning under uncertainty in a way standard SFT on oracle answers cannot, highlighting the advantage of nuanced supervision.

AI.tldr: The paper compares language models fine-tuned on Bayesian model outputs versus true oracle answers for reasoning under uncertainty, showing that Bayesian-supervised tuning installs internal Bayesian beliefs and decision processes that standard supervised fine-tuning does not.
AI.motivation: To understand whether and how language models can perform genuinely Bayesian reasoning about hidden variables from few observations, and why fine-tuning on Bayesian model outputs yields more Bayesian-like behavior than tuning on true task answers alone.
AI.method: The authors define a hierarchy of criteria for an LM to qualify as a Bayesian decision maker, assessing behavior, internal representations, and computations. They then fine-tune LMs either on outputs of an optimal Bayesian model (Bayes-trained) or on true task answers (oracle-trained) and test them on a flight recommendation task, probing intermediate-layer representations and intervening by exchanging encoded beliefs between models.
AI.result: Bayes-trained LMs behave in a Bayesian manner, encode Bayes rule quantities in intermediate layers, and partially use these beliefs for decisions. Oracle-trained LMs differ both in their internal beliefs and in how (or whether) they map beliefs to recommendations. When beliefs are swapped between models, some of the Bayesian performance advantage transfers, showing that the internal Bayesian beliefs are functionally relevant.
AI.conclusion: Fine-tuning on Bayesian model outputs installs structured, usable Bayesian beliefs and decision processes in LMs that standard supervised fine-tuning on true answers does not, demonstrating the value of nuanced Bayesian supervision for improving reasoning under uncertainty.

title: When More Data Is Not Enough: The Context-Sufficiency Frontier in Generative AI Personalization
comment: PREPRINT - SUBMITTED TO JOURNAL OF SERVICE RESEARCH (JSR)
summary: Personalization has long relied on customer data to infer what an individual is likely to value. We call this customer evidence: the customer's historical behavior and preferences. Generative AI extends personalization by allowing providers to supply changing situational information at the moment a response is produced, without encoding every condition in advance. We define this provider-side context as information about what is possible, permitted, or advisable now. This flexibility creates a new problem: once context becomes easy to supply, more is not necessarily better. We develop a theory of context sufficiency in which the relevance of context to the customer's current intent matters more than its volume. The theory identifies four states, insufficiency, sufficiency, saturation, and interference, and introduces the Context-Sufficiency Frontier to locate the minimal relevant set. In a full-factorial experiment with a generative recommender at a large home-furnishing retailer, relevant context improved appropriateness, while irrelevant context reduced it and destabilized retrieval. The framework shifts personalization from supplying more context toward identifying what the current interaction actually requires and enforcing constraints throughout the service process.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a theory and framework for determining how much and what kind of contextual information generative AI systems should use to personalize recommendations, showing that only relevant context improves outcomes.
AI.motivation: As generative AI enables providers to inject rich, dynamic contextual information at response time, firms are tempted to add more and more context under the assumption that it will enhance personalization. However, excessive or poorly chosen context may not improve, and can even harm, recommendation quality by overwhelming or distracting the model. The authors aim to understand when additional context truly helps personalization and when it becomes counterproductive.
AI.method: The authors develop a conceptual theory of context sufficiency tailored to generative AI–driven personalization. They define provider-side context and formalize four qualitative states of context usage: insufficiency, sufficiency, saturation, and interference. They then introduce the Context-Sufficiency Frontier, which characterizes the minimal set of context that remains relevant to a customer’s current intent. To empirically test the theory, they conduct a full-factorial experiment with a generative recommender system deployed at a large home-furnishing retailer, systematically varying the presence and relevance of contextual information and measuring changes in recommendation appropriateness and retrieval behavior.
AI.result: The experiment demonstrates that adding context that is relevant to the customer’s current intent improves the appropriateness of generative recommendations. In contrast, including irrelevant or extraneous context degrades recommendation quality and destabilizes the system’s retrieval behavior, confirming that more context is not always beneficial. The findings empirically support the proposed states of context use and validate the importance of locating the minimal relevant context set along the Context-Sufficiency Frontier.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that effective generative personalization depends less on maximizing the amount of contextual information and more on carefully curating context that is directly relevant to the user’s present goal. The proposed theory and Context-Sufficiency Frontier guide designers toward identifying the minimal, most relevant context and enforcing constraints on what is supplied throughout the service process. This reorients personalization strategy from indiscriminately enriching context toward context discipline, improving recommendation quality and system stability in generative AI–based services.

title: Towards Robust Numerical Claim Verification
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used for claim verification, yet remain brittle for numerical reasoning: even small changes in value can sharply degrade accuracy. We show that this brittleness persists in frontier LLMs, but can be mitigated through adversarial fine-tuning on numerically perturbed examples. Using parameter-efficient fine-tuning, small Qwen3 models (0.6B$\unicode{x2013}$8B) reach 98.7% accuracy on label-flipping perturbations, outperforming larger zero-shot models and frontier systems (GPT-5.4 Pro (74.0%) and Gemini 2.5 Flash (73.9%)). The gains generalise to unseen perturbation types, indicating robust numerical decision boundaries rather than memorised edits. Robustness also transfers without target-domain data, significantly improving cross-lingual performance in Spanish. We further show that the same fine-tuning recipe confers robustness to evidence-side perturbations, using the VitaminC dataset.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates and improves numerical robustness of LLMs used for claim verification via adversarial fine-tuning on numerically perturbed data.
AI.motivation: LLMs used for fact/claim verification are fragile when reasoning about numbers; small numerical changes in input can cause large drops in accuracy. This brittleness persists even in frontier LLMs, motivating methods to make numerical reasoning more robust without requiring huge models or extensive new data.
AI.method: The authors apply parameter-efficient adversarial fine-tuning to small Qwen3 models using training data with systematically perturbed numerical values (label-flipping perturbations and other numeric variations). They then evaluate robustness across different perturbation types, zero-shot baselines, frontier models, cross-lingual settings (Spanish), and evidence-side perturbations (VitaminC dataset).
AI.result: After adversarial fine-tuning, small Qwen3 models (0.6B–8B) achieve up to 98.7% accuracy on label-flipping numerical perturbations, outperforming significantly larger zero-shot and frontier models like GPT-5.4 Pro (74.0%) and Gemini 2.5 Flash (73.9%). The robustness generalizes to unseen numeric perturbations, transfers across languages without target-domain data (improving Spanish performance), and extends to robustness against perturbations in the evidence text as shown on VitaminC.
AI.conclusion: Adversarial fine-tuning on numerically perturbed examples can substantially harden LLMs’ numerical reasoning in claim verification, allowing relatively small models to outperform larger frontier systems in robustness. The learned robustness is not just memorization but induces more stable numerical decision boundaries that generalize across perturbation types, languages, and even to evidence-side perturbations.

title: Backdoor Containment via Expert Quarantine and Shutdown in LLMs
summary: Backdoored large language models (LLMs) can behave normally on benign inputs while producing attacker-specified outputs under hidden triggers. Existing defenses span four stages--prior-training, in-training, post-training, and inference-time--and share one of two underlying strategies: either suppress backdoor learning (by filtering poisoned data or interrupting its acquisition during optimization) or learn, then purify (by repairing model weights or gating inputs after a fully backdoored model has formed). We propose a third strategy, learn, but channel: allow backdoor formation during training but route it into a designated, quarantined component that can be disabled at deployment. To this end, we propose Quarantined Expert Shutdown QES, a computationally efficient containment strategy built in a regularization-steered MoE-like setting. Specifically, given a poisoned dataset, QES augments a Transformer-based language model with routed expert-specific LoRA branches and lightweight routers, and uses auxiliary routing objectives to attract trigger-conditioned behavior into a designated expert while preserving benign capability elsewhere. At deployment, mitigation reduces to a single constant-time operation: zeroing the quarantined expert's routing weight, without trigger screening or further updating model weights. Empirically, our methods reduce the attack success rate ASR from 100% to 0-10% on most settings across two tasks, three attacks, and four model families, while downstream utility is often preserved or only modestly affected. These results establish learn, but channel as a previously unexplored regime for backdoor containment in generative LLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes QES, a method that channels backdoor behavior into a small, quarantined expert module in an LLM so it can be disabled at deployment, substantially lowering backdoor attack success while retaining normal performance.
AI.motivation: Backdoored LLMs can behave normally on benign inputs but exhibit attacker-controlled behavior under hidden triggers. Existing defenses either try to prevent backdoors from being learned at all or attempt to repair or filter a fully trained, potentially backdoored model. Both paradigms can be computationally expensive, unreliable, or disruptive to model quality. The authors aim to explore a new defense regime that tolerates backdoor learning but structurally confines it to a controllable component that can be easily neutralized at deployment.
AI.method: They introduce Quarantined Expert Shutdown (QES) within a mixture-of-experts-like architecture for Transformer-based LLMs. The base model is augmented with expert-specific LoRA branches and lightweight routing modules. Using a poisoned training set, they apply auxiliary routing objectives that encourage any trigger-conditioned behavior to flow into a designated “quarantined” expert while maintaining normal capability in other experts. Once trained, mitigation is done by a simple operation at inference: setting the routing weight of the quarantined expert to zero, effectively disabling the backdoor without needing trigger detection or further weight updates.
AI.result: Across two tasks, three different backdoor attacks, and four LLM families, QES reduces attack success rates from 100% to between 0–10% in most tested settings. At the same time, the downstream performance on benign tasks is largely preserved or only mildly degraded, showing that the model remains useful after quarantine. The method is computationally efficient since it avoids heavy retraining or runtime screening.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates a new defense paradigm, “learn, but channel,” where backdoor behaviors are allowed to form but are structurally isolated into a quarantined expert that can be deactivated at deployment. QES provides an efficient and effective containment strategy for generative LLM backdoors, with strong empirical reductions in attack success and limited impact on benign utility, establishing this channeling approach as a promising direction for robust LLM defense.

title: How Divergence Becomes Decision Flips in Compressed Language Models
summary: Compression reports summarize how far a compressed language model moved from the dense one, usually by a KL divergence; a deployment that relies on the dense model's outputs needs to know how many of its decisions changed. We show that total variation, not KL, answers this directly. Across 802 compressed and perturbed copies of 19 open models on five corpora and nine mechanically unrelated perturbation families, the rate at which the arg-max token changes (the \emph{flip rate}) tracks total variation at a ratio with median $1.05$, with no fitted constant. KL converts into flips only through its square root and a factor that varies fourfold across models and corpora, because KL averages over tokens before the root is taken; first-order statistics averaged per token, such as Hellinger distance, avoid this, but reports rarely give them. As a result, of two compressors reported on different models and corpora whose flip rates differ by at least $10%$, KL assigns the smaller divergence to the one that changes more decisions in $11%$ of cases, total variation in $1%$. Two pre-registered tests mark the limits: on a held-out code corpus the ratio held for all eight models while three predictions about KL each failed for half of them or more, and on three new models with real kernels it stayed in its band for 37 of 38 checkpoints but fell below one on code for two models. In vLLM speculative decoding, total variation measured under teacher forcing predicts greedy draft acceptance with a mean relative error of $1.1$--$2.4%$, without the task-specific calibration that KL needs.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that total variation distance is a more direct and reliable measure than KL divergence for understanding how compression or perturbation of language models affects their discrete decisions (arg-max tokens / flips). It empirically validates a near-1:1 relationship between flip rate and total variation across many models, corpora, and perturbations, and shows that KL is less stable and needs task-specific calibration.
AI.motivation: Existing compression reports for language models typically quantify how much a compressed model deviates from its dense counterpart using KL divergence. But practitioners who rely on the dense model’s outputs care about how many decisions (arg-max tokens) actually change after compression. KL does not directly answer this, and its relationship to flip rate is model- and corpus-dependent, and only indirectly connected via inequalities. The authors aim to identify and validate a divergence measure that more directly corresponds to decision changes and works robustly across models, corpora, and perturbations.
AI.method: The authors systematically compare KL divergence, total variation distance, Hellinger distance, and related metrics on 802 compressed and perturbed variants across 19 open language models, five corpora, and nine distinct perturbation families. They define and measure the flip rate—the fraction of positions where the arg-max token changes between dense and perturbed models—and study how it correlates with each divergence. They analyze how KL theoretically translates to flip rate via its square root and model-dependent factors, whereas first-order token-wise statistics (like Hellinger and total variation) avoid this averaging issue. They run two pre-registered tests: (1) on a held-out code corpus across eight models to check stability of the flip–TV relationship and several predictions about KL, and (2) on three new models with real compression kernels across 38 checkpoints, to test the robustness and possible failure modes of the proposed relationship. They also evaluate in a practical setting: vLLM speculative decoding, where they see if total variation under teacher forcing predicts greedy draft acceptance rates without extra calibration.
AI.result: Empirically, the flip rate tracks total variation distance extremely closely, with a median ratio of 1.05 across 802 model–perturbation–corpus combinations, and this relationship holds without fitting any constant. In contrast, the mapping from KL divergence to flip rate goes only through its square root and involves a model- and corpus-dependent factor that varies by about 4×. This leads to mis-rankings: when comparing two compressors whose flip rates differ by at least 10%, KL assigns a smaller divergence to the more disruptive compressor in 11% of cases, while total variation does so in only 1% of cases. In the pre-registered held-out code corpus test, the TV–flip ratio held for all eight models, while three predictions based on KL each failed for at least half the models. In tests on three new models with actual compression kernels, the TV–flip ratio stayed within its expected band for 37 of 38 checkpoints; the only notable deviation was that it dipped below one on code for two models. In vLLM speculative decoding, total variation computed under teacher forcing predicts greedy draft acceptance rates with mean relative error of only 1.1–2.4%, whereas KL requires task-specific calibration to achieve similar performance.
AI.conclusion: Total variation distance is a more faithful and robust proxy than KL divergence for the key practical quantity in compressed language model deployment: the rate at which arg-max token decisions change (flip rate). Because KL averages over tokens before applying a square root, it introduces model- and corpus-dependent scaling factors and can mis-rank compressors in terms of how many decisions they alter. First-order per-token divergences like total variation and Hellinger correlate more linearly and consistently with flip rate, making them better suited for compression reporting and for predicting behavior in real systems like speculative decoding. The authors recommend that compression reports include total variation (and/or similar first-order metrics) instead of, or in addition to, KL, especially when the goal is to understand decision changes rather than purely distributional shifts.

title: A Simple Doxastic Deontic Logic for Norm-Guided Decision Making
comment: Manuscript accepted at PRIMA 2026. Includes an additional appendix with proofs
summary: Making decisions despite conflicting norms and incomplete or unreliable information is a fundamental challenge for autonomous systems. We introduce a simple doxastic deontic logic for this setting: a classically reducible fragment of Chellas' Minimal Deontic Logic, extended with explicit conditional norms and combined with multi-agent KD45, so that norms can depend on agents' beliefs about both facts and norms. On this logic we define the Doxastic Norm Compliance Optimization Problem, where an agent chooses a decision minimizing weighted norm violations. We distinguish subjective optimization (relative to the agent's beliefs) from objective optimization (relative to the actual facts). We give conditions under which (i) the two coincide and (ii) optimal decision-making can be reduced to weighted partial MaxSAT in polynomial time.

AI.tldr: The paper defines a logical framework and optimization problem for autonomous agents to choose actions that best comply with possibly conflicting norms under uncertainty, and shows when this can be solved efficiently via MaxSAT.
AI.motivation: Autonomous systems must act under incomplete, uncertain, and sometimes inconsistent normative requirements (e.g., rules, regulations, ethical guidelines). Existing deontic and doxastic logics often either ignore computational tractability or cannot handle norms that depend on agents' uncertain beliefs about both facts and other norms. The authors want a formalism where agents can reason about what they ought to do given uncertain, possibly wrong beliefs and conflicting conditional norms, and then compute best-possible compliant decisions in a principled, efficient way.
AI.method: They construct a simple doxastic deontic logic by taking a fragment of Chellas' Minimal Deontic Logic that is classically reducible, extending it with explicit conditional norms, and combining it with a multi-agent KD45 belief logic. This allows representing norms whose applicability depends on what agents believe about facts and norms. On top of this logic they formally define the Doxastic Norm Compliance Optimization Problem, where each possible decision is evaluated by the number and weight of norms it violates. They differentiate subjective optimization (minimizing violations relative to the agent's beliefs) from objective optimization (relative to the actual world). They then prove conditions guaranteeing that subjective and objective optimal decisions coincide and show a reduction of the optimization problem to weighted partial MaxSAT, establishing that it can be solved in polynomial time under certain structural restrictions.
AI.result: The paper delivers: (1) a combined doxastic-deontic logic with conditional norms based on multi-agent KD45 and a fragment of Chellas' Minimal Deontic Logic; (2) a formal definition of the Doxastic Norm Compliance Optimization Problem that captures weighted trade-offs among possibly conflicting norms; (3) a conceptual and formal distinction between subjective (belief-based) and objective (fact-based) norm compliance optimization; (4) sufficient conditions under which the subjectively optimal and objectively optimal decisions are identical; and (5) a polynomial-time reduction of the optimization problem to weighted partial MaxSAT, including conditions under which this reduction is computationally efficient.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that their doxastic deontic framework provides a principled and computationally tractable basis for autonomous agents to make decisions under normative conflict and uncertainty. By enabling explicit conditional norms that depend on agents' beliefs and by framing decision choice as a weighted violation minimization problem, they reconcile normative reasoning with realistic epistemic limitations. The conditions under which subjective and objective optimization coincide, together with the reduction to weighted partial MaxSAT, suggest that such norm-compliant decision-making can be implemented efficiently in practice for a useful class of problems.

title: Sequential Functional Structured Tucker Compression for Large Language Model Attentions
summary: Post-training compression of LLM attention is often formulated as independent matrix approximation, ignoring both the shared structure among attention projections and the representation shift introduced by earlier compression. We propose FTC, a sequential structured compression framework that adapts the approximation to the current compressed model while jointly exploiting the native Q/K/V head structure under a fixed storage budget. The output projection is handled separately to account for the changed post-attention representation. FTC requires neither fine-tuning nor gradient-based recovery. Across seven decoder-only LLMs from 6B to 32B parameters, FTC achieves the lowest WikiText-2 perplexity among the compared methods at every tested keep ratio on five modern GQA models, with the largest gains under aggressive compression. The improvements transfer to downstream tasks and remain substantial at the 32B scale.

AI.tldr: FTC is a post-training, sequential structured compression framework for LLM attention that exploits Q/K/V head structure and adapts each step to prior compression, outperforming existing methods in perplexity under various compression ratios without fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Existing post-training compression methods for LLM attention typically approximate each projection matrix independently, failing to exploit the shared structure among Q/K/V heads and ignoring representation shifts caused by earlier compression. This leads to suboptimal compression, especially under tight storage budgets and aggressive compression ratios. There is a need for a compression framework that is aware of the evolving compressed model and the inherent structure of attention to achieve better performance without costly fine-tuning.
AI.method: FTC introduces a sequential structured compression framework for attention in large language models. Instead of compressing attention matrices independently, it jointly leverages the native Q/K/V head structure under a global storage budget, and performs compression in a sequential, model-aware manner: each approximation step is adapted to the already-compressed state of the model. The output projection matrix is treated separately to accommodate the changed post-attention representation. The whole procedure is post-training, does not require gradients or fine-tuning, and is evaluated at different keep ratios on modern GQA-based decoder-only LLMs ranging from 6B to 32B parameters.
AI.result: On seven decoder-only GQA LLMs with sizes between 6B and 32B parameters, FTC attains the best WikiText-2 perplexity among all compared post-training compression methods at every tested keep ratio, with especially large gains under aggressive compression. Performance improvements also transfer to multiple downstream tasks, and the advantages persist even for 32B-parameter models.
AI.conclusion: By being both structure-aware (jointly compressing Q/K/V heads) and model-aware (sequentially adapting to previous compression), FTC provides a more effective post-training compression approach for LLM attention. It avoids the need for gradient-based fine-tuning while consistently outperforming alternative methods in perplexity and downstream task performance, particularly under tight storage budgets and for large-scale models.

title: Ontology-Grounded, Reasoner-Verified Benchmarks for Evaluating LLM Reasoning in Scientific AI
comment: 17 pages, 2 figures. Accepted at the AI Data Readiness for Scientific Discovery (AIDaR) Workshop at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026), Paris
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly underpin scientific AI applications that reason over structured knowledge, from biomedical question answering to materials informatics. However, their logical reasoning often falls short, producing factual inaccuracies unacceptable in these settings. Reliable evaluation remains challenging: manual dataset construction scales poorly, and LLM-based generation risks embedding the very flaws it aims to measure. High-quality benchmarks must ground both correct and incorrect labelled examples in explicit background knowledge, formally verifiable by a standard reasoner. We propose a pipeline that automatically generates ontology-grounded multiple-choice question (MCQ) benchmarks from any sufficiently axiomatised OWL 2 ontology, with correct answers grounded in the ontology by design. Distractors are generated by perturbing the right-hand-side class expressions of class definition axioms, and their incorrectness is formally verified by an OWL reasoner via entailment checks. We evaluate the pipeline on three ontologies: Pizza (small, academic), PMDco (complex, materials science), and DOID (large, biomedical), generating 112, 2,491, and 15,216 MCQs respectively. Distractors span four semantic categories from class unsatisfiability to weakened subsumptions, enabling diagnostic evaluation of specific reasoning failures. Items meet natural language quality standards: mean LLM judge scores of 4.02, 4.36, and 3.36 out of 5 confirm fluency, and correct-answer-to-distractor similarity above 0.8 shows that wrong options cannot be dismissed on surface form alone. Six LLMs evaluated zero-shot achieve 41.1-76.8% accuracy, well above the 25% random-guessing baseline, indicating the benchmarks are challenging and discriminative. This work is a step towards more reliable benchmarks for assessing logical reasoning in scientific AI.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an automated pipeline to generate ontology-grounded multiple-choice benchmarks from OWL 2 ontologies, creating formally verified correct and incorrect answers to evaluate LLM logical reasoning in scientific domains.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used in scientific AI tasks that require reasoning over structured knowledge, but they often fail at precise logical reasoning and can produce factual errors that are unacceptable in high-stakes domains. Existing evaluation benchmarks are hard to scale, and using LLMs themselves to generate benchmarks risks reproducing the same reasoning flaws. There is a need for scalable, high-quality benchmarks where both correct and incorrect answers are rigorously grounded in explicit, machine-verifiable background knowledge.
AI.method: The authors design a pipeline that takes any sufficiently axiomatised OWL 2 ontology and automatically generates multiple-choice questions. Correct options are derived directly from ontology axioms, ensuring correctness by construction. Distractor options are generated by systematically perturbing the right-hand-side class expressions in class definition axioms. An OWL reasoner is then used to formally verify that each distractor is indeed incorrect via entailment checks. The pipeline is applied to three ontologies of varying size and domain: Pizza (small, educational), PMDco (complex, materials science), and DOID (large, biomedical). Distractors are categorized into four semantic types (e.g., making the class unsatisfiable or weakening subsumption relations) to probe distinct reasoning capabilities. Natural language realizations of the questions and options are evaluated for fluency and similarity using LLM judges and embedding-based similarity measures.
AI.result: The pipeline successfully generates 112 MCQs from the Pizza ontology, 2,491 from PMDco, and 15,216 from DOID, demonstrating scalability across ontologies of different sizes and domains. Generated distractors span four semantic categories, enabling fine-grained assessment of different logical failure modes.
