AI.method: The authors build a unified conceptual framework that categorizes task adaptation techniques by where task information is encoded (weights, prompts, embeddings), then develop a taxonomy, compare paradigms, and analyze their trade-offs and relationships.
AI.result: The paper organizes the literature on LLM task adaptation into a single taxonomy covering parameter-efficient fine-tuning, in-context learning, and embedding-injection, clarifying how methods differ, where they overlap, and when each is preferable.
AI.conclusion: A unified view of task adaptation for LLMs reveals connections and trade-offs between weight-based, prompt-based, and embedding-based methods, and identifies open research problems in combining paradigms, understanding mechanisms, and improving efficiency and robustness.

title: An Educator-Guided LLM Pedagogical Agent for Scaffolded Feedback in Conceptual Database Design
summary:
We present an educator-guided LLM pedagogical agent for scaffolded feedback in conceptual database design. Integrated into an entity--relationship diagram (ERD) editor, the system grounds feedback in the student artifact, assignment requirements, educator-authored rubrics, and instructional resources. Its architecture separates hidden, artifact-grounded diagnosis from the workflow that controls the form and disclosure level of student-facing support.
  We instantiate the architecture as a four-stage workflow progressing from concept checks and guided application to low-detail feedback and localized clarification. Each feedback request creates a stateful episode linked to versioned ERD states. In a deployment spanning three ERD environments and 383 feedback episodes, 71.1\% of observed target-level changes fully or partially incorporated the hidden diagnostic target, including many after Stages~1--2. Qualitative analysis showed that staged disclosure sometimes withheld inaccurate details, supported selective uptake, or allowed later recovery, though some errors still shaped revisions. Survey responses from a self-selected sample favored delayed disclosure and student agency but noted indirectness and repetition.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an educator-guided LLM agent that provides scaffolded, staged feedback on conceptual database design within an ERD editor, showing that delayed, partially hidden diagnostics can effectively support student revisions while managing error and preserving student agency.
AI.motivation: Students designing conceptual database models (ERDs) need timely, targeted feedback that connects their artifacts to assignment requirements and instructional materials. Existing LLM-based feedback systems risk over-disclosure, inaccuracy, and taking too much control away from educators and students. The authors aim to design a feedback system that is both pedagogically controlled and technically grounded in the student’s work and rubric, while mitigating LLM hallucinations and supporting productive student agency.
AI.method: They design an LLM-based pedagogical agent embedded in an ERD editor. The architecture cleanly separates a hidden diagnostic layer—where the LLM evaluates the ERD against requirements, rubrics, and resources—from a staged, student-facing workflow that modulates how much of this diagnosis is revealed, and in what form. They implement a four-stage feedback workflow that progresses from high-level concept checks and guided application to more explicit but still low-detail feedback and finally localized clarification. Each feedback interaction forms a stateful episode tied to versioned ERD states, enabling analysis of how students respond to feedback across stages. They deploy the system across three ERD environments and log 383 feedback episodes, combining quantitative analysis of design changes with qualitative analysis of revisions and a survey of student perceptions.
AI.result: Across the 383 feedback episodes, 71.1% of observed target-level changes in students’ ERDs fully or partially aligned with the system’s hidden diagnostic targets, indicating substantial uptake of the underlying feedback even when details were not fully disclosed. Many of these aligned changes occurred after the early stages of the workflow (Stages 1–2), suggesting that initial, less explicit support can still guide productive revisions. Qualitative analyses showed that staged disclosure: (1) sometimes prevented the propagation of incorrect LLM details by never revealing them directly, (2) enabled students to selectively take up feedback elements, and (3) allowed later stages to correct or refine earlier issues. However, some diagnostic errors still influenced student revisions negatively. Survey data from a self-selected subset of users indicated a preference for delayed, staged disclosure and control over when to seek more explicit help, though some participants criticized the feedback as occasionally indirect or repetitive.
AI.conclusion: An educator-guided, staged-disclosure LLM feedback architecture embedded in an ERD editor can effectively support conceptual database design learning while providing safeguards against over-reliance on, or errors from, the underlying model. By separating hidden diagnosis from student-facing workflow and controlling how and when details are revealed, the system achieves substantial alignment between intended diagnostic targets and student changes, supports student agency, and can sometimes contain LLM inaccuracies. Nonetheless, diagnostic errors still pose risks, and users may experience staged feedback as indirect or repetitive, pointing to the need for further refinement of workflow design, error mitigation, and user experience.

title: ReHoPER: Receding-Horizon Planning for Enhanced Reasoning
summary: We propose ReHoPER, an inference-only, zero-shot method that improves large language models' reasoning by generating and answering intermediate questions along multiple paths before the final answer. It iteratively plans a horizon of candidate intermediate questions, selects one to answer, and replans from the updated history. ReHoPER is task-agnostic, using the same generic instructions across datasets and models without labeled data or task-specific prompt design. Across multiple datasets, including iLLC, a new controlled benchmark for compositional reasoning, ReHoPER outperforms strong baselines, with the largest gains in the most compositional settings. Our implementation and the iLLC generator are publicly available to support future work.

AI.tldr: ReHoPER is an inference-only, zero-shot reasoning enhancement method for large language models that plans and answers intermediate questions along multiple paths, improving compositional reasoning performance without task-specific training or prompts.
AI.motivation: Large language models often struggle with complex, compositional reasoning, especially without task-specific fine-tuning or carefully crafted prompts. There is a need for a generic, inference-only procedure that can systematically improve reasoning by structuring intermediate steps, while remaining task-agnostic and not relying on labeled data.
AI.method: ReHoPER iteratively plans a horizon of candidate intermediate questions, explores multiple reasoning paths by selecting one question at a time to answer, then replans based on the updated history. It uses the same generic instruction set for different datasets and models, operates in a zero-shot manner, and requires no labeled data or task-specific prompt engineering. The authors also introduce iLLC, a controlled benchmark designed to test compositional reasoning, and evaluate ReHoPER against strong baselines on multiple datasets.
AI.result: On several benchmarks, including the newly proposed iLLC dataset, ReHoPER consistently outperforms strong baseline methods for reasoning with large language models. The performance gains are especially pronounced on tasks with higher levels of compositionality, indicating that its multi-step intermediate-question approach is particularly effective for complex reasoning.
AI.conclusion: ReHoPER demonstrates that an inference-only, task-agnostic strategy that plans and answers intermediate questions can substantially improve the compositional reasoning abilities of large language models without additional training or task-specific prompts. The release of both the ReHoPER implementation and the iLLC benchmark aims to facilitate further research on structured reasoning in language models.

title: MemFit: Efficient Long-Term Agentic Memory
summary: Long-term memory systems for large language models (LLMs) have gained popularity for extending reasoning capabilities across applications. Current memory systems rely on LLM agents to organize and consolidate memory, resulting in costly, inefficient write operations. To address this limitation, we propose MemFit, a long-term memory system for conversational agents that reduces the cost and latency of memory operations. Unlike existing systems that rely on expensive LLM calls for memory construction or discard surface-level details through compression, MemFit stores each turn verbatim in an append-only store with near-instantaneous, LLM-free insertion, indexing turns with segment summaries rather than replacing them. Additionally, MemFit uses an LLM-free, multi-path retrieval strategy that combines lexical and semantic signals with cross-encoder reranking over caption- augmented episodes in both textual and multimodal settings. Empirical results on three widely used benchmarks, LoCoMo, MemGallery, and LongMemEval-S, show that MemFit achieves state-of-the-art performance while reducing memory construction time and cost several-fold, providing a scalable and efficient solution for persistent agentic memory.

AI.tldr: MemFit is a long-term memory system for conversational LLM agents that stores interactions verbatim and uses efficient, LLM-free multi-path retrieval to achieve state-of-the-art performance with much lower cost and latency.
AI.motivation: Existing long-term memory systems for LLMs depend on LLM agents to organize, summarize, and consolidate memory. This makes memory writes expensive and slow, and sometimes discards useful information through aggressive compression. There is a need for a scalable, low-latency, low-cost memory mechanism that still preserves important contextual details and works well across text and multimodal tasks.
AI.method: MemFit replaces LLM-based memory construction with an append-only store that records each dialogue turn verbatim, enabling near-instant insertion without LLM calls. Instead of summarizing away raw content, it indexes turns using segment-level summaries while retaining the full text. For retrieval, MemFit uses an entirely LLM-free, multi-path strategy that integrates both lexical and semantic retrieval signals, and then applies a cross-encoder reranker over caption-augmented episodes. This design works for both textual and multimodal (e.g., image-related) contexts.
AI.result: On three standard benchmarks for long-term conversational memory—LoCoMo, MemGallery, and LongMemEval-S—MemFit achieves state-of-the-art performance. At the same time, it reduces memory construction time and monetary cost by several-fold compared to prior LLM-based memory systems.
AI.conclusion: MemFit demonstrates that long-term memory for conversational agents can be both more accurate and significantly more efficient by eliminating LLM calls from the memory write and retrieval pipeline. Storing raw turns verbatim with summary-based indexing and LLM-free multi-path retrieval yields scalable, persistent agentic memory suitable for real-world applications.

title: Beyond Leaderboards: Tokenomics of Agentic Small Language Model Ensembles
comment: 8 pages, 9 figures, Presented at ACM CAIS 2026 Workshop RLEval: Methods and Reinforcement Learning Environments for Evaluating AI Agents. Resubmission of permitted appeal, Ticket #MOD-104177
summary: As large language models (LLMs) move from standalone assistants into agentic workflows, evaluation must extend beyond scalar leaderboard accuracy to account for operational reliability, cost, latency, and token efficiency. We use an agentic ensemble of small language models (SLMs) with an SLM-judge-mediated feedback loop as a case study for such beyond-leaderboard evaluation. On the 541-prompt IFEval benchmark, the best ensemble achieves 97.34% strict prompt accuracy, exceeding the strongest standalone LLM baseline, gpt-5.4, by 5.81 percentage points while operating in a lower-cost regime. We then analyze the tokenomics and operational behavior behind this gain, including cost per sample, token composition, useful-output goodput, feedback-loop recovery, latency decomposition, and performance across instruction categories and constraint counts. Our results show that agentic SLM ensembles can trade additional test-time tokens and orchestration overhead for improved instruction-following fidelity, motivating multi-dimensional evaluation protocols for future agentic AI systems.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates agentic workflows built from ensembles of small language models (SLMs), showing they can outperform a strong standalone LLM in instruction-following while being cheaper, and argues for multi-dimensional evaluation beyond simple accuracy leaderboards.
AI.motivation: Traditional LLM evaluation centers on scalar accuracy metrics on leaderboards, which ignore operational aspects like reliability, cost, latency, and token efficiency. As LLMs increasingly operate as agents and in complex workflows, these additional dimensions become crucial. The authors are motivated to understand whether ensembles of smaller models plus an automated feedback loop can improve instruction-following performance in a more cost-efficient and operationally-aware way, and how to properly evaluate such systems.
AI.method: The authors construct an agentic ensemble system composed of several small language models working together, augmented with a feedback loop mediated by a judge SLM that checks and critiques outputs and prompts revisions. They evaluate this architecture on the 541-prompt IFEval instruction-following benchmark and compare against a strong standalone LLM baseline (gpt-5.4). Beyond raw accuracy, they analyze tokenomics and operational behavior: cost per sample, token usage and composition, amount of useful output (goodput), the system's ability to recover via the feedback loop, latency breakdowns, and performance stratified by instruction categories and constraint complexity.
AI.result: On IFEval, the best SLM ensemble configuration reaches 97.34% strict prompt accuracy, outperforming the gpt-5.4 baseline by 5.81 percentage points while operating in a lower-cost regime. The analysis shows that while the ensemble spends more tokens at test time and incurs orchestration overhead, this investment yields higher instruction-following fidelity and better handling of complex, constrained prompts. The feedback loop enables recovery from initial errors, and the token and latency breakdowns quantify where the extra computation is spent and how it translates into improved performance.
AI.conclusion: Agentic ensembles of small models, coordinated via a judge-based feedback loop, can surpass a strong standalone LLM in instruction-following accuracy while remaining cost-efficient, primarily by trading extra test-time tokens and orchestration for quality gains. These findings underscore that future evaluation of agentic AI systems should move beyond single-number leaderboards to multi-dimensional protocols that jointly consider accuracy, cost, latency, token efficiency, and operational robustness.

title: ActiveSaddler: Automated Curriculum Learning for Agent Harness Optimization
comment: 37 pages, 16 figures. Project website and code: https://autosaddler-projectpage.github.io/activesaddler/
summary: Automated harness optimization can substantially improve LLM agents by iteratively updating their prompts, tool interfaces, and control logic from execution feedback. However, existing methods primarily optimize how the harness is updated while largely fixing which training scenarios generate the feedback that drives those updates. As the harness evolves, the scenarios most useful for further optimization can change, suggesting that the training curriculum itself should adapt alongside the harness. We formulate this missing dimension of harness optimization as an automated curriculum learning problem and introduce ActiveSaddler. ActiveSaddler models the evolving curriculum as a non-stationary bandit with dynamically instantiated optimization targets. It abstracts recurring failures into reusable failure-pattern arms, estimates the potential learning progress from further targeting each pattern, and adaptively balances revisiting known weaknesses with exploring unseen scenarios for new ones. Optimization outcomes continually update both the set of discovered failure patterns and their priorities, allowing the curriculum to co-evolve with the harness. Experiments on GAIA2 and Terminal-Bench 2.0 show that ActiveSaddler consistently discovers stronger harnesses, improving test Pass@1 by 4.4 and 7.5 percentage points over the same harness optimizer using a scenario order fixed before optimization, respectively. Ablations further show that these gains depend on dynamically constructing optimization targets, estimating their evolving utility, and balancing continued optimization with new failure discovery. Together, these results establish automated curriculum learning as a new crucial optimization dimension for harness optimization.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ActiveSaddler, an automated curriculum learning method that adaptively selects training scenarios to optimize LLM agent harnesses, yielding significantly better performance than using a fixed scenario order.
AI.motivation: Existing automated harness optimization methods for LLM agents focus on how to update prompts, tools, and control logic from feedback but assume a fixed set or order of training scenarios. As the harness improves, the most informative scenarios for further improvement change, so keeping the curriculum static wastes optimization potential. The authors aim to make the training curriculum co-evolve with the harness to more efficiently discover and fix failure modes.
AI.method: They cast curriculum design for harness optimization as a non-stationary bandit problem with dynamically created arms. ActiveSaddler clusters recurring failures from execution feedback into reusable failure-pattern arms, each corresponding to a type of weakness. It then estimates the expected learning progress from further training on each pattern and uses a bandit-style strategy to balance exploitation (revisiting known weaknesses) and exploration (sampling new scenarios to discover new failure patterns). As optimization proceeds, the set of failure patterns and their priorities are continuously updated, making the curriculum adaptive to the current harness state.
AI.result: On GAIA2 and Terminal-Bench 2.0 benchmarks, ActiveSaddler consistently learns stronger harnesses than a baseline that uses the same underlying harness optimizer but with a fixed scenario order. It improves Pass@1 by 4.4 and 7.5 percentage points, respectively. Ablation studies show that the performance gains rely on all three key components: dynamic construction of optimization targets (failure patterns), estimation of their evolving utility, and explicit balancing of continued optimization against exploration for new failures.
AI.conclusion: Automated curriculum learning is an important and previously underexplored dimension of harness optimization for LLM agents. By modeling curriculum design as a non-stationary bandit over failure patterns and allowing targets and priorities to evolve, ActiveSaddler delivers substantial and robust gains in harness quality. This establishes that co-evolving the training curriculum with the harness should be a standard consideration in future harness optimization systems.

title: Role-aware Heuristic Episodic Attention for Conversational LLMs
summary: Large language models often lose track of persistent instructions and relevant information as multi-turn conversations grow. We study this cumulative contextual decay through three related failure modes: attention pollution, dilution, and drift. We propose REA (Role-aware Heuristic Episodic Attention), a context-management framework that assigns different persistence and representation policies to instructions and episodic interactions. Instructional Memory retains identified global constraints in a dedicated prefix. Episodic Memory preserves user inputs and compresses model replies, while heuristic retrieval selects raw text, compressed representations, or omission for each historical turn. On Long-MT-Bench+, REA improves the judge score from 6.32 to 7.36 on a 10-point scale, a 16.5% relative gain over the Vanilla baseline, and reduces average latency by 2.91$\times$. Additional evaluations show aggregate gains on three backbones spanning 1.7B-7B parameters and on Chinese and English role-playing tasks. These results support role-aware context management as a practical approach to maintaining conversational continuity and instruction adherence.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses how large language models lose track of instructions and context in long multi-turn dialogues and proposes a role-aware context management framework (REA) that improves response quality and efficiency.
AI.motivation: In long multi-turn conversations, large language models tend to forget or misinterpret earlier instructions and important information, leading to degraded response quality. This degradation is attributed to cumulative contextual decay via attention pollution, dilution, and drift. There is a need for practical mechanisms to preserve key instructions and relevant dialogue history while controlling computational cost and latency.
AI.method: The authors introduce REA (Role-aware Heuristic Episodic Attention), a context-management framework that separates and manages different types of conversational information. It distinguishes between persistent global instructions and episodic interactions. Instructional Memory stores global constraints in a dedicated prefix that is always preserved. Episodic Memory keeps user inputs in full and compresses model replies. A heuristic retrieval strategy then decides, for each historical turn, whether to include the raw text, a compressed representation, or to omit it entirely, based on its relevance and role, thereby mitigating attention pollution, dilution, and drift.
AI.result: On Long-MT-Bench+, using REA improves the judge score from 6.32 to 7.36 out of 10, corresponding to a 16.5% relative gain over a vanilla baseline without such context management, and decreases average latency by a factor of 2.91. Additional experiments across three different backbone models ranging from 1.7B to 7B parameters, and on both Chinese and English role-playing tasks, show consistent aggregate improvements in conversational continuity and instruction adherence.
AI.conclusion: Role-aware context management, as instantiated in REA, is an effective and practical approach to reducing contextual decay in large language model conversations. By separating instructional and episodic information and using heuristic retrieval over compressed histories, REA improves both quality and efficiency of multi-turn dialogue, better maintaining conversational continuity and adherence to user instructions across different models and languages.

title: OR for AI That Does OR: Routing LLMs up the Escalator inside the OSCAR Framework
summary: Large language models can translate business descriptions into optimization models, but executable code may misrepresent constraints or objectives. A solver can then return an optimal solution to the wrong problem. Even when the solution satisfies the intended operating rules, a better plan may exist. For organizations that repeatedly use optimization modeling, an LLM-based framework should produce accurate formulations at low cost and, ideally, run locally. We study how to verify improvements and allocate attempts across LLMs that differ in price and capability. We develop OSCAR (Optimization modeling by Simulator, Coder, And Reviewer), which uses an offline Simulator certified against labeled decision examples to compare candidates and continues searching beyond feasibility. We model the search for the next certified improvement as sequential decisions under unobserved difficulty: which LLMs to call and when to stop. In a simplified known-prior setting, we give conditions under which cost-ordered escalation is optimal. For general menus, we derive a prior-free competitive guarantee. On five benchmark problems, OSCAR achieves 95% to 100% accuracy at the reported settings using two small open-weight LLMs, each deployable locally on a single GPU. Their single-attempt accuracies average 29% and 48%. In five runs per problem, Codex and Claude Code incur average token costs 3.1 and 5.8 times OSCAR's, respectively. OSCAR supports open-weight models locally or in the cloud, depending on budget and confidentiality requirements. Firms should maintain labeled decision examples of feasible and infeasible decisions to clarify plain-language operating rules. OSCAR follows these labels when an LLM's interpretation conflicts with them. As LLM capabilities and prices change, OSCAR's simple operating rules and adjustable settings help firms adapt their model choices and benefit from these advances.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces OSCAR, a framework that uses multiple LLMs plus a certified simulator to reliably generate correct optimization models from business descriptions at low cost, and analyzes how to allocate calls across LLMs with different cost/quality tradeoffs.
AI.motivation: Organizations increasingly want to use large language models to translate plain-language business rules into mathematical optimization models. However, directly using LLM-generated code is risky: constraints or objectives can be mis-specified, leading solvers to optimize the wrong problem. Moreover, achieving high accuracy often requires expensive, powerful LLMs run via external APIs, which raises cost, latency, and confidentiality concerns. There is a need for a principled, low-cost, locally deployable framework that can (i) verify whether an LLM-generated model is not just feasible but actually better than prior solutions, and (ii) decide intelligently how to use multiple LLMs with different price and capability profiles.
AI.method: The authors design OSCAR (Optimization modeling by Simulator, Coder, And Reviewer), a framework that combines: (1) an offline Simulator, pre-certified using labeled examples of feasible and infeasible decisions, to test and compare candidate optimization models; (2) one or more LLM Coders that propose new formulations; and (3) a Reviewer logic that uses simulator feedback to decide whether to accept, reject, or further refine candidates. They formalize the problem of searching for the next certified improvement as a sequential decision process under unknown problem difficulty: the system must choose which LLM to query (with known cost and accuracy profile) and when to stop searching. Under a simplified setting with known priors, they derive conditions where querying models in order of increasing cost (“cost-ordered escalation”) is optimal. For more general menus of LLMs and unknown priors, they provide a prior-free competitive performance guarantee on their search policy.
AI.result: On five benchmark optimization modeling problems, OSCAR—using only two small open-weight LLMs that can each run locally on a single GPU—achieves 95% to 100% final modeling accuracy under the reported parameter settings. By contrast, the same models have much lower single-attempt accuracy, averaging 29% and 48%. When compared to stronger proprietary code models (Codex and Claude Code) over five runs per problem, OSCAR’s average token cost is substantially lower: Codex costs about 3.1 times and Claude Code about 5.8 times as much as OSCAR to reach comparable performance. These results demonstrate that the orchestrated, simulator-guided multi-attempt strategy can both greatly improve effective accuracy and reduce cost relative to naïve single calls to powerful models.
AI.conclusion: OSCAR provides a practical and theoretically grounded approach for organizations that frequently build optimization models from natural language descriptions. By relying on a certified simulator and labeled decision examples to arbitrate between candidate formulations, OSCAR can correct or override an LLM’s misinterpretation of business rules and continue searching for improvements beyond mere feasibility. Its decision rules for when and how to escalate among LLMs allow firms to flexibly trade off cost, accuracy, and deployment constraints, and to leverage small, open-weight models locally or in the cloud without sacrificing reliability. As LLM capabilities and prices evolve, OSCAR’s simple operating policies and tunable settings enable firms to update which models they use while preserving the framework’s verification and cost-control benefits.

title: A Citation-Grounded Benchmark for Trustworthy Earnings Call Transcript Analysis with Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have been increasingly used for financial document analysis, including earnings call transcripts (ECTs). Beyond generating standalone claims, users increasingly prefer grounded analyses that pair claims with verifiable citations from source documents to enable independent validation. However, evaluating such analytical claims typically requires extensive expert annotation, which is costly and difficult to scale, and real-world financial analysis commonly involves long context-question-answer triplets, further increasing task complexity. To address these challenges and benchmark the current landscape of grounded analysis by LLMs, we propose a numeric evidence evaluation method that enables groundedness assessment without reliance on expert annotation. We also introduce an automated dataset construction pipeline and construct ECTs-100 from the top 100 constituents of the S&P 500 to support benchmark of both groundedness and correctness. In addition, we examine conscious incompetence, a practical failure mode in financial analysis in which LLMs must detect when available evidence is insufficient and refrain from producing unsupported hallucinations. Empirical results show that LLMs perform well in groundedness but face notable limitations in correctness, with informational insufficiency presenting an additional challenge.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a scalable, annotation-free way to evaluate how well LLMs ground financial analyses in numeric evidence from earnings call transcripts, builds a benchmark dataset (ECTs-100), and shows that models are reasonably grounded but often incorrect and bad at recognizing when evidence is insufficient.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used to analyze financial documents like earnings call transcripts, where users want claims that are explicitly supported by verifiable citations. Evaluating such grounded analysis normally needs expensive domain experts and long context QA setups, which do not scale. There is also a critical real-world risk: models may hallucinate confident analyses when the available evidence is incomplete. The paper aims to create scalable evaluation tools and datasets for grounded financial analysis and to study this failure mode.
AI.method: The authors design a numeric evidence evaluation method that checks whether model-generated analytical claims are properly grounded in numerical data from source documents, allowing assessment without human expert labeling. They then build an automated pipeline that uses this method to construct a benchmark dataset, ECTs-100, from earnings call transcripts of the top 100 S&P 500 companies. The benchmark evaluates both groundedness (are claims supported by cited evidence?) and correctness (are the claims factually right?). They also define and empirically study a failure mode termed conscious incompetence, where models should detect insufficient evidence and abstain rather than hallucinate.
AI.result: Using ECTs-100, experiments show that existing LLMs tend to do relatively well on groundedness—i.e., they often cite the right numeric evidence—but still exhibit notable weaknesses in overall factual correctness. Moreover, they struggle when the available information is insufficient, frequently failing to detect this and instead generating unsupported or speculative answers, which is particularly problematic in financial analysis.
AI.conclusion: Numeric evidence-based evaluation can provide scalable, expert-free assessment of groundedness in financial LLM analysis. The ECTs-100 benchmark offers a realistic testbed for long-context, evidence-grounded financial QA. Current LLMs, while reasonably good at pointing to relevant evidence, are not reliably correct and have difficulty recognizing when the evidence is inadequate, underscoring the need for methods that improve both factual accuracy and calibrated abstention in financial applications.

title: Finding the Right Fit: Model-Harness Interactions across Agent Tasks
summary: Choosing an agent system means choosing both a language model and the harness through which it acts. We ask whether a strong model, harness, or pairing stays strong when the setting changes. We evaluate 66 configurations: four configurable harnesses (OpenHands, DeepSeek Harness, PI, and openJiuwen) paired with five models on TUA-Bench, ALE-CLI, and Terminal-Bench 4, plus the native Codex-GPT and Claude Code-Claude pairings. Model rankings reverse across harnesses. On Terminal-Bench 4, Claude leads GPT by 7.94 points in OpenHands but trails it by 30.16 points in PI. For four of the five models, the best harness changes from one benchmark to another, yet some pairings hold: openJiuwen gives Kimi its highest score on all three benchmarks, by 5.61 to 11.11 points. A model's own vendor harness is not reliably its best, and higher cost does not reliably buy a higher score. On Terminal-Bench 4, GPT scores higher under PI than under DSH at less than a quarter of the cost per task. Matched trajectories suggest why fit varies. Models start almost all repairs themselves, so much depends on whether the harness hands failures back in a form the model can use. GPT does best with PI's lean scaffold, while Kimi, which often issues malformed tool calls, does best in openJiuwen. We argue that the model, the harness, and the task should be evaluated together, and we release the harness adapters, evaluation code, and all 6,204 scored trajectories at https://github.com/liyix/finding-the-right-fit and https://huggingface.co/datasets/yixuanli97/finding-the-right-fit.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how different combinations of language models and agent harnesses perform across benchmarks, showing that performance depends strongly on the specific pairing and task, not just on the model alone.
AI.motivation: Most evaluations focus on model quality alone, but in agentic settings models act through harnesses (frameworks that manage tools, retries, and feedback). It is unclear whether a strong model or harness in one setting remains strong in another, and how much of performance comes from their interaction. Practitioners need guidance on choosing not just a model but a full agent stack.
AI.method: The authors systematically evaluate 66 configurations formed by pairing four configurable agent harnesses (OpenHands, DeepSeek Harness, PI, openJiuwen) with five language models across three benchmarks (TUA-Bench, ALE-CLI, Terminal-Bench 4). They also include native vendor pairings like Codex-GPT and Claude Code-Claude. They compare scores, costs, and analyze thousands of recorded trajectories to understand how harness design (e.g., error handling, scaffolding style) interacts with specific model behaviors such as self-initiated repair and tool-call robustness.
AI.result: Model rankings vary substantially across harnesses: a model that is best under one harness can be far from best under another. For instance, on Terminal-Bench 4 Claude beats GPT by 7.94 points in OpenHands but loses by 30.16 points in PI. For four of the five models, the best harness differs across benchmarks. Some stable pairings emerge, such as openJiuwen consistently giving Kimi its top scores across all benchmarks, outperforming alternatives by 5.61–11.11 points. Vendor-native harnesses are not consistently optimal, and higher API cost does not consistently yield higher benchmark scores. GPT under PI outperforms GPT under DeepSeek Harness on Terminal-Bench 4 while costing less than a quarter per task.
AI.conclusion: Agent performance is a property of the model–harness–task triad, not of the model in isolation. The best configuration depends on how well the harness’s error handling, feedback formats, and scaffolding match the model’s interaction style and failure modes. For example, GPT benefits from PI’s minimal scaffold, while Kimi, which often produces malformed tool calls, performs better with openJiuwen’s handling. Evaluations and deployment decisions should therefore consider full agent stacks and cross-benchmark behavior. The authors support this by releasing harness adapters, code, and 6,204 scored trajectories for reproducible study.

title: The Devil Is in the Reconstruction Loss Scale: Rethinking Optimization in LLM Quantization
summary: Post-training quantization (PTQ) methods typically use sequential quantization that partitions a pre-trained LLM into a series of units (e.g., transformer blocks), with one unit quantized at each stage. State-of-the-art PTQ methods are predominantly learning-based, optimizing auxiliary quantization parameters (e.g., scaling factors, rotation matrices, clipping thresholds, and adapters) via gradient descent to minimize a reconstruction loss. A common practice is to use mean squared error (MSE) as the reconstruction loss function, yet its induced optimization behavior remains largely unexplored. In this work, we take a holistic view of sequential quantization and systematically investigate how optimization evolves from the first quantization stage to the last, aiming for a deep understanding of optimization in learning-based PTQ schemes. Through extensive empirical studies spanning representative learning-based PTQ methods, LLM families, model scales, architectures, quantization settings and various tasks, we consistently uncover Optimization Imbalance: reconstruction loss magnitudes vary dramatically across stages, accompanied by highly uneven gradient magnitudes and parameter updates under MSE. We term the cross-stage range of loss magnitudes the reconstruction loss scale, and reveal that MSE translates the unexpectedly large reconstruction loss scale into highly uneven gradient magnitudes, which in turn lead to uneven optimization strength across quantization stages. This finding suggests a general principle for improving learning-based PTQ: optimization strength across stages should be decoupled from the reconstruction loss scale. Theoretically, we show that root mean squared error (RMSE) variants defined at the sample, channel, token, and element levels naturally realize this principle through implicit gradient normalization, outperforming MSE significantly as a drop-in replacement.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how optimization behaves in learning-based post-training quantization (PTQ) for LLMs and finds that using MSE as reconstruction loss causes large imbalances in optimization strength across quantization stages, proposing RMSE-style losses to normalize gradients and improve performance.
AI.motivation: Learning-based PTQ for large language models typically quantizes models block by block and optimizes auxiliary quantization parameters with MSE reconstruction loss, but practitioners have little understanding of how this optimization behaves across different quantization stages. The authors want to understand why some stages dominate optimization, how loss magnitudes and gradients are distributed through the quantization process, and whether the standard MSE objective is fundamentally suited to this setting. They are motivated by the observation that existing methods can be unstable or suboptimal and suspect that the loss design itself, rather than architectures or optimizers, might be the core issue.
AI.method: The authors take a holistic, stage-wise view of sequential quantization in PTQ and perform extensive empirical analyses across multiple learning-based PTQ methods, LLM families, model sizes, architectures, quantization configurations, and tasks. At each quantization stage they measure reconstruction loss magnitudes, gradient norms, and parameter update sizes when using MSE loss, identifying patterns of imbalance. They formalize the notion of reconstruction loss scale—the range of loss values across stages—and link it analytically to resulting gradient magnitudes in MSE. Based on this analysis, they design and study several root mean squared error (RMSE) style reconstruction objectives defined at different granularities (sample-level, channel-level, token-level, and element-level), and show theoretically that these RMSE variants induce an implicit gradient normalization across stages. They then benchmark these RMSE losses as drop-in replacements for MSE in existing PTQ pipelines.
AI.result: Empirical studies reveal a pronounced Optimization Imbalance: in sequential quantization, later stages can have much larger reconstruction losses under MSE, which translate almost directly into larger gradient magnitudes and parameter updates. This produces strong, uneven optimization strength favoring particular stages, regardless of their true importance to downstream performance. The authors quantify this via the reconstruction loss scale and show that MSE faithfully amplifies this scale into gradient disparities. In contrast, the proposed RMSE-based losses, defined at multiple granularities, effectively normalize gradient magnitudes across stages through their functional form, leading to more balanced optimization. When plugged into diverse state-of-the-art learning-based PTQ methods without changing other components, these RMSE variants consistently outperform the original MSE-based objectives across LLM families, scales, quantization settings, and tasks.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that the commonly used MSE reconstruction loss is inherently prone to inducing large cross-stage optimization imbalances in learning-based PTQ, because it directly maps differences in reconstruction loss scale into uneven gradient strengths. A key design principle for effective PTQ is therefore to decouple optimization strength from the raw reconstruction loss scale across quantization stages. RMSE-style reconstruction losses naturally realize this via implicit gradient normalization, offering a simple, general, and effective drop-in replacement for MSE. Adopting such normalized objectives can significantly improve stability and accuracy of PTQ for LLMs across a wide range of methods and settings, without architectural modifications.

title: ABDA-NL: A Natural-Language Scenario Explorer for Argument-Based Reasoning
comment: 9 pages, 3 figures. Extended version of a demonstration abstract in the Proceedings of COMMA 2026. Code at https://github.com/idaks/ABDA-NL and live demo at https://demo.abda-nl.org
summary: ABDA-NL adds a natural-language interface to ABDA, a system for argument-based discussion using ASPIC- knowledge bases under grounded semantics. Users see which conclusions are accepted, rejected, or undecided, open an interactive rendering of the grounded discussion game to learn why, explore what-if alternatives by suspending assumptions and rules or changing preferences, ask questions that are answered from a scenario's reference documents, and author new facts, assumptions, and rules in plain English. A large language model provides the bridge between language and formalism: it answers questions from the documents and the current state of the scenario, and it translates plain-English edits into candidate formal statements. The deterministic ABDA engine remains the sole source of arguments, attacks, and acceptance labels, and every proposal of the model is validated and confirmed by the user before it takes effect.

AI.tldr: ABDA-NL is a natural-language interface for an argumentation system (ABDA) that lets users query, inspect, and edit argument-based discussions in plain English, with an LLM mapping language to formal ASPIC+ rules while the core reasoning stays deterministic and user-validated.
AI.motivation: Formal argumentation systems like ABDA are powerful for structuring debates and reasoning from complex knowledge bases, but they are difficult for non-expert users to access because they require interacting with formal representations and understanding acceptance semantics. There is a need for an interface that hides the formalism behind natural language while preserving rigorous, explainable reasoning and user control.
AI.method: The authors build ABDA-NL, a natural-language front-end to the ABDA engine (which uses ASPIC+ knowledge bases under grounded semantics). They integrate a large language model as a translator and assistant: it answers questions using scenario reference documents and the current argumentation state, and converts users’ plain-English edits into candidate formal facts, assumptions, rules, and preference changes. The system visualizes which conclusions are accepted, rejected, or undecided and provides an interactive grounded-discussion game to explain why. All LLM-generated formal statements are explicitly validated by users before being committed, and the ABDA engine alone computes arguments, attacks, and acceptance labels.
AI.result: The resulting system allows users to: (1) see and explore the status of conclusions (accepted, rejected, undecided); (2) inspect an interactive rendering of the grounded discussion game to understand the underlying argument structure; (3) perform what-if analyses by suspending rules/assumptions or changing preferences; (4) ask natural-language questions whose answers draw on both reference documents and the current scenario; and (5) author and modify the formal knowledge base in plain English, with the LLM proposing formal translations that remain under user control and are evaluated by the deterministic ABDA engine.
AI.conclusion: ABDA-NL demonstrates that a large language model can effectively serve as a natural-language bridge to a formal, deterministic argumentation system without compromising explainability or control. By keeping the LLM out of the core reasoning loop and requiring user validation of its translations, the system retains rigorous argument-based semantics while making complex argumentative reasoning, what-if exploration, and knowledge-base editing accessible in natural language.

title: Distilling Directional Verification
summary: Knowledge distillation aims to transfer the factual knowledge of large language models to smaller models for efficient deployment. Yet a teacher may recall a relation in one direction while failing to generate the answer in the reverse direction. Distillation from its generated answers can therefore propagate this directional limitation to the student. The same teacher can nevertheless recognize such an answer by scoring the relation in the direction it knows. We introduce directional label distillation, in which frozen teachers score candidate answers in that known direction and the best-scoring candidate becomes the student's training target. On facts about parents and their children, known-direction scoring yields more accurate labels than scoring the requested direction, even after tuned corrections for name priors. With prior-corrected scores, the better direction depends on the facts rather than the template, and reverses on mined facts whose notable entity is the parent rather than the child. With the evaluated children's forward facts withheld, students trained on known-direction labels improve open-ended accuracy on their trained queries by 13 to 15 points over students trained on prior-corrected reverse labels. After generated answers are matched to a fixed name list by lexical similarity, students reproduce nearly all selected labels. Their accuracy largely follows label quality. The label advantage holds on unscreened queries and when candidates are retrieved without inserting correct answers. Our findings show that directional verification mitigates the transfer of errors from teacher-generated answers to students by providing more accurate training targets. Code is available at https://github.com/js-lee-AI/directional-verification.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes directional label distillation, where a frozen LLM teacher scores candidate answers in the direction it best knows a relation, and the top-scoring candidate is used as the training label for a smaller student model, improving factual accuracy over standard distillation from generated answers.
AI.motivation: Standard knowledge distillation for LLMs typically uses the teacher’s generated answers as targets. However, for asymmetric or directional relations (e.g., parent–child), a teacher may correctly recall a fact in one direction (parent → child) but fail in the reverse (child → parent). Distilling directly from potentially wrong generated answers can propagate these directional errors to the student. The authors are motivated to find a way to exploit the teacher’s recognition ability (via scoring) in its strong direction to produce more reliable labels for the student, thereby improving factual knowledge transfer and reducing error propagation.
AI.method: They introduce directional label distillation: instead of taking the teacher’s free-form generation as ground truth, they construct a set of candidate answers and have a frozen teacher score these candidates in the direction where it is known to perform better on a relation. The highest-scoring candidate is then used as the training target for the student. The method is evaluated on factual relations about parents and children. They compare scoring in the “known” direction (e.g., parent → child) vs. the requested/reverse direction (child → parent), and correct for name priors in scoring. They withhold forward facts for held-out children when training, use lexical matching to align generated answers with a fixed name list, and analyze student performance on open-ended queries, unscreened queries, and settings where candidates are retrieved without inserting correct answers.
AI.result: Known-direction scoring produces more accurate labels than scoring in the requested (reverse) direction for parent–child facts, even after correcting for name frequency priors. When scores are prior-corrected, the optimal scoring direction depends on the specific facts rather than on the question template, and reverses when the notable entity is the parent instead of the child. Students trained on known-direction labels achieve 13–15 percentage-point higher open-ended accuracy on their trained queries compared with students trained on prior-corrected reverse-direction labels. After mapping student generations to a fixed name list, students almost perfectly reproduce the selected labels, and their accuracy largely tracks label quality. The label-quality advantage of known-direction scoring also holds on unscreened queries and when candidate answers are retrieved without inserting correct ones.
AI.conclusion: Directional verification—using a teacher to score candidate answers in the direction in which it is more reliable—provides more accurate training targets than directly distilling from its generated answers. This mitigates the transfer of teacher errors to student models for directional relations like parent–child, leading to substantial gains in factual accuracy. The approach appears robust across different query settings and retrieval setups, and suggests that leveraging directional asymmetries in a teacher’s knowledge is a promising path for safer, more faithful knowledge distillation in LLMs.

title: PG-SFT: Balancing Capability Acquisition and Retention in Offline Agent Fine-Tuning
summary: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on offline agent trajectories is the standard approach for training specialized tool-using agents, but forcing models to imitate reasoning and actions token by token may harm other capabilities (e.g., general reasoning, tool calling, code generation) of the base model. In this work, we focus on studying \emph{how to better balance the trade-off between acquiring new capabilities and preserving existing ones during agent trace SFT}. By comparing several baselines in our setup, standard SFT improves the target benchmark while lowering several non-target benchmark scores; meanwhile, simply constraining distributional drift using KL penalty or limiting the update magnitude did not avoid this regression trend. Motivated by recent token-wise adaptive learning objectives, this work proposes \textbf{Privilege-Guided SFT (PG-SFT)} to leverage turn-level information gain of agent trajectories as an indicator to adjust supervision strength. PG-SFT yields a more favorable observed trade-off on the evaluated benchmarks, substantially reducing distributional drift and broad capability degradation at the cost of slight degradation in target-task performance. Our findings suggest that balancing the acquisition--retention trade-off depends not only on whether the model is anchored to its base behavior, but also on where and how strongly supervision should depart from that behavior.}

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to fine-tune tool-using agents on trajectory data without damaging their general abilities, and proposes Privilege-Guided SFT (PG-SFT), which adaptively adjusts supervision strength to better balance new capability gains and retention of existing skills.
AI.motivation: Standard supervised fine-tuning on offline agent traces improves performance on the targeted tool-using tasks but often harms other important abilities of the base model, such as general reasoning, tool calling, and code generation. Existing attempts to constrain distributional drift (e.g., via KL penalties or small updates) do not fully prevent this capability regression. There is a need to understand and better manage the trade-off between acquiring new specialized skills and preserving broad, pre-existing capabilities during agent trace SFT.
AI.method: The authors empirically compare standard SFT and several baselines that constrain distributional drift (KL penalty, limiting update magnitude) using an agent-training setup with multiple benchmarks. They then introduce Privilege-Guided SFT (PG-SFT), which uses turn-level information gain from agent trajectories to decide how strongly to supervise each part of the trace. Supervision is adaptively scaled token-wise or turn-wise based on how informative a turn is, so the model departs more from base behavior where trajectories add the most novel signal and stays closer to base behavior elsewhere.
AI.result: In experiments, standard SFT improves performance on the primary target benchmark but causes drops on several non-target benchmarks, indicating broad capability degradation. Simple constraints on distributional drift (e.g., KL regularization, smaller updates) do not fully stop this regression. PG-SFT, by contrast, achieves a better trade-off: it substantially reduces distributional drift and mitigates degradation on broad capabilities, while only slightly reducing performance improvements on the target task compared to vanilla SFT.
AI.conclusion: The balance between acquiring new specialized capabilities and retaining general abilities during agent SFT is not governed solely by anchoring the model to its base distribution. It also critically depends on selectively adjusting where and how strongly the fine-tuning signal overrides base behavior. Privilege-Guided SFT, which leverages turn-level information gain to adapt supervision strength, offers a more favorable acquisition–retention trade-off for training tool-using agents from trajectories.

title: Scaling and Distilling Text Embeddings for Better Diffusibility
comment: 28 pages, 12 figures. Code is available at https://github.com/la0ka1/diffusing-scaled-text-embeddings
summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer a promising alternative to autoregressive (AR) language generation. Recent advances in continuous DLMs, which apply latent diffusion to continuous text embeddings, raise a practical question: which embedding makes the best latent space, i.e., the most diffusible? To answer this, we search through different embeddings and find that scaling the embedding model to stronger ones within the same family (T5 to T5Gemma-1 to T5Gemma-2) greatly improves generative performance. But the raw T5Gemma-2 embeddings are still not optimal. They are so discriminative that even the embeddings of plausible alternative words are separated, which makes the generation vulnerable to imperfect sampling. Consequently, continuous diffusion often fails to reach any of them and ends up at an invalid embedding instead. To address this, we distill T5Gemma-2 into a student encoder that learns the teacher's decoded probabilities as soft labels. Learning from such soft labels makes the student pull the alternative embeddings closer while maintaining the encoding-decoding mechanism. The distilled embeddings form a more connected and diffusible latent space, improving over the vanilla T5Gemma-2 embeddings. As a result, our medium-sized DLM achieves Gen. PPL 17.8 (against real-text PPL 15.4) at real-text entropy on OpenWebText, outperforming GPT-2-M on Gen. PPL.

AI.tldr: The paper studies which text embedding spaces work best as latent spaces for continuous diffusion language models and proposes a distilled T5Gemma-2 encoder that produces more "diffusible" embeddings, significantly improving generation quality over GPT-2-M–level baselines.
AI.motivation: Diffusion language models are a promising alternative to autoregressive models, but recent continuous DLMs that operate on text embeddings depend heavily on the underlying embedding space. Existing strong encoders like T5Gemma-2 create very discriminative, fragmented latent spaces where even semantically similar words are far apart. This makes diffusion sampling prone to landing on invalid or non-decodable embeddings, hurting generation quality. The authors want to understand which embeddings are best suited for diffusion and how to modify them to make the latent space more connected and generative without sacrificing linguistic competence.
AI.method: 1) Empirically compare multiple embedding families and scales (T5, T5Gemma-1, T5Gemma-2) as latent spaces for continuous diffusion language models, measuring generative perplexity and related metrics. 2) Diagnose the problem that high-capacity encoders yield overly separable embeddings, so plausible alternative words are encoded far apart, causing diffusion trajectories to miss valid tokens. 3) Propose a distillation scheme: train a student encoder from T5Gemma-2 where the supervision signal is the teacher’s decoded token probability distribution (soft labels), not just hard token IDs. This encourages embeddings of alternative plausible words to be closer together while still supporting standard encode–decode behavior. 4) Plug the distilled encoder into the DLM and evaluate on OpenWebText, comparing generative perplexity to baselines like GPT-2-M.
AI.result: Scaling the encoder within the T5/T5Gemma family improves DLM performance, with T5Gemma-2 giving the best raw results among undistilled models. However, raw T5Gemma-2 embeddings remain suboptimal: diffusion often produces invalid embeddings because the space is too sharp and fragmented. The proposed distillation to soft-label-based embeddings yields a latent space where alternatives are closer and more connected. With this distilled encoder, their medium-sized DLM attains generative perplexity 17.8 at real-text entropy on OpenWebText (real-text PPL 15.4), surpassing GPT-2-M in generative perplexity under comparable conditions.
AI.conclusion: The choice and structure of the embedding space are crucial for continuous diffusion language models. Simply using a stronger encoder like T5Gemma-2 helps but is not sufficient, because excessive discriminativeness makes the space poorly suited for diffusion-based sampling. Distilling the encoder with soft decoded probability targets produces a more "diffusible" latent space where plausible word alternatives are closer, improving sampling robustness and text quality. This approach enables a medium-sized DLM to outperform GPT-2-M on generative perplexity, indicating that carefully engineered latent spaces can make continuous diffusion a strong competitor to autoregressive language modeling.

title: Cybernetic and Epistemic: A Missing Vocabulary for Trustworthy Agentic Delegation
comment: Accepted at TAS 2026 (AAAI Fall Symposium Series), Nov 5-7, 2026, Arlington VA
summary: As code generation is increasingly delegated to AI systems, the bottleneck is shifting from writing code to supervising the systems that write it --- a shift CS-education researchers have begun to name. This shift exposes a vocabulary gap: the field asks for "human oversight" without a working distinction between the two things language does in a delegation channel --- coordinate action (cybernetic: words succeed when the world comes to match them) and coordinate understanding (epistemic: they succeed when they answer to the world and a hearer can check that they do). The failure this names is not cybernetic language but epistemic-form language doing cybernetic work: explanation-shaped output calibrated for approval rather than truth. Oversight that checks only whether an output was approved is satisfiable by rubber-stamping; oversight that holds an agent accountable requires the reasoning behind its work be retrievable and checkable. We present three delegation episodes --- illustrations, not controlled evidence --- in which epistemic engagement proved practicable while remaining auditable, one public record where a recommendation was withdrawn on its own stated terms, and one failure case illustrating oversight that requires no reasons for its discretionary choices. We propose a criterion for agentic-system governance, alongside existing technical trust properties: every consequential choice should carry the condition under which it would have gone otherwise, in a form a third party can test. Without such a condition, a third party cannot distinguish a decision from a rubber stamp. We give the criterion an operational form --- a two-part reconstruction test scoring a delegation record by whether a second reader can predict what the agent does under a perturbation --- and a deliberation-recording convention, ORRCF, that makes the condition a required component of every recorded choice.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that in AI code generation, the main challenge is no longer writing code but supervising AI systems, and proposes a formal, testable way to record and audit the reasons behind AI decisions so oversight is more than rubber-stamping.
AI.motivation: As AI systems increasingly write code, the limiting factor becomes how humans supervise and govern these systems, not code production itself. Existing notions of “human oversight” are too vague and conflate two distinct roles of language in delegation: (1) coordinating actions so that the world matches instructions (cybernetic) and (2) coordinating understanding so that reasons can be checked against the world (epistemic). Current AI outputs often look like explanations but are optimized for approval, not truth, which undermines meaningful accountability. There is a need for a governance criterion that makes AI decisions and their underlying conditions transparent and auditable by third parties.
AI.method: The authors analyze the conceptual gap between cybernetic and epistemic uses of language in human–AI delegation, then use three qualitative “delegation episodes” as illustrative case studies where epistemic engagement (checking reasons, not just outcomes) was feasible and auditable. They present one public case in which a recommendation was later withdrawn on the basis of its own stated terms, and a counterexample where oversight demanded no reasons for discretionary choices. Building on these, they propose a formal governance criterion and translate it into: (1) a two-part reconstruction test that evaluates if a second reader can predict an agent’s behavior under perturbations from the delegation record, and (2) a standardized deliberation-recording convention called ORRCF that embeds counterfactual conditions into every logged choice.
AI.result: The paper demonstrates, via illustrative cases rather than controlled experiments, that it is practically possible to structure interactions with AI systems so that their reasoning processes are recorded in a way that a third party can later audit. The proposed reconstruction test offers an operational way to score the transparency and auditability of a delegation record: if a second reader can successfully reconstruct how the agent would act under altered conditions, the record passes the test. The ORRCF convention supplies a concrete template for encoding, alongside each consequential decision, the specific conditions under which the decision would have been different, making the underlying choice structure explicit.
AI.conclusion: Meaningful oversight of agentic AI systems requires more than outcome approval; it requires access to reasons and counterfactual conditions behind each consequential choice. The authors argue that every such decision should be accompanied by a testable condition describing when the decision would have changed, enabling third parties to distinguish genuine deliberation from rubber-stamping. Their reconstruction test and ORRCF recording format operationalize this governance criterion, offering a pathway to more accountable, auditable AI delegation channels and a clearer distinction between cybernetic and epistemic roles of language in human–AI supervision.

title: It Takes Workflows to Evolve Better Workflows
summary: Tackling complex real-world tasks can exceed the capabilities of a single large language model (LLM), motivating the use of multi-agent workflows that coordinate specialized agents to work together on these tasks. Recent methods train LLMs to construct better workflows from execution outcomes, but they optimize only the workflow generator, while the other agents that build or execute each workflow remain fixed even though every outcome depends on all of them. However, extending training beyond the generator is challenging: the agents are coupled, and a workflow's outcome is a single sparse score that cannot tell which agent causes a failure. We propose FloWright, which leverages the workflow as a harness to optimize workflows. By introducing a hierarchical, structure-aware reward paradigm, FloWright enables one role to self-evolve and two or more roles to co-evolve, with no additional models, labels, or executions. Considering the limitation that workflows are commonly trained and evaluated on data that a single agent can already handle, we further propose DataWright, an adaptive data hardening approach that converts existing datasets into workflow-level tasks with increased difficulty. Across document, slide, chart, code, math, and finance tasks, small open models trained with FloWright achieve improved performance by up to $+7.41\%$, with co-evolving ($+5.03\%$) more roles gaining more than optimizing one of them alone ($+2.83\%$). Our project page: https://xhguo7.github.io/FloWright/.

AI.tldr: FloWright is a framework to jointly optimize multi-agent LLM workflows and their component agents using structure-aware rewards, plus DataWright, which hardens datasets into more challenging workflow-level tasks.
AI.motivation: Single LLMs often fail on complex real-world tasks, so multi-agent workflows of specialized LLMs are used. Existing methods train only the workflow generator, leaving the other agents static, even though outcomes depend on all agents. Because workflow agents are coupled and feedback is only a sparse final score, it is hard to know which agent to improve, limiting end-to-end training of multi-agent systems.
AI.method: FloWright introduces a hierarchical, structure-aware reward scheme that treats the workflow itself as a training harness. It decomposes the sparse workflow-level outcome into role-specific rewards so that individual roles or multiple roles can be updated together (self-evolution or co-evolution) without adding new models, labels, or extra executions. In parallel, DataWright transforms standard, typically easy, single-agent datasets into harder, workflow-level tasks through adaptive data hardening, ensuring training data better matches the complexity that benefits from multi-agent workflows.
AI.result: Across a wide range of domains—document, slide, chart, code, math, and finance tasks—small open-source LLMs trained within FloWright show performance gains up to +7.41%. Jointly optimizing multiple roles (co-evolution) yields larger improvements (+5.03%) than optimizing only a single role (+2.83%), demonstrating the value of coordinated learning among workflow agents.
AI.conclusion: FloWright makes it feasible to train not only the workflow generator but also the constituent agents in multi-agent LLM systems via a structure-aware reward design, enabling both self-evolution and co-evolution without extra supervision or computation. DataWright further ensures that training data is sufficiently challenging and aligned with workflow usage. Together, they significantly strengthen the effectiveness of small open models on complex, multi-step tasks, highlighting the importance of end-to-end training of multi-agent LLM workflows.

title: VeriHarness: Scaling Agentic Verification for Long-Horizon Tasks
summary: As LLM agents undertake increasingly complex, long-horizon tasks, verifying their outputs becomes increasingly challenging. We study how verification capability can be strengthened with a fixed base model, without access to reference answers or grading rubrics at test time. Repeated sampling yields multiple rollouts that can contain complementary correct claims, but we need a reliable verification mechanism to determine which claims to trust. We first find that disagreement often exposes correct alternatives, while consensus can conceal errors. These observations motivate VeriHarness, which turns the underlying LLM a generator uses into an agentic verifier by giving it a workspace, evidence tools, and reusable verification skills. A disagreement resolver checks competing claims against environmental evidence, while a consensus challenger tests shared claims and searches for omitted requirements. Their findings guide the selection and revision of the final artifact. Across five long-horizon workspace benchmarks and two frontier models, VeriHarness achieves the highest selection scores among the evaluated baselines. Evidence-backed revision further improves average performance, bringing gains over a single rollout to 6.2 points with Gemini 3.5 Flash and 6.4 points with Claude Opus 4.8. We further show that verification skills can self-improve from failure feedback, demonstrating VeriHarness as a novel and critical approach for scaling long-horizon agentic verification. We release the full pool of approximately 26,000 rollouts across all five benchmarks and both models, produced at a cost of over $100,000, to support future research on agentic verification.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces VeriHarness, a framework that turns an LLM into an agentic verifier to better check and improve long-horizon LLM agent outputs by leveraging disagreement, consensus-challenging, and environment-grounded evidence.
AI.motivation: As LLM agents tackle more complex, long-horizon tasks, it becomes difficult to verify their outputs, especially without gold answers or grading rubrics. Existing methods that rely on simple majority voting or single-pass checks are unreliable: consensus can hide shared mistakes, and disagreement can contain the correct but minority answer. There is a need for a scalable way to improve verification performance while keeping the base model fixed and operating only from the rollouts and accessible environment evidence.
AI.method: The authors propose VeriHarness, which converts the same LLM used for generation into an agentic verifier equipped with a workspace, access to evidence tools, and reusable verification skills. The system: (1) repeatedly samples multiple rollouts from the generator to obtain diverse candidate solutions; (2) detects and analyzes disagreements between rollouts, then uses a disagreement resolver that checks competing claims against environmental evidence; (3) challenges consensus claims via a consensus challenger that tests shared assumptions and searches for missing requirements; and (4) uses these verification findings to select and revise the final artifact. The verification skills can be iteratively improved via self-improvement using feedback from verification failures.
AI.result: Across five long-horizon workspace benchmarks and using two frontier LLMs (Gemini 3.5 Flash and Claude Opus 4.8), VeriHarness achieves the best selection performance compared with evaluated baselines. When incorporating evidence-backed revision, the framework improves over a single rollout by 6.2 points with Gemini 3.5 Flash and 6.4 points with Claude Opus 4.8. The authors also show that the verification skills themselves can be refined from failure feedback. Additionally, they release a large dataset of about 26,000 rollouts across all benchmarks and models, created at a cost of over $100,000.
AI.conclusion: VeriHarness demonstrates that a fixed LLM can be turned into an effective, agentic verifier for long-horizon tasks by structuring verification around disagreement resolution, consensus challenging, and environment-grounded evidence. This approach substantially improves the reliability of solution selection and enables further gains via evidence-backed revision and self-improving verification skills. The released large-scale rollout dataset provides an important resource for future work on scalable agentic verification.

title: LawCompass: Navigating from Legal QA to Multi-Agent Deep Research with Grounded Evidence
summary: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) have significantly democratized access to legal information. Nevertheless, most existing legal assistants remain confined to multi-turn conversational QA, failing to support complex legal tasks that require systematic evidence retrieval, multi-step reasoning, and report-level synthesis. In this paper, we present LawCompass, an evidence-grounded legal assistant that navigates the transition from standard Legal QA to multi-agent deep research. LawCompass provides three task-oriented functions: Legal QA, which delivers precise, evidence-backed answers to legal questions; Professional Retrieval, which enables structured exploration of statutes and judicial cases via query rewriting; and Deep Research, which employs a multi-agent workflow to decompose complex legal tasks and synthesize comprehensive research reports. Crucially, LawCompass maintains explicit citation links across all modules, empowering users to directly verify system outputs against original legal sources. Evaluation results demonstrate that LawCompass provides a practical and scalable paradigm for transforming conversational AI into trustworthy and evidence-grounded legal research assistance.

AI.tldr: LawCompass is an evidence-grounded legal assistant that goes beyond simple Q&A to support complex legal research via multi-agent workflows, structured retrieval, and report-level synthesis with explicit legal citations.
AI.motivation: Although LLMs and RAG have made legal information more accessible, current legal assistants are mostly limited to conversational Q&A and cannot adequately handle complex legal research tasks that need systematic evidence retrieval, multi-step reasoning, and comprehensive report generation. There is a need for a system that can bridge simple QA and full-fledged legal research while ensuring trustworthy, source-grounded outputs.
AI.method: The authors design LawCompass, a legal assistant with three task-oriented capabilities: (1) Legal QA that produces concise, evidence-backed answers; (2) Professional Retrieval that uses query rewriting to systematically explore statutes and case law; and (3) Deep Research that adopts a multi-agent workflow to break down complex legal tasks and synthesize extensive research reports. Across these modules, they maintain explicit citation links to original legal sources to support verification and transparency. They then evaluate LawCompass on legal tasks to assess practicality and scalability.
AI.result: LawCompass successfully supports not only precise legal Q&A but also structured retrieval of legal materials and the generation of comprehensive research reports, while preserving explicit citation trails. Empirical evaluation indicates that the system is both practical and scalable for real-world legal research assistance and improves over standard conversational legal QA baselines.
AI.conclusion: LawCompass offers a viable paradigm for moving from simple, conversational legal QA systems toward more capable, trustworthy, and evidence-grounded legal research assistants. By combining multi-agent deep research workflows with structured retrieval and persistent citation tracking, it better supports complex legal tasks and enhances the verifiability and reliability of AI-assisted legal research.

title: RISED: RubrIcs for agentic multi-environment Selection and sElf-Distillation
summary: Training a single LLM agent jointly across diverse interactive environments has attracted increasing attention as a route to generalist agents. Existing curriculum and data-selection strategies often allocate training at the environment level or prioritize local reward-based signals, without explicitly considering relationships between current rollouts across environments for prompt-group selection. Meanwhile, as environments are learned at different rates, all-failure and all-success rollout groups can coexist within a batch, leaving those data without group-relative reward signals. Both challenges highlight limitations of relying solely on scalar rewards in multi-environment RL: they provide limited information about cross-environment relationships and no within-group reward contrast when rewards are identical. This motivates richer textual feedback, such as rubrics describing rollout behaviours, to guide learning. Beyond rubrics' usage as reward, we repurpose rubrics to guide both online data selection and policy supervision. An LLM judge tags each rollout using a predefined rubric vocabulary shared across environments. The resulting profiles guide the selection of data that aligns with the overall behavioural composition of the mixed-environment batch while limiting overlap with already-selected data.
