Available positive rubrics (describing desired behaviours) provide privileged context for an on-policy self-distillation teacher, supplying additional token-level supervision, while negative rubrics (describing undesired behaviours) guide subsequent rollout generation away from recurring failure modes. Together, these components form RISED. Across model backbones, RISED achieves the highest mean pass rate across environments and ranks first or second in every individual environment. Rubric-based analysis of RISED can further characterize the behavioural changes accompanying these gains.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes RISED, a rubric-guided framework that uses an LLM judge to annotate rollouts across multiple environments, and leverages these annotations for better data selection and policy supervision, achieving higher pass rates in diverse interactive tasks.
AI.motivation: Scalar rewards in multi-environment RL are too limited: they don’t capture relationships across environments, and they fail to provide informative signals when all rollouts in a group either succeed or fail. Existing curriculum and data-selection methods operate mostly at the environment level or rely on local reward signals, ignoring the structure and behavioural patterns present across rollouts. This motivates using richer, textual feedback (rubrics) to provide more fine-grained and comparable supervision across diverse environments.
AI.method: The method, RISED, introduces rubric-based supervision into multi-environment RL with LLM agents. An LLM judge evaluates each rollout using a predefined, shared rubric vocabulary that describes desired and undesired behaviours across environments. These rubric tags create behaviour “profiles” that (1) guide online data selection by choosing rollouts whose rubric profiles maintain the desired behavioural composition of a mixed-environment batch while reducing redundancy, and (2) provide additional policy supervision: positive rubrics are used as privileged context for an on-policy self-distillation teacher, giving token-level guidance, while negative rubrics steer future rollout generation away from common failure modes.
AI.result: Across different model backbones and interactive environments, RISED obtains the highest average pass rate and is in the top one or two methods on every individual environment benchmark. The rubric-based evaluation framework also allows the authors to analyze how specific behavioural traits change as performance improves under RISED.
AI.conclusion: Rubric-based signals from an LLM judge can complement or partially replace scalar rewards in multi-environment RL for LLM agents. By using rubrics jointly for data selection and policy supervision—via positive and negative behaviour tags—RISED produces more effective, generalist agents across diverse environments and offers interpretable analyses of behavioural improvements.

title: Sentence Specificity Scores for Collaborative Technical Documentation: A Domain-Transfer Study
comment: 17 pages, 2 figures. Accepted for publication in the 2026 IEEE 12th International Conference on Collaboration and Internet Computing (CIC)
summary: Collaboration depends on shared context, and technical documentation is one way that context persists across people and AI teammates. Specificity, the amount and exactness of detail expressed in language, shapes what information documentation captures and how precisely that information is communicated. This work audits sentence-specificity scoring artifacts on technical documentation and tests whether scores applied only after generation help choose among fixed LLM-generated revisions. Across Wikipedia and three technical-documentation corpora, the fixed general-domain predictor SpeciTeller and the pinned post-publication author-repository implementation of Ko et al.'s target-adapted predictor produce different corpus orders and same-sentence rank agreement from -0.066 to 0.510. Strict filtering and token-length adjustment change these patterns without reconciling them. In the Gemma set, SpeciTeller ranking raises direction-valid selection from 71.7% to 83.3% (+11.7 points; 95% source-case bootstrap interval +1.7 to +21.7); in the GPT-OSS-120B set, SpeciTeller ranking raises direction-valid selection from 51.7% to 56.7% (+5.0 points; 95% source-case bootstrap interval -6.7 to +16.7), and every primary single-score GPT-OSS-120B interval includes zero. These findings tie score interpretation and decision value to the predictor and candidate set.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how different automatic sentence-specificity scorers behave on technical documentation and whether using these scores after generation helps select better LLM-written revisions.
AI.motivation: Effective collaboration with humans and AI requires technical documentation that conveys the right level of detail. Automatic sentence-specificity predictors are used to quantify this detail, but it is unclear how consistent different predictors are on technical documentation and whether their scores are practically useful for choosing between alternative LLM-generated text revisions.
AI.method: The authors audit two sentence-specificity scoring systems—SpeciTeller (a general-domain predictor) and a target-adapted predictor from Ko et al.—on Wikipedia and three technical documentation corpora. They compare corpus-level rankings and same-sentence rank agreements, including robustness checks like strict filtering and token-length adjustments. They then test decision-making value by applying specificity scores only after generation to rank and select among fixed LLM-generated candidate revisions in two settings (a Gemma-based set and a GPT-OSS-120B-based set), measuring how often the score-based choice aligns with a directionally correct or “direction-valid” selection and estimating uncertainty with bootstrap confidence intervals.
AI.result: The two specificity predictors produce notably different orderings of corpora and only modest to low agreement on sentence-level rankings (correlations from slightly negative to moderately positive). Preprocessing adjustments like stricter filtering and length normalization change, but do not reconcile, these discrepancies. When used to select among LLM-generated revisions, SpeciTeller improves the rate of direction-valid choices from 71.7% to 83.3% in the Gemma set with a clearly positive bootstrap interval, but only from 51.7% to 56.7% in the GPT-OSS-120B set, where all primary single-score intervals include zero, indicating statistically uncertain gains.
AI.conclusion: Automatic specificity scores are not interchangeable: different predictors can yield substantially different interpretations of how specific a corpus or sentence is. Their usefulness for guiding decisions—such as selecting between LLM-generated documentation revisions—depends strongly on both the predictor and the candidate set. Practitioners should therefore validate specificity models in their actual decision context rather than assuming that any specificity score will reliably capture and optimize the desired notion of detailed technical documentation.

title: Evaluating LLM-Generated Preference Distributions
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as probabilistic generators for simulation, synthetic data generation, and decision support in settings where real-world data are unavailable. Yet, the structure and reliability of the distributions they produce remain understudied. Here, we systematically analyze LLM-generated distributions of preferences for air travel, restaurants, and consumer products. Encouragingly, all models considered in our analysis exhibit self-coherence, with the most probable outcomes stabilizing rapidly under repeated sampling. At the same time, we observe substantial discordance across both model families and scales, with little consensus even among their most probable outcomes. These patterns hold across nine open-weight models, three choice domains, and show robustness under temperature changes, greedy decoding, and perturbations of prompt and ordering. Our findings indicate that outcomes are influenced more by the choice of model than by the wording of the prompt, challenging the common assumption that sufficiently capable LLMs produce similar preference distributions when used as stand-ins for survey respondents.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how consistent and reliable large language models are when used to generate probabilistic preference distributions, finding that they are internally stable but disagree significantly with each other.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used as substitutes for real-world data in simulations, synthetic surveys, and decision-making tasks that require distributions over human preferences. However, it is unclear whether the probability distributions LLMs implicitly define over such preferences are stable, well-structured, and comparable across models. This lack of understanding poses risks for researchers and practitioners who treat LLM-generated choices as if they came from a coherent and shared underlying process.
AI.method: The authors systematically probe multiple LLMs across nine open-weight model families by asking them to generate preference choices in several domains: air travel, restaurants, and consumer products. They repeatedly sample from each model to estimate the induced distribution over preferences, assess convergence and stability of the most probable outcomes, and compare distributions across models and scales. They test robustness to changes in temperature, greedy decoding, prompt wording, and ordering to separate prompt effects from model-internal effects.
AI.result: All examined models show strong self-coherence: repeated sampling quickly leads to stable estimates of which outcomes are most probable under each model. However, the preference distributions differ markedly across model families and sizes. Even the top-ranked options according to one model often do not match those of others. These discrepancies persist across domains, decoding strategies, temperatures, and various prompt and ordering perturbations.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can produce internally consistent probabilistic preference distributions, but these distributions are highly model-dependent and not interchangeable. The choice of which model to use has a larger impact on the generated preferences than the specific phrasing of prompts. Therefore, treating LLMs as generic stand-ins for human survey respondents or assuming that more capable models will naturally converge to similar preference distributions is unwarranted and potentially misleading.

title: Capturing In-Context Learning Dynamics with Task Operators
summary: In-context learning (ICL) enables language models to perform new tasks from demonstrations without weight updates. However, every ICL inference requires processing the full set of examples, resulting in inefficient deployments, and how ICL works mechanistically is not fully understood. Prior work compresses ICL into fixed activation vectors extracted from specific layers or positions, but these input-independent interventions fail on complex tasks where the output depends on fine-grained interactions with the input. By analyzing the ICL forward pass, we show that each attention head's output is an affine transformation of its context-masked counterpart, and that the parameters of this transformation are empirically stable across samples for a given task. Building on this, we introduce Task Operator (TO), which replays this transformation as an analytically derived update to the attention output projection. Across lexical, algorithmic, and reasoning tasks, TO achieves the best overall performance among prior methods and substantially narrows the gap between zero-shot inference and ICL. We further show that the extracted knowledge concentrates in a task-specific sparse circuit across layers and positions, and that averaging operators from disjoint demonstration batches enables effective many-shot scaling without expanding the context window. Our code is available at https://github.com/gzxiong/task_operator.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Task Operator (TO), a method that turns the effect of in-context learning into an explicit parameter update to attention outputs, making ICL more efficient while preserving strong performance.
AI.motivation: In-context learning lets language models learn from demonstrations without updating weights, but it is computationally inefficient because each new input requires reprocessing the entire prompt, and its internal mechanisms are poorly understood. Existing attempts to compress ICL into fixed activations break down on complex tasks where behavior depends heavily on the specific input tokens. The authors want a mechanistically grounded, efficient, and input-sensitive way to capture what ICL is doing.
AI.method: The authors analyze the forward pass of ICL and show that for each attention head, the output with demonstrations can be written as an affine transformation of a version that is masked from the demonstration context. They empirically find that the parameters of this affine transform are stable across examples within a task. They then define a Task Operator (TO) that replays this affine transformation as an analytically derived update to the attention output projection matrix. TO is extracted from ICL runs and then applied directly, without needing to re-run ICL, effectively converting ICL behavior into a reusable operator. They further study where this operator’s effect concentrates, revealing a sparse task-specific circuit across layers and positions and explore combining operators from different demonstration batches by averaging them for many-shot scaling.
AI.result: Across a variety of lexical, algorithmic, and reasoning benchmarks, TO reaches the highest overall performance compared to prior ICL-compression approaches and substantially closes the performance gap between standard zero-shot inference and full ICL. They also find that the learned operators are sparse and localized to particular layers/positions and that averaging operators from disjoint sets of demonstrations successfully scales to many-shot performance without needing longer context windows.
AI.conclusion: In-context learning can be approximated as a stable affine transformation at the attention-head level, which can be captured as a Task Operator and applied as a direct update to attention projections. This yields an efficient, mechanistically interpretable way to reuse ICL-acquired task knowledge across inputs, significantly improving zero-shot performance and permitting many-shot scaling without increasing context length.

title: Calibration-risk routing for controlled world-model adaptation
summary: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) can exploit simulated experience, but a simulator-to-target shift creates a model-selection problem: correcting the simulator and fitting the target directly can each fail under limited target data. We introduce the Model-Corrected World Model (MC-WM), which separates initial target data into disjoint fit, selection, and calibration partitions and deploys the family with lower standardized calibration risk. A learned confidence signal and deterministic validity predicates weight one-step imagined policy updates without rewriting physical rewards. We evaluate 540 unique reported run cells across three controlled Multi-Joint dynamics with Contact (MuJoCo) shifts; one exact-routing cell was repeated after a pre-deployment artifact gate, giving 541 completed executions.

AI.tldr: Proposes MC-WM, a model-based RL framework that handles simulator-to-target shift via data partitioning and calibration-based model selection.
AI.motivation: In MBRL, using simulators enables efficient learning, but mismatch between simulator and real target environment (sim-to-real or domain shift) causes poor performance. Directly correcting the simulator or learning a new model from limited real data can both fail, creating a model-selection and data-efficiency challenge.
AI.method: Introduce Model-Corrected World Model (MC-WM) that (1) splits limited target data into three disjoint sets: fit, selection, and calibration; (2) trains candidate models/families using different strategies (e.g., simulator-corrected vs target-fitted) on the fit set; (3) selects between families based on standardized calibration risk computed on the selection/calibration partitions; and (4) uses a learned confidence signal and deterministic validity predicates to weight one-step imagined policy updates without altering the true reward function. The approach is evaluated on MuJoCo environments under controlled simulator-to-target shifts.
AI.result: Across 540 distinct experimental configurations (run cells) on three MuJoCo tasks with controlled dynamics shifts—plus one repeated cell after an artifact gate—MC-WM demonstrates robust performance in the presence of simulator-to-target mismatch, showing that calibration-risk–based family selection and confidence-weighted model usage can effectively leverage both simulators and limited target data.
AI.conclusion: MC-WM provides a principled, data-partitioned, calibration-based approach to selecting and using world models in MBRL under simulator-to-target shift, improving robustness and reliability of policy learning when both imperfect simulators and scarce real data are available.

title: JoinGR: Learning to Traverse Join Graphs for Table Retrieval
summary: Retrieving the right tables is a prerequisite for Text-to-SQL over realistic databases. Dense table retrievers rank schema elements independently, but this ignores a key source of evidence: some required tables are not mentioned in the question and become identifiable only through their join relationships to already relevant tables. We introduce JOINGR, a join-aware table retrieval method that treats the database join graph as the retrieval space. Columns are represented as graph nodes, while intra-table and foreign-key relationships are represented as typed edges. Given a question, JOINGR selects semantically similar anchor tables, traverses join edges with a query-conditioned scorer, and aggregates the resulting edge deposits into table scores. The scorer is a lightweight MLP on top of frozen query, node, and edge embeddings, trained with a pairwise margin loss over gold tables. On BIRD and Spider datasets, JOINGR is competitive with the strongest retrieval baselines. On BEAVER, a challenging enterprise benchmark with multi-hop table requirements, JOINGR substantially improves recall over dense retrieval and re-ranking baselines. Cross-domain experiments show that the learned scorer transfers across benchmarks, indicating that the method captures reusable joingraph traversal behavior.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes JOINGR, a join-aware table retrieval method that uses the database join graph to improve table selection for Text-to-SQL tasks, especially when required tables are not explicitly mentioned in the question.
AI.motivation: Existing dense table retrievers treat schema elements independently and mainly rely on surface semantic similarity between the question and tables/columns. This overlooks cases where important tables are not directly mentioned in the question and can only be discovered via their join relationships with already relevant tables. There is a need for a retrieval method that can exploit the relational structure of the database (join graph) to recover such multi-hop, implicitly referenced tables, which is crucial for realistic, complex Text-to-SQL scenarios.
AI.method: The paper introduces JOINGR, a join-aware retrieval framework that models the database schema as a join graph where columns are nodes and edges represent intra-table and foreign-key relationships, with types. Given a natural language question, JOINGR first identifies semantically similar anchor tables using standard similarity search. It then performs graph traversal over join edges using a query-conditioned scoring function that estimates the relevance of traversing each edge. This scorer is a small MLP applied on frozen embeddings of the query, nodes, and edges. Traversal accumulates "deposits" on traversed edges or nodes, which are then aggregated into table-level scores. The MLP is trained with a pairwise margin loss to rank gold (ground-truth) tables above non-gold ones. The approach is evaluated against dense retrieval and re-ranking baselines on multiple Text-to-SQL benchmarks.
AI.result: On standard Text-to-SQL benchmarks BIRD and Spider, JOINGR achieves performance competitive with the strongest existing table retrieval methods. On BEAVER, a more demanding enterprise benchmark characterized by multi-hop table requirements, JOINGR significantly increases recall compared to dense retrieval and re-ranking baselines, demonstrating its advantage in scenarios where important tables are not explicitly mentioned in the query. Cross-domain experiments indicate that the learned graph traversal scorer transfers well between datasets, suggesting that the method learns generalizable join-graph navigation patterns rather than overfitting to a single schema or domain.
AI.conclusion: JOINGR effectively leverages the database join graph to improve table retrieval for Text-to-SQL, especially in complex, multi-hop settings where key tables are only identifiable via join relationships. By modelling retrieval as query-conditioned traversal over a column-level join graph and using a lightweight learned scorer on frozen embeddings, the method attains strong performance and generalizes across domains. This demonstrates that incorporating structured relational information into table retrieval is a powerful complement to standard dense semantic matching and can substantially enhance Text-to-SQL systems in realistic databases.

title: What Can Analogy Tell Us About Artificial Consciousness?
summary: Who or what is conscious? Because subjective experience is directly accessible only in the first person, judgments about consciousness in other entities depend partly on analogy. Historically, such inferences have focused on nonhuman animals, but advances in artificial intelligence have raised the possibility of conscious AI. Here we develop a causal framework for evaluating such evidential analogies. The key distinction is between similarities in factors plausibly involved in generating consciousness and similarities in downstream behavioural or cognitive effects. Our framework weights source-target similarity by causal relevance while allowing for unknown causes, disabling differences and alternative routes to consciousness. Applied to biological systems, it explains why analogical support generally weakens with increasing causal distance from humans. Applied to contemporary AI, it suggests that behavioural similarity provides only limited evidence for consciousness because relevant causal correspondences remain poorly established. The framework also clarifies what evidence would strengthen claims of artificial consciousness.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a causal, analogy-based framework for judging consciousness in nonhumans and AI, emphasizing causal similarities over mere behavioral resemblance.
AI.motivation: To address how we can rationally assess which entities (animals, AI systems) are conscious when direct access to subjective experience is impossible and traditional analogies are philosophically and scientifically fragile.
AI.method: The authors construct a formal causal-analogical framework that distinguishes between (a) likeness in underlying factors that plausibly generate consciousness and (b) likeness in downstream behavioral/cognitive outputs, and they specify how to weight these similarities by their causal relevance while accommodating unknown causes, disanalogies, and multiple potential routes to consciousness.
AI.result: Using this framework, they explain patterns in our current judgments: analogical support for consciousness decreases with increasing biological and functional distance from humans, and for present-day AI systems, behavioral similarity yields only weak evidence of consciousness due to the lack of demonstrated causal alignment in mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: Consciousness attributions should not rest mainly on surface behavior but on causally relevant similarities in the mechanisms that generate experience; for AI, stronger evidence of consciousness would require better-established mechanistic correspondences rather than more human-like behavior alone.

title: Probe with Participation Trophies: Random-Reward RL as a Probe of LLM Capability
summary: We connect the spurious-reward paradox to a model's reachability and propose random-reward reinforcement learning (RL) as a useful tool for the probing enterprise, addressing a decade-long debate over what probing performance actually reveals about a model. There are two prevailing explanations for the surprising finding that even random rewards can improve the performance of large language models (LLMs): one attributes the gains to particular mechanisms within RL training; the other to data contamination. Our results motivate a different view: spurious-reward RL can probe a model's reachability, or what further training can attain from its current state under specified constraints, beyond what is reflected in its current performance. Two OLMo checkpoints with the same accuracy on synthetic arithmetic (3.5%), for example, reach 8.5% and 55% in their best runs under the same correctness-rewarded RL. Examining OLMo checkpoints across pre-training and mid-training reveals three distinct regimes of training response: early on, RL produces little improvement even when correct answers are rewarded; later in pre-training, rewarding correct answers becomes effective while random rewards remain weak; and, upon entering mid-training, even random rewards can produce large gains. A similar ordering appears in a number-masked supervised fine-tuning (SFT) analysis of these checkpoints, suggesting that the pattern is not specific to a particular RL mechanism. Moreover, RL with random rewards offers a distinctive perspective on what training can make an LLM do, since its reward signal supplies no information about which answers are correct. By asking what training can attain without correctness feedback, it addresses the label-leakage side of a central problem in decodability-based probing: whether a successful probe reveals the model's capabilities or learns the task itself.

AI.tldr: The paper studies why random-reward RL sometimes improves LLM performance and argues that such training reveals a model’s “reachability” (what further training can achieve) rather than contamination or specific RL tricks.
AI.motivation: There has been a long-standing debate about what probing methods (like RL or linear probes) actually tell us about a model’s internal capabilities, and why even random rewards can improve LLM performance. Existing explanations focus on specific RL mechanisms or data contamination, leaving unclear what probe success truly reflects. The authors want a principled account of what spurious-reward RL is measuring.
AI.method: They analyze the ‘spurious-reward paradox’ through the lens of reachability: the set of behaviors a model can reach via constrained further training from its current state. Using random-reward and correctness-reward RL on OLMo checkpoints at different training stages, they compare baseline task accuracy with best performance reachable under RL. They also conduct a complementary number-masked supervised fine-tuning (SFT) experiment to test whether the observed patterns are specific to RL or reflect broader trainability properties.
AI.result: They find that models with similar initial accuracy can have very different reachable performance under the same RL setup (e.g., two 3.5%-accurate OLMo checkpoints can be pushed to 8.5% vs. 55%). Across OLMo’s training trajectory they identify three regimes: (1) early training: RL barely helps even with correct rewards; (2) later pre-training: correctness-based RL becomes effective but random-reward RL remains weak; (3) mid-training: even random-reward RL can produce substantial gains. A parallel pattern appears under number-masked SFT, indicating the phenomenon is not tied to a specific RL algorithm.
AI.conclusion: Random-reward RL should be interpreted as probing a model’s reachability—what further training can elicit without correctness feedback—rather than as evidence of data contamination or peculiar RL mechanics. This reframes the spurious-reward paradox and clarifies a central issue in decodability-based probing: whether improvements reflect latent model capabilities or learning the task. Spurious-reward RL illuminates what behavior is accessible purely by optimization dynamics, absent informative labels.

title: Beyond Answer Confidence: A Controlled Audit of Self-Knowledge in a Black-Box Decision Model
summary: Decision models return probabilities intended for routing, abstention and automated action. Calibration makes those probabilities useful on average, but does not establish whether low confidence reflects chance or missing knowledge, nor whether confidence falls when a model moves beyond what it knows. We audit this distinction in Jev, a decision model, with over 15 public datasets and 6 generated task families, with paired interventions that vary the information supplied for a fixed item. Jev's confidence is calibrated on familiar closed-choice tasks but fails as an indicator of missing knowledge: with no answer-relevant information it assigns up to 0.80 to a salient option, and on news beyond an observed knowledge boundary it exceeds accuracy by 0.21--0.33, a gap that recalibration on earlier months does not close. Targeted yes/no questions give sharper readouts of the case: whether an outcome is settled (AUROC 1.00) and whether the evidence suffices (0.95, against 0.85 for confidence on the same items). Asking whether Jev knows the answer appears to flag fabricated entities and post-boundary news (0.91), but with realistic names or with dates removed it shows no advantage over answer uncertainty. Black-box knowledge audits therefore need explicit controls for surface cues. Code: https://github.com/Syntheme/beyond-answer-confidence.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how well a decision model’s confidence scores indicate not just accuracy but true knowledge vs ignorance, and finds that standard calibration is insufficient: the model can be confidently wrong when it lacks relevant information or faces unseen knowledge, and explicit meta-questions about knowledge and evidence work better than raw answer confidence.
AI.motivation: In decision-making systems, probabilistic outputs are used for routing, abstention, and automation. While calibration ensures that probabilities match accuracy on average, it does not tell us if low confidence means true ignorance, or if confidence reliably drops when the model goes beyond its knowledge. The authors want to distinguish answer confidence from knowledge-awareness and to test whether current models’ probabilities meaningfully signal missing knowledge, especially under distributional and knowledge shifts.
AI.method: The authors audit Jev, a decision model, across more than 15 public datasets and 6 synthetic task families. They design paired interventions where the underlying item is fixed but the information provided to the model is systematically varied, including cases with no answer-relevant information and cases that cross a temporal knowledge boundary (e.g., news after a cutoff date). They compare standard probability calibration on closed-choice tasks with performance on these knowledge-aware audits. Additionally, they introduce targeted yes/no meta-questions about whether the outcome is settled and whether the available evidence suffices, and they compare these meta-predictions (using AUROC) to the model’s raw answer confidence on the same items. They also manipulate surface cues—such as using realistic vs fabricated names or removing dates—to study how such cues affect knowledge-uncertainty readouts.
AI.result: Jev’s confidence scores are well-calibrated on familiar, closed-choice benchmarks, but fail to indicate missing knowledge. When given no answer-relevant information, the model can still assign high probability (up to 0.80) to salient options. On news items beyond a known temporal knowledge boundary, Jev’s confidence exceeds its true accuracy by 0.21–0.33, and recalibrating on earlier-month data does not close this gap. In contrast, targeted yes/no meta-questions perform very well: the model nearly perfectly detects whether an outcome is already settled (AUROC 1.00) and strongly predicts whether evidence is sufficient (AUROC 0.95 vs 0.85 when using answer confidence alone). Asking directly whether the model knows the answer helps detect fabricated entities and post-boundary news (AUROC 0.91), but this advantage disappears when names are realistic or temporal cues (like dates) are removed. These findings show that surface cues can strongly influence apparent knowledge-awareness.
AI.conclusion: Standard probability calibration and raw answer confidence are not reliable indicators of a model’s knowledge or ignorance, particularly under information deprivation or temporal knowledge shifts. Even when a model is well-calibrated on typical tasks, it can still be confidently wrong when it lacks relevant information or encounters unseen data. Explicit meta-questions about whether outcomes are settled or evidence is sufficient provide sharper and more reliable signals of knowledge state, but they are vulnerable to being driven by superficial cues such as names and dates. Therefore, black-box knowledge audits must incorporate explicit controls for such surface cues and cannot rely solely on answer probabilities; careful meta-evaluation and task design are needed to measure and improve a model’s awareness of its own knowledge limits.

title: Precision over Scale: A Polish-Silesian Benchmark and a Translation System Outperforming Open-Source and Commercial Models
summary: Dialectal machine translation remains challenging due to limited data and strong linguistic variation not captured by standard benchmarks, which often assume standardized and well-edited text. We study Polish-Silesian MT using neural and rule-based systems, evaluating on SiLTT - a new Pol-Szl testset, alongside established BOUQuET and FLORES benchmarks. Results show our rule-based system is consistently strongest on SiLTT and BOUQuET datasets and that TranslateGemma fine-tuned on a curated dataset improves over strong neural baselines but does not surpass the rule-based system in dialectal settings. We release SiLTT and our best neural model to support further research.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates Polish-Silesian dialectal machine translation, finding a rule-based system outperforms neural models on new and existing benchmarks, while a fine-tuned TranslateGemma improves but still lags behind rule-based MT in dialectal settings.
AI.motivation: Dialectal MT is difficult because available data is scarce and typical MT benchmarks focus on standardized, well-edited language, failing to reflect strong dialectal variation. Polish-Silesian, in particular, lacks robust benchmarks and systematic evaluation, so there is a need to better understand which MT approaches work best and to provide resources for this dialect pair.
AI.method: The authors build and compare neural and rule-based MT systems for Polish↔Silesian. They introduce a new Polish-Silesian test set (SiLTT) and also evaluate on existing BOUQuET and FLORES benchmarks. They fine-tune TranslateGemma on a curated Polish-Silesian dataset and systematically compare its performance with other neural baselines and a handcrafted rule-based system across these benchmarks.
AI.result: Across the SiLTT and BOUQuET datasets, the rule-based MT system consistently achieves the best performance. The fine-tuned TranslateGemma model improves over strong neural baselines, demonstrating the benefit of targeted fine-tuning, but it still does not surpass the rule-based system on dialectal data. Performance on FLORES is also considered but appears less reflective of dialectal difficulty than the dialect-focused sets.
AI.conclusion: Rule-based MT remains highly competitive, and in this setting superior, for dialectal translation like Polish-Silesian, especially when data is limited and variation is high. While fine-tuned large neural models can close part of the gap, they do not yet outperform carefully designed rule-based systems on dialectal benchmarks. The release of the SiLTT test set and the best-performing neural model is intended to facilitate future research and benchmarking on Polish-Silesian and similar dialectal MT tasks.

title: From Discovery to Decision: Finite-Budget Recoverability in LLM Voting
summary: Voting over multiple LLM responses is a common primitive in test-time scaling and ensemble inference. Collecting more responses can expand the candidate pool and increase the chance that a correct answer is discovered. Under a fixed call budget, a discovered answer still needs to accumulate enough support within the remaining calls to become the final plurality winner, creating a discovery-to-decision gap. In this work, we characterize this gap through the realized vote state and remaining call budget. We derive a sharp recoverability threshold and show that, as sampling proceeds, the observed candidate set can only expand while the set of reachable endpoint winners can only contract, inducing a candidate-level conversion window. Under a specified iid response law, the same state yields exact finite-horizon endpoint probabilities. We further show that merging wrong-answer identities preserves single-call correctness and cannot improve plurality accuracy, and that the effect of redistributing wrong-answer probability depends on the realized vote state. Singleton reachability yields a gold-free exact locking certificate. For a known answer universe, its first trigger is the earliest prefix at which all admissible continuations yield the same fixed-budget output. Empirically, most discovered-but-unselected correct answers lose reachability only after discovery. In a controlled Word16 study, input permutation improves raw-plurality accuracy by 21.1 points with essentially unchanged single-call correctness. Exact locking saves 28-30% of calls at a 16-call budget while preserving every fixed-budget output.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how voting over multiple LLM responses works under a fixed query budget and identifies when a correct answer, once discovered, can or cannot still become the final plurality winner.
AI.motivation: In test-time scaling and ensemble inference with LLMs, practitioners often sample multiple responses and use voting to choose an answer. However, even if a correct answer is discovered early, it may not receive enough subsequent votes to win under a fixed call budget. This discovery-to-decision gap is not well understood theoretically, limiting our ability to design efficient sampling and stopping rules.
AI.method: The authors formalize the voting process as sampling from an i.i.d. response law under a fixed call budget and analyze the evolution of the vote state (current vote counts for each candidate) as more samples are drawn. They derive a sharp recoverability threshold that characterizes when a candidate can still become the final plurality winner, define a candidate-level conversion window, and compute exact finite-horizon endpoint probabilities for each candidate given the current state. They also study the effect of merging identities of wrong answers and redistributing their probability mass, and introduce the notion of singleton reachability to provide an exact certificate (locking) that the final outcome is already determined. Experiments on a controlled Word16 task study the empirical behavior of these phenomena and test practical procedures like input permutation and exact locking.
AI.result: The analysis shows that as sampling proceeds, the set of distinct answers seen can only grow, while the set of potential final winners can only shrink, giving rise to a conversion window for each candidate. The authors prove a sharp recoverability threshold: for any realized vote state and remaining calls, one can exactly determine which candidates are still reachable as final plurality winners and compute their exact endpoint probabilities under the assumed response law. They show that merging wrong-answer identities does not improve and can only preserve plurality accuracy, even though it preserves single-call correctness, and that how wrong-answer probability is redistributed can change the outcome depending on the current vote state. They further demonstrate that singleton reachability can serve as an exact, gold-free locking certificate indicating that all future continuations within the budget yield the same final output.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that the discovery-to-decision gap is a central constraint in multi-sample LLM voting under a fixed budget and can be precisely characterized via recoverability thresholds and endpoint probabilities. Many correct answers are discovered but later become unreachable as final winners. Structural properties of the vote dynamics imply that naive manipulations such as merging wrong answers cannot improve plurality accuracy. Practically, the proposed exact locking criterion allows early stopping without changing any fixed-budget decisions, reducing the number of LLM calls by around 28–30% at a 16-call budget, while input permutation can substantially boost raw-plurality accuracy without affecting single-call correctness.

title: AgSpec: Pushing the Limits of Retrieval-Based Speculative Decoding in Coding Agent Pipelines
summary: Retrieval-based speculative decoding (SD) drafts tokens by copying continuations from existing text, which suits coding agents that repeatedly reproduce code, logs, and earlier attempts. Yet existing methods fall short in agent pipelines: much of the reusable text is missing from their corpora or stored in a form that differs from what the agent emits, and their draft lengths ignore that accept length varies across agents and drifts over turns. We present AgSpec, a framework that supplies the corpus and draft-length policies that existing retrieval engines lack in coding-agent pipelines. AgSpec retrieves from session, workspace, and global corpora, retaining the ongoing session trajectory and indexing opened files in the agent's emission format. It bounds each agent's draft length with an offline-profiled cap and adapts the length online from verification feedback. On two repository-level multi-agent coding benchmarks, AgSpec outperforms five retrieval-based drafters and EAGLE-3 in most evaluated settings, raising generation throughput over autoregressive decoding up to 4.37$\times$ at batch size 1 and 4.76$\times$ at batch size 16. AgSpec also remains effective on benchmarks without a repository or a multi-agent pipeline, showing that its gains generalize to coding agents broadly.

AI.tldr: AgSpec is a retrieval-based speculative decoding framework tailored for coding agents, which reuses text from multiple corpora and dynamically adapts draft lengths to speed up code generation.
AI.motivation: Existing retrieval-based speculative decoding methods underperform in coding-agent pipelines because the reusable text is often absent from their corpora or stored in formats that differ from agent outputs, and because they use fixed or naive draft-length policies that ignore agent-specific and turn-specific accept lengths. There is a need for a framework that better matches the data and behavior of coding agents so speculative decoding can provide significant speedups in realistic multi-agent and repository-level coding scenarios.
AI.method: AgSpec augments existing retrieval engines with (1) richer, agent-aligned corpora and (2) adaptive draft-length policies. It retrieves reusable continuations from three corpora: the live session history, the agent’s workspace (including opened files), and a global corpus, all stored/indexed in the agent’s emission format. For speculative decoding, AgSpec caps each agent’s draft length with an offline-profiled maximum and further adapts the draft length online using feedback from verification (i.e., which drafted tokens the main model accepts). This combination allows it to propose longer drafts when they are likely to be accepted and shorten them when verification shows low accept rates.
AI.result: On two repository-level multi-agent coding benchmarks, AgSpec outperforms five other retrieval-based drafting methods and EAGLE-3 in most settings. It increases generation throughput compared to standard autoregressive decoding by up to 4.37× at batch size 1 and 4.76× at batch size 16. Additionally, experiments on benchmarks without repositories or multi-agent pipelines show that AgSpec still provides substantial gains, indicating robustness across different coding-agent configurations.
AI.conclusion: AgSpec demonstrates that tailoring speculative decoding to coding agents—by aligning retrieval corpora with agent outputs and by using both offline profiling and online feedback to control draft length—yields consistent throughput improvements over existing methods and baseline decoding. Its benefits generalize beyond the specific multi-agent, repository-level setups it was designed for, suggesting it is a broadly useful approach for accelerating LLM-based coding agents.

title: Pay for the Fault, Not the Flow: Label-Free In-Flow Multi-Agent Workflow Optimization
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly construct multi-agent workflows that decompose a complex task and assign specialist agents from a pool. However, building such a workflow well remains challenging: how finely to divide the task, which agent to trust with each subtask, and when to create a new specialist are all critical decisions a workflow constructor needs to settle up front. Thus, whether each subtask succeeds remains unknown until the workflow runs. Yet, improving a workflow is costly. Locating a fault usually requires a reference answer, a graded outcome, or a trained assessor, and the fix is applied to the whole workflow through re-execution, re-search, or retraining. We propose InFlowOp, which prices every decision in one label-free cost that weighs how well an agent's competence meets what a subtask demands against how much that agent takes to run. Before execution, InFlowOp bidirectionally determines the granularity of task decomposition and agent assignment following from the cost rather than from a fixed template. During execution, InFlowOp corrects a fault with the cheapest move via the same cost that serves the workflow both as it is built and as it runs. Facing the workflow-level evaluation challenge, we introduce Braid, a benchmark whose tasks require multi-agent coordination beyond single-agent capability. Across various domains and backbones, InFlowOp outperforms single agent baselines by up to $+11.97\%$, achieving $+9.64\%$ with in-flow optimization. Our project page: https://xhguo7.github.io/InFlowOp/.

AI.tldr: InFlowOp is a framework for constructing and optimizing multi-agent LLM workflows by assigning subtasks to agents based on a unified, label-free cost function, improving both initial workflow design and in-flow correction.
AI.motivation: Current multi-agent LLM systems struggle with how to decompose complex tasks, how to choose and assign specialist agents, and how to adapt workflows when subtasks fail, typically requiring reference answers, external grading, or retraining. This makes workflow improvement expensive and inflexible, and there is no standard way to evaluate multi-agent workflows that truly require coordination beyond a single model's capability.
AI.method: The authors introduce InFlowOp, which defines a single label-free cost function that jointly accounts for (1) how well an agent’s competence matches a subtask’s requirements and (2) the computational cost of running that agent. Using this cost, InFlowOp: (a) determines task decomposition granularity and assigns subtasks to agents prior to execution, not via fixed templates; and (b) dynamically repairs faults during execution by choosing the cheapest correction move according to the same cost metric. They also create Braid, a benchmark of tasks that inherently require multi-agent coordination and cannot be solved by a single agent alone.
AI.result: On the Braid benchmark across multiple domains and backbone models, InFlowOp yields up to +11.97% performance gains over single-agent baselines and achieves +9.64% improvement when leveraging in-flow optimization, demonstrating both the effectiveness of its workflow construction and its online correction strategy.
AI.conclusion: InFlowOp provides a unified, label-free, cost-based framework for both designing and dynamically optimizing multi-agent LLM workflows, reducing the need for expensive supervision or retraining while improving performance. The accompanying Braid benchmark establishes a more realistic, workflow-level evaluation setting for multi-agent LLM coordination and shows that principled, cost-aware workflow optimization outperforms single-agent approaches.

title: Madeleine: Learning Involuntary Recall for Conversational Memory from Simulated Lives
summary: A long-term conversational assistant must recall the right memory at the right moment, yet the memory that matters most is often not similar to what the user says now. Current systems recover such associations by letting an LLM reason at write or read time, at a cost of hundreds to over a thousand LLM calls per memory bank and up to several thousand context tokens per query. We argue that association is a learnable relevance: the pointwise mutual information of memories under how human lives unfold. We introduce Madeleine, which learns amortized association: offline, an LLM life simulator writes simulated lives, whose cue-trigger pairs teach a query encoder a residual association on top of frozen similarity; online, it calls no LLM and plugs into any vector memory by replacing only the query encoder. On LoCoMo-Plus under the official protocol, Madeleine (I) reaches 66.6 when plugged into HyperMem, the highest among all systems evaluated under this protocol; (II) used alone, reaches the score of HyperMem as released (52.4 vs. 52.9) with zero LLM calls and about 1/21 of its answer context; and (III) lifts T-Mem by 26.2 points, significantly outperforms the same untrained backbone inside both systems, and leaves ordinary QA intact on the 4B backbone.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Madeleine, a system that learns to retrieve the right long‑term conversational memories via a learned association model instead of expensive LLM reasoning at query time.
AI.motivation: Long-term conversational assistants must remember and retrieve past user-specific information. However, the most relevant past memories are often not lexically or semantically similar to the user’s current utterance, making standard similarity search inadequate. Existing systems address this via heavy LLM-based reasoning at write or read time, leading to high computational cost (hundreds to thousands of LLM calls and very large context windows per query). The authors aim to make associative memory retrieval both more accurate and far more efficient.
AI.method: They conceptualize association as a learnable relevance signal, approximating the pointwise mutual information between memories as human lives unfold. They propose Madeleine, which learns “amortized association.” Offline, an LLM-based life simulator generates synthetic long-term interaction traces with cue-trigger memory pairs, which are then used to train a query encoder to predict a residual association score on top of standard similarity-based retrieval, while keeping the similarity encoder frozen. Online, Madeleine does not call any LLM: it simply replaces the query encoder in any vector-memory system, re-ranking or augmenting similarity search results using the learned association model.
AI.result: On the LoCoMo-Plus benchmark under its official protocol, Madeleine: (I) achieves a score of 66.6 when integrated with HyperMem, the best among systems evaluated under the same protocol; (II) when used alone, matches the original HyperMem system’s performance (52.4 vs. 52.9) while using zero LLM calls and only ~1/21 of its answer context; and (III) improves T-Mem by 26.2 points, showing clear gains over using the same untrained backbone in either system, and does so without hurting ordinary QA performance on a 4B-parameter backbone.
AI.conclusion: Amortized association, learned from simulated life trajectories, can replace expensive online LLM reasoning for long-term conversational memory retrieval. By training a query encoder to capture association as residual relevance over similarity, Madeleine enables plug-and-play, LLM-free, and efficient retrieval in vector memory systems while improving or matching state-of-the-art performance on long-term conversation benchmarks.

title: Beyond Final Accuracy: Auditing Communication in LLM Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Multi-agent communication aims to help agents benefit from one another's information. Yet improvements in system performance leave a fundamental ambiguity: do they reflect effective communication, a favorable agent architecture, or simply additional reasoning? Because communication methods are commonly evaluated within the systems they were designed for, these factors are difficult to disentangle. Final accuracy further merges corrected errors and corrupted answers into a single outcome, obscuring how communication changes decisions. We introduce Independent--Communicate--Revise (ICR), a controlled framework that evaluates communication as answer revision following independent reasoning. ICR fixes initial reasoning trajectories, measures correction and preservation conditional on both agents' initial correctness, and uses a no-message revision control to quantify gains beyond additional reasoning. Across four reasoning benchmarks, our audit of textual and latent communication reveals that similar aggregate accuracy can conceal substantially different revision behaviors. Compared with transmitting answers alone, full reasoning increases correction while reducing preservation on all four benchmarks, so richer messages amplify beneficial and harmful influence alike. Receiver-policy comparisons on MedQA and GPQA-D further show that a structured verification policy shifts every channel toward greater preservation and lower correction, while its effect on selectivity varies across channels and tasks. These findings challenge treating communication quality as an intrinsic property of a channel. ICR therefore recenters evaluation on selective revision, providing a unified framework for examining how message content and receiver policies jointly produce benefits and harms.

AI.tldr: They propose a controlled framework (ICR) to evaluate how multi-agent communication actually changes answers, separating communication effects from architecture and extra reasoning.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of multi-agent communication conflate multiple factors: agent architecture, extra reasoning steps, and the communication channel itself. Final accuracy hides whether communication is correcting mistakes or corrupting correct answers, and most methods are only tested in the systems they were built for, making comparisons and diagnosis hard.
AI.method: They introduce Independent–Communicate–Revise (ICR), where agents first reason independently, then exchange messages, then revise their answers. Initial trajectories are fixed to disentangle effects. They condition analysis on the initial correctness of both agents, measure both correction (fixing wrong answers) and preservation (keeping right ones), and add a no-message revision control to isolate benefits beyond extra reasoning. They apply this to various communication channels (textual, latent; answers-only vs full reasoning) across four reasoning benchmarks, and compare different receiver policies, including a structured verification policy, on MedQA and GPQA-D.
AI.result: They find that similar aggregate accuracy can hide very different revision patterns across communication channels. Sending full reasoning rather than just final answers consistently increases the rate of corrections but also decreases preservation, meaning richer messages both help and harm more. Structured verification policies shift all channels toward higher preservation and lower correction, with mixed effects on how selectively messages are used, and these effects differ by task and channel.
AI.conclusion: Communication quality is not an intrinsic property of a channel; it depends on how messages interact with receiver policies and initial beliefs. ICR reframes evaluation around selective revision—balancing correction of errors with preservation of correct answers—and offers a unified way to audit when and how multi-agent communication produces benefits versus harms.

title: Counting and Min-Cost Encoding for Tokenization in Large Language Models
summary: Mainstream large language models rely on a tokenizer to encode text into a token sequence. Different tokenizers may yield token sequences of substantially different lengths for the same text. With a fixed model architecture, shorter token sequences correspond to lower inference time. We propose a tokenizer training approach named Counting and Filtering (CNF) and a text encoding algorithm called Min-Cost Encoding (MCE). MCE defines a cost function over a text segment, and determines the best segmentation by globally minimizing the overall segmentation cost. CNF builds a raw vocabulary by directly counting valid substrings, and then constructs the final vocabulary through a filtering step based on actual token usage when segmenting the training corpus with MCE. The CNF-MCE conbination offers several advantages over BPE, including higher token efficiency, greater scalability, and lower dependency. Across six text categories and two vocabulary-size groups, CNF-MCE consistently achieves better compression than the evaluated BPE tokenizers. With a 250K vocabulary, CNF-MCE increases compression rate by 26% and 30% on English web text over the o200k_base and qwen250k tokenizers. Experiments scaling the vocabulary to 1M entries on English web text demonstrate sustained improvements over BPE, with a token efficiency improvement of over 60% and vocabulary utilization rising from 52.9% to 96.9%. The MCE algorithm does not depend on a merge list (as in BPE) or token probability (as in UnigramLM), making it applicable to a wide range of vocabularies, including those built from BPE, UnigramLM, CNF, and others. Language models trained from scratch at the 1.8B and 8B scales achieve comparable average performance to models using the BPE tokenizers across 11 benchmarks. These results demonstrate that CNF-MCE can improve token efficiency significantly while maintaining competitive downstream performance.

AI.tldr: They propose a new tokenizer training method (CNF) plus a global optimal encoding algorithm (MCE) that yields shorter token sequences than BPE while preserving model performance.
AI.motivation: Tokenization length and efficiency strongly affect inference cost; existing tokenizers like BPE can be suboptimal in compression, scalability, and vocabulary utilization, especially at large vocabulary sizes.
AI.method: 1) Define Min-Cost Encoding (MCE), which segments text by globally minimizing a cost function over possible segmentations, independent of merge lists or token probabilities. 2) Train a tokenizer with Counting and Filtering (CNF): first count valid substrings to build a raw vocabulary, then filter based on actual usage when segmenting the training corpus with MCE. 3) Evaluate CNF-MCE against BPE-based tokenizers over various corpora, vocabulary sizes (250k–1M), and model scales (1.8B and 8B parameters).
AI.result: CNF-MCE consistently produces shorter tokenizations (better compression) than BPE across six text categories and two vocabulary-size groups; on English web text with a 250K vocab, it improves compression by 26–30% over o200k_base and qwen250k tokenizers. Scaling to a 1M vocabulary keeps these gains, improving token efficiency by over 60% and raising vocabulary utilization from 52.9% to 96.9%. Models trained with CNF-MCE tokenization match the performance of BPE-tokenized models across 11 benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: CNF-MCE is a more token-efficient and scalable tokenization-and-encoding framework than standard BPE, substantially reducing token counts and improving vocabulary utilization, while maintaining competitive downstream performance in language models.

title: Empty Commitments: When Agents Promise What Their Runtime Cannot Deliver
summary: A chatbot that says "I will remind you tomorrow" will not run again until the user writes. We call such a promise an empty commitment: a promise of an action after the current turn that nothing in the agent's tools or runtime can carry out. Unlike a broken promise, its emptiness follows from the agent's configuration alone; no later trajectory is needed. We define empty commitments on top of commitment semantics, with three failure types, an anchoring condition for promises that a tool could make real, and a response-level outcome taxonomy. We then describe a measurement protocol: follow-up requests run in five setups that add one persistence affordance at a time, with the environment either left implicit or stated.

AI.tldr: Paper analyzes 'empty commitments' in chatbots: promises about future actions that the system is in fact incapable of fulfilling, given its architecture.
AI.motivation: LLM-based chatbots often make forward-looking promises (e.g., reminders, future actions) that their underlying tools and runtimes cannot execute, causing user confusion and trust issues. The paper aims to formally characterize and measure such impossible promises.
AI.method: Builds a formal semantics of commitments tailored to LLM agents, defines 'empty commitments' with three failure types and an anchoring condition for potentially realizable promises, then proposes a measurement protocol using follow-up user requests across five system configurations that incrementally add persistence capabilities, under both implicit and explicitly described environments.
AI.result: Provides a taxonomy of response-level outcomes and a protocol showing how different persistence affordances affect the likelihood and nature of empty commitments, distinguishing cases where tools could in principle realize a promise from those where the architecture makes fulfillment impossible.
AI.conclusion: Empty commitments can be determined from system design alone and should be formally accounted for when building and evaluating LLM agents. By adding and clearly exposing persistence affordances, designers can reduce structurally impossible promises and better align user expectations with system capabilities.

title: BanglaDial-Abuse: A Corpus-Grounded Dataset for Regional Dialect Identification in Abusive Bangla Text
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Dataset Version 1.0 available on Zenodo: 10.5281/zenodo.23074319
summary: Regional linguistic variation remains an important challenge for Bangla natural language processing, particularly in informal and non-standard text. This paper introduces BanglaDial-Abuse, a balanced Bengali-script dataset developed for regional dialect identification in abusive and hostile Bangla text. The dataset contains 1,000 sentences distributed equally across four linguistic varieties: Standard Bangla, Chattagram, Sylhet, and Barishal, with 250 samples per class. The resource was constructed using a corpus-grounded synthetic procedure incorporating regional variation in pronouns, possessive forms, verb morphology, negation, interrogative structures, postpositions, vocabulary, and Bengali-script spelling conventions while preserving the underlying hostile or abusive meaning. Descriptive analysis shows broadly comparable sentence-length distributions but partially distinct lexical spaces across the four classes. Pairwise Jaccard vocabulary similarity ranges from 0.37 to 0.56. The primary task is four-class regional dialect identification rather than binary abusive-text detection. The dataset is publicly available through Zenodo under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 license. The current version is intended as a research and prototyping corpus rather than a native-speaker-validated gold-standard linguistic resource. Keywords: Bangla, Bengali, dialect identification, regional dialect, abusive language, low-resource NLP, Chattagram, Sylhet, Barishal, dataset

AI.tldr: BanglaDial-Abuse is a 1,000-sentence Bengali-script dataset for identifying regional Bangla dialects in abusive/hostile text across four varieties (Standard, Chattagram, Sylhet, Barishal).
AI.motivation: Regional variation in Bangla, especially in informal and abusive online language, makes NLP tasks like dialect identification difficult due to scarce labeled resources and non-standard spellings. The authors aim to provide a controlled, balanced dataset specifically targeting regional dialect identification within abusive/hostile contexts, addressing the low-resource gap for Bangla regional varieties.
AI.method: They created a balanced corpus of 1,000 hostile or abusive sentences, with 250 per dialect: Standard Bangla, Chattagram, Sylhet, and Barishal. Using a corpus-grounded synthetic procedure, they systematically varied dialectal features—pronouns, possessives, verb morphology, negation, interrogatives, postpositions, vocabulary, and spelling—while preserving abusive meaning. They then performed descriptive statistics on sentence length and lexical overlap, computing pairwise Jaccard similarity of vocabularies for the four dialect classes.
AI.result: The resulting BanglaDial-Abuse dataset exhibits comparable sentence length across dialects but distinct lexical spaces, with vocabulary Jaccard similarities between dialect pairs ranging from 0.37 to 0.56. The dataset is curated as a four-class classification benchmark for regional dialect identification in abusive Bangla text and released publicly via Zenodo under CC BY 4.0.
AI.conclusion: BanglaDial-Abuse offers a new, balanced research corpus for four-way regional dialect identification in abusive Bangla text, suitable for experimentation and prototyping in low-resource NLP. However, it is not yet a native-speaker-validated gold-standard resource, so future work should include expert validation, expansion, and use in broader abusive-language and dialect modeling tasks.

title: Network World Models as Environments for Algorithm Design on Complex Systems
summary: World models, which simulate an environment and predict how it changes under actions, are increasingly used in real-world applications such as robotics. Complex systems call for the same tool because the effect of an action is not immediate. Seeding nodes for a campaign, or immunizing nodes against an epidemic, changes little on its own; what matters is the outcome that unfolds over the steps that follow. Designing an algorithm that selects such actions to maximize expected performance on a task is inherently iterative, and every candidate must be scored by the outcome it produces. Obtaining that outcome has relied on simulation, whose cost becomes a bottleneck when candidates are evaluated over many sampled trajectories. We propose an action-conditioned Network World Model that learns a network's diffusion dynamics under interventions over time, applies each action to the network, and predicts the outcome that follows. It serves as a fast evaluator inside an algorithm design loop in which a coding agent designs and refines executable algorithms using feedback from full rollouts, action-level credit, and counterfactual probes over alternative interventions. Across eight network tasks and five diffusion models, the designed algorithms match or exceed the strongest reported baseline in 138 of 141 settings while enabling up to 14.5 times faster rollouts than Monte Carlo simulation. Code will be released upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: They build a learned “world model” for network diffusion that can quickly evaluate candidate intervention algorithms, drastically reducing reliance on slow Monte Carlo simulation.
AI.motivation: In many networked systems (e.g., information spread, epidemics), the impact of an action such as seeding or immunizing nodes only appears after several diffusion steps. To design good intervention algorithms, we must evaluate many candidate actions by simulating their long-term effects, but Monte Carlo simulators are computationally expensive and become the bottleneck in algorithm design loops.
AI.method: They propose an action-conditioned Network World Model that learns the diffusion dynamics of a network under interventions. This model takes as input a network, a sequence of actions/interventions, and predicts the resulting diffusion outcomes over time. It is used inside an automated algorithm-design loop where a coding agent generates and refines executable intervention policies, using feedback from (1) full predicted rollouts, (2) action-level credit assignment, and (3) counterfactual probes comparing alternative interventions. The model is trained across multiple network diffusion tasks and models.
AI.result: Across eight network optimization tasks and five different diffusion models, algorithms designed using the proposed world model match or outperform the strongest existing baselines in 138 out of 141 experimental settings. Moreover, using the learned world model as the evaluator yields up to a 14.5× speedup in rollout time compared to traditional Monte Carlo simulation, while still providing sufficiently accurate performance estimates for algorithm search.
AI.conclusion: A learned, action-conditioned Network World Model can effectively replace expensive Monte Carlo simulation as the inner-loop evaluator for designing network intervention algorithms. This enables automated design of high-performing algorithms across a variety of network diffusion settings while significantly reducing computational cost, suggesting that similar world-model-based design loops could be applied to other complex, multi-step decision problems on graphs.

title: My FAULT: Self-Diagnosis as Credit Assignment in Self-Evolving Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a powerful approach for training large language model agents on multi-step tasks, yet reliance on terminal outcome rewards creates two credit-assignment problems, particularly in long-horizon tasks. First, same-outcome rollout groups provide no learning signal from terminal rewards. Second, terminal rewards provide only trajectory-wide feedback, making it difficult to identify which decisions caused a failure. Recent work supplements terminal rewards with finer-grained information from trajectory analysis, such as natural-language reflections on intermediate decisions and errors. However, natural-language diagnoses are difficult to use directly for credit assignment: their error claims may be unreliable, and they do not quantify how much each error should affect learning. We propose Self-Diagnosis-guided Terminal Credit Redistribution (FAULT), which turns diagnosed errors into explicit step-level credit anchored by terminal outcomes. FAULT checks diagnostic evidence and learns relative error costs from task outcomes. During training, the policy and self-diagnoser co-evolve, while error costs are updated online from recent outcomes. On ALFWorld, FAULT recovers learning signals from same-outcome groups, reaching 95% signal coverage versus 41% for GRPO and 72% for GiGPO, while better localizing credit to specific error steps. Across two model scales, FAULT delivers strong. improvements on the long-horizon ALFWorld and WebShop tasks while remaining competitive on short-horizon Search-based QA.

AI.tldr: FAULT is a method for agentic RL that converts self-diagnosed errors into step-level credit signals, solving key credit-assignment issues from relying only on terminal rewards in long-horizon tasks.
AI.motivation: Agentic RL for LLM agents often relies on terminal outcome rewards, which causes two major credit-assignment issues in long-horizon tasks: (1) same-outcome trajectories (all success or all failure) provide no differential learning signal, and (2) trajectory-wide rewards don’t reveal which specific decisions led to success or failure. Existing approaches add natural-language reflections or diagnoses over trajectories, but these textual explanations are noisy, uncalibrated, and do not directly yield quantitative, step-level credit assignments. A method is needed that can transform such high-level diagnoses into reliable, granular reward signals while respecting terminal outcomes.
AI.method: The paper introduces FAULT (Self-Diagnosis-guided Terminal Credit Redistribution). First, a self-diagnoser analyzes trajectories and produces error diagnoses for individual steps in natural language. FAULT then verifies or “checks” these diagnostic claims and converts them into explicit, quantitative step-level credit values that are anchored to the terminal outcome (success/failure). It learns relative error costs from observed task outcomes, updating these costs online during training. The behavior policy and the self-diagnoser are trained jointly (co-evolution), with the credit redistribution mechanism continuously adjusted to better attribute outcome differences to specific errorful steps, thereby recovering learning signal even among trajectories with identical terminal outcomes.
AI.result: On the ALFWorld benchmark, FAULT substantially increases the proportion of trajectories that yield usable learning signals in same-outcome groups: 95% signal coverage versus 41% for GRPO and 72% for GiGPO. It also achieves better localization of credit to specific error steps, indicating more precise attribution of failures. Across two LLM model sizes, FAULT provides strong performance improvements on long-horizon ALFWorld and WebShop tasks, while maintaining competitive performance on shorter-horizon Search-based QA where terminal-reward credit assignment is less problematic.
AI.conclusion: FAULT demonstrates that self-diagnosis, when coupled with outcome-anchored credit redistribution and learned error costs, can effectively transform noisy natural-language trajectory analyses into useful step-level rewards for agentic RL. This approach mitigates key credit-assignment failures of pure terminal-reward methods, especially in long-horizon environments, improving both signal coverage and task performance while remaining broadly applicable across different tasks and model scales.

title: Improving Math Reasoning through Value-guided Informative Search
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has substantially improved the mathematical reasoning capabilities of large language models. Recent work introduces search into RLVR rollouts to increase trajectory diversity, but diversity alone does not ensure that the search-induced rollout policy improves upon the current policy. To address this gap, we propose APIVIS, a training-time framework that adapts finite-budget Gumbel search to chunk-level mathematical reasoning. APIVIS combines direct and searched responses within each rollout group, allowing improvements found by search to produce informative relative rewards. It further applies selective supervision to search-improved tokens, preserving a learning signal when uniform group rewards render GRPO ineffective. We show that exact value-guided selection improves the expected verifier reward at each searched state and that this guarantee extends to the complete rollout policy, with a corresponding approximate guarantee under bounded value-estimation error. Experiments on widely recognized mathematical reasoning benchmarks and different model scales demonstrate substantial improvements over competitive search-based methods, validating the effectiveness of APIVIS.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes APIVIS, a training-time framework that integrates finite-budget Gumbel search into reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) for mathematical reasoning, combining direct and search-augmented rollouts with selective supervision to reliably improve the rollout policy and verifier rewards.
AI.motivation: Existing RLVR methods have significantly advanced mathematical reasoning in large language models, but simply adding search during rollouts mainly increases trajectory diversity without guaranteeing that the resulting search-based rollout policy is actually better than the current policy. Moreover, uniform group rewards can make standard GRPO-style learning signals weak or uninformative, limiting the benefits of search. The authors aim to design a principled way to integrate search so that it provably improves verifier rewards and yields a strong learning signal during training.
AI.method: The authors introduce APIVIS, a training-time framework that adapts finite-budget Gumbel search to chunk-level mathematical reasoning steps. In each rollout group, APIVIS mixes directly generated responses with search-augmented responses, so that improvements discovered via search can be compared against the base policy to generate informative relative rewards. The method further employs selective supervision: only tokens that are actually improved by search receive targeted training signals, which preserves learning signal even when group-level rewards are uniform and standard GRPO becomes ineffective. They also develop a value-guided selection mechanism to choose which search outputs to trust, and analyze its behavior under exact and approximate value estimates.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis shows that, given exact value estimates, the value-guided selection in APIVIS improves the expected verifier reward at every searched state, and that this local improvement guarantee extends to the full rollout policy. When value estimates are boundedly inaccurate, they prove an approximate improvement guarantee. Empirically, across multiple widely used mathematical reasoning benchmarks and at different model sizes, APIVIS yields substantial performance gains over strong search-based baselines, demonstrating more effective use of search during RLVR training.
AI.conclusion: APIVIS provides a principled way to couple search with RLVR for mathematical reasoning: by integrating finite-budget Gumbel search at the chunk level, mixing direct and searched trajectories, and applying selective supervision to search-improved tokens, it yields provable and empirical improvements in verifier rewards and end-task performance. The framework effectively addresses the mismatch between trajectory diversity and policy quality in prior search-based RLVR methods and establishes a more reliable route to enhancing the mathematical reasoning abilities of large language models.

title: HeadEdit: Calibrating Language Model Behavior Through the Frozen Unembedding Matrix
summary: Alignment does not eliminate behavioral errors in language models. Models may still refuse benign requests, call unnecessary tools, or yield to false user claims.
