Current methods mitigate such errors as a computation problem, and rarely explore if the desired behavior is already encoded in the model's representation. Motivated by the observation that behavior-relevant information remains linearly decodable from the final hidden state even when the resulting logits produce the undesired behavior, we introduce HeadEdit, a gradient-free method that calibrates model behavior through the unembedding matrix. HeadEdit extracts a low-rank behavioral subspace from paired completions and uses each prompt's coordinates within it to generate a vocabulary-wide correction, thereby implementing implicitly adaptive steering without manually specified target tokens or parameter updates. HeadEdit improves all nine experimental settings across three tasks and three model families, with negligible inference overhead and no systematic loss of general capabilities. It also reveals a connection to gradient-based alignment. HeadEdit's low-dimensional representation partly predicts how preference tuning changes output logits on unseen prompts. The subspace learned from the model can also be reused after tuning, improving performance without re-extracting or retuning. These results show that HeadEdit provides a practical, lightweight, and interpretable way to calibrate model behavior through the unembedding matrix.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces HeadEdit, a gradient-free technique that uses a low-rank subspace in the unembedding matrix to correct misaligned behaviors in language models without affecting general capabilities.
AI.motivation: Aligned language models still show behavioral errors such as refusing benign requests, overusing tools, or accepting false user claims. Existing alignment and steering methods largely treat this as an optimization or tuning problem and rarely investigate whether the correct behavior is already encoded in the model’s internal representations. The authors are motivated by the observation that behavior-relevant information is linearly decodable from final hidden states even when the model’s output logits correspond to undesired behaviors, suggesting that alignment might be achieved by better decoding this existing information rather than retraining the whole model.
AI.method: They propose HeadEdit, a gradient-free, post-hoc calibration method that operates on the unembedding matrix. From paired completions (good vs bad behavior), they extract a low-rank “behavioral subspace” in logit space. For each new prompt, they project its final hidden state into this subspace to obtain coordinates that generate a vocabulary-wide logit correction, effectively steering the model’s output distribution. HeadEdit does not require explicit target tokens, gradient-based updates, or full parameter finetuning, and acts as an implicitly adaptive steering mechanism through a small set of learned directions in unembedding space.
AI.result: Across three tasks and three model families, HeadEdit improves performance in all nine experimental settings, reducing behavioral errors such as unnecessary refusals and tool calls, while incurring negligible inference overhead. The method does not cause a systematic drop in general capabilities. Empirically, the learned low-dimensional subspace correlates with how gradient-based preference tuning modifies logits, and the same subspace remains useful even after the model is further tuned, allowing reuse without retraining the subspace.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that HeadEdit is a practical, lightweight, and interpretable approach for calibrating language model behavior by editing the unembedding matrix rather than retraining the model. The existence and effectiveness of a low-rank behavioral subspace shows that correct behaviors are often already encoded in the model’s representations, and that small, structured adjustments to the decoding process can reliably reduce misalignment while preserving general performance. The discovered link to gradient-based alignment suggests that such subspace methods capture core aspects of alignment updates and can complement or enhance standard tuning pipelines.

title: YouRA: A Persistent-State Architecture for Evidence-Traceable Autonomous Research Agents
comment: Accepted to the AACL-IJCNLP 2026 Main Conference. 21 pages, 5 figures, 17 tables
summary: End-to-end research agents can now produce complete scientific papers, yet manuscript claims often diverge from executed experiments. This gap is structural: research state, failure histories, and claim-evidence alignment are not maintained as persistent, verifiable state across long-horizon pipelines. We present YouRA (Your Research Agent), an architecture for stateful, evidence-traceable autonomous research. YouRA preserves research state, execution evidence, and failure history across the research trajectory by integrating three components: a Verification State Architecture (VSA) that tracks hypotheses, gates, and evidence pointers; an Independent Controller that turns state and reflection records into lifecycle, recovery, and debate/review control while separating control from execution; and Stateful Reflection that logs failures as structured lessons and routes recovery through bounded repair, redesign, or reset. On MLR-Bench's predefined ten-task end-to-end subset, YouRA improves over both MLR-Agent and AI Scientist V2 on scalar Overall across all three matched backbones. An automated diagnostic using MLR-Bench's hallucination taxonomy reports intersection/union counts for four fact-based failure types, and data-provenance diagnostic shows more real-data-based outputs. Ablating each of the four components (the VSA, the Independent Controller, MCP tool access, and reflection-guided recovery) supports their separable contributions. Removing either core-state component drops YouRA below the full system. Code: https://github.com/PrayPrey/Your-Research-Agent.

AI.tldr: YouRA is an architecture for autonomous research agents that keeps verifiable, persistent research state so claims stay aligned with actual experiments, achieving better performance and fewer hallucinations than prior systems on MLR-Bench.
AI.motivation: Existing end-to-end research agents can write full scientific papers but often produce claims that do not accurately reflect the experiments they actually ran. This mismatch stems from a lack of persistent, verifiable state that tracks hypotheses, experimental history, evidence, and failures across long, multi-step research processes. The paper aims to close this structural gap so that autonomous research outputs are more trustworthy, traceable, and grounded in real data and executed procedures.
AI.method: The authors propose YouRA, an autonomous research architecture composed of: (1) a Verification State Architecture (VSA) that explicitly represents hypotheses, decision gates, and pointers to underlying evidence; (2) an Independent Controller that uses the maintained state and reflection logs to orchestrate the research lifecycle (planning, execution, review, and recovery) while decoupling control from task execution; and (3) Stateful Reflection mechanisms that store failures as structured lessons and direct recovery strategies via bounded repair, redesign, or full reset. They evaluate YouRA on the ten-task end-to-end subset of MLR-Bench using three different backbone models, perform hallucination diagnostics based on MLR-Bench’s taxonomy, analyze data provenance, and run ablations that remove each core component (VSA, Independent Controller, MCP tool access, and reflection-guided recovery) to quantify their contributions.
AI.result: Across all three backbone models and on MLR-Bench’s ten-task end-to-end subset, YouRA achieves higher scalar Overall scores than both MLR-Agent and AI Scientist V2. Automated hallucination diagnostics show that YouRA reduces fact-based failure types (measured via intersection/union counts) and produces more outputs that are demonstrably grounded in real data. Ablation experiments reveal that each component—VSA, Independent Controller, MCP tool access, and reflection-guided recovery—provides separable benefits, and that removing either of the two core state components (VSA or Independent Controller) degrades performance enough to bring YouRA below the full system’s performance.
AI.conclusion: YouRA demonstrates that making research agents stateful and evidence-traceable substantially improves reliability and grounding of autonomous research. By explicitly tracking hypotheses, gating decisions, evidence references, and structured failure histories, and by separating control from execution, YouRA reduces hallucinations and improves benchmark performance compared with prior end-to-end agents. The results support the view that verifiable, persistent research state and structured recovery processes are key architectural elements for building trustworthy, long-horizon autonomous research systems.

title: Temporally-Resolved Token Attribution Reveals the Generation Dynamics of Diffusion Language Models
summary: This work presents Diffusion Layer Integrated Gradients (DLIG), a token attribution method for diffusion language models (DLMs) that extends Integrated Gradients (IG~\cite{sundararajan2017axiomatic}) to arbitrary layers and denoising steps. DLIG attributes a DLM's progressive commitment to a self-generated or fixed completion for an input prompt. We establish direct correspondences between DLIG and the IG axioms of completeness, implementation invariance, linearity, and symmetry preservation. As a lightweight complement to interventional analysis, DLIG provides an inexpensive first check of mechanistic hypotheses across the denoising trajectory. We demonstrate this on word-sense disambiguation, multi-hop graph reasoning, and sentence infilling, revealing how DLMs draw on inputs across positions, layers, and denoising steps.

AI.tldr: Proposes DLIG, a token attribution method for diffusion language models that generalizes Integrated Gradients across layers and denoising steps.
AI.motivation: Existing attribution methods like Integrated Gradients are designed for standard feedforward models and do not directly handle the multi-step denoising process and layered structure of diffusion language models, limiting mechanistic interpretability of these models.
AI.method: Extend Integrated Gradients to diffusion language models by defining attributions over arbitrary layers and denoising steps, tracking the model’s evolving commitment to a given completion. The method preserves key IG axioms (completeness, implementation invariance, linearity, symmetry) and is computationally lightweight compared to interventional analyses.
AI.result: DLIG successfully attributes how different tokens and positions influence the generation process across denoising steps and layers. Empirical studies on word-sense disambiguation, multi-hop graph reasoning, and sentence infilling show that DLIG can reveal when and where the model uses specific input information along the diffusion trajectory.
AI.conclusion: DLIG is a principled and efficient attribution tool for diffusion language models that adheres to IG axioms and serves as a practical first-pass method for testing mechanistic hypotheses about how these models use input tokens across layers and denoising steps.

title: Beyond State-of-the-Art: Standardising Environmental Impact Metrics for AI Research
summary:
As the capabilities and ubiquity of Large Language Models (LLMs) grow, so does their environmental footprint. Despite calls for responsible AI, the machine learning community lacks standardised practices for carbon accounting. Our automated literature review of the 5,285 papers accepted to NeurIPS 2025 reveals that reporting of environmental impact is nearly non-existent. To catalyse a shift toward sustainable AI, we define standardised sustainability metrics for evaluating model training efficiency, accompanied by simple heuristics to estimate the carbon cost of LLM inference. We implement these metrics in carbonbenchmark, a drop-in software solution for tracking and reporting emissions.
  Finally, to combat the pursuit of marginal accuracy gains at disproportionate environmental costs, we formalise the `Smallest Model that Achieves the Job' (SMAJ), a framework which challenges the field to prioritise computational efficiency and environmental accountability alongside traditional `State-of-the-Art' (SotA) accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that as LLMs grow, their environmental impact is ignored, proposes standardised sustainability metrics and carbon estimation heuristics, implements them in a tool, and introduces the SMAJ framework to prioritise efficiency over marginal accuracy gains.
AI.motivation: The motivation is the growing environmental footprint of increasingly large and ubiquitous LLMs, combined with the lack of standardised carbon accounting practices and the near-absence of environmental impact reporting in leading ML venues such as NeurIPS 2025.
AI.method: The authors conduct an automated literature review of 5,285 NeurIPS 2025 papers to assess current reporting practices, define standardised sustainability metrics for training efficiency, design simple heuristics to estimate carbon cost of LLM inference, and implement these in a drop-in software package called carbonbenchmark.
AI.result: The literature review finds that environmental impact reporting is almost entirely absent in NeurIPS 2025 papers. The authors provide concrete sustainability metrics, practical heuristics for inference carbon estimation, and a working software solution (carbonbenchmark) that can be integrated into ML workflows to track and report emissions.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that the ML community currently neglects environmental reporting, and to move toward sustainable AI, it should adopt standardised sustainability metrics, use tools like carbonbenchmark for systematic emissions tracking, and embrace the SMAJ framework to value the smallest adequate model instead of relentlessly chasing SotA accuracy at high environmental cost.

title: AGO AI Quality Gate: Evidence-First Release Decisions for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
comment: 14 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables. Submitted version (pre-review). Accepted at NFMCP 2026, ECML PKDD 2026 Workshops
summary: Enterprises adopting retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) face a recurring operational decision: promote, revise, or block a system version. The evidence is incomplete and the metrics come from fallible LLM judges. We report on AGO AI Quality Gate (AGO), an evidence-first quality-gate framework deployed in industrial RAG assessment engagements. AGO integrates four key components: a four-state decision model that treats missing data and judge errors as explicit outcomes; layered scoring combining deterministic checks, local guardrails, and structured LLM evaluation; a stratified beta-binomial gate that quantifies regression risk probabilistically; and a mandatory meta-evaluation protocol to validate the LLM judge before it influences decisions. Since engagement data is proprietary, we evaluate the judge layer on RAGBench, a public benchmark of 100k annotated RAG traces across 12 datasets. On identical stratified test samples (N=1200 per judge), a low-cost judge (gpt-4.1-nano) detects non-adherent answers barely above chance (AUROC 0.603 [0.570, 0.634]), despite producing flawless protocol output, while gpt-4o reaches 0.783 [0.756, 0.807] -- yet its per-domain performance still ranges from 0.62 to 0.88. A fixed-seed gate study spanning regression, no change, and improvement quantifies unsafe promotion, false-alarm cost, and improvement throughput. Under regression, the decision-grade profile reduces unsafe promotion to 22.2%-35.1%, against 29.3%-41.8% for a naive gate. These results support the design choices that judge quality must be measured per engagement and that point estimates alone are not a release decision.

AI.tldr: The paper presents AGO, an evidence-first quality gate framework for deciding whether to promote, revise, or block RAG system versions, accounting for incomplete evidence and imperfect LLM judges.
AI.motivation: Enterprises using RAG must frequently decide if a new system version is safe to release, but available metrics are noisy, incomplete, and often based on fallible LLM judges, making naive gating risky for production use.
AI.method: The authors design AGO, which combines: (1) a four-state decision model that explicitly handles missing data and judge errors; (2) layered scoring with deterministic checks, local guardrails, and structured LLM judging; (3) a stratified beta-binomial gate that expresses regression risk probabilistically; and (4) a meta-evaluation protocol to validate any LLM judge before it is used in decisions. They empirically assess the judge layer using RAGBench (100k annotated traces across 12 datasets) and run fixed-seed gate simulations under regression, no-change, and improvement scenarios.
AI.result: On RAGBench with equal-sized stratified samples (N=1200 per judge), a cheap model (gpt-4.1-nano) barely exceeds chance at detecting non-adherent answers (AUROC 0.603 with 95% CI [0.570, 0.634]), whereas gpt-4o performs substantially better (AUROC 0.783 [0.756, 0.807]) but still shows large domain variance (0.62–0.88 AUROC). In gate simulations, AGO’s decision-grade profile cuts unsafe promotion rates under regression to 22.2–35.1%, compared to 29.3–41.8% for a naive gate, while also explicitly quantifying false alarms and improvement throughput.
AI.conclusion: AGO’s evidence-first design, including mandatory judge meta-evaluation and probabilistic gating, leads to safer and more informative release decisions for RAG systems than naive point-estimate thresholds. Judge quality must be evaluated per engagement and point estimates alone are insufficient as a release criterion.

title: AbsorbEvo: An Agentic Framework for Autonomous Inverse Design of Microwave Absorbers
summary: Designing high-performance microwave absorbers requires specialized expertise in electromagnetic theory, materials science and simulation programming, and entails time-consuming optimization. Here, we present AbsorbEvo, an agentic framework for autonomous inverse design that translates natural-language performance objectives into designs verified by full-wave simulations. Its candidate evolution strategy integrates language reasoning, physics-based prediction and historical feedback. A large language model proposes the directions and magnitudes of parameter adjustments based on task objectives and computational history. The system combines directed increments with global sampling to generate candidates and uses a low-cost predictive model as a physics prior to rank them. Only high-ranking designs undergo full-wave simulation. Results passing physical validity checks are used to evaluate performance and guide subsequent search. Experience from training tasks is further distilled into textual skills, which are independently validated before use in new tasks. Under identical proposal budgets on held-out AbsorbBench-36 tasks, AbsorbEvo achieved a task success rate of 79.17%, versus 25.00% for a generic agent and 12.50% for random search. Its mean best coverage was 0.7816, compared with 0.6434 and 0.6448, respectively. By integrating language reasoning and physics-based feedback into design decisions, AbsorbEvo provides a methodological foundation for natural-language-driven autonomous inverse design of microwave absorbers.

AI.tldr: AbsorbEvo is an autonomous, language-driven inverse design framework that efficiently designs microwave absorbers by combining an LLM, physics-based prediction, and simulation feedback, substantially outperforming generic agents and random search.
AI.motivation: Designing high-performance microwave absorbers is complex and requires deep expertise in electromagnetics, materials, and simulations, along with time-consuming manual or heuristic optimization. There is a need for an automated system that can take intuitive, natural-language performance goals and reliably produce validated absorber designs, reducing expert effort and accelerating innovation.
AI.method: The authors build AbsorbEvo, an agentic framework where a large language model interprets natural-language objectives and computational history to suggest parameter adjustment directions and magnitudes. Candidate designs are generated via a mix of directed local increments and global sampling. A low-cost predictive model acts as a physics prior to rank candidates, and only top-ranked ones undergo expensive full-wave electromagnetic simulations. Designs that pass physical sanity checks are used to assess performance and inform subsequent candidate proposals. Knowledge from training tasks is distilled into textual “skills” that are independently validated and then reused in new design tasks. Performance is benchmarked on AbsorbBench-36 under fixed proposal budgets against a generic agent and random search.
AI.result: On the AbsorbBench-36 benchmark with identical proposal budgets, AbsorbEvo attained a 79.17% task success rate, compared with 25.00% for a generic agent and 12.50% for random search. Its mean best coverage metric reached 0.7816, outperforming the generic agent (0.6434) and random search (0.6448). These metrics demonstrate improved efficiency and quality of designs discovered by AbsorbEvo.
AI.conclusion: Integrating language-based reasoning with physics-based prediction and simulation feedback enables AbsorbEvo to autonomously perform inverse design of microwave absorbers from natural-language specifications, significantly outperforming baseline search methods. The framework offers a methodological foundation for scalable, natural-language-driven autonomous design in this domain and potentially other physics-based design problems.

title: ASCRIBE: Atomic and Significance-Based Reasoning for Thai Clinical SOAP Note Generation
summary: Automatic SOAP note generation can ease the documentation burden on physicians, but existing reasoning methods often omit clinically important information and generate unsupported content. Progress in Thai is further hindered by the lack of publicly available datasets. We propose ASCRIBE, a physician-inspired reasoning framework that ascribes a clinical-significance level to each extracted atomic fact in the conversation before summarization, making a general-purpose LLM a more reliable scribe. We also release ThaiClinicBench, the first de-identified Thai clinical summarization benchmark of real encounters, together with a synthetic training corpus derived from real clinical notes. As a prompt, ASCRIBE outperforms chain-of-thought prompting on GPT-5.4 and Gemini 3.1 Pro across the physician-aligned LLM-judge metrics and improves on standard prompting by up to 10.3 points on the completeness LLM-judge metric. As a GRPO reward, it enables a Gemma-4-E4B model trained solely on synthetic data to match Gemini 3.1 Pro in factual precision and surpass it in completeness. Code and data can be found at https://github.com/loolootech/ascribe.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ASCRIBE, a clinical-significance–aware reasoning framework and a new Thai clinical summarization benchmark, showing improved SOAP note generation in terms of completeness and factuality, even for models trained only on synthetic data.
AI.motivation: Clinical SOAP note generation can reduce physicians’ documentation workload, but current LLM reasoning methods often miss key clinical details and hallucinate unsupported content. These issues are exacerbated for low-resource languages like Thai due to a lack of public datasets. The paper aims to make LLMs more clinically reliable scribes and to bootstrap Thai clinical NLP research by providing appropriate data resources.
AI.method: The authors design ASCRIBE, a physician-inspired reasoning framework where conversations are decomposed into atomic facts that are each assigned a clinical-significance level prior to summarization. This significance-aware fact selection guides the LLM to focus on clinically important information and avoid unsupported details. ASCRIBE is used both as a prompting strategy for general-purpose LLMs (e.g., GPT-5.4, Gemini 3.1 Pro) and as a GRPO-based reward signal to train a smaller Gemma-4-E4B model on synthetic data. They also build ThaiClinicBench, a de-identified Thai clinical summarization benchmark from real encounters, and construct a synthetic training corpus from real clinical notes.
AI.result: As a prompt, ASCRIBE outperforms chain-of-thought prompting on GPT-5.4 and Gemini 3.1 Pro on multiple physician-aligned LLM-judge metrics and yields up to a 10.3-point gain in completeness over standard prompting. As a GRPO reward for training Gemma-4-E4B solely on synthetic data, ASCRIBE enables the smaller model to match Gemini 3.1 Pro in factual precision and exceed it in completeness. The authors also publicly release ThaiClinicBench and accompanying synthetic data.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating explicit clinical-significance reasoning into LLM workflows substantially improves the quality of automatic SOAP note generation, especially in terms of completeness and factual fidelity. ASCRIBE proves effective both as a prompting framework for large general LLMs and as a reward mechanism for training smaller models, while the new ThaiClinicBench dataset lays foundational infrastructure for Thai clinical summarization research.

title: CortexBridge: Cortical Alignment of EEG Montages for Foundation Models
summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) foundation models are often pretrained with a fixed channel vocabulary or a limited set of montages, making transfer difficult when electrode layouts change. We propose CortexBridge, a lightweight adapter that combines EEG features with electrode and atlas coordinates to map arbitrary montages into a shared cortical latent space. Evaluated with three frozen foundation models on five brain-computer interface (BCI) datasets from the Mother of All BCI Benchmarks (MOABB), CortexBridge improves performance in 13 of 15 evaluations. The gains in balanced accuracy average 0.80% for EEGPT, 0.70% for LaBraM, and 3.26% for CBraMod, with a maximum gain of 13.02% on 12-class steady-state visual evoked potential (SSVEP) classification. Visualizations of the learned atlas representations reveal task-dependent spatial patterns, with SSVEP showing a more concentrated representation in the Yeo Visual network than auditory P300. These results establish cortical alignment as a learnable and anatomically grounded routing mechanism from heterogeneous EEG montages to pretrained foundation models.

AI.tldr: CortexBridge is a lightweight adapter that aligns EEG data from arbitrary electrode montages into a shared cortical latent space using anatomical coordinates, improving transfer to frozen EEG foundation models.
AI.motivation: Existing EEG foundation models assume fixed channel layouts or a small set of montages, which breaks transferability when real-world electrode configurations differ, limiting generalization and practical deployment across diverse EEG setups.
AI.method: The authors design CortexBridge, an adapter that augments EEG features with electrode and atlas-based cortical coordinates, and learns a mapping from any montage into a shared cortical latent space. This adapter is trained while keeping the downstream EEG foundation model frozen, and is evaluated across multiple datasets and tasks from MOABB with several different pretrained models.
AI.result: Across five MOABB BCI datasets and three frozen EEG foundation models (EEGPT, LaBraM, CBraMod), CortexBridge improves performance in 13 out of 15 evaluation settings. Average balanced accuracy gains are 0.80% for EEGPT, 0.70% for LaBraM, and 3.26% for CBraMod, with a peak improvement of 13.02% on a 12-class SSVEP classification task. Visualization of learned atlas embeddings shows task-specific spatial organization, such as stronger concentration in the Yeo Visual network for SSVEP than for auditory P300.
AI.conclusion: CortexBridge demonstrates that cortical alignment can be learned as an anatomically grounded routing layer, enabling heterogeneous EEG montages to interface effectively with fixed-vocabulary EEG foundation models. This approach mitigates montage-dependence, improves cross-dataset performance, and provides interpretable spatial patterns aligned with known functional networks.

title: Harness Annealing: Learning to Act with Less External Control
summary: Language agents rely on external harnesses to track state, organize workflows, and verify answers. Beyond providing tools and information, these harnesses supply control decisions about what to investigate, whether to revise, and when to stop. Training on successful harness-supported trajectories can improve task performance while leaving these decisions dependent on runtime intervention. We ask whether harness-supported experience can also teach the model to make these decisions, allowing the division of control to change as the model learns. We call this objective harness internalization: learning to assume specified control responsibilities while retaining task performance after the corresponding support is withdrawn. We introduce HARNESS ANNEALING TRAINING (HAT), which combines explicit control supervision with a curriculum over teacher trajectories collected under progressively weaker harnesses. Experiments with 9B and 35B models on SWE-QA and SWE-QA-Pro evaluate every checkpoint under four deployment harnesses. Selected annealed checkpoints operating with tools alone achieve scores close to those of their respective starting checkpoints deployed with the full harness. The benefits vary with model scale and deployment configuration, and further annealing does not uniformly improve performance. These findings suggest that harness-supported experience can help reduce the runtime control required by a trained agent.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a training method that lets language models internalize control decisions previously handled by external agent harnesses, so they can operate with less runtime orchestration while maintaining performance.
AI.motivation: Current language agents depend heavily on external harnesses to manage control flow: choosing what to investigate, when to use tools, whether to revise answers, and when to stop. While models can be trained on trajectories generated under these harnesses, the resulting systems still rely on runtime control logic, which is complex and brittle. The authors want to know if experience gained under strong harness supervision can be transformed into internal capabilities of the model itself, reducing or shifting the need for external control without sacrificing task performance.
AI.method: They define the objective of "harness internalization," where a model gradually takes over specific control decisions previously provided by the harness. To achieve this, they introduce HARNESS ANNEALING TRAINING (HAT), which combines (1) explicit supervision of control decisions and (2) a curriculum of teacher trajectories produced with progressively weaker harnesses. As training progresses, the external harness assistance is reduced (“annealed”), encouraging the model to assume more control. They evaluate 9B and 35B models on SWE-QA and SWE-QA-Pro, checking every training checkpoint under four different deployment harness configurations to see how well control behavior and task performance are retained as harness support is reduced.
AI.result: For both 9B and 35B models, certain intermediate annealed checkpoints can operate effectively with only tools (minimal harness) while achieving scores close to their respective initial checkpoints that used the full, strong harness. The magnitude of the benefit depends on model size and on the particular deployment harness. However, continuing the annealing process does not monotonically improve performance; after some point, further reduction of harness support during training may degrade results.
AI.conclusion: Harness-supported trajectories can be used not only to improve task skill, but also to teach models to take over parts of the control logic that were previously handled externally. The proposed HAT procedure shows that some harness functionality can be internalized: appropriately chosen checkpoints can run with weaker harnesses and still perform well. Nonetheless, the gains are sensitive to model scale and deployment details, and there are diminishing or even negative returns from excessive annealing, suggesting a need for careful design of curricula and stopping criteria when reducing external control.

title: Grounding Large Language Models in DSGE Simulators for Policy Generation and Forecasting
summary:
Large language models can produce economic policy responses that sound reasonable, but this does not show that their actions are consistent with economic dynamics. We test this by placing an instruction-tuned language model inside six Snowdrop-backed dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) simulators. At each turn, the model observes the economy and a change in economic discourse, selects a bounded policy action, and receives the next simulated state and an economic reward. We implement a common Python interface for repeated rollouts, persistent shocks, state cloning, and rolling-horizon simulation.
  This setting creates a long-horizon credit-assignment problem. Policy effects may appear several quarters after an action is taken. PPO has a learned value function that can propagate delayed reward to earlier tokens through generalized advantage estimation. GRPO has no learned value function and instead assigns a group-relative advantage from complete rollout returns. It therefore cannot distinguish which earlier turn caused the outcome; if every rollout receives the same return, the normalized advantage is zero. We use PPO as the primary method and GRPO as a matched critic-free baseline. The experiments also test directional semantic signals, reward horizon, trajectory warm starts, cross-simulator transfer, and historically anchored pandemic and monetary-policy shocks. The objective is to judge policy actions by their simulated economic consequences rather than by plausible language alone.

AI.tldr: The paper embeds an instruction-tuned large language model as a policy-maker in DSGE macroeconomic simulators to test whether it can learn effective economic policies based on simulated outcomes rather than plausibility of text alone.
AI.motivation: Large language models often give economic policy advice that sounds plausible in natural language, but it is unclear whether these suggestions are consistent with underlying dynamic economic models. There is a need to move beyond linguistic plausibility and evaluate policy quality using formal macroeconomic simulations that capture delayed and complex effects of policy decisions.
AI.method: The authors integrate an instruction-tuned LLM into six Snowdrop-backed DSGE simulators via a unified Python interface that supports repeated rollouts, persistent shocks, state cloning, and rolling-horizon simulation. At each time step, the LLM observes the current economic state and discourse change, chooses a bounded policy action, and receives the resulting next state and scalar reward. They frame this as a long-horizon credit-assignment RL problem and primarily use PPO, which leverages a learned value function and generalized advantage estimation to handle delayed rewards. GRPO, which lacks a value function and uses group-relative advantages from full rollout returns, is used as a critic-free baseline. They also run experiments on directional semantic reward signals, varying reward horizons, warm-starting trajectories, cross-simulator transfer, and historically-inspired shocks like pandemics and monetary policy shifts.
AI.result: PPO can propagate delayed rewards across long horizons and thus can learn from DSGE rollouts which policy actions lead to better simulated economic outcomes, while GRPO struggles with credit assignment when many rollouts obtain similar total returns because its normalized advantage collapses toward zero. The framework enables systematic testing of how well LLM-based policy agents respond to persistent shocks, transfer across different DSGE environments, and perform under various reward shaping and horizon configurations, though the abstract does not give specific numerical performance metrics.
AI.conclusion: Embedding LLMs as decision-making agents in DSGE simulators provides a way to evaluate and train their economic policy behavior based on formal macroeconomic dynamics rather than text plausibility alone. Algorithms with value functions like PPO are better suited to this long-horizon credit-assignment setting than critic-free methods like GRPO. The proposed interface and experiments demonstrate a path toward more rigorous, simulation-based assessment of LLM-generated economic policy recommendations.

title: Evaluating the Robustness of Japanese LLMs to IME-Related and Typographical Errors
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance across various natural language processing tasks. However, their robustness to typographical errors remains underexplored, particularly in Japanese, where text input involves multiple writing systems and IME-based conversion. In this study, we evaluate the robustness of Japanese LLMs against realistic Japanese-specific typos. We introduce five typo categories: Character Transposition, Character Replacement, Homophone Conversion, Japanese IME Conversion, and Full-Width Conversion. These perturbations are applied to three Japanese benchmark datasets (JMMLU, JCommonsenseQA, and JamC-QA), and eleven Japanese and multilingual LLMs are evaluated. The results show that Character Transposition and Character Replacement typos consistently reduce accuracy across benchmarks, whereas IME Conversion, Full-Width Conversion, and Homophone Conversion have relatively limited impact. These findings reveal that current Japanese LLMs remain vulnerable to realistic Japanese typing errors, particularly those that substantially distort the original input, highlighting the importance of robustness evaluation in practical input environments.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how robust Japanese LLMs are to realistic Japanese-specific typos, finding that certain typo types significantly harm performance.
AI.motivation: While LLM robustness to noise has been explored mostly in English, Japanese poses unique challenges due to multiple writing systems and IME-based input. There is a lack of systematic evaluation of Japanese LLM robustness to realistic typing errors common in real-world use.
AI.method: The authors define five realistic Japanese-typing typo categories (Character Transposition, Character Replacement, Homophone Conversion, Japanese IME Conversion, Full-Width Conversion). They automatically inject these perturbations into three Japanese benchmarks (JMMLU, JCommonsenseQA, JamC-QA), then measure the performance degradation of eleven Japanese and multilingual LLMs under each typo type.
AI.result: Character Transposition and Character Replacement typos consistently and substantially lower accuracy across all benchmarks and models. In contrast, IME Conversion, Full-Width Conversion, and Homophone Conversion introduce only modest or limited drops in performance.
AI.conclusion: Japanese LLMs are still vulnerable to realistic Japanese typing errors, especially those that strongly distort the surface form of the input. This underlines the need to evaluate and improve robustness in real, IME-based Japanese input scenarios when designing and deploying LLMs.

title: Auditing Action Settlement in LLM Agent Environments: Order, Progress, and Replay
summary: Concurrent actions in large language model (LLM) agent environments require arbitration even when each proposal is individually valid. We implement a typed snapshot-settlement contract and audit three distinct properties: order sensitivity, useful progress, and replay consistency. Five settlement policies are tested in 28,800 exhaustive permutation trials and 2,160 scripted multistep episodes. Joint policies are spatially order-invariant conditional on fixed priorities, yet conservative rejection completes only 31.25% of agents in a six-agent doorway task versus 90.28% for random tickets; the paired improvement is 59.03 percentage points (95% bootstrap interval: 50.00-68.06). All policies preserve the tested spatial constraints, and priority arbitration still misses the independent small-instance optimum. A separate full-state journal audit exactly replays 156 checkpoints and rejects 1,332 constructed corruptions with a retained terminal anchor. The evidence concerns execution semantics, not human realism or long-run fairness.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to fairly and reliably choose between multiple concurrent action proposals from LLM agents using a formal “snapshot-settlement” mechanism and evaluates several arbitration policies.
AI.motivation: In LLM agent environments, multiple agents or tools may propose concurrent actions that are individually valid but mutually incompatible (e.g., multiple agents trying to pass through a doorway at once). There is a need for principled, auditable execution semantics to arbitrate among these actions while preserving constraints, ensuring progress, and enabling reproducible replays of system behavior.
AI.method: The authors implement a typed snapshot-settlement contract that defines how to choose and apply a subset of proposed actions under spatial and logical constraints. They define and audit three properties of the settlement process: order sensitivity (whether outcome depends on proposal order), useful progress (how often agents achieve their goals), and replay consistency (whether the same sequence can be exactly reproduced). They then instantiate five concrete settlement policies and evaluate them via 28,800 exhaustive permutation trials and 2,160 scripted multistep episodes, including a six-agent “doorway” coordination task. They also build a full-state journal and run a corruption audit across 1,488 cases (156 valid checkpoints and 1,332 synthetic corruptions).
AI.result: Joint policies are spatially order-invariant when priorities are fixed, meaning that reordering actions in space does not change the outcome under the same priorities. However, conservative rejection policies substantially limit task completion (31.25% success in the six-agent doorway task) compared with a random-ticket arbitration policy (90.28% success), giving a 59.03 percentage point improvement (95% bootstrap CI: 50.00–68.06). All tested policies respect the designed spatial constraints, but even priority-based arbitration fails to reach the theoretically optimal solution for small independent instances. The journal-based replay mechanism exactly reproduces all 156 valid checkpoints and successfully detects and rejects 1,332 deliberately corrupted states while maintaining a consistent terminal anchor.
AI.conclusion: The study shows that formal snapshot-settlement contracts can provide constraint-preserving, auditable execution semantics for concurrent LLM agent actions, but the choice of arbitration policy critically affects system-level performance and coordination. Conservative policies may overly sacrifice progress, while random or ticket-based approaches can achieve much higher completion rates without violating constraints. Additionally, robust journaling can guarantee replay consistency and detect corruption. The work focuses on execution semantics and correctness properties, not on simulating human behavior or addressing long-run notions of fairness among agents.

title: Right Answers, Wrong States: Hidden Information Failures in Multi-Agent Collaboration
summary: Multi-agent systems are often judged by whether they reach the correct answer. This can miss a distinct failure: collaboration may leave behind a corrupted information state even when the immediate decision is correct. We call this an off-query failure. To study this failure in collaborative decision support, we introduce OffQuery, which separately evaluates evidence verification (T1), shared-state reconstruction (T2), and task resolution (T3) in two representative high-stakes settings: healthcare and disaster response. Across GPT, Gemini, and Qwen models, standard collaboration shows much stronger task performance than state reliability. Averaged over 21 model--setting combinations, task resolution reaches 64.7%, while evidence verification and state reconstruction reach only 14.3% and 43.1%. We trace this gap to selective information use: current queries often bypass corrupted facts, which become consequential when later tasks require them. We further introduce ReGround, which resolves conflicting evidence, verifies shared facts, reconstructs a trusted state, and reasons over that state. Across seven models from three families, ReGround improves all three capabilities in every evaluated setting, with average relative gains of 309.0%, 82.9%, and 17.6% on T1, T2, and T3. Reliable collaboration therefore requires both a correct decision and a reliable shared state for future reasoning.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that multi-agent systems can appear successful by giving correct answers while still leaving behind corrupted shared information states, and introduces benchmarks (OffQuery) and a method (ReGround) to evaluate and improve this hidden aspect of reliability.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of multi-agent systems focus mainly on whether the final answer to a query is correct. This overlooks a critical failure mode in collaborative settings: agents may agree on a correct solution for the current task while corrupting or failing to maintain a trustworthy shared information state that will be reused later. Such "off-query" failures are especially dangerous in high-stakes domains like healthcare and disaster response, where future decisions may depend on incorrectly stored or unverified facts. The authors aim to define, measure, and mitigate these failures so collaborative AI systems can be trusted not only for single outputs but for ongoing workflows.
AI.method: The authors define and operationalize "off-query failure" in a new evaluation framework, OffQuery, which decomposes collaborative decision support into three stages: (T1) evidence verification, (T2) shared-state reconstruction, and (T3) task resolution. They instantiate this benchmark in two high-stakes domains—healthcare and disaster response—and test a range of large language models (GPT, Gemini, Qwen) in multi-agent collaboration setups. They then introduce ReGround, a procedure that explicitly: (1) resolves conflicting evidence, (2) verifies shared facts, (3) reconstructs a trusted shared state, and (4) reasons over that state. They evaluate ReGround across seven models from three model families on all OffQuery tasks and settings, comparing performance with standard collaboration baselines.
AI.result: In standard multi-agent collaboration settings, models achieve relatively high task resolution performance (T3), with an average of 64.7% accuracy across 21 model–setting combinations. However, they perform much worse on evidence verification (T1) and shared-state reconstruction (T2), which reach only 14.3% and 43.1% on average, respectively. This reveals a large gap between solving the immediate task and maintaining a reliable shared information state. The authors attribute this to selective information use—models often succeed by relying only on a subset of evidence, leaving unverified or corrupted facts in the shared state that later become problematic. When applying ReGround, all three capabilities improve in every evaluated setting: average relative gains of 309.0% on T1, 82.9% on T2, and 17.6% on T3 are reported across seven models from three families.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that evaluating and designing multi-agent systems purely based on final task performance is insufficient and potentially misleading, especially in high-stakes domains. Reliable collaboration requires not just a correct final answer but also a trustworthy, well-maintained shared information state that remains robust for future reasoning. OffQuery provides a structured way to measure off-query failures via evidence verification, state reconstruction, and task resolution, revealing that current systems underperform severely on the first two despite decent task success. The proposed ReGround procedure substantially improves state reliability and also enhances task performance, demonstrating that explicit verification, conflict resolution, and state reconstruction are key ingredients for dependable collaborative decision support systems.

title: ReSolve: Reusing Candidate Reasoning through Selective Generative Moderation
summary: Sampling multiple solutions spends computation on intermediate deductions and unfinished arguments as well as final answers. We introduce ReSolve, a training-free inference procedure that reuses this candidate reasoning through selective generative moderation. An answer-distribution controller invokes a model to examine existing derivations when candidates disagree or lack a parseable answer, then incorporates the generated solution into a bounded loop. Under Hybrid scoring on 130 competition-mathematics problems evaluated with two independently sampled candidate pools, ReSolve obtains 100 and 99 correct answers, compared with 91 and 92 for voting over the same four candidates, with no correct-to-incorrect changes relative to that vote in either pool. Eight-sample self-consistency obtains 94 and 96 correct answers while consuming substantially more tokens; ReSolve uses 46.3% and 47.2% fewer tokens in the two evaluations. A controlled ablation removes visible derivations while retaining answer keys, vote counts, and the per-state output-cap rule, reducing accuracy from 100 to 93 correct despite increasing computation. Selective and always-on Uniform moderation both solve 97 problems, while selectivity reduces moderation tokens by approximately 54% and total pipeline tokens by 6.2%. These results support candidate reasoning as reusable inference computation. They do not establish an accuracy advantage over additional sampling or a distinct benefit from specialized route instructions.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces ReSolve, a training-free inference method that reuses intermediate reasoning from multiple sampled solutions to improve accuracy and efficiency in solving competition math problems.
AI.motivation: Standard multi-sampling strategies (like majority voting or self-consistency) waste computation on intermediate reasoning steps that are discarded, and they can be token-inefficient. The authors want to see whether partial reasoning from candidate solutions can be reused as a form of inference computation, improving performance without extra training or large increases in token use.
AI.method: The authors design ReSolve, an answer-distribution controller that selectively calls a language model to review and moderate existing derivations when candidate solutions disagree or fail to yield a valid answer. The system operates in a bounded loop, where the model examines prior candidate chains-of-thought, generates a new solution conditioned on them, and feeds this back into the candidate pool. They test a Hybrid scoring regime using two independently sampled pools of four candidates each on 130 competition math problems, and compare ReSolve against simple voting, self-consistency with more samples, and ablations that remove access to intermediate reasoning or modify the moderation policy (selective vs always-on Uniform moderation).
AI.result: On the 130-problem benchmark, ReSolve achieves 100 and 99 correct answers on the two candidate pools, versus 91 and 92 for majority voting over the same four candidates. Eight-sample self-consistency gets 94 and 96 correct but uses far more tokens; ReSolve cuts token usage by roughly 46–47% relative to that baseline. An ablation without visible derivations but with access to answer keys and vote counts drops accuracy from 100 to 93 even with more computation, showing the value of reusing reasoning traces. Both selective and always-on Uniform moderation solve 97 problems, but the selective variant uses about 54% fewer moderation tokens and 6.2% fewer total tokens.
AI.conclusion: ReSolve demonstrates that intermediate candidate reasoning can be reused as inference computation to improve accuracy and token efficiency on math problems, relative to simple voting and token-heavy self-consistency, without any additional model training. The experiments indicate that seeing derivations, not just answers and votes, materially contributes to performance. However, the work does not show a clear accuracy benefit over simply increasing sample counts in general, nor a distinct advantage from specialized routing/moderation instructions, so further research is needed to characterize when and how such moderation-based reuse is most beneficial.

title: Science Utopia? Closed-Loop LLM Simulation of Academic Research Ecosystems
summary: Scientific progress emerges from a longitudinal ecosystem in which researchers, institutions, funding agencies, collaboration networks, and the scientific literature co-evolve. As AI becomes increasingly involved throughout the scientific research cycle, understanding these interconnected and evolving processes becomes increasingly important. We introduce SciUtopia, a persistent, closed-loop LLM-agent simulation framework for studying academic research ecosystems. SciUtopia models interconnected scientific processes such as research-direction choice, collaboration, submission, peer review, resubmission, citation, funding, and researcher attrition, while maintaining evolving states across simulated years. Its configurable institutional mechanisms and information channels provide a controlled testbed for matched counterfactual experiments and targeted interventions. Across 61 simulation worlds, SciUtopia simulates over 40,000 researchers from 8,000 institutions, producing around 400,000 publication decisions and 1.2 million LLM-generated peer reviews. Using these longitudinal simulations, we find that rejection-driven resubmission substantially amplifies reviewer burden beyond population growth alone, cautious exploration balances citation impact with career success and long-term topic diversity, and resource inequality can emerge even without detectable cumulative advantage from narrowly winning early funding. Code is available at https://github.com/Ahren09/ScienceUtopia.

AI.tldr: SciUtopia is a large-scale, persistent LLM-agent simulation that models how researchers, institutions, and funding systems co-evolve, enabling controlled experiments on policies in academic ecosystems.
AI.motivation: To understand and evaluate how complex, interdependent components of the scientific ecosystem—researcher decisions, collaboration, peer review, funding, and citations—jointly shape long-term scientific progress, especially as AI increasingly participates in these processes. Traditional empirical studies lack experimental control and counterfactual analysis across decades-long timescales, so a configurable simulation is needed to explore policy interventions and systemic dynamics safely and systematically.
AI.method: The authors build SciUtopia, a closed-loop multi-agent framework where LLM-based agents simulate researchers, reviewers, and institutions over many years. The system explicitly models processes such as choosing research directions, forming collaborations, submitting manuscripts, peer reviewing, resubmitting after rejection, receiving citations, obtaining grants, and dropping out of academia. It maintains evolving states for agents and institutions, and allows configurable institutional rules and information structures to run matched counterfactual experiments. They instantiate 61 different “simulation worlds” with varying policies and conditions, simulating 40,000 researchers from 8,000 institutions, around 400,000 publication decisions, and 1.2M LLM-generated peer reviews.
AI.result: Across the simulated worlds, the authors observe: (1) Rejection-driven resubmission cycles dramatically increase reviewer workload, above what would be expected from growth in researcher numbers alone. (2) A cautious exploration strategy—balancing novel topics with stable, safer directions—optimizes both citation impact and career success, while also maintaining long-run topic diversity. (3) Significant resource inequality can arise even in the absence of strong cumulative advantage from early, marginal funding wins, meaning structural factors alone can generate unequal outcomes.
AI.conclusion: SciUtopia offers a scalable, configurable simulation testbed for studying the long-term behavior of scientific ecosystems and assessing policy interventions. The initial experiments suggest that current norms around resubmission, exploration strategies, and funding allocation can unintentionally increase reviewer burden, shape topic diversity, and generate resource inequality. The framework enables counterfactual analysis of such mechanisms and can inform more balanced, equitable, and efficient designs for future research systems, particularly as AI agents increasingly participate in the scientific process.

title: When Does Exercise-Specific Joint Selection Help? An Audit of Evaluation and Control Design
comment: Exploratory offline audit of subject-disjoint skeleton-based exercise correctness evaluation; 5 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables
summary: Exercise-specific joint selection can improve skeleton-based correctness classification, but what does that gain establish? We audit 1,057 repetitions from ten REHAB24-6 subjects, separating evaluation aggregation, subset structure, and temporal representation. The manual-subset kNN gain changes from 0.055 for pooled out-of-fold AUROC to 0.020 for equal-weight within-person AUROC; both paired intervals include zero. Among 1,000 dimension-matched random maps, 14 match or exceed the manual pooled result, versus 145 when bilateral structure and trunk inclusion are also matched. RBF-SVM retains a positive within-person gain, whereas logistic regression and a random-convolution comparator have negative point gains under that estimand. Sequence-order and paired-seed controls further qualify the interpretation. This exploratory audit shows why joint-selection claims require explicit estimands and structurally appropriate controls; it does not establish a new algorithm or clinical benefit.

AI.tldr: This paper audits whether hand-picked joint subsets genuinely improve correctness classification in skeleton-based exercise analysis, finding small, estimation-dependent gains that often vanish under stricter evaluation and controls.
AI.motivation: Prior work claims that selecting specific joints from skeletal motion data improves classification of exercise correctness, but typically lacks clarity on what performance measure (estimand) is targeted and whether reported gains are robust to appropriate baselines and controls. This paper aims to critically examine those claims rather than propose a new model, clarifying how evaluation choices, subset structure, and temporal representation affect the apparent benefit of joint selection.
AI.method: The authors analyze 1,057 repetitions from ten subjects in the REHAB24-6 dataset. They compare a manually designed joint subset to many random joint maps under several conditions: pooled out-of-fold AUROC versus equal-weight within-person AUROC; different assumptions about subset structure (e.g., bilateral symmetry and trunk inclusion); and different temporal representations. They test multiple classifiers (kNN, RBF-SVM, logistic regression, and a random-convolution baseline) and use controls such as sequence-order shuffling and paired random seeds to isolate the effect of joint selection from confounders. Performance gains are quantified and compared with distributions from 1,000 random, dimension-matched subsets.
AI.result: The reported performance gain from the manual joint subset depends strongly on how performance is aggregated and what structural constraints are imposed. The kNN AUROC gain drops from 0.055 under pooled out-of-fold evaluation to 0.020 under equal-weight within-person evaluation, and in both cases the confidence intervals include zero. When comparing the manual subset against 1,000 random, dimension-matched subsets, 14 random maps match or exceed the manual subset under basic matching, and 145 do so when bilateral structure and trunk inclusion are also matched. RBF-SVM maintains a positive within-person gain for the manual subset, while logistic regression and the random-convolution comparator show negative gains under that estimand. Additional sequence-order and paired-seed controls further limit strong interpretations of the manual subset’s advantage.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that the supposed benefits of manual joint selection in skeleton-based correctness classification are fragile and highly dependent on evaluation choices and control conditions. Small gains can disappear or reverse under more appropriate estimands and structurally matched baselines, indicating that joint-selection claims must be framed with explicit estimands and rigorously controlled comparisons. The work is an exploratory audit rather than a proposal of a new algorithm or demonstration of clinical benefit.

title: Know When to Hold 'em: Correct-Token Retention in Uniform-State Diffusion Language Models
summary: Uniform-state diffusion models (USDMs) can revise any token at any denoising step, which lets them correct their own mistakes, a key advantage over masked diffusion. Self-correction, however, requires both revising incorrect tokens and retaining correct ones, and we show that current USDMs lack the latter. Even under greedy-tail decoding, state-of-the-art USDMs (DUO, UDLM, and uniform-noise SEDD) keep revising 173--270 of 512 positions at every step, and these large, uncoordinated edits collapse sample diversity. A random-token corruption experiment traces this deficit to the models themselves: they reconstruct clean and corrupted tokens with nearly identical accuracy, even though clean tokens are easier targets. A decomposition of the validation NELBO shows that training barely rewards retention: incorrect predictions are heavily penalized at corrupted positions but almost free at clean ones. We propose Correct-Token Retention Regularization (CTR-Reg), a simple but effective auxiliary loss that trains the model to retain tokens left unperturbed by the forward process and requires no change to the sampler. CTR-Reg improves clean-token accuracy by 26.5 percentage points on average across six benchmarks, while leaving corrupted-token accuracy virtually unchanged, and its per-step revisions converge to only 3--11 positions. With just five greedy-tail steps, generative perplexity more than halves under CTR-Reg for all three models while diversity is preserved, and these gains hold across sampling budgets. Our results identify correct-token retention as a key missing ingredient for self-correcting diffusion language models, and demonstrate an effective fix.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies that uniform-state diffusion language models revise too many tokens at each step, harming diversity, and introduces a simple regularization (CTR-Reg) that teaches models to retain already-correct tokens, greatly improving efficiency and quality.
AI.motivation: Uniform-state diffusion models can theoretically self-correct any token at any step, but in practice they constantly revise a large fraction of tokens, even ones that are already correct. This behavior undermines sample diversity and indicates that models are not learning to distinguish clean from corrupted tokens. The authors want to understand why this happens—diagnosing both the models and the training objective—and to design a simple modification that encourages models to preserve correct tokens while still fixing incorrect ones, thereby realizing the promise of self-correcting diffusion language models.
AI.method: 1) Empirically measure how many token positions state-of-the-art USDMs (DUO, UDLM, uniform-noise SEDD) revise at each denoising step under greedy-tail decoding. 2) Run a random-token corruption experiment where some tokens are left clean and others are corrupted, then compare reconstruction accuracy on clean vs corrupted positions to test whether models preferentially retain correct tokens. 3) Decompose the validation NELBO to quantify how the training objective rewards (or fails to reward) correct-token retention at clean positions vs correction at corrupted ones. 4) Propose Correct-Token Retention Regularization (CTR-Reg), an auxiliary loss that explicitly trains the model to keep tokens that were unperturbed by the forward diffusion process, without changing the sampler. 5) Evaluate CTR-Reg across six benchmarks and three USDM architectures, measuring clean-token and corrupted-token accuracy, number of per-step revisions, generative perplexity, and sample diversity under various sampling budgets.
AI.result: Baseline USDMs revise a large number of positions—173–270 out of 512—at every step, which leads to uncoordinated, diversity-collapsing edits. In the random corruption test, models reconstruct clean and corrupted tokens with nearly identical accuracy, showing little preference for retaining already-correct tokens. NELBO decomposition reveals that the standard training objective strongly penalizes errors on corrupted positions but barely penalizes mistakes on clean ones, so retention is weakly incentivized. With CTR-Reg, clean-token accuracy improves by an average of 26.5 percentage points over six benchmarks, while accuracy on corrupted tokens remains essentially unchanged. The number of revised positions per step drops dramatically to only 3–11. Using just five greedy-tail denoising steps, generative perplexity is more than halved for all three tested models and sample diversity is maintained; these improvements persist across different sampling budgets.
AI.conclusion: Correct-token retention is a central but previously missing capability in uniform-state diffusion language models. Standard training objectives do not sufficiently encourage models to preserve uncorrupted tokens, leading to excessive token revisions and reduced diversity. The proposed CTR-Reg auxiliary loss directly addresses this by rewarding retention of clean tokens, substantially improving clean-token accuracy and reducing unnecessary edits without harming corrupted-token correction. As a result, USDMs become more efficient and more diverse generators, showing that explicit retention training is an effective and simple ingredient for truly self-correcting diffusion language models.

title: Federated Agent Optimization
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate in private environments and accumulate valuable experience from task execution, tool use, feedback, and local knowledge. Yet such experience is distributed across organizations and cannot be directly shared because of privacy and proprietary constraints. Conventional federated learning is insufficient for this setting, as agent capabilities extend beyond model parameters to memory, tools, rewards, skills, and structured knowledge. In this paper, we formulate \textbf{Federated Agent Optimization (FAO)}, which studies how distributed agents can collaboratively improve through controlled information exchange while keeping raw data, complete trajectories, and private knowledge local. We define FAO as a multi-objective problem balancing agent utility, privacy leakage, and communication cost, and organize its optimization space across policy, memory, tool use, reward, and structured knowledge and skills. We further characterize how private experience can be abstracted, protected, aggregated, and adapted into transferable capabilities, providing a unified view of how agents can benefit from one another without direct experience sharing. Finally, we identify the key challenges of FAO and outline several promising directions for future research toward trustworthy federated agent systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Federated Agent Optimization (FAO), a framework for enabling multiple LLM-based agents to collaboratively improve while keeping their private data and experiences local.
AI.motivation: LLM agents are increasingly deployed in private, proprietary environments where they gather rich experience (task traces, tool use patterns, feedback, local knowledge). This experience is valuable but cannot be directly shared due to privacy and ownership constraints. Existing federated learning only focuses on model parameters and does not capture the full range of agent capabilities such as memory, tools, rewards, and structured skills. There is a need for a principled way for these agents to learn from each other without exposing raw data or full trajectories.
AI.method: The authors formalize Federated Agent Optimization (FAO) as a multi-objective optimization problem, where multiple distributed agents coordinate to improve their performance while respecting constraints on privacy leakage and communication cost. They decompose the FAO design space along several axes—policy, memory, tool use, reward, and structured knowledge/skills—and propose ways to abstract, protect, aggregate, and adapt private experiences into transferable representations that can be shared among agents. This yields a unified conceptual framework for thinking about what, how, and at what granularity agents should exchange information.
AI.result: The paper does not present empirical benchmark results in the abstract; instead, it offers conceptual results: a formal definition of FAO, a taxonomy of optimization dimensions (policy, memory, tools, rewards, knowledge/skills), and a characterization of mechanisms for converting private experience into shareable, privacy-preserving capabilities. It also systematizes the trade-offs between utility, privacy, and communication in federated agent systems.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that FAO provides a unifying lens for designing collaborative yet privacy-preserving learning schemes for LLM agents whose capabilities go beyond static model parameters. They argue that future research should address open challenges—such as better abstractions for experience, stronger privacy guarantees, and efficient communication protocols—to realize trustworthy federated agent ecosystems where agents can benefit from each other without sharing raw data or full trajectories.

title: What Wins a Vote? Formatting, Length, and Lexical Diversity in the French Compar:IA LLM Arena
summary: LLM arenas turn pairwise human preferences into model rankings. Those preferences may reflect how an answer is presented as well as what it says. We take a stylometric approach to 137,293 decisive French-language votes from the July 2026 Compar:IA release; the primary formatting analysis includes 137,113 battles across 116 models, and the joint estimates use the 127,092 battles with all required measurements. For each battle, we reconstruct the response visible when the user voted. We then compare the raw ranking with rankings adjusted for formatting, length, readability, vocabulary variety, and sentence structure. Presentation is associated with winning, but length, bold text, and lists tend to occur together, making their individual contributions hard to separate. Across the measured features, two associations change least across specifications: bold usage (+11.0% win odds per standard deviation in the joint model) and moving-average type-token ratio (MATTR), a measure of vocabulary variety that is less sensitive to answer length (+16.8%). The bold association is substantially smaller in observed multi-turn conversations, whereas the MATTR association changes little; because users choose whether to continue, this difference is descriptive rather than causal. The full adjustment moves 36 of 116 models by at least ten ranks. Yet comparisons with external benchmarks do not show that adjusted rankings better measure capability. We therefore recommend publishing raw and adjusted rankings side by side as a transparent sensitivity analysis.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how stylistic and formatting features of LLM answers (like bolding, length, and vocabulary variety) influence win rates in a large French-language human-preference arena, and how adjusting for these features changes model rankings.
AI.motivation: LLM leaderboards built from pairwise human preferences may conflate model capability with presentation style: users might prefer answers that look nicer or seem more polished, regardless of their substantive quality. The authors want to quantify how much such stylistic factors bias arena results and whether adjusting for them yields rankings that better reflect underlying model capability.
AI.method: Using 137k+ decisive French-language votes from the Compar:IA July 2026 arena (116 models), the authors reconstruct the exact responses seen by voters. They extract multiple stylometric features—formatting (e.g., bold, lists), length, readability metrics, vocabulary variety (especially MATTR), and sentence structure. They then estimate how each feature is associated with win odds via regression-style joint models and compare raw model rankings with rankings adjusted for these features. They also compare single-turn vs observed multi-turn conversations to see how associations change when users choose to continue or stop.
AI.result: Formatting and presentation correlate with a higher chance of winning, but many features (length, bold, lists) are highly collinear, making it difficult to tease apart individual causal effects. Two features show robust associations across model specifications: bold usage, which raises win odds by ~11% per SD, and MATTR (vocabulary variety), which raises win odds by ~16.8% per SD. In multi-turn conversations, the effect of bold text is much smaller, while the MATTR effect stays similar. Adjusting arena results for all measured features significantly reshuffles rankings; 36 of 116 models move by at least 10 positions. However, comparison to external benchmarks does not show that the adjusted rankings better track true capabilities than the raw rankings.
AI.conclusion: Stylistic and formatting choices meaningfully influence LLM arena outcomes and can materially change model rankings when adjusted for. Yet, because these adjustments do not clearly improve correlation with external capability benchmarks, they should not replace raw rankings. Instead, the authors advocate publishing both raw and style-adjusted rankings as a form of transparent sensitivity analysis, highlighting the degree to which presentation affects perceived model quality without over-interpreting adjusted scores as more accurate measures of capability.

title: Dependency-Aware Reward Shaping for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: When training large language models with reinforcement learning, terminal rewards provide little guidance about which steps matter. Common methods for assigning step credit overlook that work built on uncorrected mistakes is wasted while independent work remains valid. With only a final success/failure reward, every step in a failed episode has zero total future reward, even when it made progress. We propose Dependency-Aware Reward Shaping (DARS), which represents task progress as predicates linked by prerequisite relations and assigns step-level credit over the dependency graph. An annotator marks which predicates each step verifies, invalidates, or repairs. Verified predicates are discounted according to graph distance from the nearest broken prerequisite, while independent predicates are unaffected. Repairs update these weights based on any errors that remain; invalidated predicates need re-verification to regain credit. A fixed potential converts these annotations into signed per-step rewards. A common reward and annotation interface allows DARS to integrate with a range of reasoning and agentic training methods, such as GiGPO and ARPO/AEPO, without changing their rollout strategies or optimizers. Across five task families and models from 1.5B to 8B, DARS improves success by up to 10 points over GiGPO trained with the same budget and harness (ALFWorld), raises the WebShop task score and Search-R1 QA accuracy, complements AEPO's entropy-based training on AIME24/25 with a Python interpreter, and exceeds OmniOPD in controlled tool-free reasoning comparisons at 1.7B and 4B. Ablations show that step-level credit, dependency attenuation, and graph topology each contribute. On ALFWorld, a distilled 8B annotator matches the API annotator, enabling DARS to run efficiently without a frontier judge. Code is available at https://github.com/JianhuiWei7/DARS.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Dependency-Aware Reward Shaping (DARS), a method to assign fine-grained, structure-aware step rewards when training LLM agents with RL, improving performance across several reasoning and agentic benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Standard RL training of language agents often relies on terminal, episode-level rewards (success/failure), which provide no information about which intermediate steps were useful. Existing step-credit methods typically treat all past work in a failed trajectory as equally bad, ignoring that parts of the trajectory may be correct and reusable while other parts rest on earlier mistakes. The authors want a principled way to propagate credit and blame along the logical/prerequisite structure of multi-step tasks so that models are rewarded for genuine progress and penalized for error cascades, thereby improving reasoning and tool-use performance.
AI.method: They propose Dependency-Aware Reward Shaping (DARS). First, they represent task progress as a set of predicates connected via a prerequisite dependency graph. Human or model annotators label each step in a trajectory with which predicates it verifies (achieves), invalidates (breaks), or repairs. For each predicate, DARS maintains a potential value that depends on its status and its graph distance from any broken prerequisites. Verified predicates get discounted credit when they depend—directly or indirectly—on unresolved errors; independent predicates retain full credit. When a step repairs errors, the potentials are updated to reflect restored validity; when it invalidates predicates, those lose credit until reverified. A fixed potential-based shaping scheme transforms these evolving predicate-level potentials into signed, per-step rewards. Because it is implemented as an interface layer (a reward/annotation API), DARS can plug into existing RL training methods (e.g., GiGPO, ARPO/AEPO) without modifying their rollout or optimization algorithms. They also train a distilled 8B annotator model to replace an external API-based annotator, making DARS practical at scale.
AI.result: On a range of benchmarks and model sizes (1.5B–8B parameters), DARS consistently improves agent performance. On ALFWorld, it yields up to a 10 percentage point improvement over GiGPO trained under the same budget and harness. It also increases scores on WebShop and Search-R1 QA, and further improves AEPO’s performance on AIME24/25 when used with a Python interpreter. In controlled, tool-free reasoning experiments, DARS-trained models outperform OmniOPD at 1.7B and 4B parameters.
