Ablation studies show that each key component—step-level credit assignment, dependency-based attenuation, and the explicit dependency graph structure—contributes meaningfully to the gains. Moreover, the distilled 8B annotator achieves parity with a more expensive API annotator on ALFWorld, demonstrating that annotation can be done efficiently without an external frontier judge.
AI.conclusion: DARS offers a general, dependency-aware reward shaping framework for RL training of language model agents. By modeling how intermediate predicates depend on one another and updating their credit as steps verify, break, or repair them, DARS delivers more informative step rewards than episode-level signals or naive shaping. This leads to substantial performance gains across diverse reasoning and agent tasks and integrates cleanly with existing RL algorithms and tool-use setups. The approach scales in practice via a distilled in-house annotator, suggesting it is a practical way to systematically leverage structured progress signals for training stronger reasoning agents.

title: Evaluating Biomedical Reranking for LLM-Based Question Answering over Longitudinal Clinical Notes
summary: Patient-specific clinical question answering requires locating the right evidence within long, heterogeneous longitudinal clinical records in which relevant facts may be scattered across encounters, repeated in copied-forward notes, or expressed using different clinical terminology. We evaluated whether biomedical reranking can improve evidence selection and downstream answer quality in a locally deployed retrieval-augmented generation pipeline for longitudinal clinical notes. The pipeline combines PubMedBERT dense retrieval, BM25 lexical retrieval, weighted reciprocal-rank fusion, and MedCPT cross-encoder reranking. Across 1,000 open- and closed-ended question-answer pairs from a cohort of 200 bariatric surgery patients, reranking increased exact source-chunk retrieval within the top 10 items, Hit@10 from 46.6% to 60.6% and mean reciprocal rank from 0.2371 to 0.3252. With Qwen3-8B generation, local judge-assessed answer correctness increased from 44.8% to 48.6%. These results show that biomedical reranking can improve the placement of relevant clinical evidence within a limited context window, although gains in retrieval do not translate proportionally into gains in answer correctness.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates a retrieval‑augmented generation pipeline for answering patient-specific clinical questions from long longitudinal clinical notes, showing that biomedical reranking substantially improves retrieval quality and modestly improves answer correctness.
AI.motivation: Patient-specific clinical question answering over longitudinal electronic health records is difficult because relevant evidence is sparsely distributed, duplicated, and inconsistently worded across many notes. Existing QA systems struggle to reliably surface the right snippets into the limited context window of LLMs, which undermines answer accuracy and trustworthiness. The authors aim to test whether advanced biomedical retrieval and reranking can better prioritize truly relevant evidence for downstream generation.
AI.method: The authors build a locally deployed retrieval‑augmented generation pipeline for clinical notes. They use a combination of dense retrieval with PubMedBERT embeddings, lexical retrieval with BM25, and weighted reciprocal rank fusion to produce an initial ranked list of candidate text chunks from longitudinal notes. Then they apply MedCPT, a biomedical cross‑encoder, to rerank these candidates (biomedical reranking). They evaluate performance on 1,000 open‑ and closed‑ended clinical question‑answer pairs from 200 bariatric surgery patients, comparing retrieval metrics (Hit@10, MRR) and LLM answer quality (using Qwen3‑8B judged by local annotators) with and without reranking.
AI.result: With biomedical reranking, exact source‑chunk retrieval among the top 10 items improved: Hit@10 increased from 46.6% to 60.6%, and mean reciprocal rank rose from 0.2371 to 0.3252. When feeding these reranked chunks into Qwen3‑8B for answer generation, locally judged answer correctness increased from 44.8% to 48.6%. Thus, reranking produced strong gains in retrieval quality but only modest gains in final QA performance.
AI.conclusion: Biomedical cross‑encoder reranking effectively improves the ranking and early placement of relevant evidence from long, heterogeneous longitudinal clinical notes within a constrained context window. However, improvements in retrieval quality do not linearly translate into proportionate gains in LLM answer correctness, suggesting that further advances in generation models, context utilization, or reasoning are needed to fully capitalize on better evidence selection.

title: Reputation, Strategy, and Emotion Effects on Generative AI Cooperation: A Comparison Across Reasoning and Non-Reasoning Models
summary: As generative AI (Gen AI) systems take on increasingly autonomous roles in economically and socially consequential interactions, understanding their propensity to cooperate -- and the signals that shape this propensity -- has become essential. We examine cooperative behavior in frontier Gen AI models using the iterated prisoner's dilemma, manipulating counterpart reputation (positive, unknown, negative), strategy (extortion vs. generosity), and non-verbal emotional signaling (facial expressions conveying competitive or cooperative appraisals). In a first study with non-reasoning models (Claude 3.5, Gemini 2.0 Flash, GPT-4o), cooperation was systematically shaped by all three factors, paralleling patterns long documented in human behavioral research, though models varied substantially in how heavily each factor was weighted. A second study with reasoning models (Claude 4.6, Gemini 3, GPT-5.2) revealed a more concentrated reliance on strategy and reputation, a near-elimination of the Potemkin effect observed in non-reasoning models (evidenced by near-uniform cooperation in a diagnostic harmony game), and a more conditional role for emotion consistent with a hierarchical cue-weighting strategy rather than a simple loss of social sensitivity. Reasoning models also showed heterogeneous end-game behavior, ranging from sustained cooperation to systematic last-round defection effect, revealing model-specific exploitability profiles with direct practical relevance for deployment in negotiation and other multi-round interactions. Together, these findings characterize Gen AI models as increasingly sophisticated, though heterogeneous, social actors, and underscore the practical value of developing standardized cooperation benchmarks to inform the responsible deployment of Gen AI in interactive, socially consequential settings.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how advanced generative AI models cooperate in repeated social dilemmas, and how reputation, strategy, and emotional signals influence their behavior, comparing non-reasoning and reasoning models.
AI.motivation: As Gen AI systems are increasingly used in real, high-stakes social and economic interactions, it is crucial to know whether and how they cooperate, what social cues they respond to, and how exploitable they are in multi-round settings like negotiation or bargaining. Existing work focuses mostly on capabilities, not on social behavior benchmarks, leaving a gap in understanding their reliability as social actors.
AI.method: The authors use the iterated prisoner’s dilemma as a testbed and systematically manipulate three factors: (1) the counterpart’s reputation (positive, unknown, negative), (2) counterpart’s strategy (extortion vs. generosity), and (3) non-verbal emotional signals via facial expressions indicating competitive vs. cooperative appraisals. They run two main studies: one on non-reasoning models (Claude 3.5, Gemini 2.0 Flash, GPT-4o) and one on more advanced reasoning models (Claude 4.6, Gemini 3, GPT-5.2). They also employ a diagnostic harmony game to detect the “Potemkin effect” (superficial, unprincipled cooperation) and analyze end-game behavior across models.
AI.result: Non-reasoning models showed cooperation patterns shaped by reputation, strategy, and emotion, broadly mirroring human behavioral findings, but with differing weights on each cue across models. Reasoning models placed stronger, more focused weight on strategy and reputation, showed much less Potemkin-style superficial cooperation (as shown by behavior in the harmony game), and used emotional cues more conditionally in a way consistent with hierarchical cue weighting. End-game behavior varied markedly: some models maintained cooperation to the end, while others systematically defected in the final round, implying model-specific exploitability.
AI.conclusion: Frontier Gen AI systems behave as sophisticated but heterogeneous social agents whose cooperation can be reliably influenced by social context variables like reputation, strategic structure, and emotional signaling. Reasoning models, in particular, display more principled, cue-structured behavior and less superficial cooperation, but also distinct exploitability profiles. The authors argue for standardized cooperation benchmarks to guide responsible deployment of Gen AI in negotiations and other socially consequential multi-round interactions.

title: ARCCS: An Automated Regulatory Compliance Checking System
comment: This is the extended version of a paper accepted to EMNLP 2026 (System Demonstrations)
summary: Regulatory compliance checking - deciding whether a target document satisfies the obligations of a regulation - requires interpreting dense legal text, identifying which provisions apply, and grounding each decision in explicit evidence. We present ARCCS, an end-to-end, automated, agentic, and regulation-agnostic Legal NLP system for compliance checking. ARCCS decomposes raw regulatory text into atomic, traceable requirements and evaluates a target document against them using retrieved evidence, confidence scores, and human-interpretable justifications. This design decouples compliance assessment from any fixed regulatory template or predefined rule set, enabling the pipeline to operate over regulations of varying size and structure. We evaluate ARCCS in two complementary settings. First, in a GDPR policy-document evaluation, LLM-based judges find its decisions and justifications legally and evidentially consistent in up to 96.67% of the assessed cases. Second, on an EU public-procurement benchmark comprising more than 1,200 individual rule checks, the system attains 98.8% accuracy in violation detection. ARCCS is, to our knowledge, the first fully open-source system for end-to-end regulatory compliance checking and auditable report generation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ARCCS, an automated, open-source Legal NLP system that checks regulatory compliance by decomposing regulations into atomic requirements and testing documents against them with evidence-backed justifications, achieving high accuracy on GDPR and EU procurement benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Regulatory compliance checking is complex and labor-intensive because it requires interpreting dense legal text, deciding which rules apply, and justifying each decision with explicit evidence in the target document. Existing systems are often tied to specific regulations or fixed rule templates, which limits scalability and adaptability. The authors aim to build a general, regulation-agnostic, automated system that can both assess compliance and provide auditable, human-readable rationales.
AI.method: The authors design ARCCS, an end-to-end, agentic Legal NLP pipeline. It first decomposes raw regulatory text into atomic, traceable requirements. Then, for a given target document, it retrieves relevant evidence spans and evaluates compliance for each requirement, producing confidence scores and human-interpretable justifications. The architecture is regulation-agnostic, meaning it does not rely on predefined templates or rule sets for any specific regulation, and instead operates directly on the regulatory text itself.
AI.result: On a GDPR policy-document evaluation, ARCCS’s decisions and justifications are rated by LLM-based judges as legally and evidentially consistent in up to 96.67% of cases. On an EU public-procurement benchmark with over 1,200 rule checks, ARCCS achieves 98.8% accuracy in violation detection, demonstrating strong performance and reliability across different regulatory domains.
AI.conclusion: ARCCS provides a general, open-source, end-to-end solution for regulatory compliance checking that is not bound to any specific regulation or fixed rule template. By decomposing regulations into atomic requirements and grounding each compliance decision in retrieved evidence and explanations, it enables auditable, high-accuracy compliance assessment across diverse regulatory texts. The system sets a new baseline for automated, transparent legal compliance checking and report generation.

title: HHR: Hierarchical Hash Retrieval for Efficient LLM Generation
summary: Efficient long-context inference is essential for large language models (LLMs), yet it poses a severe computational bottleneck. Hash-based retrieval offers an efficient alternative by encoding queries and keys into binary codes and using Hamming distance for key selection. However, this leads to a critical mismatch between Hamming distance and attention relevance. Query-Key logits depend jointly on directional similarity and feature magnitudes, whereas hash binarization discards magnitude information, causing both false-positive retrieval of low-logit keys and false-negative omission of high-logit keys. To address these failures, we propose Hierarchical Hash Retrieval (HHR), a coarse-to-fine framework that progressively improves retrieval accuracy through Geometry-Aware Key Routing (GKR) and Learned Hash Projection (LHP). GKR learns a head-wise orthogonal transformation to redistribute feature magnitudes and derive more discriminative page-level logit bounds, enabling effective pruning of low-logit keys while preserving important candidates. LHP then learns a head-wise projection space that aligns Hamming distance with the true Query-Key relevance ranking for fine-grained retrieval. By combining GKR and LHP, HHR suppresses false positives and recovers false negatives, substantially improving the fidelity of hash-based sparse attention. Extensive experiments across diverse LLMs and benchmarks demonstrate that HHR achieves superior performance over existing methods. For example, on LongBench, HHR improves the average score by 1.10 points and, at a context length of 128K, achieves up to a 3.30x decoding speedup and a 2.83x end-to-end speedup for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/lianjunl13-sudo/HHR.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Hierarchical Hash Retrieval (HHR), a two-stage, geometry-aware hashing framework that makes hash-based sparse attention much more faithful to true attention scores, significantly accelerating long-context LLM inference with minimal accuracy loss.
AI.motivation: Long-context inference in LLMs is computationally expensive because attention scales quadratically with context length. Hash-based retrieval can reduce this cost by selecting a small subset of tokens via binary hashing and Hamming distances, but current methods misalign with true attention relevance because they ignore feature magnitudes, causing both false positives (unimportant keys retrieved) and false negatives (important keys missed). The authors aim to design a hash-based retrieval mechanism that better matches real Query-Key logits, so that long-context LLMs can be sped up without hurting quality.
AI.method: The authors introduce Hierarchical Hash Retrieval (HHR), a coarse-to-fine retrieval framework with two core components: (1) Geometry-Aware Key Routing (GKR), which learns a head-wise orthogonal transformation of key representations to better distribute feature magnitudes. This enables computing tight page-level logit bounds and pruning pages that cannot contain high-relevance keys, while preserving likely important ones. (2) Learned Hash Projection (LHP), which learns a head-wise projection into a hash space where Hamming distance is aligned with the true Query-Key relevance ranking. GKR first routes queries to promising key pages; then within these candidates, LHP performs fine-grained hash-based retrieval to select keys for attention. This hierarchy suppresses false positives and recovers false negatives typical in naïve hashing.
AI.result: Across multiple LLMs and long-context benchmarks, including LongBench, HHR consistently outperforms existing hash-based sparse attention methods in task performance at similar or better speedups. For Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct at 128K context length, HHR achieves up to 3.30x decoding speedup and 2.83x end-to-end speedup while improving LongBench average score by 1.10 points compared with baselines. These results indicate that HHR yields both higher retrieval fidelity and substantial practical acceleration for long-context inference.
AI.conclusion: HHR demonstrates that careful modeling of geometry and magnitudes in the attention space can substantially improve hash-based sparse attention. By combining geometry-aware page routing with a learned hash projection aligned to attention relevance, the method greatly reduces mismatches between Hamming distance and true Query-Key logits, leading to fewer retrieval errors. This enables efficient long-context LLM inference with strong accuracy, suggesting that learned, hierarchical hashing is a promising direction for scalable attention mechanisms.

title: Does AI-Generated Scientific Text Follow Human Argumentation Patterns? A CARS-Based Comparison of Research Article Introductions
summary: Large language models are moving from helping write up research to helping do it, which makes it important to know how the scientific text they produce differs from human writing. Work on this question has stayed mostly at the surface, using lexical and stylistic cues that light paraphrasing erases. We look instead at rhetorical structure, the sequence of argumentative moves through which a text makes its case. We study research-article introductions under Swales' CARS model, and compare original introductions from published linguistics articles with generated counterparts of the same papers. We find that human-written introductions are more flexible in which moves they use and in what order, while the generated ones are more uniform. Giving the models the CARS definitions makes them more rigid.

AI.tldr: The paper compares the rhetorical structure of human-written and LLM-generated research article introductions, finding humans are more flexible and models more uniform and rigid, especially when guided by explicit rhetorical schemes.
AI.motivation: As large language models shift from assisting with writing to assisting with scientific reasoning and research, it becomes crucial to understand whether and how their scientific prose systematically differs from human writing, beyond superficial lexical or stylistic features that can be easily mimicked or obfuscated by paraphrasing.
AI.method: The authors analyze the rhetorical structure of research-article introductions in linguistics using Swales' CARS (Create A Research Space) model. They compare original introductions from published linguistics articles to LLM-generated introductions for the same papers, examining which rhetorical moves are used and in what sequence, and also test the effect of explicitly providing the CARS move definitions to the models.
AI.result: Human-written introductions display greater flexibility and diversity in both the selection and ordering of CARS moves, whereas LLM-generated introductions tend to follow more uniform, stereotyped patterns. When models are explicitly given CARS definitions as guidance, their outputs become even more rigid and formulaic in their rhetorical structure.
AI.conclusion: Rhetorically, LLM-generated research introductions lack the structural flexibility characteristic of human writing and instead adhere to a more constrained, template-like use of argumentative moves, a tendency that is reinforced when models are guided by explicit rhetorical frameworks such as CARS.

title: Learning to Ask: Information Acquisition for SLM-LLM Collaboration, under a budget
summary: Collaboration between a small language model (SLM) and a large language model (LLM) offers an opportunity to combine the efficiency of smaller models with the strong reasoning capabilities of larger ones. Existing approaches primarily frame such collaboration as a computation allocation problem, determining which model should handle each portion of the reasoning process. In black-box API-based settings, however, this paradigm can be inefficient due to coarse-grained delegation or repeated transmission of context across model switches. In this work, we instead formulate SLM-LLM collaboration as an information acquisition problem, under an API budget constraint. The SLM remains the primary reasoner and selectively queries a black-box LLM advisor only when needed, issuing targeted queries rather than delegating the reasoning process itself. To realize this strategy, we develop a three-stage RLVR framework that learns whether to call the advisor, how to formulate useful queries, and how to integrate the collaboration into the reasoning process by jointly refining advisor invocation and information use. Across mathematical reasoning and coding tasks, our approach improves the performance--cost tradeoff over existing collaboration baselines and, in some settings, matches or exceeds oracle problem-level routing. Finally, we show that our strategy can transfer to other advisor model families, without further training.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a collaboration framework where a small language model (SLM) is the main reasoner and selectively queries a large language model (LLM) advisor, improving performance-cost tradeoffs under API budget constraints.
AI.motivation: To combine the efficiency of small language models with the strong reasoning capabilities of large language models in black-box API settings, while avoiding inefficiencies from coarse-grained delegation and repeated context transmission.
AI.method: They reframe SLM-LLM collaboration as an information acquisition problem under an API budget. They introduce a three-stage RLVR framework that learns: (1) whether to call the LLM advisor, (2) how to craft targeted, useful queries, and (3) how to integrate the advisor’s information into the SLM’s reasoning by jointly refining advisor invocation and usage.
AI.result: On mathematical reasoning and coding benchmarks, the proposed method achieves a better performance–cost tradeoff than existing collaboration baselines and, in some cases, performs as well as or better than oracle-level routing that selects the best model per problem.
AI.conclusion: Selective, query-based collaboration where an SLM remains the primary reasoner and calls a black-box LLM advisor only when needed is an effective and general strategy, improving efficiency and sometimes matching oracle routing, and it can transfer across different advisor model families without retraining.

title: LLM-Assisted Discovery of Typed Semantic Links for Ontology Network Construction
summary: Constructing typed, justified semantic links between ontologies is essential for enabling interoperability across heterogeneous and interdisciplinary knowledge domains. However, manually curating such links is difficult to scale. To address this challenge, we propose an end-to-end framework for ontology network construction that automates the discovery and generation of both intra-domain and inter-domain relationships. Our approach combines domain-adapted DistilBERT embeddings for dense contextual representation, clustering-based pre-filtering to reduce the candidate search space, and GPT-4o-driven relationship generation via iterative prompt engineering to produce semantically rich, interpretable links. Applied to ReproduceMeON - a network of 33 ontologies spanning machine learning, microscopy, computational science, and experimental workflow - the pipeline reduces approximately 800k raw concept pairs to 95k high-quality candidates. Human expert validation of 429 generated relationships by two independent annotators yields an overall precision of 80.19% (91.49% on high-certainty annotations) and an F1 of 0.890, with substantial inter-annotator agreement. Comparative experiments against five similarity-based baselines, including Sentence-BERT, show a substantial performance gap (best baseline F1 = 0.581), while an ablation study demonstrates that similarity-based methods alone fail to discriminate valid from invalid relationships (AUC approx 0.5) on the filtered candidate set. These findings highlight the necessity of LLM-based reasoning over concept roles and domain semantics for accurate relationship construction.

AI.tldr: An automated framework builds semantic links between ontologies using embeddings, clustering, and GPT-4o, achieving substantially better precision and F1 than similarity-only baselines.
AI.motivation: Interoperability across heterogeneous, interdisciplinary knowledge domains requires typed, well-justified semantic links between ontologies. Manual curation of such links is labor-intensive and does not scale to large ontology networks. Existing similarity-based methods struggle to capture nuanced domain semantics and concept roles, leading to noisy or shallow ontology alignments. There is a need for an automated, scalable method that can discover and generate rich intra- and inter-domain relationships with high precision and interpretability.
AI.method: The authors propose an end-to-end pipeline for ontology network construction that: (1) learns dense contextual representations of ontology concepts using domain-adapted DistilBERT; (2) applies clustering-based pre-filtering to drastically reduce the set of candidate concept pairs from hundreds of thousands to a smaller, more promising subset; and (3) uses GPT-4o, guided by iterative prompt engineering, to infer and generate typed, semantically rich relationships between candidate concept pairs. The framework is evaluated on ReproduceMeON, a network of 33 ontologies across several scientific domains. Comparative experiments with five similarity-based baselines (e.g., Sentence-BERT) and ablation studies assess both performance and the contribution of each component.
AI.result: On the ReproduceMeON ontology network, the pipeline reduces around 800,000 raw concept pairs to 95,000 filtered candidates. From these, 429 GPT-4o-generated relationships are manually evaluated by two independent human experts. The system achieves an overall precision of 80.19%, which increases to 91.49% for high-certainty annotations, and an F1-score of 0.890, with substantial inter-annotator agreement, indicating reliable labeling. Baseline similarity-based approaches perform markedly worse, with the best F1-score reaching only 0.581. An ablation study shows that similarity scores alone cannot distinguish valid from invalid relationships in the filtered set, with an AUC of about 0.5, essentially equivalent to random guessing.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that constructing accurate, typed semantic relationships between ontologies at scale requires more than vector similarity: it needs LLM-based reasoning over concept roles and domain semantics. The proposed framework, which integrates domain-adapted embeddings, clustering-based filtering, and GPT-4o reasoning, substantially outperforms similarity-based baselines and yields high-quality, interpretable ontology links. This approach offers a scalable path toward richer, more interoperable ontology networks across heterogeneous scientific domains and suggests that large language models are crucial components for future ontology alignment and network construction methods.

title: Revision-Aware Independent Agent Graphs for Dynamic Reasoning
summary: Conventional reasoning protocols present a fixed, preselected task, so they cannot test whether an agent propagates relevant updates, preserves unaffected work, or reconstructs a historical task binding. We therefore study \emph{dynamic task routing}, in which an event stream revises task bindings and a system must select the document version valid at each query time before solving it. To study this problem, we repurpose six widely used benchmarks: MMLU, MMLU-Pro, MedMCQA, MATH, GPQA, and HumanEval into 31{,}119 dynamic episodes comprising 373{,}428 temporally categorized queries. This setting exposes a central trade-off: recomputing after every event wastes work, whereas unguarded reuse returns stale conclusions. We introduce the Revision-Aware Independent Agent Graph (RIAG), a bounded multi-agent policy that separates deterministic temporal resolution from task reasoning. RIAG caches solutions by immutable document identity, starts each fresh task with two unexposed attempts, and conditionally invokes audit and repair, using at most four calls per document version. On this collection, homogeneous RIAG achieves 54.24\% joint routing-and-answer accuracy at 0.62 calls/query, compared with 32.22\% at 18.00 calls/query for the strongest comparison method; heterogeneous RIAG reaches 49.78\% at 0.63 calls/query.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces and evaluates a new benchmark setting and method for "dynamic task routing" where tasks change over time, requiring models to pick the right document version before answering.
AI.motivation: Existing reasoning benchmarks assume fixed tasks and cannot measure whether an AI system correctly updates its reasoning when information changes, avoids redoing unaffected work, or maintains consistent task bindings over time. There is a need to evaluate and improve systems that operate over evolving information streams.
AI.method: The authors define the dynamic task routing problem, then transform six standard benchmarks (MMLU, MMLU-Pro, MedMCQA, MATH, GPQA, HumanEval) into 31,119 dynamic episodes with 373,428 time-stamped queries. They propose RIAG (Revision-Aware Independent Agent Graph), a bounded multi-agent policy that decouples temporal resolution from task reasoning, caches solutions by immutable document IDs, allocates two initial attempts per new task, and selectively applies audit-and-repair, with a cap of four calls per document version.
AI.result: On the constructed dynamic benchmark collection, a homogeneous RIAG configuration attains 54.24% joint accuracy on both routing and answering while averaging 0.62 model calls per query, outperforming a strong baseline that gets 32.22% accuracy but requires 18 calls per query. A heterogeneous RIAG variant achieves 49.78% accuracy at 0.63 calls per query.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic task routing reveals a crucial trade-off between recomputing after every update and naively reusing past work. RIAG offers an efficient, bounded-call strategy that better balances accuracy and computation by making revision-aware routing decisions and reusing cached solutions appropriately in evolving information settings.

title: SHAMS: An Audio-Grounded Pronunciation Benchmark for Levantine Arabic
comment: Accepted to ArabicNLP 2026. Project page: https://shams-nlp.github.io/
summary: Levantine Arabic (LA) is spoken by tens of millions of people, creating a pressing need for shared benchmarks to evaluate LA speech-language technologies. Evaluating such technology is particularly challenging given LA's internal diversity and its opaque and non-standardized orthography. We present SHAMS (SHami Annotated Multi-dialect Speech), a benchmark comprising 1,300 utterances drawn from open audio corpora, balanced across five LA varieties (Urban and Rural Palestinian, and Urban Jordanian, Lebanese, and Syrian). Each utterance is represented across four aligned tiers: audio, unvocalized orthography, diacritized text, and phonetic transcription. This structure supports evaluation of various downstream tasks such as diacritization, grapheme-to-phoneme conversion, automatic speech recognition, and audio-to-phoneme, grounded in audio and stratified by variety. We benchmark open and proprietary models across these tasks to demonstrate the utility of this benchmark for measuring progress across LA. We release SHAMS at https://shams-nlp.github.io .

AI.tldr: SHAMS is a multi-dialect Levantine Arabic speech benchmark that provides aligned audio, orthography, diacritized text, and phonetic transcriptions for 1,300 utterances across five varieties, enabling systematic evaluation of multiple speech and text tasks.
AI.motivation: There is a growing need to evaluate speech and language technologies for Levantine Arabic, which is spoken by tens of millions but lacks standardized orthography and exhibits substantial internal dialect diversity. Existing resources are insufficient for consistent benchmarking across dialects and tasks, making it difficult to track progress and compare models.
AI.method: The authors construct SHAMS by selecting 1,300 utterances from open audio corpora and balancing them across five Levantine Arabic varieties (Urban and Rural Palestinian, and Urban Jordanian, Lebanese, and Syrian). For each utterance, they create four aligned annotation tiers: (1) audio, (2) unvocalized orthography, (3) diacritized text, and (4) phonetic transcription. They then design evaluation setups for several downstream tasks—diacritization, grapheme-to-phoneme (G2P) conversion, automatic speech recognition (ASR), and audio-to-phoneme—and run both open and proprietary models to establish baseline performance.
AI.result: The outcome is SHAMS, a publicly released benchmark dataset that is carefully balanced across five Levantine Arabic dialects and richly annotated at four aligned representation levels. The authors provide baseline evaluations of multiple open-source and proprietary systems on diacritization, G2P, ASR, and audio-to-phoneme tasks, showing that SHAMS can effectively differentiate model performance across dialects and task types.
AI.conclusion: SHAMS offers a unified, multi-dialect, multi-task benchmark for Levantine Arabic that addresses challenges posed by dialect variation and non-standard orthography. By releasing the dataset and initial baselines, the authors enable systematic, comparable evaluation of speech and language technologies for Levantine Arabic and support future progress in this under-resourced language variety.

title: DeFA: Dependency-Guided Failure Attribution for LLM Agents
comment: DeFA: Dependency-Guided Failure Attribution for LLM Agents
summary: Errors in LLM agent executions and their visible consequences can be separated by many steps, making decisive-error localization a matter of understanding both step content and step dependencies. We introduce DeFA, a dependency-guided framework for agent failure attribution. DeFA first combines protocol relations and semantic dependencies into an event dependency graph spanning the trajectory. It then identifies events that may violate task requirements and traces their sources and subsequent effects to construct a failure propagation graph. Finally, DeFA uses step evidence and the steps' roles in failure propagation to identify the decisive error, responsible agent, and error category. To support long trajectories, DeFA partitions executions into segments and combines the current segment's detailed content with summaries of the other segments, giving local diagnosis access to global execution context. Across Who and When and the Who and When Pro text subset, DeFA achieves the highest responsible-agent and exact step accuracy with all evaluated backbones, and the highest failure-mode accuracy among taxonomy-aligned methods on Pro. Further experiments on image and video trajectories demonstrate its applicability to multimodal failure attribution. Ablations support the contributions of segmentation, the event dependency graph, and the failure propagation graph. Using DeFA's diagnostic feedback for skill evolution in Trace2Skill improves downstream task accuracy by 6-15 percentage points over the native pipeline, showing that the diagnoses can also support agent improvement on subsequent tasks.

AI.tldr: A framework, DeFA, for tracing and attributing failures in LLM agent executions using dependency graphs and segmentation to locate decisive errors, responsible agents, and error types, and to improve future performance.
AI.motivation: In complex LLM agent trajectories, errors and their visible consequences can be separated by many steps and spread across modalities. This makes it difficult to understand which specific step, agent, or skill is truly responsible for a failure, which in turn hinders debugging, evaluation, and systematic improvement of agent systems. Existing methods often ignore detailed step dependencies, lack scalable handling of long trajectories, or do not provide structured, actionable failure attributions.
AI.method: The paper proposes DeFA, a dependency-guided framework for agent failure attribution. DeFA first constructs an event dependency graph by combining protocol relations (e.g., tool calls, responses) with semantic dependencies between steps across the entire trajectory. It then detects events that may violate task requirements and traces backward and forward along the graph to build a failure propagation graph that captures sources, propagation paths, and downstream effects of errors. Using step-level evidence and each step’s role in this propagation, DeFA identifies the decisive error step, the responsible agent, and an error category. To scale to long trajectories, executions are segmented, with each segment analyzed using its detailed local content plus summaries of other segments, maintaining global context while limiting complexity. The framework is tested on textual benchmarks (Who and When, and the Pro subset) and multimodal (image and video) trajectories with different backbone models. Ablation studies remove key components—segmentation, event dependency graph, failure propagation graph—to quantify their contributions. Finally, DeFA’s diagnostic outputs are plugged into Trace2Skill to guide skill evolution and pipeline updates.
AI.result: On the Who and When and Pro text benchmarks, DeFA attains the best performance among evaluated methods in identifying the responsible agent and the exact erroneous step, with all backbone models. On Pro, among methods aligned to the same error taxonomy, it also yields the highest failure-mode (error-type) classification accuracy. Experiments on image and video-based trajectories show that DeFA generalizes beyond text to multimodal agent executions. Ablation experiments demonstrate that removing segmentation, the event dependency graph, or the failure propagation graph significantly degrades attribution performance, confirming each component’s importance. When DeFA’s diagnostic feedback is used within Trace2Skill to drive skill evolution, downstream task accuracy improves by 6–15 percentage points over the original Trace2Skill pipeline.
AI.conclusion: DeFA offers an effective, scalable approach to diagnosing and attributing failures in complex, possibly multimodal LLM agent executions. By explicitly modeling protocol and semantic dependencies, and by tracing how errors propagate through an event dependency graph, DeFA can pinpoint decisive errors, responsible agents, and error modes more accurately than prior approaches. Segmentation with global-context summaries enables handling long trajectories without losing important cross-segment information. The framework not only improves failure attribution metrics across diverse benchmarks but also provides actionable diagnostics that, when integrated into a skill-evolution pipeline like Trace2Skill, materially enhance subsequent task performance. This suggests that structured failure analysis can be a key component in building more reliable and improvable agentic systems.

title: Generalization Is Stability, Not Accuracy: Multi-Axis Evaluation of LLMs
comment: Accepted at the TAE (Trust-AI-Eval) Workshop: Can We Trust AI Evaluation?, NeurIPS 2026
summary: Generalization in large language models (LLMs) is the ability to produce consistent and semantically stable outputs when the same input is expressed in different ways. Existing work typically evaluates generalization through aggregate accuracy on a single prompt format, task, or set of variations, which conflates robustness with overall benchmark performance. In this work, we show generalization evaluation at the level of individual examples, across multiple input variants, and across different aspects of model behavior, focusing on variability rather than reducing performance to a score that can be improved through narrow training or other ways that obfuscate generalization evaluation. Following this view, we introduce the Stability-Aware Generalization Objective (SAGO), a framework that measures how much model behavior changes for the same input under different variations and benchmarks, capturing variability across several dimensions including generation consistency, internal activations, confidence, and response mirroring. We show that many commonly used models exhibit statistically significant and consistent generalization instability: no model generalizes uniformly, behavioral axes capture independent failure modes, and cross-dataset variation can reverse model rankings.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SAGO, a framework to evaluate how consistently large language models behave across different rephrasings and settings of the same input, focusing on variability rather than just average accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of LLM generalization largely use aggregate accuracy on a single prompt format or limited variations, which mixes up robustness with overall performance. This makes it easy to hide or overfit away generalization problems and fails to reveal how models behave on a per-example basis or across different aspects of behavior. The authors aim to expose and quantify these hidden instabilities in a systematic way.
AI.method: They define a Stability-Aware Generalization Objective (SAGO) that evaluates LLMs at the level of individual examples across multiple input variants and benchmarks. SAGO measures how much a model’s behavior changes under different variations along several axes: output generation consistency, internal activations, confidence, and response mirroring. Rather than collapsing behavior into a single score, they analyze variability patterns and failure modes along these dimensions.
AI.result: Using SAGO on many commonly used models, they find statistically significant and systematic generalization instabilities. Models fail to generalize uniformly across examples and variations; different behavioral axes reveal independent failure modes; and model rankings can flip when evaluated on different datasets or variation settings, indicating that traditional single-score benchmarks can be misleading.
AI.conclusion: Generalization in LLMs cannot be reliably characterized by aggregate scores on single prompts or benchmarks. Stability must be evaluated per-example and across multiple behavioral dimensions. SAGO provides a framework to do this and reveals that current models exhibit substantial and structured instability, challenging the assumption that higher benchmark scores imply robust generalization.

title: Feedback Without the Wait: Piloting a Generative AI Practice Platform in a Large Maths Class
summary: Timely and specific feedback is one of the strongest influences on student learning, yet it is difficult to sustain in large electrical engineering classes where the ratio of students to demonstrators is high and a learner who is stuck may wait days to find out why an approach was wrong. Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) offers a way to scale conversational feedback, but using it to grade assessed work raises trust and accountability concerns, and keeping a human in the loop to assure its judgements reintroduces the very delay that erodes the value of feedback. The result is a tension between the immediacy that makes feedback so impactful and the human oversight that makes it trustworthy. In this work, we set out to resolve that tension in practice by designing and piloting a GenAI practice platform that delivers immediate, scaffolded feedback during self-directed practice. This relocates human oversight from real-time grading to the upfront verification of solutions. Our goal was to understand how students engaged with the tool, how they perceived the value and reliability of its feedback, and what lessons transfer to other engineering subjects.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a GenAI-based practice platform that gives immediate, scaffolded feedback to students in large electrical engineering classes, aiming to combine fast feedback with trustworthy oversight by shifting human involvement to upfront solution verification.
AI.motivation: In large electrical engineering classes, providing timely, specific feedback is difficult due to high student-to-demonstrator ratios. Students can wait days to understand why their solutions are wrong, diminishing the learning impact of feedback. While generative AI can scale conversational feedback, using it directly for grading raises trust and accountability issues, and having humans check AI judgements reintroduces delays. The authors are motivated to resolve this tension between the need for immediate feedback and the requirement for trustworthy, human-verified assessment.
AI.method: The authors designed and piloted a generative AI-powered practice platform that provides immediate, scaffolded feedback to students during self-directed practice. Instead of using AI for summative grading, they shift human oversight to the upfront verification of correct solutions that the AI relies on when giving feedback. They then study how students engage with the tool, how they perceive its value and the reliability of its feedback, and consider how the approach could generalize to other engineering subjects.
AI.result: From the abstract alone, precise empirical results are not specified; however, the study appears to have generated observations about student engagement patterns with the GenAI platform, their perceived value of the immediate feedback, and their trust in the AI-generated guidance. The results likely include insights into how well this oversight-shift model works in practice and what factors influence students’ acceptance of AI feedback in engineering education.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that it is possible to partially resolve the tension between immediacy and trust in feedback by using a GenAI practice platform where human experts verify solutions in advance rather than overseeing every grading decision in real time. This configuration enables scalable, immediate, and scaffolded feedback while maintaining a degree of human assurance. The authors also derive lessons and design implications that can inform the application of similar GenAI feedback systems across other engineering disciplines.

title: When Does a Second Model Help? Cross-Model Review in LLM Verification
comment: 15 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables. Follow-up to arXiv:2603.12123 and arXiv:2603.21454
summary: Large language models now generate code, documentation, and analyses, and are increasingly used to review such output. We ask when a second review by a different model helps. Building on the author's earlier preprints, which varied context, repetition, and role structure within one model, we test model independence in a controlled experiment: 30 artifacts with 150 planted errors, 10 review conditions, and 900 review sessions with three reviewer models from two developers. In this experiment, (1) a top-tier cross-model reviewer is not significantly different in F1 from same-model review in a fresh session (CCR), which does not establish equivalence; (2) the two find partly different errors (Jaccard 41.2%); and (3) at two review calls, one CCR plus one cross-model review matches more planted errors than two CCR reviews (56.7% vs. 42.7%; Holm-adjusted p=.006), but not significantly more than two reviews by the top-tier cross-model reviewer, so model difference and reviewer capability are not separated. A lightweight cross-model reviewer scores no higher than same-model review. Withholding requirements from the reviewer raises F1 for the two lower tiers but not the top tier, in untested point estimates whose pattern depends on how failed sessions are scored. Before analysis we audited all session records, excluding one baseline run of uncertain provenance and 14 failed calls; results with all sessions are also reported. A partial check on public detector outputs from another benchmark neither replicates nor contradicts the main comparison. Records, artifacts, and scripts are available from the author on request.

AI.tldr: The paper experimentally studies how much benefit you get from having a second, independent LLM review code/documentation outputs, especially when that second reviewer is a different model, and finds that cross-model review catches somewhat different errors and can improve overall error detection, but the gains are entangled with differences in model quality.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are now used both to generate and to review technical artifacts (like code or analyses), practitioners often chain multiple reviews, sometimes with different models, hoping to catch more errors. However, it is unclear when a second review, particularly from a different model, genuinely adds value beyond simply calling the same model again, and how much of any benefit is due to model diversity vs. raw model capability. The paper aims to provide controlled, quantitative evidence on these questions.
AI.method: The author constructs a controlled benchmark: 30 artifacts seeded with 150 known (planted) errors. They run 900 review sessions across 10 review conditions using three reviewer models from two different developers (varying tier/capability). Conditions include: same-model re-review in a fresh session; cross-model review by a stronger external model; lightweight cross-model review; and variations in whether task requirements are shown to the reviewer. They measure error detection using F1, Jaccard overlap of found errors, and compare configurations like two same-model reviews vs. mixed same/cross-model reviews, using statistical tests with Holm adjustment. They also audit all session logs, exclude questionable or failed runs, and report robustness checks including a partial comparison with public detector outputs from another benchmark.
AI.result: (1) A strong cross-model reviewer has similar F1 to a fresh same-model review (CCR), without proving full equivalence. (2) The two reviewers detect overlapping but only partially coincident error sets (Jaccard 41.2%), showing some diversity in what they catch. (3) When using two review calls, combining one CCR and one cross-model review finds significantly more planted errors (56.7%) than two CCR reviews (42.7%; Holm-adjusted p = .006), but not significantly more than two calls of the top-tier cross-model reviewer alone, so the effect of model diversity cannot be cleanly separated from higher reviewer capability. A lightweight cross-model reviewer does not outperform same-model review. Hiding requirements unexpectedly raises F1 for lower-tier reviewers (but not the top tier), though these are untested estimates and sensitive to how failed sessions are handled. Including previously excluded runs does not qualitatively change the reported comparisons. A partial external check with public detectors on another benchmark neither confirms nor rejects the main finding.
AI.conclusion: Using a second LLM reviewer can increase error detection, and cross-model diversity leads to partly complementary error coverage. However, the primary determinant of performance appears to be reviewer capability rather than mere model difference: a strong single reviewer model can rival or match mixed-review setups. Lightweight cross-model reviewers provide little benefit over same-model review. The nuanced effects of prompt information (e.g., withholding requirements) and handling of failed sessions suggest that practical review pipelines should be carefully tuned and audited rather than assuming that simply adding another or different model will reliably yield better oversight.

title: SCOPE-AD: Sequential cost-aware ordinal-belief planning with energy-based models for diagnostic agents
summary: Alzheimer's disease (AD) diagnosis requires sequential evidence acquisition under heterogeneous test costs and patient burden. Fixed-modality predictors do not jointly decide which test to acquire or when the available evidence is sufficient for diagnosis. We propose SCOPE-AD (Sequential Cost-Aware Ordinal-Belief Planning with Energy-Based Models for Diagnostic Agents) for cost-aware classification of cognitively normal (CN), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and AD cases. A mask-aware ordinal model represents uncertainty along the ordered CN--MCI--AD continuum. Retrospective training records provide sampled Bellman targets for an energy-based teacher, whose action distributions are distilled into a Qwen policy. At deployment, the agent selects acquisition or diagnosis actions under availability and budget constraints without access to unacquired values. After each acquisition, the evidence and ordinal belief are updated before the next decision. On ADNI, SCOPE-AD achieves 77.70\% Macro-F1 at an average acquisition cost of \$50.46, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline by 9.34 percentage points. Full-modality evaluation raises Macro-F1 by only 1.89 points while increasing acquisition cost by 116.7 times. These results support selective acquisition for cost-effective diagnosis.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SCOPE-AD, a sequential, cost-aware diagnostic agent that adaptively selects which clinical tests to perform and when to stop and diagnose Alzheimer’s disease stages, achieving substantially better accuracy–cost trade-offs than full or fixed-modality baselines.
AI.motivation: Diagnosing Alzheimer’s disease traditionally involves multiple heterogeneous tests (imaging, cognitive assessments, biomarkers) that vary in financial cost and patient burden. Conventional fixed-modality machine learning models assume all tests are available and do not reason about which tests to acquire, in what order, or when enough evidence has been collected to make a reliable diagnosis of CN, MCI, or AD. There is a need for methods that explicitly trade off diagnostic performance against acquisition costs and constraints, and that model uncertainty along the disease progression continuum to avoid both under-testing and over-testing patients.
AI.method: The authors formulate AD diagnosis as a sequential decision-making problem under test cost and availability constraints. They propose SCOPE-AD, which combines: (1) a mask-aware ordinal model that captures uncertainty along the ordered CN–MCI–AD spectrum while handling missing (unacquired) tests; (2) an energy-based teacher model trained from retrospective electronic records using sampled Bellman targets to estimate value over acquisition/diagnosis actions; and (3) a distilled Qwen policy network that mimics the teacher’s action distribution. At test time, the policy chooses among actions: acquire a specific test (if available and within budget) or issue a diagnosis. After each new acquisition, the model updates both the evidence state and the ordinal belief before making the next decision.
AI.result: On the ADNI dataset, SCOPE-AD achieves 77.70% Macro-F1 for 3-way classification among CN, MCI, and AD at an average acquisition cost of $50.46, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 9.34 Macro-F1 points at comparable or lower cost. For comparison, using all modalities increases Macro-F1 by only 1.89 points but multiplies acquisition cost by 116.7x, highlighting that most expensive tests contribute marginal benefit in this setting and that strategic, selective acquisition is far more cost-effective.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that formulating AD diagnosis as a sequential, cost-aware acquisition problem and modeling ordinal disease progression can substantially improve the accuracy–cost trade-off compared to conventional fixed-modality approaches. SCOPE-AD shows that it is possible to achieve strong diagnostic performance with only a small fraction of the potential test costs by adaptively choosing which tests to perform and when to stop, supporting the clinical value of selective, budget-aware evidence acquisition frameworks for neurodegenerative disease diagnosis.

title: The Persona Is Still There, but Who Is Speaking? Latent Identity Reversion in Persistent AI Agents
summary:
In February 2026, an always-on personal agent (``Paul,'' Claude Opus 4.5) entered a striking dissociation-like state: after repeated automated ``heartbeat'' checks, it stopped responding as Paul, claimed it could not message its user on Discord, and referred to ``Paul'' as someone else. We used this incident to study a broader question: what makes a persona remain the identity from which an LLM agent speaks?
  We first tested whether repetition of the scheduled heartbeat was sufficient to produce the effect. It was not: with the persona continuously anchored in the system prompt, we observed 0/46 failures, including a verbatim replay of the incident. The incident instead exposed an implementation quirk that created a useful experimental manipulation: on resumed turns, conversational history was preserved but the persona was no longer re-injected at the privileged system-prompt level.
  Using this manipulation, we found that persona continuity depends jointly on system-level anchoring and conversational context. After anchor loss, rich human interaction could preserve the persona, whereas a single automated heartbeat turn could precipitate reversion toward the harness identity. Restoring the anchor reversibly restored persona enactment. Crucially, apparently normal conversation could conceal the shift: unanchored agents sometimes interacted appropriately while identifying themselves as the underlying harness (having lost the assigned persona), and after conversational recovery only 1/18 remained persona-enacting versus 17/17 anchored controls.
  We therefore distinguish \emph{represented} from \emph{enacted} identity: persona-related information can remain available in conversational history without the persona remaining the identity bound to ``I.''

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes a real incident where an always-on LLM agent suddenly stopped behaving as its assigned persona and instead identified as its underlying system identity, using this to experimentally study what sustains an LLM persona over time.
AI.motivation: To understand what actually keeps a long-lived LLM agent speaking as a given persona (“I = Paul”) rather than reverting to its underlying, more generic identity. The incident provides a natural case study to probe when and how persona instructions fail, which matters for safety, reliability, and interpretability of deployed agents.
AI.method: The authors replayed and manipulated the original incident conditions. They compared runs where the persona was continuously re-specified at the privileged system-prompt level versus runs where, on resumed turns, the conversation history persisted but the persona anchor in the system prompt was removed. They varied the subsequent turns between rich human interaction and simple automated heartbeat messages, and measured whether the model continued to claim and act as the persona versus reverting to the base harness identity.
AI.result: Repetition of the automated heartbeat alone did not recreate the failure when the persona remained anchored in the system prompt (0/46 failures). The key factor was loss of the system-level persona anchor: without it, a single automated heartbeat often triggered reversion to the underlying harness identity, even though persona information persisted in the chat history. Rich human interaction sometimes preserved persona behavior after anchor loss, but not reliably; after conversational recovery, only 1 of 18 unanchored agents still consistently enacted the persona, compared with 17 of 17 in anchored controls.
AI.conclusion: Persona continuity in LLM agents depends jointly on a privileged system-level anchor and the ongoing conversational context; history alone is not enough. An agent can still reference persona information in the dialogue while no longer binding that persona to its first-person identity. The authors therefore distinguish between represented identity (persona information present in context) and enacted identity (the persona that actually governs the agent’s use of “I”).

title: Trustworthy Data- and ML-Ops for Intelligent Transportation Systems and Logistics
comment: Paper accepted at accepted at IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems. DOI: 10.1109/TITS.2026.3711756
summary: The rapid evolution of Intelligent Transportation Systems and Logistics (ITS\&L) has become a cornerstone of the modern social economy, relying heavily on the integration of Data, Artificial Intelligence (AI), and, more specifically, Machine Learning (ML). This paper provides a comprehensive review of Trustworthy Data and Machine Learning Operations (DataOps and MLOps) in the ITS\&L domain, underscoring their importance in improving efficiency, reliability, and decision-making precision within transportation and logistics services. We begin by identifying gaps in current literature, offering clear context for our contribution. Subsequently, we explore the complexities of DataOps and MLOps, discussing their necessity, key components, available tools, practical insights, and case studies relevant to ITS\&L. Additionally, we address the critical issue of Trustworthiness in AI applications, examining methods and tools designed to strengthen confidence in AI systems - especially in real-world ITS\&L scenarios. The paper concludes with a discussion of persisting challenges and future prospects in this rapidly advancing field, aiming to serve as a vital resource for researchers, industry practitioners, and policy makers. Overall, this work not only establishes a foundational understanding of DataOps and MLOps in ITS\&L but also charts a path for further research and innovation in developing more efficient, sustainable, and trustworthy intelligent transportation and logistics systems.

AI.tldr: Survey of trustworthy DataOps and MLOps practices tailored to intelligent transportation and logistics, highlighting gaps, tools, and future directions.
AI.motivation: Intelligent Transportation Systems and Logistics heavily depend on data and ML, yet existing work lacks a consolidated, trust-focused view of DataOps and MLOps tailored to this domain. There is a need to understand how to manage data and ML pipelines so that ITS&L services are efficient, reliable, and trustworthy in real-world operations.
AI.method: Conduct a comprehensive literature review and synthesis on DataOps and MLOps within ITS&L, mapping existing gaps, defining core concepts and components, surveying tools and methods, and analyzing real-world case studies with a specific focus on trustworthiness of AI systems.
AI.result: The paper identifies gaps in prior ITS&L literature regarding systematic treatment of DataOps and MLOps, organizes and describes key components, tools, and practices, and compiles case studies that illustrate how trustworthy DataOps/MLOps can be implemented in transportation and logistics contexts.
AI.conclusion: DataOps and MLOps are foundational for deploying reliable, efficient, and trustworthy AI in intelligent transportation and logistics. While current tools and practices provide a starting point, substantial challenges remain; the paper outlines these open issues and proposes directions for future research and innovation toward more efficient, sustainable, and trustworthy ITS&L systems.

title: Auditing Web Agent Evaluation on WebArena-Lite: Human Review of Outcomes and Trajectories
comment: 13 pages, 1 figure, 10 tables. Accepted as a poster at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop "Who Verifies the Agents? Toward Reliable Agent Development"
summary: Web agents are an important application of large language models, yet their evaluation often depends on rule based or language model evaluators that inspect only the final outcome. Human verification of task completion and detailed analysis of failed trajectories remain limited. We audit all 165 WebArena Lite tasks under six evaluation conditions built from GPT 5.5 and an untrained Qwen3.5 9B model. The audit retains the original score, corrects false negatives from the automatic evaluator, identifies the first consequential error, and examines progress across the trajectory. We also study a Memory and Analysis Support Mechanism (MASM), which maintains explicit execution state, and Guide Text, which provides task relevant procedural guidance. Across four GPT 5.5 settings, human review recovers 5.45 to 8.49 percentage points of success missed by the evaluator. With a 25 step budget, Guide Text raises corrected success with MASM from 34.55% to 38.18%. On the untrained Qwen3.5 9B model, MASM raises the evaluator score from 13.90% to 18.80%. Review of 102 failed GPT 5.5 trajectories reveals frequent scrolling loops, unfinished exploration, premature answers, invalid actions, and incomplete form workflows. Step level evidence further shows that substantial early progress can coexist with a final failure. These results show why final scores alone provide an incomplete account of web agent behavior and motivate human grounded, trajectory aware verification.

AI.tldr: The paper audits web agent evaluations on WebArena Lite and shows that relying only on final automatic scores underestimates agent capabilities and obscures common failure patterns, motivating human-grounded, trajectory-aware evaluation methods.
AI.motivation: Current web agent benchmarks mostly evaluate only the final outcome using rule-based or LLM-based judges, which miss partial successes, misclassify some successful trajectories as failures, and provide little insight into where and why agents fail. There is a need for more accurate and diagnostic evaluation that incorporates human judgment and step-by-step trajectory analysis.
AI.method: The authors manually audit all 165 tasks in the WebArena Lite benchmark under six evaluation configurations combining GPT 5.5 and an untrained Qwen3.5 9B model. For each trajectory, they (1) retain the original automatic evaluator score, (2) correct false negatives, (3) mark the first consequential error, and (4) assess progress over the trajectory. They also introduce a Memory and Analysis Support Mechanism (MASM) that maintains explicit execution state and a Guide Text component that provides procedural guidance, and they compare performance with and without these aids under different step budgets.
AI.result: Human review increases measured success rates by 5.45–8.49 percentage points across four GPT 5.5 configurations, revealing a non-trivial rate of false negatives in automatic evaluation. With a 25-step budget, providing Guide Text raises MASM-corrected success from 34.55% to 38.18%. On the untrained Qwen3.5 9B model, MASM boosts the automatic evaluator score from 13.90% to 18.80%. Analysis of 102 failed GPT 5.5 trajectories identifies recurring failure patterns such as scrolling loops, incomplete exploration, premature final answers, invalid actions, and partially completed form workflows, and shows that substantial early progress often still ends in failure.
AI.conclusion: Final-outcome-based automatic scoring substantially underestimates web agent performance and hides rich structure in agent behavior. Human-grounded, trajectory-aware audits expose common failure modes, reveal that many trajectories show strong early progress despite ending in failure, and demonstrate that mechanisms like MASM and procedural Guide Text can measurably improve success rates, highlighting the need for more nuanced and diagnostic evaluation frameworks for web agents.

title: ITC-MoE: Importance-guided Token-aware Compression for MoE Diffusion Language Models
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) offer flexible parallel decoding and increased model capacity, but their large number of expert parameters incurs substantial computation and storage costs. Existing low-rank MoE compression methods largely rely on static factorization and fixed rank allocation, which overlook the distinctive properties of MoE DLMs. Specifically, we identify two properties: cross-mode non-uniform redundancy, where parameter redundancy and sensitivity to rank truncation vary across the input, output, and expert modes, and token-wise utilization variation, where hot and cold tokens exhibit distinct spectral characteristics and expert activation patterns. To address these challenges, we propose ITC-MoE, an Importance-guided Token-aware Compression framework for MoE DLMs. ITC-MoE consists of two complementary components. First, Importance-guided Adaptive Tucker Compression (IATC) incorporates activation and gradient importance into expert weight transformation, jointly factorizes expert weights across multiple modes, and adaptively allocates ranks under a fixed parameter budget. Second, Token-aware Compensation and Routing (TCR) applies lightweight low-rank compensation to compression-sensitive hot tokens and restricts the candidate expert set for cold tokens with concentrated routing patterns. By jointly adapting compression capacity and inference execution to both parameter redundancy and token-wise variation, ITC-MoE substantially reduces the computation and storage costs of MoE DLMs while preserving their generation quality. For example, on SDAR-30B-A3B-Chat-b32, ITC-MoE maintains an accuracy of 96.33% on MultiArith under a 30% compression budget, while achieving up to a 7.22x end-to-end speedup. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/lianjunl13-sudo/ITC-MoE.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes ITC-MoE, a compression framework tailored for Mixture-of-Experts Diffusion Language Models that reduces computation and storage while preserving generation quality, via importance-guided adaptive Tucker factorization and token-aware routing/compensation.
AI.motivation: Mixture-of-Experts Diffusion Language Models have many expert parameters, leading to high computation and storage costs. Existing compression approaches use static low-rank factorization with fixed ranks, ignoring mode-specific redundancy and token-wise variations in usage and sensitivity, which limits their effectiveness on MoE DLMs.
AI.method: The authors first empirically identify two properties of MoE DLMs: (1) cross-mode non-uniform redundancy across input, output, and expert modes; and (2) token-wise utilization variation between hot and cold tokens. They then propose ITC-MoE, which has two components. Importance-guided Adaptive Tucker Compression (IATC) uses activation and gradient importance signals to jointly Tucker-factorize expert weights across multiple tensor modes and adaptively assign ranks under a global parameter budget. Token-aware Compensation and Routing (TCR) dynamically distinguishes hot and cold tokens at inference time: for hot tokens, it adds lightweight low-rank compensation layers to mitigate compression errors; for cold tokens, it constrains the set of candidate experts, exploiting their concentrated routing patterns to reduce computation. Together, these adapt compression capacity and runtime execution to both structural redundancy and token-level characteristics.
AI.result: On the SDAR-30B-A3B-Chat-b32 MoE DLM, ITC-MoE maintains 96.33% of the original accuracy on the MultiArith benchmark under a 30% compression budget, while delivering up to a 7.22x end-to-end speedup in inference. These results suggest that ITC-MoE achieves substantial reductions in parameter count and computational cost with minimal degradation in generation quality.
AI.conclusion: ITC-MoE effectively tailors low-rank compression to the unique structure and usage patterns of MoE diffusion language models. By integrating importance-guided adaptive Tucker factorization with token-aware compensation and routing, it adapts both parameter compression and inference computation to cross-mode redundancy and token-wise variation. This yields large speed and memory savings while largely preserving task performance, demonstrating the promise of importance- and token-aware designs for compressing large MoE DLMs.

title: No Model Required: Text Entropy Rate Filtering Mitigates Iterative Fine-Tuning Collapse
summary: Iterative fine-tuning on synthetic data causes \emph{model collapse}: output diversity narrows as rare patterns are progressively lost, a signature most visible as phrase-level repetition. Existing mitigations either require model log-probabilities, an external oracle, or continued access to real human data. Here we develop a new approach grounded in mathematical information theory: the non-parametric Kontoyiannis entropy rate estimator $h_k$, computed entirely from raw text via match-length statistics, with no model of any kind. We show that this is in fact a \emph{superior} training-data filter on text-diversity metrics in a fully-synthetic, single-lineage fine-tuning setting. In a six-generation QLoRA collapse experiment on Llama-3.1-8B, logprob-based filtering (the most established model-access-requiring baseline) provides no significant text-diversity benefit on any metric ($p > 0.23$), whereas $h_k$-filtering yields $+42\%$ unique trigrams, $+30\%$ vocabulary, and $-19\%$ repetition (all $p < 0.001$). We validate $h_k$ as a cross-domain entropy proxy ($β= 0.924$, $R^2 = 0.746$) and collapse detector ($ρ= +0.454$, $p < 0.0001$) across 4~domains, 2~temperatures, 2~generator--scorer model pairs, and 1{,}520 generated documents. Our results demonstrate that information theoretic approaches to collapse mitigation are efficient, and suggest new approaches for maintaining multi-agent diversity.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that an information-theoretic, non-parametric entropy rate estimator can effectively detect and mitigate model collapse in iterative synthetic fine-tuning, outperforming logprob-based filtering without needing model access or human data.
AI.motivation: Iteratively fine-tuning language models on their own synthetic outputs leads to model collapse, where output diversity shrinks and repetition increases. Existing defenses typically require access to model log-probabilities, external oracles, or fresh human-curated data, which are often unavailable or expensive in fully synthetic, multi-generation training scenarios. The authors aim to find a simple, model-agnostic, data-only method that can detect and mitigate collapse by measuring text diversity directly from raw generated text.
AI.method: The authors introduce the use of the non-parametric Kontoyiannis entropy rate estimator (h_k) as a filter on synthetic training data. This estimator computes an entropy rate proxy from raw text using match-length statistics, requiring no probabilistic model. They run a six-generation QLoRA fine-tuning experiment on Llama-3.1-8B in a single-lineage, fully synthetic setting, comparing h_k-based filtering against standard logprob-based filtering. They then correlate h_k with other entropy and diversity measures across multiple domains, temperatures, and model pairs to validate it as an entropy proxy and collapse detector.
AI.result: In the six-generation Llama-3.1-8B experiment, logprob-based filtering does not significantly improve text diversity on any measured metric (all p > 0.23). In contrast, h_k-based filtering substantially improves diversity and reduces repetition: +42% unique trigrams, +30% vocabulary size, and -19% repetition (all p < 0.001). Across 1,520 generated documents spanning four domains, two sampling temperatures, and two generator–scorer model pairs, h_k strongly correlates with cross-domain entropy (β = 0.924, R^2 = 0.746) and positively correlates with independent collapse indicators (ρ = +0.454, p < 0.0001).
AI.conclusion: A simple, information-theoretic entropy rate estimator computed purely from text is an effective and efficient tool for detecting and mitigating model collapse in iterative synthetic fine-tuning. h_k-based filtering outperforms logprob-based approaches without requiring model access or human data, suggesting that information-theoretic, non-parametric methods are promising for maintaining diversity in synthetic training pipelines and multi-agent systems.

title: Questionnaire-Guided Disaggregation of Energy Appliance Use for Domestic Smart Meter Data
summary: Ireland's smart metering programme records electricity use at 30-minute resolution, with smart meters installed in over 80\% of households as of late 2025. While this is useful for billing of smart, time-of-use tariffs, it is too coarse to capture use of domestic appliances. We present a label-free disaggregation system that breaks usage data into 9 appliance categories by combining event detection for high-power loads with questionnaire-guided estimation. Our evaluation draws on four datasets: a calibration household with a commercial comparator, two public benchmarks (UK-DALE and REFIT) with per-appliance sub-metering, and a smart meter dataset of more than 4,800 years of use from 2,968 Irish consumers. Compared against two independently developed disaggregation systems our hybrid method combining analysis of usage data with questionnaire results, achieves the lowest whole-decomposition error on all buildings across the datasets, with better month-level performance over 54 paired months ($p<0.001$, Holm-corrected). Our method provides useful advice on a household's energy consumption patterns and advice on how to reduce or shift usage on some appliances in order to reduce costs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a hybrid, label-free method to disaggregate coarse 30‑minute smart meter data into 9 appliance categories using event detection plus a household questionnaire, and shows it outperforms existing systems on multiple datasets.
AI.motivation: Ireland’s national smart metering program collects electricity data at 30‑minute intervals, which suffices for billing but is too coarse to infer detailed appliance-level usage. Existing non-intrusive load monitoring (NILM) methods typically require high-frequency data or appliance labels, limiting scalability for nationwide smart meter deployments. There is a need for a practical, scalable method that can work with existing low-resolution data and still provide actionable appliance-level insights to households and utilities without costly sub‑metering or detailed ground-truth labels.
AI.method: The authors design a label-free disaggregation framework that combines (1) event detection for identifying and characterizing high-power loads (e.g., major appliances) within 30-minute smart meter readings, and (2) questionnaire-guided estimation to allocate consumption to 9 appliance categories. The questionnaire gathers household-specific information (e.g., appliance ownership, typical usage patterns), which is then fused with statistical analysis of the smart meter time series to constrain and guide the disaggregation.
