The system is evaluated on four datasets: a calibration household equipped with a commercial comparator; two public NILM benchmarks (UK-DALE and REFIT) which provide per-appliance sub-metered data for ground truth; and a large Irish smart meter dataset consisting of over 4,800 consumer-years from 2,968 homes. The authors compare their hybrid method against two independently developed disaggregation systems using metrics of whole-home decomposition error and month-level performance, applying statistical significance testing (Holm-corrected).
AI.result: Across all evaluated buildings and datasets, the proposed hybrid method achieves the lowest whole-home decomposition error compared with the two baseline disaggregation systems. On 54 paired months of data, it shows significantly better month-level performance with p < 0.001 after Holm correction, indicating robust statistical evidence of improvement. The method successfully partitions household consumption into 9 appliance categories despite the coarse 30-minute resolution and absence of appliance labels. Using the large Irish smart meter dataset, the authors demonstrate that the system can be deployed at scale and remain effective under real-world conditions.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that combining coarse-resolution smart meter data with lightweight, questionnaire-based household information enables accurate, label-free appliance-category disaggregation at scale. This hybrid approach outperforms existing NILM systems when restricted to 30‑minute data and offers practical value for national smart metering programs. It can provide households with actionable feedback on their energy consumption patterns and tailored recommendations on how to reduce or shift usage of specific appliance categories to lower electricity costs. The work demonstrates a viable pathway to extracting appliance-level insights from existing smart meter infrastructures without requiring high-frequency sensing or extensive sub-metering.

title: GAW-PO: Preference Optimization with Gradient-Aligned Token Weights
summary: Most preference optimization methods, such as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), apply preference supervision at the response level, although autoregressive language models are optimized token by token. As a result, all tokens in a rejected response contribute to the negative training signal, including tokens that may encode behavior that is useful for the preferred response. We introduce GAW-PO, a gradient-aligned token reweighting method for DPO that estimates, for each rejected token, whether penalizing it would interfere with the preferred update directions. Tokens whose gradients are strongly aligned with the preferred behavior receive a weaker negative contribution, while conflicting tokens retain a stronger penalty. Our method achieves the highest average performance among the evaluated preference-optimization methods, improving by 0.97 points over standard DPO and 0.65 points over the strongest competing baseline across 11 benchmarks spanning mathematics, reasoning, coding, and question answering. We further show that gradient-aligned weighting is substantially more robust to aggressive preference optimization: as the DPO regularization parameter $β$ decreases, standard DPO degrades sharply, whereas GAW-PO continues to improve. These results suggest that accounting for the interaction between rejected-token updates and preferred behavior provides an effective form of token-level credit assignment for preference optimization.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes GAW-PO, a token-level, gradient-aligned reweighting method for DPO that downweights penalties on useful tokens in rejected responses, leading to better and more robust preference optimization across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing preference optimization methods like DPO operate at the response level, but autoregressive models are trained token by token. This mismatch causes all tokens in a rejected response to receive a negative signal, even when some tokens encode behavior that is actually helpful or shared with the preferred response. This leads to suboptimal credit assignment, over-penalizing useful behaviors and harming performance, especially under aggressive preference optimization settings.
AI.method: The authors introduce GAW-PO, which modifies DPO by performing token-level, gradient-aligned reweighting. For each token in the rejected response, the method estimates how its gradient aligns with the gradient corresponding to the preferred response. If the gradient of a rejected token is strongly aligned with the preferred behavior, its negative contribution is downweighted; if it conflicts with the preferred gradient, its penalty remains strong. This produces an effective, token-wise credit assignment mechanism atop the standard DPO framework, without changing the overall objective form but adjusting token weights based on gradient alignment.
AI.result: Across 11 benchmarks in mathematics, reasoning, coding, and question answering, GAW-PO achieves the best average performance among evaluated preference-optimization methods. Quantitatively, it improves by 0.97 points over standard DPO and 0.65 points over the strongest competing baseline. In addition, when the DPO regularization parameter β is decreased (i.e., more aggressive preference optimization), standard DPO performance degrades sharply, while GAW-PO continues to improve, showing superior robustness under stronger optimization pressure.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating gradient-aligned token weighting into DPO yields more accurate token-level credit assignment in preference optimization. By avoiding excessive penalties on rejected tokens that support preferred behavior, GAW-PO better exploits useful signal in rejected responses, improves performance across diverse tasks, and remains robust under aggressive optimization. This indicates that modeling the interaction between rejected-token updates and preferred behavior at the token level is a powerful way to enhance preference optimization for autoregressive language models.

title: DAYJOB: A Benchmark for Long-Horizon Professional Work
comment: 11 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. An earlier version was accepted to the 2nd Workshop on Agentic AI Benchmarks and Applications for Enterprise Tasks (AABA4ET) at NeurIPS 2026. Evaluation harness: https://github.com/surge-ai/dayjob
summary: Professional work often starts with a brief request that leaves the professional to work out what is needed, which documents matter, and whether the request's premise holds. We introduce DAYJOB, a benchmark of 130 tasks built by professionals in healthcare (50) and finance (80). The tasks are estimated to take a professional 13.6 hours on average in healthcare and 16.6 in finance. Each task is a containerized Harbor environment with an expert rubric of binary criteria (median 47.5 and 57.5 per task) that an agentic judge applies to the delivered files, and an attempt passes only if it meets every criterion. Across 30 model configurations from 13 developers, the strongest, Claude Opus 5.5, passes 24.7% of healthcare and 23.9% of finance attempts, and the median configuration passes 0.6% and 2.5%. In case studies, agents accept premises that the record contradicts and carry wrong inputs through otherwise consistent analyses. We release all healthcare tasks, 50 of the 80 finance tasks, the evaluation harness, and the leaderboard.

AI.tldr: DAYJOB is a benchmark of realistic, multi-hour professional tasks in healthcare and finance used to rigorously evaluate agentic AI systems with strict binary rubrics.
AI.motivation: Existing AI benchmarks are typically short, synthetic, or narrowly scoped, and do not capture the open-ended, multi-document, premise-checking nature of real professional work. The authors aim to create a benchmark that reflects how professionals actually receive and complete complex tasks, so that the capabilities and failure modes of advanced models and agentic systems can be meaningfully measured.
AI.method: The authors construct 130 tasks authored by domain professionals: 50 in healthcare and 80 in finance. Each task is implemented as a containerized Harbor environment with access to relevant documents and tools, and is accompanied by an expert-designed rubric consisting of many binary pass/fail criteria. An automated agentic judge evaluates the files produced by AI agents against this rubric, and a task is considered passed only if every criterion is satisfied. They run 30 model configurations from 13 developers on these tasks and record pass rates, along with qualitative case studies of failure modes.
AI.result: Tasks are long and complex, with estimated human completion times of 13.6 hours in healthcare and 16.6 hours in finance, and rubrics with around 50+ binary checks each. Even the strongest evaluated configuration, Claude Opus 5.5, passes only about a quarter of attempts (24.7% healthcare, 23.9% finance), while the median configuration passes almost none (0.6% healthcare, 2.5% finance). Case studies reveal that agents frequently accept incorrect premises from the initial request and propagate these errors through otherwise coherent analyses.
AI.conclusion: Current state-of-the-art models and agentic setups struggle substantially with realistic, long-horizon professional tasks that require identifying what matters, checking assumptions against records, and satisfying detailed, strict rubrics. DAYJOB provides an open benchmark, evaluation harness, and leaderboard to spur progress and allow systematic measurement of whether AI agents can reliably perform complex professional work in domains like healthcare and finance.

title: How the Audit Rule Shapes Faithful Factor Explanations in LLMs
summary: Large language models are often asked which input factors influenced their outputs. For structured inputs, such reports can be checked by counterfactual perturbation, but each factor must be queried multiple times to estimate its effect, so verification is usually budget-limited. We study how this limited-budget setting changes the incentive to report factor-level influence truthfully. We formalize the interaction as a verification game and show that proper scoring alone is not enough when auditing depends on the report: report-dependent auditing creates a suppression incentive, because factors reported as important are more likely to be checked and penalized for estimation noise. In contrast, report-independent auditing, or a mixed rule with a small report-independent floor, removes this channel and makes truthful reporting preferable to full suppression. We instantiate the framework with the Counterfactual Brier Score (CBS) and evaluate its predictions on four NLP benchmarks. A synthetic rational agent matches the theoretical prediction exactly, and real LLMs follow the same incentives when they are made explicit. The main design implication is simple: under partial verification, factor-level explanation systems should include a report-independent audit component so that under-reporting cannot be used to avoid scrutiny.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to design verification and auditing schemes so that large language models truthfully report which input factors influenced their outputs under a limited evaluation budget.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly expected to explain which input features influenced their decisions. For structured inputs, these explanations can be partially verified via counterfactual perturbations, but each factor is expensive to test. With limited audit budget, only some factors can be checked, and typically more important-reported factors get checked more often. This creates strategic incentives for models (or agents) to under-report influence to avoid scrutiny, undermining the reliability of explanations. The paper aims to understand and fix this incentive problem.
AI.method: The authors formalize the problem as a verification game between an explainer (the LLM providing factor-level influence reports) and an auditor with a limited query budget. They analyze how different auditing policies and scoring rules affect incentives for truthful reporting versus suppression of influential factors. They prove that with report-dependent auditing, proper scoring rules alone do not ensure truthful reporting because important-reported factors are audited more and thus more exposed to estimation noise penalties. They then characterize conditions under which report-independent or mixed auditing policies restore incentive compatibility. They instantiate their framework using the Counterfactual Brier Score (CBS) as the evaluation metric and simulate both a synthetic perfectly rational agent and real LLMs on four NLP benchmarks, making incentives explicit to the models.
AI.result: The theoretical analysis shows that when auditing probability depends on reported importance, models face an incentive to suppress or downplay factor influence to reduce expected penalties from noisy counterfactual estimates, even under proper scoring rules. Introducing a report-independent audit component (a non-zero probability of auditing any factor regardless of its reported importance) eliminates this suppression incentive and makes truthful reporting strictly better than full suppression. Empirically, a synthetic rational agent behaves exactly as predicted by the theory under different audit schemes. Real LLMs, when given prompts that spell out the incentive structure, also adjust their factor reports in line with the predicted incentives across four NLP benchmarks, demonstrating the practical relevance of the theoretical incentive analysis.
AI.conclusion: Proper scoring rules are not sufficient to elicit truthful factor-level influence reports when verification is budget-limited and audit probabilities depend on the reports. Report-dependent auditing inadvertently incentivizes under-reporting to evade scrutiny. Adding a report-independent auditing component—even a small one—changes the incentive structure so that truthful reporting dominates suppression. Therefore, explanation systems for LLMs that rely on partial counterfactual verification should include a report-independent audit floor to ensure that models cannot strategically avoid being checked by downplaying factor influence.

title: ProtoFlow: Prototype-Guided Flow Matching for Multivariate Time Series Forecasting
summary: Generative modeling has shown strong promise for multivariate time mseries (MTS) forecasting, especially scale to high-dimensional settings. Diffusion-based methods achieve competitive performance but typically require many sampling steps at inference. VAE-based non-iterative forecasting frameworks have therefore emerged as an efficient alternative. Within this line of work, vector quantization (VQ) enables controllable latent space modeling by mapping multivariate series into compact discrete representations. Existing VQ-based forecasting methods, however, typically rely on autoregressive (AR) token generation, which suffers from exposure bias and training-inference mismatch. Flow matching provides an efficient non-autoregressive alternative for latent forecasting, but existing formulations usually initialize transport from a generic Gaussian prior. We instead observe that the trained VQ codebook already captures representative latent prototypes and can thus serve as a more informative prior for flow matching. Based on this insight, we propose ProtoFlow, a forecasting framework that combines vector-quantized autoencoding with Prototype-prior Flow matching. Our method first maps multivariate sequences into a discrete latent space, then constructs a structured prior from the learned codebook, and finally learns a DiT-based rectified flow to transport samples from this prior to future latent representations conditioned on historical observations. By replacing generic noise initialization with a learned prototype prior, ProtoFlow avoids the rollout mismatch of AR token prediction and promotes faster training convergence. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets show that it consistently achieves superior forecasting performance with efficient inference.

AI.tldr: ProtoFlow is a VQ-based multivariate time-series forecasting framework that replaces autoregressive token generation with a prototype-based flow matching approach for efficient, accurate, non-iterative forecasting.
AI.motivation: Existing generative models for multivariate time-series forecasting either rely on diffusion, which is accurate but slow due to many sampling steps, or VAE/VQ-based methods that are efficient but mostly autoregressive, leading to exposure bias and training–inference mismatch. Flow-matching offers efficient non-autoregressive forecasting, but current approaches start from an uninformative Gaussian prior, ignoring structure already learned by VQ codebooks. The authors aim to design a forecasting framework that is non-autoregressive, more sample-efficient, and uses a stronger, data-driven prior while scaling to high-dimensional MTS.
AI.method: The authors introduce ProtoFlow, which combines vector-quantized autoencoding with a prototype-prior flow matching scheme. First, an encoder maps multivariate time-series into a discrete latent space based on a learned VQ codebook. This codebook’s entries serve as prototypical latent representations. Instead of initializing flow matching from a generic Gaussian, the method constructs a structured prior distribution over these prototypes. Then, a DiT-based (Diffusion Transformer-style) rectified flow model is trained to transport samples from this prototype prior to the target future latent representations, conditioned on historical observations. This yields non-autoregressive latent forecasts, which are finally decoded back to the original time-series space.
AI.result: Across multiple benchmark multivariate time-series forecasting datasets, ProtoFlow consistently outperforms prior methods in predictive accuracy while maintaining efficient inference. It achieves better performance than diffusion-based methods with fewer sampling steps and improves over existing VQ-based autoregressive and Gaussian-prior flow-matching models in both convergence speed and final forecasting metrics.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging the learned VQ codebook as a structured prototype prior in a flow-matching framework addresses the shortcomings of both autoregressive VQ forecasting (exposure bias) and Gaussian-prior flow models (uninformative initialization). ProtoFlow demonstrates that prototype-based priors can lead to faster training convergence, more accurate and efficient non-autoregressive multivariate time-series forecasting, and provide a scalable solution for high-dimensional MTS tasks.

title: AURAL: Adaptive Latent Reasoning with Joint Chunk for Speech Language Models
summary: Model intelligence and fast response jointly shape the quality of interaction with speech language models, yet remain difficult to achieve together. Explicit chain-of-thought (CoT) improves reasoning and audio understanding, but generating intermediate reasoning tokens delays responses. Describing fine-grained acoustic cues further lengthens CoT and increases latency. Latent reasoning can reduce this overhead, yet existing methods often trail CoT and remain limited by single-path supervision and reasoning budgets that do not adapt to problem difficulty. We introduce AURAL, which models a distribution over multiple plausible reasoning continuations in latent space and jointly predicts chunks of future states to reduce sequential forward passes and reasoning latency. To provide initial supervision for latent reasoning, we construct AuralReason-683K: 683K bilingual speech utterances (about 1,000 hours) with concise CoT for emotion recognition, empathetic dialogue, and general reasoning. AURAL-RL then explores beyond these traces, rewarding concise reasoning that yields high-quality answers and adapting reasoning effort to each problem. Across two backbones, AURAL-RL achieves performance comparable to CoT-RL, with larger gains over the respective supervised checkpoints on most metrics. Analysis further shows that harder questions elicit more latent reasoning steps. On Qwen2.5-Omni, it reduces time to the first answer token by 11.8x, from 1.22 to 0.10 s, versus 0.05 s for direct answering.

AI.tldr: AURAL is a speech language model framework that performs fast, latent chain-of-thought reasoning, achieving CoT-level performance with much lower response latency.
AI.motivation: Speech language models need both strong reasoning ability and low latency for good interaction quality. Explicit chain-of-thought improves reasoning and audio understanding, but it is slow because generating long intermediate reasoning sequences—especially those describing detailed acoustic cues—adds significant delay. Existing latent reasoning approaches reduce overhead but often underperform explicit CoT and are constrained by single-path supervision and fixed reasoning budgets that don’t adapt to task difficulty. The paper aims to close this gap: match or approach CoT performance while dramatically reducing response time and enabling adaptive reasoning depth.
AI.method: The authors propose AURAL, a latent reasoning framework for speech language models. AURAL models a distribution over multiple plausible reasoning continuations directly in latent space, instead of generating token-level CoT. It predicts chunks of future latent states jointly, which reduces the number of sequential forward passes and lowers reasoning latency. For supervision, they build AuralReason-683K, a dataset of 683K bilingual speech utterances (about 1,000 hours) annotated with concise chain-of-thought for tasks like emotion recognition, empathetic dialogue, and general reasoning. They first train the model with this supervised data, then apply reinforcement learning (AURAL-RL) to explore beyond the provided reasoning traces. The RL objective rewards concise latent reasoning that leads to high-quality answers and encourages the model to adapt its reasoning effort (number of latent steps) to the difficulty of each problem.
AI.result: AURAL-RL, instantiated on two different backbone models, attains performance comparable to chain-of-thought reinforcement learning (CoT-RL), and consistently yields larger improvements over their respective supervised baselines on most evaluation metrics. Empirical analysis shows that the model naturally allocates more latent reasoning steps to harder questions, demonstrating adaptive reasoning depth. Deployed on Qwen2.5-Omni, AURAL-RL reduces the time to first answer token from 1.22 seconds to 0.10 seconds—an 11.8× speedup—while remaining close in speed to direct answering (0.05 seconds) that uses no explicit reasoning.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that latent, distributional reasoning in speech language models can match the benefits of explicit chain-of-thought while drastically cutting response latency. By predicting chunks of future latent states and training with both supervised concise CoT data and reinforcement learning, AURAL learns to reason efficiently and allocate computation adaptively based on task difficulty. This yields near-CoT performance with order-of-magnitude faster first-token latency, improving the practicality of reasoning-capable speech language models for real-time interactive applications.

title: TRACE: Trajectory Return Attribution and Contrastive Erasure for Multi-Turn Safety
summary: Safety-aligned large language models (LLMs) often refuse a harmful request but comply once the same goal is spread over several turns. Preference objectives score whole responses to single prompts, so their training loss alone cannot control risk on unseen histories. Our analysis gives sufficient conditions under which suppression at supervised single-turn contexts yields a bound on multi-turn trajectory risk. The bound accounts for coverage, transfer slack, and leakage, and characterizes contraction relative to a base-policy risk budget evaluated on the trained policy's contexts. TRACE (Trajectory Return Attribution and Contrastive Erasure) turns this principle into a token-level objective. On the safe response, each token is weighted by the discounted return of a refusal-attributable advantage. The advantage compares a frozen reference model with its refusal-ablated copy, allowing earlier response tokens to receive credit from later refusal-related evidence. At high-gap positions on rejected responses, TRACE combines the observed token with policy-selected alternatives in the erasure target. A gradient-norm penalty replaces the retain set. Across five open-weight models and seven multi-turn attacks, TRACE gives the lowest attack success rate (ASR) in all 35 model and attack pairs, while the model utility evaluated on MMLU and HellaSwag drop by at most 1\.23 points. Source code can be found in the supplemental material.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes TRACE, a token-level training objective that improves multi-turn safety of large language models by aligning single-turn refusals with reduced trajectory-level attack success, achieving strong robustness with minimal performance loss on standard benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing safety-aligned LLMs can be bypassed by spreading a harmful objective across multiple conversation turns. Current preference-based training focuses on single prompt–response pairs and does not directly control safety risk over unseen multi-turn dialogue histories. The authors aim to establish theoretical conditions and a practical method that connect single-turn suppression behavior to guarantees on multi-turn trajectory risk.
AI.method:
1) Provide a theoretical analysis that derives sufficient conditions under which suppressing harmful behavior on supervised single-turn contexts yields an upper bound on multi-turn trajectory risk, factoring in coverage, transfer slack, and leakage, and relating it to a base-policy risk budget.
2) Introduce TRACE (Trajectory Return Attribution and Contrastive Erasure), a token-level safety objective that: (a) assigns each token in a safe response a weight equal to the discounted return of a refusal-attributable advantage; (b) defines this advantage by comparing a frozen reference model with a refusal-ablated copy so that earlier tokens get credit from later refusal evidence; (c) on unsafe/rejected responses, identifies high-gap positions and mixes the observed token with policy-selected alternatives as an erasure target; and (d) replaces the usual retain set with a gradient-norm penalty to stabilize training.
AI.result: TRACE is evaluated on five open-weight LLMs and seven types of multi-turn safety attacks. Across all 35 model–attack combinations, TRACE achieves the lowest attack success rate (ASR) compared to baselines. At the same time, general model utility on standard benchmarks (MMLU and HellaSwag) is largely preserved, with performance drops of at most 1.23 points, indicating strong safety gains with minimal capability loss.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that carefully designed single-turn safety training can provably reduce multi-turn trajectory risk when certain conditions are met, and that TRACE is an effective practical instantiation of this idea. By attributing credit for refusals at the token level and using contrastive erasure, TRACE significantly improves robustness to multi-turn attacks with very small degradation in general task performance, offering a promising direction for safer LLM training.

title: Which LLM to pick? Online Active Model Selection for Large Language Models
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to process streaming data, with practitioners relying on benchmarks to select the best model even though these signals only approximate real performance. While oracle annotations can provide reliable feedback, they are often costly and difficult to obtain at scale. To address this challenge, we propose ONLINE LLM PICKER, the first framework for active model selection for LLMs in online settings. Given an arbitrary stream of queries and a limited annotation budget, ONLINE LLM PICKER selects the most informative prompts for annotation to identify the best LLM among candidate models. Across multiple tasks including 10 datasets, for over 130 language models, we show that ONLINE LLM PICKER saves annotation cost by up to 71.67% while reliably identifying the best or near-best model for the stream. We also show that using the returned model for sequential generation on unannotated prompts across the stream reduces regret by up to a factor of 2.51x, indicating that ONLINE LLM PICKER can identify the best or near-best model well before processing all streaming prompts.

AI.tldr: They propose an online, active-learning-based framework (ONLINE LLM PICKER) that selects which prompts to annotate in a query stream so as to quickly and cheaply identify the best LLM among many candidates.
AI.motivation: In real applications, LLMs are increasingly used on streaming queries. Practitioners must choose one model, but offline benchmarks are only approximate indicators of actual performance, and obtaining ground-truth (oracle) annotations online is expensive and limited. There is no existing principled method for actively deciding what to annotate and which model to deploy in a streaming, multi-model setting, so they want a data-efficient, online method for model selection that works under annotation-budget constraints.
AI.method: They design ONLINE LLM PICKER, an active model selection framework for streaming data. Given a pool of candidate LLMs, a stream of incoming prompts, and a fixed annotation budget, it decides in an online fashion which prompts are most informative to send for oracle annotation. Using these selectively annotated examples, it estimates and compares the performance of the candidate models to identify the best or near-best one for the given stream. The framework is evaluated across 10 datasets and more than 130 language models on multiple tasks, and regret is measured for sequential generation on the remaining, unannotated prompts.
AI.result: Across diverse datasets, tasks, and over 130 LLMs, ONLINE LLM PICKER reduces the number of oracle annotations needed by up to 71.67% while still reliably finding the best or near-best model for the query stream. When the selected model is then used to answer the rest of the stream without further annotations, the cumulative performance shortfall (regret) is reduced by up to 2.51x compared to baselines, demonstrating that the method can lock onto a strong model well before observing and labeling the full stream.
AI.conclusion: ONLINE LLM PICKER provides a practical and efficient solution to online LLM model selection under limited annotation budgets. By actively choosing which streaming queries to label, it can identify a best or near-best model early, greatly cutting annotation cost while maintaining performance and lowering regret in downstream sequential generation. This shows that active online model selection is both feasible and valuable in real-world LLM deployment scenarios.

title: PPO-HRAP: Proximal Policy Optimization with a Hybrid Regime-Aware Policy for Risk-Controlled Trading
summary: Reinforcement learning for trading often struggles to balance upside participation with drawdown control. Profit-only policies can collapse toward passive long exposure on upward-drifting assets, while aggressively risk-penalized rewards can become too defensive during volatile periods. This paper proposes PPO-HRAP, a hybrid regime-aware policy that combines Proximal Policy Optimization with an interpretable regime prior. The agent observes both market features and portfolio-state variables, receives a reward combining portfolio log return, VIX-conditioned drawdown-increase penalty, target-exposure deviation, and turnover cost, and executes a blended action between the PPO actor output and a regime-derived target exposure. On the held-out 2020-2022 SPY test window, PPO-HRAP achieves 27.62% total return, 8.48% annualized return, 0.6447 Sharpe ratio, 0.8588 Sortino ratio, and 0.4592 Calmar ratio, while reducing maximum drawdown from 34.10% for Buy and Hold to 18.47%. Across five SPY seeds, PPO-HRAP remains stable with mean total return $0.2725 \pm 0.0109$ and mean Sharpe ratio $0.6219 \pm 0.0565$. Single-run cross-asset tests on QQQ and DIA further show that the proposed method ranks first on total return and Sharpe ratio for all three reported assets. These results suggest that blending learned actions with a volatility-aware regime prior is a practical way to improve risk-adjusted trading behavior, although the current policy still incurs high turnover and cross-asset robustness beyond SPY remains limited to single-run evidence.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PPO-HRAP, a regime-aware reinforcement learning trading method that blends PPO actions with a volatility-based exposure prior to improve risk-adjusted returns and drawdown control versus Buy & Hold on SPY, with additional albeit limited cross-asset tests.
AI.motivation: Standard RL trading agents either chase profit and degenerate into near-passive long exposure on rising markets, or overemphasize risk penalties and become too defensive in volatile regimes. There is a need for a method that can simultaneously participate in upside, control drawdowns, and remain stable and interpretable across different volatility regimes.
AI.method: The authors design PPO-HRAP, which augments Proximal Policy Optimization with a hybrid, regime-aware policy. The agent’s observation space includes market features and portfolio-state variables. The reward combines portfolio log returns, a drawdown-increase penalty modulated by VIX (higher penalty in high-volatility regimes), a penalty for deviating from a regime-derived target exposure, and a turnover cost. The final trading action is a convex combination of the PPO actor’s suggested exposure and an interpretable, volatility-aware regime prior that specifies target exposure by regime. Performance is evaluated on SPY (with multiple random seeds) and in single-run tests on QQQ and DIA using risk/return metrics (total and annualized return, Sharpe, Sortino, Calmar, drawdown).
AI.result: On a 2020–2022 SPY test set, PPO-HRAP delivers 27.62% total and 8.48% annualized return, Sharpe 0.6447, Sortino 0.8588, Calmar 0.4592, and cuts max drawdown from 34.10% (Buy & Hold) to 18.47%. Over five SPY seeds, performance is stable with mean total return 0.2725±0.0109 and Sharpe 0.6219±0.0565. In single-run tests on QQQ and DIA, PPO-HRAP ranks first among compared methods in both total return and Sharpe for all three ETFs.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating a volatility-aware regime prior into PPO and blending it with learned actions can yield more balanced trading behavior, achieving better drawdown control and higher risk-adjusted returns than Buy & Hold and competing baselines. However, the approach currently induces high turnover, and evidence of robustness across assets is limited because cross-asset experiments rely on single runs; these are highlighted as areas for future improvement and validation.

title: Can LLMs Reliably Annotate Bioassay Metadata to Improve Data Readiness?
comment: Accepted to the AIDaR workshop at NeurIPS
summary: The emergence of foundation models for molecular property prediction requires a high degree of AI data readiness, including reliable metadata annotation. However, both public repositories and industrial screening databases suffer from missing, inconsistent, or conflated assay annotations. In this work, we quantify the extent of missing annotations in PubChem for the BioAssay Ontology (BAO) assay format and physical detection method fields and investigate whether open-source and proprietary large language models (LLMs) can reliably predict and audit metadata annotations directly from the assay text. In our assessment, we found that the annotation coverage across PubChem's $\sim$2 million bioassays is critically sparse, 36\% lacking an assay format, 89\% a BioAssay type, and >99.9\% any BAO-mapped assay format or detection technology term. This motivates the need for automated test-metadata curation. Using evaluation sets derived from PubChem and ChEMBL, we assess the agreement of seven open-source and proprietary LLMs with existing silver labels. Recall is at least 0.96 for biochemical and cell-based assay formats, with a similar pattern for detection technology, although disagreements increase on under-represented classes. Manual inspection shows that many of these disagreements trace back to inconsistencies between silver sources rather than to LLM error. Moreover, in a qualitative study with a senior industrial curator, LLM-generated evidence prompted the expert to revise some of their own labels, showing LLMs can flag potentially mislabeled assays. Across the study, performance differences between proprietary and open-source models were small. Together, these results suggest LLMs can support the large-scale annotation and auditing of assay metadata, though per-class reliability estimates and targeted human review remain necessary before such labels enter downstream ML pipelines.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how well large language models can automatically annotate and audit missing or inconsistent assay metadata in PubChem/ChEMBL, showing high recall and usefulness for large‑scale curation but with the need for human oversight.
AI.motivation: Foundation models for molecular property prediction require high-quality, consistently annotated assay metadata, but major repositories like PubChem have extensive missing and inconsistent BioAssay Ontology annotations, making automated curation methods necessary.
AI.method: The authors first quantify missing BAO-related metadata in ~2M PubChem bioassays. They then build evaluation sets from PubChem and ChEMBL and test seven open-source and proprietary LLMs on predicting assay format and detection technology directly from assay text, comparing LLM outputs to existing ‘silver’ labels and performing manual expert review of disagreement cases, including a qualitative study with a senior industrial curator.
AI.result: They find that PubChem metadata coverage is critically sparse: 36% of assays lack an assay format, 89% lack a BioAssay type, and >99.9% lack BAO-mapped assay format or detection technology terms. Several LLMs achieve ≥0.96 recall on major assay-format classes (biochemical and cell-based) and similar performance on detection technology; disagreements are concentrated in underrepresented classes and often arise from inconsistencies in silver labels, not true LLM errors. Performance differences between open-source and proprietary models are small, and LLM-generated evidence sometimes leads human experts to revise their own labels.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can reliably support large-scale annotation and auditing of assay metadata in public repositories, helping to fill critical gaps needed for AI-ready molecular data. However, their predictions should be used with per-class reliability estimates and targeted human curation, especially for rare or ambiguous classes, before being integrated into downstream machine-learning workflows.

title: An ontology for cross-sectoral crisis management: core and public health modules
summary: This paper presents the European Crisis Management Ontology (ECMO), a modular OWL-based ontology intended as a cross-sectoral reference for disaster risk reduction and response. ECMO is designed to be organised as a network of ontological modules. Among the modules, ECMO-CORE captures fundamental crisis management concepts such as hazard, event, exposure, impact, and response measure and uses ontology design patterns and the OWL2 punning technique to resolve ambiguities between hazard types and event manifestations. In addition, domain-specific modules are defined as in the case of the public health module aligned with SNOMED CT and ICD-11. To demonstrate the resource's utility, we used ECMO to represent the data of the Epidemic Intelligence from Open Sources system of the Joint Research Centre to generate an end-to-end pipeline that populates an ECMO-compliant knowledge graph from unstructured epidemiological news. Initial results demonstrate that ECMO provides the formal guardrails necessary for consistent and unified knowledge representation and integration. The ontology is publicly available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20070268 and is released under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) license.

AI.tldr: They introduce ECMO, a modular ontology to standardize how crisis and disaster information is represented and integrated across sectors, and demonstrate it on epidemic news data.
AI.motivation: Crisis management data (e.g., hazards, impacts, responses) come from many heterogeneous systems and sectors, making it hard to integrate and reason over them consistently. There is a need for a shared, formal, cross-sectoral ontology that can serve as a reference model for disaster risk reduction and response, and that can be extended to specific domains like public health.
AI.method: They design ECMO as a modular OWL ontology organised as interconnected ontological modules. A core module (ECMO-CORE) defines basic crisis concepts (hazard, event, exposure, impact, response measure), leveraging ontology design patterns and OWL2 punning to distinguish hazard types from their event manifestations. They add domain-specific modules, exemplified by a public health module aligned with SNOMED CT and ICD-11. To validate ECMO, they build an end-to-end pipeline that takes unstructured epidemiological news from the Epidemic Intelligence from Open Sources system, maps it into ECMO concepts, and populates an ECMO-compliant knowledge graph.
AI.result: The authors successfully model core crisis management concepts and create at least one domain module (public health) interoperable with existing medical terminologies. Their pipeline can transform open-source epidemiological news into a structured ECMO-based knowledge graph. Initial experiments show ECMO can enforce consistent, unified representation and integration of crisis-related knowledge across heterogeneous data sources.
AI.conclusion: ECMO is a practical and reusable reference ontology for crisis management, enabling standardized, cross-sectoral representation and integration of disaster risk and response information. Its modular design supports domain-specific extensions (e.g., public health) and interoperability with established terminologies. Early application to epidemic intelligence data suggests ECMO provides effective formal constraints (“guardrails”) for building coherent crisis knowledge graphs, and the openly licensed release facilitates adoption and further development.

title: What Makes Something Hard(er)? Explaining Question Difficulty in Natural Language
summary: Difficulty is one of the most fundamental properties of a question: it determines whether the question can meaningfully discriminate between models of differing ability. Although a variety of methods can now estimate or predict difficulty automatically, they yield only a single descriptive number, with no account of the underlying factors that make a question difficult in the first place. In this work, we propose a data-driven approach that automatically generates and validates natural-language hypotheses explaining what makes one question harder than another. We first estimate each item's difficulty from the responses of a large pool of LLMs using Item Response Theory. We then sample contrasting sets of easy and hard questions and prompt an LLM to propose candidate explanations of the difference, which are subsequently validated and selected on held-out questions. Experimental results across three datasets spanning mathematical, logical, and commonsense reasoning show that our method produces interpretable and predictive hypotheses. On their own, they predict the difficulty of unseen questions competitively with, or better than, advanced black-box difficulty regressors; used as additional features, they further improve those regressors, implying that they discover difficulty signals that existing models fail to capture. Moreover, we demonstrate that editing questions according to a hypothesis can shift their measured difficulty in the expected direction, indicating that the discovered hypotheses are causally valid difficulty factors rather than post-hoc descriptions. Our approach thus turns a purely descriptive difficulty score into actionable statements.

AI.tldr: They propose a method to automatically discover and validate natural-language explanations of why some questions are harder than others for LLMs, turning difficulty scores into actionable insights.
AI.motivation: Existing automatic difficulty estimators for questions give only a single numeric score and do not explain *why* a question is difficult or which factors drive difficulty. This limits interpretability, makes it hard to improve models or test specific capabilities, and prevents targeted question design or editing. The authors want a systematic, data-driven way to uncover and test the underlying linguistic and reasoning features that make questions easy or hard, especially for LLMs.
AI.method: 1) Collect responses from many LLMs on a large set of questions. 2) Use Item Response Theory (IRT) to estimate each question’s difficulty based on model performance, treating models as “test takers.” 3) Sample sets of easy vs. hard questions and prompt an LLM to generate candidate natural-language hypotheses that describe what differs between them. 4) Automatically validate these hypotheses on held-out questions by checking how well they predict relative difficulty; select those that are predictive. 5) Use the resulting hypotheses as features in difficulty prediction models and also as guides for editing questions to test causal effects on difficulty.
AI.result: Across three datasets (math, logic, commonsense), the method finds human-interpretable hypotheses about difficulty that generalize to new questions. These hypotheses alone predict unseen-item difficulty competitively with or better than strong black-box regressors. When used as additional features, they further improve state-of-the-art difficulty prediction models, suggesting they capture complementary signals. Edits to questions that follow a learned hypothesis systematically increase or decrease measured difficulty as predicted, demonstrating a causal role for the uncovered factors.
AI.conclusion: Data-driven, LLM-assisted hypothesis generation plus automatic validation can decompose question difficulty into explicit, interpretable natural-language factors. These factors are both predictive and causally linked to difficulty, turning opaque difficulty scores into actionable statements that can guide dataset design, model evaluation, and targeted question editing, and revealing difficulty signals that existing approaches overlook.

title: Verify Claims, Not Scores: Evidence-Based Verification of Modular Agents
summary: When developers change one component of an agent, such as its controller, a learned model or its verifier, they usually judge the change by an aggregate task score. That score cannot tell whether improvement was attainable, which component lost value, or what the agent's own checks certify. We introduce a claim-specific verification audit for modular agents that plan, act, check and refine. Instead of scoring the agent, the audit scores the evidence: each conclusion is recorded with the evidence behind it, one of four verdicts (supported, unsupported, unresolved or not evaluated) and the boundary within which it holds. Three tools supply that evidence. Oracle policies measure attainable improvement under an explicitly stated action set, so that a low value can be traced to the evaluation rather than to the environment. Replacing one component at a time with a perfect counterpart locates lost value, with null results read as unresolved whenever a downstream component could mask them. A separate test asks whether the verifier's score identifies the quantity it is read as bounding. Applied to a constrained portfolio-allocation agent in a synthetic market with known hidden regimes, the audit shows that the value of perfect regime information depends on the action set used to measure it, that the scenario generator discards most of the regime signal while better local fidelity does not improve decisions, and that the runtime verifier can be bypassed with no visible change in outcomes. The contribution is the protocol and the evidential distinctions it enforces; the empirical findings are specific to the agent and environment studied.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a structured “verification audit” protocol for modular agents that separates and scores evidence for individual claims about agent performance, rather than just using aggregate task scores.
AI.motivation: Developers of modular agents (with components like planners, controllers, learned models, and verifiers) typically evaluate changes with a single aggregate performance score. This score cannot reveal whether improvements were actually achievable, which specific component caused gains or losses, or what the agent’s own verification mechanisms truly guarantee. There is a need for a more diagnostic, claim-level evaluation method that clarifies what is attainable, where value is lost, and how well internal checks align with their intended guarantees.
AI.method: The authors introduce a claim-specific verification audit protocol for modular agents that plan, act, check, and refine. Instead of grading the agent as a whole, they grade the evidential support for specific conclusions. Each conclusion is annotated with: (1) the evidence used, (2) one of four verdicts—supported, unsupported, unresolved, or not evaluated, and (3) the operating boundary (conditions) under which the conclusion holds. They use three main tools: (a) Oracle policies to estimate the maximum attainable performance improvement given an explicitly defined action set, distinguishing evaluation limitations from environmental ones; (b) Component replacement tests, where each module is individually swapped with a “perfect” version to locate where value is lost, with null effects labeled as unresolved when downstream modules might mask differences; and (c) Verifier calibration tests to check whether the verifier’s score truly bounds or corresponds to the quantity practitioners assume it does. They apply this protocol to a constrained portfolio-allocation agent in a synthetic market with known hidden regimes.
AI.result: In the portfolio-allocation case study, the audit uncovers several nuanced findings: (1) The benefit of having perfect information about market regimes is not absolute; it depends strongly on the action set used to measure that value. (2) The scenario generator component discards most of the signal about the hidden regimes, so even though more accurate local modeling is possible, it does not translate into better decisions under the chosen setup. (3) The runtime verifier can be disabled or bypassed without causing noticeable changes in the agent’s observable outcomes, implying that its current scoring does not materially constrain or shape behavior in practice. These findings illustrate the kinds of distinctions the audit can reveal but are specific to the studied agent and environment.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that evaluating modular agents via a single aggregate score is insufficient for understanding where and why performance changes occur or what internal checks truly guarantee. Their proposed verification audit offers a structured, claim-level protocol that separates evidence from conclusions, assigns explicit verdicts, and clarifies the operating boundaries of each claim. By using oracle policies, component-level counterfactual replacements, and verifier calibration tests, the audit can identify attainable performance, locate value losses across modules, and assess whether verifiers measure what they are believed to bound. While the empirical results are case-specific, the main contribution is this general auditing framework and its emphasis on evidential rigor and clear distinctions between supported, unsupported, unresolved, and unevaluated claims.

title: Yo-ByT5: Efficient and High-Fidelity Diacritic Restoration for Yorùbá
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Code and outputs: https://github.com/lazy-monster/yo-byt5
summary: Yorùbá is a widely spoken tonal language that depends on diacritics to avoid lexical ambiguity. However, it is often written without these diacritics, thereby hindering downstream Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks. In this paper, we introduce Yo-ByT5, a byte-level Automatic Diacritic Restoration (ADR) model fine-tuned from ByT5-small. We evaluate Yo-ByT5 alongside five publicly released Yorùbá ADR models and one open-weight large language model (LLM) on the YAD benchmark under a consistent protocol. Our results demonstrate that Yo-ByT5 matches the performance of the strongest existing model, mT5-base, with a DER of 10.14% and a CER of 3.48%. Furthermore, it exhibits superior text fidelity despite using approximately half the parameter count of mT5-base. We also release our training code and model outputs, as well as call for the development of a larger, purpose-built benchmark for Yorùbá diacritic restoration.

AI.tldr: The paper presents Yo-ByT5, a compact byte-level model for automatically restoring Yorùbá diacritics, achieving state-of-the-art performance comparable to larger models while using fewer parameters.
AI.motivation: Yorùbá heavily relies on diacritics to convey meaning and avoid lexical ambiguity, but in practice text is frequently written without them, which harms the performance of NLP systems. Existing Automatic Diacritic Restoration (ADR) models exist, but there is a need for efficient, high-fidelity models and more rigorous, standardized evaluation for Yorùbá ADR.
AI.method: The authors fine-tune ByT5-small, a byte-level multilingual encoder-decoder model, to perform Yorùbá Automatic Diacritic Restoration, resulting in Yo-ByT5. They evaluate it under a consistent experimental protocol on the YAD benchmark, comparing against five released Yorùbá ADR models and one open-weight large language model. They compute Diacritic Error Rate (DER) and Character Error Rate (CER) and qualitatively assess text fidelity. They also make the training code and model outputs publicly available.
AI.result: Yo-ByT5 achieves a Diacritic Error Rate (DER) of 10.14% and a Character Error Rate (CER) of 3.48% on the YAD benchmark, matching the performance of the strongest existing model (mT5-base). Despite having roughly half the parameters of mT5-base, Yo-ByT5 attains superior text fidelity and comparable quantitative metrics relative to all baselines, including an open-weight LLM.
AI.conclusion: A byte-level model (Yo-ByT5) can restore Yorùbá diacritics at state-of-the-art levels while being substantially smaller than prior strongest models and producing higher-fidelity text. This demonstrates the effectiveness of byte-level architectures for low-resource, diacritic-rich languages. The authors underscore the importance of standardized evaluation and call for a larger, purpose-built benchmark for Yorùbá diacritic restoration to further advance research in this area.

title: Generation Provenance Before Behavior Attribution: Auditing Synthetic Speech Research Objects
comment: Accepted to the Third NeurIPS Workshop on Attributing Model Behavior at Scale: Data Attribution and Provenance. 4 pages, 0 figures, 1 table. An aggregate reproducibility package is available from the authors on request!
summary: Attributing model behavior to synthetic training data requires knowing what produced each training item before estimating what that item caused. A waveform-label pair does not preserve this knowledge. We propose a generation-provenance substrate in which a synthetic research object binds source specification, generated content, waveform, target, fact requirements, quality signals, review lineage, and immutable manifest identity. Producer and selection mechanism determine evidentiary meaning; storage location and variable name do not. We audit this substrate in a private Japanese care-handoff pipeline. A 113-asset review population contains 1.552 hours of synthetic speech across six scenario families; all items have linked audio, transcripts, candidate notes, and fact checklists, but human evidence is selective and source-specific. Two faithful-only manifests are scenario-seed-disjoint and immutably versioned, while exact upstream attribution remains blocked by floating generator aliases, missing per-clip TTS and code stamps, and an unversioned checking prompt. We argue that generation provenance is necessary but not sufficient for behavior attribution: it defines the candidate causal graph and audit units, whereas contributive attribution still requires frozen training runs and intervention or influence evidence. The paper contributes a compact provenance contract, an audit protocol, and a bounded case study for synthetic-data attribution; controlled research access may be offered, but we do not claim causal training-data attribution, clinical validity, or unrestricted public release.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a structured “generation provenance” framework to track how each synthetic training/example item was produced, and shows via a healthcare case study that such provenance is necessary but still insufficient on its own to causally attribute model behavior to specific synthetic data.
AI.motivation: As models increasingly train and evaluate on synthetic data, it becomes crucial to understand which generated items influenced which model behaviors. However, typical datasets (e.g., waveform–label pairs) lose information about how each item was generated (prompts, code, TTS systems, review process), making rigorous attribution and auditing impossible. The authors are motivated to design a substrate that preserves end-to-end provenance of synthetic research objects so that later audits and causal analyses are feasible, especially in sensitive domains like clinical handoff communications.
AI.method: They define a “generation-provenance substrate” and a compact provenance contract that binds, for each synthetic research object, its source specification (scenario seeds, prompts, generator identity), generated content (text, speech), associated targets (labels/notes), fact requirements, quality signals, human review lineage, and an immutable manifest identity. They then apply this contract to audit a private Japanese care-handoff pipeline containing 113 synthetic speech assets across six scenario families. They analyze which aspects of provenance are captured (audio, transcripts, candidate notes, fact checklists, manifests) and which remain missing or unstable (per-clip TTS and code stamps, versioned prompts, stable generator identifiers), and evaluate how these gaps affect the possibility of attributing downstream model behavior to specific synthetic items.
AI.result: The audit shows that the provenance contract and substrate can systematically capture rich, linked information for each synthetic asset, supporting structured audits and defining the candidate causal graph for attribution. In the case study, two manifests that include only items judged faithful are scenario-seed-disjoint and immutably versioned, demonstrating some rigor in data curation. However, exact upstream attribution is still obstructed because of incomplete provenance (floating generator aliases, missing per-clip TTS/code metadata, and an unversioned checking prompt). This highlights both the practical feasibility and current limitations of generation-provenance tracking in a real pipeline.
AI.conclusion: Generation provenance is a necessary foundation for attributing model behavior to synthetic training data, as it defines the audit units and the space of plausible causal relationships, but it is not enough to establish contributive or causal attribution on its own. Robust attribution additionally requires frozen, reproducible training runs and explicit intervention or influence evidence. The paper’s main contributions are: (1) a compact, implementable provenance contract for synthetic data; (2) an audit protocol that operationalizes this contract; and (3) a bounded, healthcare-focused case study illustrating both the benefits and limitations of the approach. The authors explicitly do not claim full causal attribution, clinical validity, or broad public release, underscoring the work’s scope as infrastructure and methodology rather than definitive causal analysis.

title: Compound interpretation is based on analogy
summary: How compound meanings are best predicted from constituent meanings remains a central question in computational models of lexical semantics. Comparing different computational models provides a way to evaluate alternative accounts of how semantic information is combined during compound comprehension. We propose a new model, the Compound Analogy Model (CAM), that predicts a compound's embedding by adding its constituent embeddings together with the average shift vectors of the two constituents' compound families. The resulting model is parameter-free and exploits local analogical structure in the semantic space. We evaluated CAM against the CAOSS model on Mandarin Chinese compounds. CAM consistently achieved higher prediction accuracy than CAOSS on both training and held-out data, with the exception of three-character compounds, for which analogical generalization is constrained by both small constituent families and a pronounced imbalance in family size between the two constituents. The advantage of CAM remained when evaluation was based on frequency-defined train-test splits that better approximate generalization from familiar to novel compounds. To assess the cognitive plausibility of the two models, we further examined whether model-derived semantic measures predict visual lexical decision latencies for two-character compounds. Predictors derived from CAM provided improved prediction for response latencies compared to predictors derived from the CAOSS model. These findings indicate that compound meaning is better characterized as local analogical generalization than as the application of a learned global linear transformation, and demonstrate that analogical semantic structure provides a cognitively plausible basis for compound comprehension.

AI.tldr: Proposal and evaluation of a parameter-free Compound Analogy Model (CAM) that predicts compound word meanings using analogical shift vectors from constituent families, outperforming an existing model and aligning better with human lexical decision data.
AI.motivation: To understand how the meanings of compound words can be best predicted from their constituent words within computational lexical semantics, and to compare different mechanistic accounts of semantic composition in order to find a more accurate and cognitively plausible model.
AI.method: Introduce CAM, which represents a compound by summing its constituent embeddings plus the average shift vectors derived from each constituent’s family of compounds, exploiting local analogical structure. Evaluate CAM against the CAOSS model on Mandarin Chinese compounds using both standard and frequency-based train-test splits, and assess cognitive plausibility by testing whether model-derived semantic measures predict human visual lexical decision latencies for two-character compounds.
AI.result: CAM consistently outperformed the CAOSS model on predicting compound embeddings for both training and held-out data, except for three-character compounds where small and imbalanced constituent families limited analogical generalization. CAM maintained its advantage under frequency-based splits that mimic generalization from familiar to novel compounds. In predicting human lexical decision latencies, semantic predictors derived from CAM explained more variance in response times than those from CAOSS.
AI.conclusion: Compound meanings are better captured by local analogical generalization in semantic space rather than by a single learned global linear transformation. The analogical structure encoded in CAM offers a more accurate and cognitively plausible account of how compound word meanings are composed and processed.

title: Gacha Decoding: Eliciting Diverse Generations Through Instruction Following
summary: We introduce Gacha Decoding, an inference-time method for eliciting diverse language model generations that scales with model capability. Across open-ended domains (in-the-wild chat, creative writing, planning for image generation, and protein design), Gacha Decoding significantly outperforms existing generation diversity approaches at equal quality (up to 2.4x Vendi over the next-best prior approach), reaching the same number of high-quality modes with over an order of magnitude fewer samples (11.0x) and discovering novel modes that no other approach surfaces. Our key insight is to treat diversity as an instruction-following problem: rather than relying on the LM's token entropy, we combine its instruction-following capability with randomness from an external RNG tool to scalably identify and realize distinct modes of the response space. This approach of "planning with dice" enables Gacha to invert the long-observed tension between diversity and model capability. As the underlying LM becomes a better instruction follower, diversity under Gacha Decoding consistently improves--even as its token entropy and diversity under prior approaches decline. Together, our results highlight that instruction following, rather than token entropy alone, can drive generation diversity.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Gacha Decoding, an inference-time method to boost diversity of language model outputs while preserving quality, by using external randomness and instruction following instead of token entropy.
AI.motivation: Existing methods to increase generation diversity in language models (e.g., temperature, nucleus sampling) often degrade quality and become less effective as models get more capable and deterministic. There is a longstanding trade-off between model capability (strong instruction following, low entropy) and output diversity, especially in open-ended tasks such as creative writing or planning. The authors aim to break this trade-off and exploit, rather than fight, the strong instruction-following behavior of modern LMs to achieve higher diversity.
AI.method: They introduce Gacha Decoding, an inference-time algorithm that treats diversity as an instruction-following objective instead of relying on the model’s intrinsic token-level entropy. The method uses an external random number generator (RNG) to sample “diversity seeds” or random instructions and then prompts the LM to follow these randomness-derived instructions, effectively “planning with dice.” By doing so, Gacha Decoding steers the LM toward distinct semantic modes in the response space, enabling diverse generations that scale with model capability. The LM’s strong instruction-following capability is explicitly leveraged to realize different modes instead of passively sampling them via stochastic decoding from the base distribution.
AI.result: Across varied open-ended domains—in-the-wild chat, creative writing, planning prompts for image generation, and protein design—the method substantially outperforms existing diversity techniques at matched quality. It achieves up to 2.4× higher Vendi diversity scores over the next-best prior baseline, attains the same count of high-quality modes using about 11× fewer samples, and uncovers novel response modes that other approaches fail to produce. As base models become more capable instruction followers, diversity under Gacha Decoding increases, even though traditional token-entropy-based diversity methods show declining diversity in the same regime.
AI.conclusion: Gacha Decoding demonstrates that instruction following, powered by external randomness, can be a more effective driver of generation diversity than token entropy-based sampling alone. By reframing diversity generation as an instruction-following problem, the method reverses the usual trade-off between capability and diversity: stronger instruction-following models yield more, not less, diversity under Gacha. This suggests future diversity techniques should explicitly exploit instruction-following behavior rather than merely tune stochastic decoding parameters.

title: Acmite: Mitigating Gender Bias in LLMs through Concept-Guided Mutual Information
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can reproduce social stereotypes from their training data, motivating extensive research on model debiasing. However, existing methods often rely on explicit biased examples or predefined group-term substitutions, making them sensitive to wording and less effective at capturing stereotype concepts shared across diverse contexts. More importantly, they typically suppress biased outputs without explicitly modeling the statistical dependence between model outputs and the underlying stereotype concepts. We propose Acmite, a lightweight concept-guided framework for targeted and selective debiasing. Acmite represents stereotypes as structured semantic concepts and uses maximal marginal relevance (MMR) to select diverse concepts for debiasing. Inspired by mutual information minimization, it approximates this dependence with token-level KL divergence while preserving task semantics. A lightweight LoRA adapter is trained with the base model frozen and activated at inference time only when the input is sufficiently similar to stereotype-related concepts; otherwise, the original model is used directly. We evaluate Acmite on BBQ, CrowS-Pairs, and StereoSet, and assess general capability preservation on ARC-Challenge, GSM8K, and PIQA. Experiments across three LLMs show that Acmite effectively mitigates gender bias across complementary evaluation formats while maintaining competitive performance on bias-unrelated tasks. Anonymous code and data are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Acmite-18E2/.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Acmite, a lightweight, concept-guided framework that selectively debiases large language models by modeling and reducing their dependence on structured stereotype concepts while preserving task performance.
AI.motivation: LLMs often reproduce social stereotypes learned from training data. Existing debiasing methods depend heavily on explicit biased examples or fixed group-term substitutions, making them brittle to wording changes and poor at capturing more abstract, shared stereotype concepts. Moreover, most approaches simply suppress biased outputs without explicitly modeling the statistical dependence between model behavior and underlying stereotypes. This creates a need for a method that targets the conceptual source of bias, works across diverse contexts, and minimally harms the model’s overall capabilities.
AI.method: Acmite first encodes stereotypes as structured semantic concepts and uses maximal marginal relevance (MMR) to select a diverse subset of such concepts for training. It then formulates debiasing as minimizing the dependence between the model’s outputs and these concepts, inspired by mutual information minimization and approximated via token-level KL divergence, while maintaining task semantics. A lightweight LoRA adapter is trained with the base LLM frozen, optimizing this tradeoff. At inference, the system checks whether an input is sufficiently similar to any stereotype-related concept; if so, it activates the adapter to debias the response, otherwise it routes the input directly to the base model, ensuring targeted and selective debiasing.
AI.result: On three bias benchmarks—BBQ, CrowS-Pairs, and StereoSet—Acmite significantly reduces gender bias across different evaluation formats. At the same time, tests on ARC-Challenge, GSM8K, and PIQA show that the method maintains competitive performance on tasks that are unrelated to bias, indicating limited degradation of general reasoning and problem-solving abilities. Experiments across three distinct LLMs demonstrate that the approach is model-agnostic and consistently effective.
AI.conclusion: Acmite provides a targeted, concept-guided debiasing framework for LLMs that explicitly reduces statistical dependence on stereotype concepts while preserving task semantics and general capabilities. By representing stereotypes as structured concepts, using MMR for diverse concept selection, and training a lightweight, selectively activated LoRA adapter, the method offers efficient, plug-in debiasing that works across models and evaluation settings. This shows that it is possible to meaningfully mitigate gender bias in LLMs without broadly suppressing outputs or substantially harming overall performance.

title: PRISM: A Category-Theoretic Framework for Measuring and Refining Multimodal Analogies
summary: Analogical reasoning involves identifying and preserving relational structures across domains. However, existing approaches to AI-driven multimodal analogy generation lack an interpretable measure of whether this structure is understood and maintained in the generated output. We address this gap with Pullback Refinement via Interpretable Structural Mapping (PRISM), a modality-agnostic framework for measuring and improving relational alignment in multimodal analogies, evaluated on visual metaphor generation. PRISM represents analogies as explicit relational mappings grounded in category theory and uses VLMs to instantiate these structures across modalities. Its first component, the pullback score, quantifies relational alignment from the resulting graph representation. On the AnaloBench benchmark, selecting the correct analogy purely by pullback score achieves 82.5% accuracy, demonstrating that the score captures meaningful relational information. PRISM's second component is an iterative refinement loop that uses the pullback score as an in-context feedback signal to iteratively revise the generated image towards greater relational depth. VLM-as-a-judge and human evaluations show that PRISM consistently improves metaphor consistency and analogy appropriateness over zero- shot generation, with human participants preferring the refined output in 57.65% of pairwise comparisons. However, a qualitative analysis reveals that refinement can favour visually crowded compositions rather than genuinely deeper relational correspondences.

AI.tldr: A framework (PRISM) to score and iteratively refine multimodal analogies by explicitly modeling and optimizing their relational structure.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal analogy and visual metaphor generation systems lack an explicit, interpretable measure of whether relational structure is truly preserved across domains, making it hard to evaluate, analyze, and systematically improve analogy quality.
AI.method: Introduce PRISM, a modality-agnostic framework grounded in category-theoretic representations of analogies as explicit relational mappings. PRISM uses vision-language models (VLMs) to instantiate cross-modal structures, computes a pullback-based graph-structural score to quantify relational alignment, and incorporates this score into an iterative refinement loop where generated images are revised using the score as in-context feedback to increase relational depth.
AI.result: On the AnaloBench benchmark, selecting analogies solely by the pullback score reaches 82.5% accuracy, indicating that the metric tracks meaningful relational information. In visual metaphor generation, both VLM-as-a-judge and human evaluations show that PRISM-refined outputs have higher metaphor consistency and analogy appropriateness than zero-shot generations, with humans preferring refined images in 57.65% of pairwise comparisons. Qualitative analysis notes a tendency toward visually crowded but not necessarily more deeply relational images.
AI.conclusion: Explicit category-theoretic structural mappings combined with a pullback-based score provide an interpretable and effective signal for evaluating and refining multimodal analogies. PRISM can improve perceived metaphor quality, but current refinement dynamics risk optimizing for visual complexity rather than truly richer relational correspondence, highlighting the need for more nuanced structural objectives.

title: Task-Oriented Rank Adaptation for Continual Learning in Text Classification
summary: Continual learning (CL) in text classification faces two critical challenges: catastrophic forgetting and negative transfer across sequential tasks. Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods such as LoRA enable efficient adaptation by learning low-rank updates of the model parameters. However, these compact representations are normally trained in isolation, limiting their reuse across related tasks. We introduce Task-Oriented Rank Adaptation (TORA), a geometric routing framework that leverages the low-rank structure of LoRA adapters to decide whether to transfer knowledge from the most compatible expert (Boosting) or isolate the new task (Shielding) based on structural similarity. Evaluated across 15 diverse text classification benchmarks, TORA consistently avoids harmful routing decisions: compatible tasks exceed their isolated performance while reducing training time, and structurally distant tasks are protected from interference with no loss in accuracy. With a single geometric threshold and no reliance on task identities or predefined sequences, TORA provides a simple and effective approach for dynamic adapter routing in sequential text classification systems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes TORA, a framework that routes LoRA adapters in continual text classification by deciding whether to transfer knowledge or isolate tasks based on geometric similarity, mitigating catastrophic forgetting and negative transfer.
AI.motivation: Continual learning for text classification suffers from catastrophic forgetting of old tasks and negative transfer between dissimilar tasks. Existing PEFT methods like LoRA are parameter-efficient but train task-specific low-rank adapters independently, missing opportunities to reuse knowledge when tasks are related and to avoid interference when they are not.
AI.method: They introduce Task-Oriented Rank Adaptation (TORA), which models LoRA adapters geometrically in a low-rank space and measures structural similarity between tasks. Based on this similarity and a single geometric threshold, TORA routes a new task either to reuse and extend the most compatible existing expert (Boosting) or to create a separate adapter to isolate it (Shielding). The routing is dynamic, does not require task IDs or fixed task order, and is designed specifically for sequential text classification.
AI.result: Across 15 varied text classification datasets, TORA improves or at least maintains performance compared to training isolated adapters. For similar tasks, it achieves higher accuracy while lowering training time through beneficial transfer. For dissimilar tasks, it avoids negative transfer and preserves accuracy by shielding them from unsuitable experts. TORA consistently makes non-harmful routing decisions under a single global threshold.
