AI.conclusion: TORA offers a simple yet effective geometric routing strategy for continual text classification with LoRA adapters, addressing catastrophic forgetting and negative transfer without needing explicit task identities or sequence information. It demonstrates that structural similarity in low-rank parameter space can guide when to share or isolate knowledge, enabling robust and efficient continual learning.

title: AiSearch: Interactive Multi-Modal Search with VLMs
comment: The demo paper with 1 page main paper, 7 pages supplementary material accepted and presented in ECCV 2026
summary: Modern retrieval systems must both be automated and interactive, allowing users to search and refine results in real time. We present AiSearch, a flexible multimodal retrieval framework that leverages the zero shot capabilities of Vision Language Models (VLMs) for natural language search over images and videos. AiSearch supports interactive search refinement through user feedback to tailor results to the user's intent, and allows visual benchmarking across multiple VLMs, enabling users to select the most suitable model for their task.

AI.tldr: AiSearch is a multimodal, interactive retrieval framework that uses vision‑language models for natural-language search over images and videos, supports iterative user feedback for refining results, and can benchmark different VLMs visually.
AI.motivation: Traditional retrieval systems often separate text and visual search, lack flexibility across different models, and provide limited mechanisms for users to iteratively refine results based on their intent. With the rise of powerful zero-shot vision-language models, there is an opportunity to unify natural-language search over images and videos, support real-time interaction, and give practitioners tools to compare and choose among different VLMs for their specific tasks.
AI.method: The authors design AiSearch, a framework that connects natural-language queries to visual content (images and videos) using zero-shot vision-language models. It offers an interactive loop where users can provide feedback on retrieved results to refine subsequent rankings, and integrates multiple VLM backends so that search quality from different models can be visualized and compared within the same interface or pipeline.
AI.result: AiSearch enables effective natural language retrieval over multimodal data without task-specific training, allows users to steer search results through feedback, and provides a practical environment for visually comparing the retrieval performance of different VLMs. The abstract implies that experiments or demonstrations show the system to be flexible and useful for real-time, interactive retrieval scenarios.
AI.conclusion: A unified, interactive multimodal retrieval framework built on zero-shot VLMs can support real-time natural language search over images and videos, adaptable refinement through user feedback, and practical benchmarking across multiple models, helping users select and tune models for their own retrieval tasks.

title: A Matryoshka Hierarchical RAG for Efficient Multi-Hop Question Answering
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems for multi-hop Question Answering (QA) must balance retrieval quality with computational cost. This cost is incurred during indexing time, through the use of expensive Knowledge Graphs (KGs) or Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate summaries, or during querying, through iterative LLM-driven retrieval. To reduce it while maintaining retrieval quality, we present MatRAG, a hierarchical framework that combines RAG systems with Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL). MatRAG addresses both kinds of cost by aligning the semantic hierarchy of a clustering structure with the nested structure of MRL. Specifically, it organizes the corpus of documents into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of clusters with progressively coarser granularity. Each level is indexed by a lower Matryoshka dimension. MatRAG pairs an iterative, top-down traversal of the DAG with an entity-driven mechanism that controls the hop budget and re-ranks candidates. We evaluated MatRAG on three standard multi-hop QA benchmarks against seven representative baselines. MatRAG outperforms its strongest competitors in terms of retrieval quality; furthermore, it reduces indexing costs by avoiding KG construction and LLM-based summarization, and lowers query-time costs through dimension-aware similarity.

AI.tldr: MatRAG is a hierarchical, cluster-based RAG framework that uses Matryoshka Representation Learning to cut both indexing and query-time costs for multi-hop QA while improving retrieval quality.
AI.motivation: Multi-hop QA RAG systems are expensive either at indexing time (e.g., building knowledge graphs, LLM-based summaries) or at query time (iterative LLM retrieval loops). There is a need for a method that preserves or improves retrieval quality but significantly lowers both types of computational costs, especially in large corpora requiring multi-step reasoning.
AI.method: MatRAG builds a hierarchical clustering of the document corpus organized as a DAG, where each higher level contains coarser clusters. It leverages Matryoshka Representation Learning so that each level is indexed with a progressively lower-dimensional embedding, aligned with the hierarchy granularity. At query time, it performs an iterative top-down traversal of the DAG, using low-dimension similarity search at higher levels and refining as it descends. An entity-driven mechanism manages the hop budget (how many retrieval steps are used) and re-ranks candidate documents to support multi-hop reasoning efficiently.
AI.result: On three standard multi-hop QA benchmarks and against seven representative RAG baselines, MatRAG achieves better retrieval quality than the strongest competing methods. It also empirically reduces indexing costs by removing the need for knowledge graph construction and LLLM-based document summarization, and lowers query-time costs by using dimension-aware similarity within the hierarchical embedding structure.
AI.conclusion: Aligning a hierarchical cluster structure with Matryoshka nested embeddings enables a RAG framework that is both more accurate and more efficient for multi-hop QA. MatRAG demonstrates that dimension-aware, top-down retrieval can replace more expensive components such as KGs and LLM summarization, offering a practical path to scalable, cost-effective multi-hop question answering.

title: Contrastive Attention Mitigates Spectral Bias in Spiking Transformers
summary: Spiking Transformers merge the energy-efficiency of spiking neural networks (SNNs) with the representational power of self-attention, creating a promising architecture for high-performance, energy-efficient computation. However, a performance gap persists versus its counterparts in artificial neural networks (ANNs). Unlike prior works attributing this to binary activations, we reveal that both spiking neurons and spiking self-attention (SSA) act as low-pass filters through multiscale spectral analysis. This characteristic leads to the dissipation of high-frequency components. To address this issue, we propose the Spiking Contrastive Attention (SCA) paradigm, which draw inspiration from the edge-detection and differential sensing properties of biological visual system. By extracting contrast prototypes via global contrastive aggregation and applying local differential refinement, SCA effectively enhances high-frequency information. Extensive experiments show that SCA is a general module that consistently boosts Spiking Transformers across image classification, semantic segmentation, and event-based tracking. Furthermore, it achieves lower complexity, offering superior efficiency over original SSA. These results establish its potential as a fundamental building block for energy-efficient Spiking Transformers.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a spectral low-pass limitation in Spiking Transformers and introduces Spiking Contrastive Attention (SCA), which enhances high-frequency information and improves performance and efficiency across multiple vision tasks.
AI.motivation: Spiking Transformers are attractive for their energy efficiency and strong representational power, but they still underperform comparable artificial neural network (ANN) models. Prior work mainly blames binary activations, without deeply analyzing the underlying cause of the performance gap. The authors aim to diagnose and address the fundamental limitations in how Spiking Transformers process information, especially from a spectral perspective, to close this gap while retaining energy efficiency.
AI.method: The authors conduct multiscale spectral analysis of both spiking neurons and spiking self-attention (SSA) modules, showing that they behave as low-pass filters that suppress high-frequency components. Motivated by biological visual systems (edge detection and differential sensing), they propose Spiking Contrastive Attention (SCA). SCA consists of two key stages: (1) global contrastive aggregation to extract contrast prototypes that emphasize differences across the input, and (2) local differential refinement to further amplify high-frequency and edge-like information. SCA is designed as a drop-in attention module that replaces SSA in Spiking Transformers, with lower computational complexity.
AI.result: Experiments across various vision tasks—image classification, semantic segmentation, and event-based tracking—demonstrate that integrating SCA into Spiking Transformers consistently improves accuracy/performance compared with models using standard SSA. Additionally, SCA reduces computational complexity, achieving higher efficiency and lower resource usage. The performance gains are robust across different benchmarks, indicating that SCA is a general and effective enhancement for Spiking Transformer architectures.
AI.conclusion: Spiking neurons and conventional spiking self-attention inherently behave as low-pass filters, causing a loss of high-frequency information and contributing to the performance gap between Spiking Transformers and ANNs. The proposed Spiking Contrastive Attention (SCA) counteracts this limitation by enhancing contrastive, high-frequency features via global contrastive aggregation and local differential refinement. SCA functions as a general, efficient module that not only boosts performance across multiple vision tasks but also reduces complexity, suggesting it can serve as a core building block for future energy-efficient Spiking Transformers.

title: The Asymptotics of Language Model Alignment with Memory
summary: Language model (LM) alignment broadly aims to perturb a given LM $Q$ into an aligned LM $q$ such that i) the outputs produced by $q$ and $Q$ are 'close' in probability, ii) $q$ has a higher expected reward than $Q$. Two common techniques for LM alignment are: KL-constrained RL, which requires knowledge of the LM distribution and is computationally expensive, and the best-of-$n$ algorithm, which requires only sampling from the LM. The work of Yang et al. established asymptotic closeness between the distributions produced by the two alignment methods for an $m$--length i.i.d. token sequence output by the LM, in the limit as $m$ increases to infinity. However, the i.i.d. assumption is not representative of practical LMs, whose output sequences often have memory. In this paper, we extend the asymptotic closeness result to the case when the $m$--length token sequence outputted by the LM is Markovian. Further, for finite-length output sequences -- particularly, when $m=1$ -- we provide a complete characterization of LM distributions and reward functions for which the KL-divergence between the distributions produced by the two alignment methods is zero -- a question first posed in Yang et al.

AI.tldr: The paper compares two language model alignment methods (KL-constrained RL and best-of-n) and shows when and how they produce similar distributions, extending prior results from i.i.d. tokens to Markovian outputs and characterizing exact agreement for short sequences.
AI.motivation: Existing alignment methods either require expensive access to full model probabilities (KL-constrained RL) or only sampling (best-of-n). Prior work showed that, under an unrealistic i.i.d. token assumption and asymptotically long sequences, these two methods produce similar aligned distributions. Real LMs are not i.i.d. and often operate at short sequence lengths, so it is unclear when the simpler best-of-n method is theoretically equivalent to the more expensive KL-constrained RL.
AI.method: The authors model the language model output as a Markov process over tokens instead of i.i.d. draws, then analyze and compare the distributions obtained by (1) KL-constrained reinforcement learning alignment and (2) best-of-n sampling with a reward function. They extend asymptotic analysis to Markovian sequences of length m and derive conditions under which the KL divergence between the two resulting distributions is zero for finite m, especially the single-token case m=1.
AI.result: They prove that for Markovian language models, as the sequence length m goes to infinity, the distributions induced by KL-constrained RL and best-of-n alignment remain asymptotically close, generalizing the earlier i.i.d. result. For finite-length sequences, and in particular for m=1, they give a complete characterization of the combinations of base LM distributions and reward functions for which the KL divergence between the distributions produced by the two alignment methods is exactly zero.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that the equivalence between KL-constrained RL and best-of-n alignment methods is not limited to i.i.d. token models but also holds asymptotically for Markovian language models. Moreover, it clarifies precisely when, for short sequences, the cheaper best-of-n approach can replicate the distribution of the more computationally intensive KL-constrained RL, guiding when practitioners can safely use best-of-n as a theoretically justified surrogate.

title: Beyond Memory: Harnessing Long-Horizon Agents with Explicit Belief States
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents can now undertake increasingly complex tasks, but the way they organize interaction history into memory does not ensure a coherent understanding of the current world. We introduce PoS, an inference-time framework that constructs and continually maintains explicit belief states as the agent's decision context. Each belief combines an estimate of the current world state with unresolved task requirements, making explicit what the agent still needs to learn and accomplish. To keep this belief reliable and actionable, PoS validates its consistency and monitors task progress to detect Belief Trapping, where the agent continues to act without making meaningful progress toward the goal. Recovery is then tailored to both the trapping pattern and the type of unresolved task requirement. Experiments on four benchmarks spanning execution and diagnosis show that PoS achieves the highest overall performance on every benchmark with all three LLM backbones. Ablations demonstrate the importance of consistency validation and recovery, while context-scaling experiments show resilience to context growth. Together, these results support belief construction and continual maintenance as a foundation for long-horizon context management beyond history retention and compression.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes PoS, an inference-time framework that builds and maintains explicit belief states for LLM agents, improving long-horizon task performance and robustness to context growth.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agents rely on interaction history as memory but lack an explicit, coherent representation of the current world and remaining task requirements. This leads to issues such as acting on outdated or inconsistent information, failing to track what is still unknown, and getting stuck making unproductive actions (Belief Trapping). There is a need for a principled way to manage long-horizon context that goes beyond basic history retention or compression.
AI.method: The authors introduce PoS, which constructs explicit belief states that combine estimates of the current world with unresolved task requirements. PoS continually updates these beliefs during inference, validates their internal consistency, and monitors task progress to detect Belief Trapping—situations where the agent acts without meaningful progress. Upon detecting trapping, PoS invokes tailored recovery strategies based on the trapping pattern and the nature of the unresolved requirements. The framework is applied on top of multiple LLM backbones and evaluated across diverse benchmarks involving execution and diagnostic tasks.
AI.result: Across four benchmarks, PoS yields the best overall performance on each benchmark for all three tested LLM backbones. Ablation studies show that both consistency validation and recovery mechanisms are crucial to achieving these gains. Additional experiments that increase context size demonstrate that PoS maintains strong performance even as context grows, indicating robustness to long-horizon scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Explicit belief construction and continual belief maintenance at inference time provide a strong foundation for managing long-horizon context in LLM agents. By making world state estimates and unresolved task requirements explicit, validating consistency, and recovering from Belief Trapping, PoS surpasses approaches that rely solely on history retention or compression, suggesting a promising direction for building more reliable and effective LLM agents on complex, extended tasks.

title: Cross-Lingual Alignment for Decoder-Only Models using MoE Routers
summary: Cross-lingual contrastive learning has been a core component of multilingual encoder training, but the ability to explicitly align representations is not possible in decoder-only LLMs because of varying multilingual tokenization. However, a growing amount of research suggests that even in LLMs, higher cross-lingual representational alignment leads to improved cross-lingual transfer. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to reimagine cross-lingual contrastive learning given the architectural constraints of modern LLMs. Rather than applying an auxiliary alignment loss on hidden states, we propose using the outputs of the mixture-of-experts (MoE) routers as the target for alignment. Router outputs lend themselves better to pooling over many tokens, enabling more reliable cross-lingual comparisons at the sequence-level. Controlled continual pre-training experiments on four open-source MoEs show that incorporating this routing loss also aligns the underlying hidden representations across languages. Most importantly, this loss improves multilingual performance on our diverse evaluation suite, demonstrating the potential of cross-lingual MoE router alignment.

AI.tldr: They introduce a new way to do cross-lingual contrastive learning for decoder-only MoE LLMs by aligning mixture-of-experts router outputs across languages, which improves multilingual transfer and also aligns hidden states.
AI.motivation: Cross-lingual contrastive learning is effective for multilingual encoders but hard to apply to decoder-only LLMs because different languages use different tokenizations, making explicit alignment of hidden states difficult. Yet, evidence shows that better cross-lingual alignment in LLMs improves transfer. The authors want a way to recover the benefits of cross-lingual alignment within the architectural constraints of modern, MoE-based, decoder-only LLMs.
AI.method: Instead of adding an auxiliary contrastive loss directly on token-level hidden representations, they focus on the mixture-of-experts router: for a given sequence, the router selects experts and outputs routing scores. They compute pooled, sequence-level router outputs and apply a cross-lingual alignment (contrastive) loss on these router representations between parallel or comparable sentences in different languages. They run controlled continual pre-training experiments on four open-source MoE LLMs, adding this new routing loss during training to evaluate its effects on alignment and downstream performance.
AI.result: The routing alignment loss encourages router outputs for semantically equivalent sequences in different languages to be similar. Empirically, they find that this training regime not only aligns router outputs but also induces better alignment in the underlying hidden representations across languages. Across four open-source MoE models, models trained with this loss achieve better multilingual performance on a diverse evaluation suite than baselines without the loss.
AI.conclusion: Aligning MoE router outputs provides an effective, architecture-compatible way to introduce cross-lingual contrastive learning into decoder-only LLMs. This router-level alignment improves both representational alignment and multilingual downstream performance, showing that MoE router signals are a powerful handle for cross-lingual training in modern LLMs.

title: SpikeMoE: Brain-Inspired Competitive Routing for Flexible Spiking Mixture-of-Experts
summary: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) enable event-driven computation through biologically inspired dynamics at the neuronal scale, while Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) perform conditional computation through expert selection at the model scale. Integrating their strengths offers potential for flexible neural architectures. A key challenge, however, lies in designing an expert selection mechanism based on spiking activity. To address this, we introduce a spike-based k-WTA Router inspired by competition-inhibition observed in the hippocampal CA1 region. The router incorporates lateral inhibition and refractory period to select Top-K experts according to discrete spike counts. Building on this, we present SpikeMoE, a framework that integrates neuronal-scale spiking dynamics with model-scale expert selection. To address incomplete multisensory inputs in multimodal tasks, we further equip SpikeMoE with a two-stage missing-modality modeling module that combines empirical prototypes from an observed-modality pool with modality-specific learnable embeddings to construct missing-modality representations. Experiments on vision, language, and multimodal benchmarks demonstrate that SpikeMoE achieves state-of-the-art performance among the SNN baselines, matches or exceeds the performance of ANN counterparts, and maintains robustness across diverse missing-modality conditions. These results demonstrate a favorable trade-off between performance and energy efficiency, validating the integration of spiking dynamics with sparse expert computation and highlighting SpikeMoE as a promising approach to energy-efficient brain-inspired computing.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SpikeMoE, a framework combining spiking neural networks with mixture-of-experts using a spike-based k-WTA router, achieving strong accuracy and energy efficiency, especially in multimodal and missing-modality settings.
AI.motivation: Spiking Neural Networks are energy-efficient and biologically inspired, but lack flexible model-scale conditional computation. Mixture-of-Experts architectures enable conditional expert selection but are typically used with conventional ANNs. There is a gap in how to perform expert selection driven directly by spiking activity, and how to handle incomplete multisensory inputs in multimodal tasks within such an SNN–MoE framework.
AI.method: The authors design a spike-based k-Winners-Take-All (k-WTA) router inspired by competition and inhibition in the hippocampal CA1 region. This router uses lateral inhibition and a refractory period to select the Top-K experts based on discrete spike counts. On top of this router, they build SpikeMoE, which integrates neuronal-level spiking dynamics with model-level expert selection. For multimodal tasks with missing modalities, they add a two-stage missing-modality modeling module that blends empirical prototypes from an observed-modality pool with modality-specific learnable embeddings to form representations for missing modalities.
AI.result: Across vision, language, and multimodal benchmarks, SpikeMoE reaches state-of-the-art results among SNN baselines and matches or surpasses ANN counterparts. It also remains robust under various missing-modality conditions. The framework exhibits a good balance between accuracy and energy consumption.
AI.conclusion: Integrating spiking dynamics with sparse expert computation via a spike-based k-WTA router is effective and energy-efficient. SpikeMoE emerges as a promising architecture for brain-inspired computing, particularly for multimodal scenarios with incomplete sensory data, offering both strong performance and robustness with favorable energy trade-offs.

title: A rubric landscape for evaluating clinical reasoning in large language models: what exists, what is missing, and what needs to be combined
summary:
Exam-style accuracy does not establish whether large language models (LLMs) reason well over clinical records. We define clinical reasoning as integrating and updating evidence across time and sources to form, revise and justify a patient's problem representation and a defensible plan.
  This structured narrative review maps three literatures: medical education assessment instruments, clinical LLM benchmarks published from 2023 onwards, and general-domain methods for evaluating long-form generation. We examine six dimensions: problem representation, temporal synthesis, differential and management reasoning, counterfactual reasoning, calibrated uncertainty, and reasoning faithfulness. Preprints are included and flagged.
  No single instrument covers all six dimensions. Problem representation and differential or management reasoning are reasonably covered, although reliability varies by instrument and setting. TIMER-Eval targets temporal synthesis, and ER-Reason assesses sequential diagnostic belief updating. Dedicated uncertainty and counterfactual evaluations are emerging, but their applicability to longitudinal free-text reasoning remains limited. Factual completeness is well theorised in general-domain evaluation, with early clinical evidence of important omissions. Faithfulness remains the weakest dimension, with one identified clinical causal-ablation study on multiple-choice questions.
  Existing tools should be combined through binary rubric items, separate completeness and correctness scores, case-specific importance weighting with non-compensable safety caps, temporal order-consistency checks, and chance-corrected reliability reporting. Further design work is needed for calibrated uncertainty, counterfactual reasoning and faithfulness over longitudinal free-text records. This review provides a design rationale, not a validated instrument.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that current exam-style benchmarks are insufficient to assess large language models’ clinical reasoning over longitudinal records and proposes a multidimensional framework and design principles for better evaluation tools.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM benchmarks in medicine mostly focus on exam-like questions, which do not capture real clinical reasoning: integrating evidence over time, revising problem representations, and justifying management plans. There is a need to understand what aspects of reasoning current instruments cover and where major gaps remain, especially for longitudinal, free-text clinical records.
AI.method: The authors conduct a structured narrative review across three bodies of work: (1) medical education assessment instruments for clinical reasoning, (2) clinical LLM benchmarks published from 2023 onwards, and (3) general-domain methods for evaluating long-form text generation. They map these against six predefined dimensions of clinical reasoning: problem representation, temporal synthesis, differential and management reasoning, counterfactual reasoning, calibrated uncertainty, and reasoning faithfulness. They also note whether works are preprints.
AI.result: They find that no existing instrument spans all six reasoning dimensions. Problem representation and differential/management reasoning are reasonably well covered but with variable reliability. Some newer tools, such as TIMER-Eval and ER-Reason, target temporal synthesis and sequential diagnostic belief updating. Emerging methods address uncertainty and counterfactual reasoning, but they are not yet well-suited for longitudinal free-text. General-domain work has strong concepts for factual completeness, with clinical evidence showing important omissions by LLMs. Faithfulness is the least developed area, with only one clinical causal-ablation study focused on multiple-choice questions.
AI.conclusion: To better evaluate clinical reasoning in LLMs, the authors recommend combining existing tools using binary rubric items, separate completeness vs correctness scores, case-specific importance weighting with non-compensable safety caps, temporal order-consistency checks, and chance-corrected reliability metrics. Substantial further work is needed to design robust measures of calibrated uncertainty, counterfactual reasoning, and faithfulness for longitudinal clinical text. The paper offers a conceptual design rationale rather than a ready-to-use validated instrument.

title: A Deterministic and Auditable AI Security Risk Assessment Framework with ATLAS Aligned Executable Rules and Formal Verification
summary: Artificial intelligence systems are increasingly deployed in high impact and safety critical settings, yet security assessment remains difficult to reproduce and defend under audit. Existing approaches often rely on narrative checklists or assessor driven scoring, and they lack an explicit, machine evaluable mapping from observable engineering artefacts to stable technique level outcomes. We present an evidence driven AI security assessment framework that operationalises assessment as a deterministic decision function. The framework normalises heterogeneous artefacts into a project independent Control ID taxonomy scored on a bounded four level ordinal scale, compiles technique level predicates from a pinned MITRE ATLAS snapshot via an explicit mitigation to control mapping, and outputs technique indexed feasibility and impact levels with traceable links back to the triggering evidence. We package all normative choices as a versioned assessment policy object to support repeatable reassessment across snapshots. To ensure semantic correctness, we formally verify boundedness, totality, ordered semantic consistency, and monotonicity of the compiled evaluator over the full declared score domain. We evaluate the framework on five public open source AI projects pinned to explicit repository snapshots, quantify before and after changes under a unified hardening intervention, and validate responsiveness to real engineering changes through fork based implementations of Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) generation and Continuous integration (CI) security scanning gates. Results show consistent downward shifts in feasibility profiles under strengthened observable controls, while worst case residual feasibility persists when technique specific core controls remain absent from the evidence scope.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a deterministic, evidence-based framework for AI security assessment that maps observable engineering artefacts to technique-level security outcomes, enabling reproducible, auditable evaluations.
AI.motivation: Security assessments of AI systems in high-impact, safety-critical settings are hard to reproduce and defend under audit. Current practices rely on qualitative checklists and subjective scoring, lacking a machine-evaluable, explicit link between observed security controls in a system and their impact on concrete adversarial techniques. This makes it difficult to compare assessments over time, across projects, or across different assessors, and to demonstrate rigor to regulators and auditors.
AI.method: The authors design an evidence-driven framework that treats AI security assessment as a deterministic decision function. They standardize heterogeneous engineering artefacts into a project-independent Control ID taxonomy scored on a four-level ordinal scale. Using a fixed snapshot of MITRE ATLAS, they build explicit mappings from mitigations to these controls and then compile technique-level predicates that, given the control scores, output feasibility and impact levels for each attack technique. All normative assumptions and mappings are encapsulated in a versioned assessment policy object. They formally verify properties of the evaluator—boundedness, totality, ordered semantic consistency, and monotonicity—over the entire score domain. Finally, they apply the framework to five open-source AI projects at pinned repository snapshots, including controlled hardening interventions and fork-based implementations of SBOM generation and CI security scanning to test responsiveness to real engineering changes.
AI.result: Across the five open-source AI projects, the framework produced technique-indexed feasibility and impact profiles that shifted in a consistent and interpretable way when observable security controls were strengthened. After applying a unified hardening intervention and adding SBOM and CI security scanning controls in project forks, the assessed attack feasibility generally decreased (downward feasibility shifts), demonstrating sensitivity to concrete engineering changes. However, for techniques where key core controls were still missing from the observed artefacts, high residual feasibility remained, showing that partial hardening does not eliminate certain attack paths.
AI.conclusion: An evidence-driven, formally specified and verified AI security assessment framework can provide reproducible, auditable, and technique-level evaluations of AI system security. By normalizing artefacts into a Control ID taxonomy, explicitly mapping to MITRE ATLAS mitigations, and capturing normative choices in a versioned policy, the approach yields consistent, traceable outputs that respond meaningfully to real engineering changes. Nonetheless, robust reductions in attack feasibility require coverage of technique-specific core controls, highlighting the importance of comprehensive evidence collection and control deployment.

title: Universal Byte-Level Encoding: UTF-8/UTF-16 Routing to Reduce Cross-Script Token-Budget Disparities
summary: Byte-level byte-pair encoding (BBPE) tokenizers are attractive for multilingual large language models (LLMs) because they cover all Unicode text. In UTF-8-based BBPE, however, many scripts start from a higher fallback cost than English: when no learned merges can be applied, a multibyte character requires multiple byte-derived symbols. We call this worst-case pre-merge cost the encoding floor. A higher floor can increase token counts and per-request cost and shrink usable context. Changing the text encoding can reduce this gap, but a single global encoding can make already-efficient English spans more expensive in mixed-script text. We propose Universal Byte-Level Encoding (UBE), a dual-alphabet tokenizer that keeps 1-2-byte UTF-8 characters on the UTF-8 path while routing 3-4-byte UTF-8 characters through UTF-16. This lowers the encoding floor for 3-byte Basic Multilingual Plane (BMP) characters in scripts with high token premiums (token counts relative to English) without raising it for already-efficient spans in mixed-script text. UBE changes only the byte representation presented to byte-pair encoding (BPE); the merge rule remains standard, and exact decoding is preserved. UBE also composes with alternative boundary policies and morphology-based representations. In a Unicode 17 audit, UBE exactly round-trips all Unicode scalar values and all inputs in the official normalization, grapheme-break, and emoji test suites. Across intrinsic evaluations, UBE lowers dispersion in English-normalized token-count ratios, reducing cross-lingual token-budget disparity. In multilingual language model (LM) experiments, UBE matches BBPE's LM quality. In the main multilingual settings, UBE reduces token counts most for high-premium scripts and slightly lowers English token counts, yielding more usable context under fixed token budgets and faster prompt processing in content-matched benchmarks.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Universal Byte-Level Encoding (UBE), a dual-encoding scheme that combines UTF-8 and UTF-16 byte views to reduce cross-lingual tokenization disparities for multilingual LLMs, especially for high-cost scripts, without hurting English efficiency or model quality.
AI.motivation: Byte-level BPE tokenizers are attractive for multilingual LLMs because they can cover all Unicode, but UTF-8-based BBPE creates a higher worst-case tokenization cost (encoding floor) for many non-Latin scripts that need 3–4 byte sequences. This leads to more tokens, higher cost, and less usable context for those languages, creating cross-lingual inequity in token budgets. Existing fixes via a single alternative encoding can improve some languages but usually make English or mixed-script spans worse. The authors aim to design an encoding that reduces this disparity, especially for scripts with high token premiums, while preserving efficiency for already well-served languages like English and maintaining compatibility with standard BPE and Unicode semantics.
AI.method: The authors propose Universal Byte-Level Encoding (UBE), a dual-alphabet tokenizer scheme. UBE routes characters differently depending on their UTF-8 length: 1–2-byte UTF-8 characters (e.g., basic Latin) are kept on the standard UTF-8 byte path, while 3–4-byte UTF-8 characters (e.g., many BMP and non-BMP scripts) are represented via their UTF-16 byte sequences before BPE is applied. This lowers the encoding floor for those scripts because UTF-16 uses fewer code units for them than UTF-8. The BPE merge algorithm itself is unchanged; only the byte representation fed into it differs by character class. The authors verify exact round-tripping via a Unicode 17 audit and conformance tests (normalization, grapheme-break, emoji). They evaluate the approach intrinsically by analyzing token-count ratios normalized to English across languages, and extrinsically via multilingual LM experiments comparing token counts, effective context length, prompt processing speed, and LM quality against standard UTF-8 BBPE.
AI.result: UBE reduces the encoding floor for 3-byte BMP characters, leading to lower token premiums for many non-Latin scripts that were previously disadvantaged under UTF-8 BBPE. It equalizes English-normalized token-count ratios across languages, i.e., lowers cross-lingual dispersion in token costs. In multilingual LLM experiments, UBE matches the language modeling quality of standard BBPE while decreasing token counts most for high-premium scripts and slightly also for English. Under fixed token budgets, this translates into more usable context in those languages and faster prompt processing for content-matched multilingual benchmarks. UBE is shown to exactly round-trip all Unicode scalar values and pass official Unicode normalization, grapheme-break, and emoji test suites.
AI.conclusion: Universal Byte-Level Encoding is an effective drop-in modification to byte-level BPE tokenizers that changes only the underlying byte representation while preserving standard BPE merges and exact decoding. By combining UTF-8 for short code points and UTF-16 for longer ones, UBE lowers the encoding floor and token premiums for many high-cost scripts without penalizing English or mixed-script spans. This yields more equitable token budgets across languages, larger effective context windows, and faster processing, all while maintaining the quality of multilingual language models and remaining compatible with Unicode standards and additional tokenization policies.

title: DRelay: Global Draft Context for Prefix-Aware Parallel Speculative Decoding Repair
summary: Parallel drafting reduces the drafting overhead of speculative decoding for large language models (LLMs), but its gains remain limited by the accepted prefix length. Even when the correct token is present in the candidate pool, a single early selection error prevents subsequent predictions from being used. We propose DRelay, which uses global information from the entire draft block to perform prefix-aware selective repair of candidate selections before target-model verification. DRelay bases its decisions on candidate correlations and the selected path: a global reader extracts predictive information across positions for each candidate. While a causal selector combines candidate-level information extracted by the global read with the tokens selected at preceding positions to determine whether the native choice at the current position is consistent with the global evidence and the selected prefix. It then decides whether to retain or replace the token, thereby repairing early errors and extending the accepted prefix. We further jointly train the draft backbone and the selector, combining candidate-support learning with a repair objective, while weighting the repair loss according to each block position's potential contribution to the consecutive accepted prefix. Across eight diverse benchmarks on an H800 GPU, DRelay consistently improves both average acceptance length and end-to-end decoding performance over DFlash, Domino, and DSpark. Under SGLang serving, DRelay improves average end-to-end speedup over DFlash, Domino, and DSpark by 14.7%-16.8%, 8.7%-9.3%, and 8.1%-9.3%, respectively.

AI.tldr: DRelay improves speculative decoding for LLMs by repairing early draft errors using global information, leading to longer accepted prefixes and faster end-to-end decoding than existing methods.
AI.motivation: Speculative decoding with parallel drafting speeds up LLM inference, but its efficiency is constrained by short accepted prefixes: a single early incorrect token choice in the draft invalidates subsequent otherwise-correct predictions. Existing systems cannot effectively recover from such early errors and thus underutilize the candidate pool, limiting speedups.
AI.method: DRelay introduces a two-stage mechanism: (1) a global reader that scans the entire draft block to extract predictive, correlation-based features for each candidate token across positions; and (2) a causal selector that, at each position, combines this global candidate information with the already-selected prefix to judge whether the current draft token is globally consistent. If inconsistent, it selectively repairs (replaces) the token before sending the sequence to the target model for verification. The draft backbone and selector are jointly trained with a combined objective: standard candidate-support learning plus a repair loss that is position-weighted by each token’s potential to extend the consecutive accepted prefix.
AI.result: On eight diverse benchmarks using an H800 GPU and SGLang serving, DRelay consistently increases both average accepted prefix length and overall decoding throughput, outperforming prior speculative decoders DFlash, Domino, and DSpark. In terms of average end-to-end speedup over these baselines, DRelay yields improvements of about 14.7%-16.8% over DFlash, 8.7%-9.3% over Domino, and 8.1%-9.3% over DSpark.
AI.conclusion: By using global draft-block information and prefix-aware selective repair, DRelay mitigates the impact of early draft errors in speculative decoding, leading to longer accepted prefixes and higher end-to-end speedups than state-of-the-art methods. This demonstrates that learning to repair draft sequences—rather than only generate them—can significantly improve practical LLM inference efficiency.

title: Mem++: Non-Destructive Memory for Long-Term Organizational LLM Agents
summary: Large Language Model (LLM) agents now take part in organizational work, where many authors record decisions across documents over months. Because a revised decision arrives as a new document rather than an edit, answering a question requires knowing which version held at a given time. However, most memory systems compress the record at write time. By distilling each document into facts, notes or graph edges, these methods fix what can be answered before any question is asked. To address this, we propose Mem++, a non-destructive memory framework shifting from write-time distillation to read-time selection. Mem++ stores every document whole with its date and author, and it calls no generative model at write time. At read time, it retrieves only documents dated up to the time a question asks about and fuses lexical and semantic rankings. Unlike systems that overwrite older versions, Mem++ keeps them and leaves the choice to the answering model. Evaluations on the organizational benchmark OrgMemBench demonstrate that Mem++ surpasses the strongest memory system baseline by 8.0 to 13.1 points across two answering models. With gpt-4.1-mini, it also achieves the best overall score, 2.6 points above RAG. In addition, Mem++ achieves the best average LLM-judge score on LoCoMo and ranks second on LongMemEval-S, behind only its entity-graph variant. Code for benchmark evaluation is available at https://github.com/AIDAChip-Inc/mem-plus-plus.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Mem++, a non-destructive memory framework for LLM agents that preserves all document versions and performs intelligent retrieval at query time, significantly improving question answering over organizational records.
AI.motivation: Existing memory systems for LLM agents typically compress or distill documents at write time into facts, notes, or graph edges. This premature distillation fixes what can be answered in the future and often loses important temporal and contextual information, especially in organizational settings where decisions evolve and are recorded as new documents rather than edits. There is a need for a memory framework that can handle versioned decisions over time without losing information due to write-time compression.
AI.method: Mem++ stores every document in full, tagged with its date and author, and deliberately avoids invoking generative models at write time. At query time, it restricts retrieval to documents whose dates are earlier than or equal to the time reference in the question, and it combines lexical and semantic retrieval signals to select relevant documents. Rather than overwriting or merging document versions, Mem++ retains all versions and delegates the final choice of which version to rely on to the answering LLM. The framework is evaluated on multiple long-context and organizational memory benchmarks.
AI.result: On the OrgMemBench organizational benchmark, Mem++ outperforms the strongest memory-system baseline by 8.0–13.1 points across two different answering models. Using gpt-4.1-mini as the answering model, Mem++ also achieves the best overall score, exceeding a standard RAG baseline by 2.6 points. Beyond OrgMemBench, Mem++ attains the highest average LLM-judge score on the LoCoMo benchmark and ranks second on LongMemEval-S, surpassed only by its own entity-graph variant.
AI.conclusion: Shifting from write-time distillation to read-time selection yields a more flexible and effective memory system for LLM agents operating over evolving organizational records. By storing full document histories with temporal metadata and applying constrained, hybrid retrieval at query time, Mem++ improves question answering performance across multiple benchmarks. The results suggest that non-destructive, temporally-aware memory architectures are a promising direction for robust LLM-based organizational assistants.

title: A Multi-Agent LLM Framework for Personalized Health Checkup Interpretation and Guidance
summary: Personalized interpretation of health checkup results requires reasoning across longitudinal records, medical knowledge, lifestyle guidance, and healthcare navigation. We present a multi-agent large language model (LLM) system that identifies multiple intents, maps each to a task-specific agent, executes them in parallel, and synthesizes their outputs. We compared answers generated in Single Agent and Multi Agent settings on 120 Korean compound queries combining two to four requirements, using synthetic health checkup records. The Multi Agent improved the weighted LLM-judge score from 1.695 to 1.797 (p = 0.027), and three additional LLM judges showed consistent improvements ($Δ$ = +0.111 to +0.186, all p < 0.05). The gains came from usefulness, consistency, and the handling of every requirement in compound queries, whereas numerical accuracy and grounding improved significantly under only one of the four judges and medical safety did not differ, and critical failures occurred at similar rates (Single Agent 15.0% vs. Multi Agent 13.3%). Two human evaluators preferred Multi Agent in 66.7% and 68.3% of pairwise comparisons. Multi Agent execution increased latency and cost by 1.31$\times$ and 2.02$\times$, respectively. In exploratory subgroup analyses, the improvement was concentrated in queries involving personal-record lookup.

AI.tldr: A multi-agent LLM system improves the quality of personalized explanations of health checkup results for complex, multi-part user queries compared with a single-agent setup, at higher latency and cost.
AI.motivation: Interpreting health checkup results for individuals is complex: it requires integrating longitudinal health records, medical domain knowledge, lifestyle advice, and navigation of healthcare options. Single LLM agents often struggle with compound queries that contain multiple distinct user intents (e.g., explanation, risk assessment, lifestyle change, and care navigation) because they must juggle all subtasks in a single reasoning stream. The authors aim to test whether a multi-agent architecture—where each sub-intent is handled by a specialized agent—can yield better, more comprehensive and reliable answers without compromising safety.
AI.method: The authors design a multi-agent LLM system that: (1) detects multiple intents within a user’s compound health query, (2) assigns each intent to a specialized task-specific agent, (3) executes these agents in parallel, and (4) synthesizes their outputs into one response. They construct 120 Korean compound queries that combine 2–4 requirements and use synthetic health checkup records as input context. They then compare answers from a Single Agent vs. Multi Agent configuration. Evaluation is performed primarily via LLM judges using a weighted scoring scheme, with four different LLM judges assessing dimensions like usefulness, consistency, coverage of all requirements, numerical accuracy, grounding, and medical safety. Additionally, two human evaluators conduct pairwise preference judgments. They also measure latency and monetary cost and conduct exploratory subgroup analysis, especially for queries involving personal-record lookup.
AI.result: Compared with the Single Agent setup, the Multi Agent system achieved a higher weighted LLM-judge score (1.695 → 1.797, p = 0.027). Three additional LLM judges confirmed consistent improvements, with score gains between +0.111 and +0.186 (all p < 0.05). The main benefits were better usefulness, more consistent reasoning, and more complete handling of all sub-requirements in compound queries. Numerical accuracy and grounding showed significant improvement only under one of the four judges. Medical safety scores did not significantly differ, and critical failure rates were similar (15.0% for Single Agent vs. 13.3% for Multi Agent). Human evaluators preferred the Multi Agent responses in roughly two-thirds of comparisons (66.7% and 68.3%). However, Multi Agent execution incurred higher computational overhead: latency increased by 1.31× and cost by 2.02×. Subgroup analyses suggested that most of the performance gain concentrates in queries that require looking up and using personal health records.
AI.conclusion: A multi-agent LLM architecture provides measurable improvements over a single-agent setup for answering complex, multi-intent health checkup queries, especially in terms of usefulness, consistency, and comprehensive handling of all requested aspects, and is preferred by human raters. Safety levels and critical failure rates remain similar to single-agent performance, indicating that multi-agent coordination alone does not substantially enhance safety. The benefits come at the cost of increased latency and monetary expense, and the gains are particularly pronounced for queries involving personal-record lookup. The work suggests that structured, specialized multi-agent designs can meaningfully enhance user-facing quality in personalized health explanation tasks, but further research is needed to improve safety and efficiency.

title: Controllable Multi-label Video Safety Detection via Adaptive Tversky Policy Optimization
summary: The rapid growth of video-based social media has increased users' exposure to harmful content, creating a need for reliable automated video safety detection. Although recent Vision-Language Models (VLMs) show strong video understanding capabilities, existing harmful video detection systems face two key limitations: they typically reduce safety detection to binary classification, overlooking the inherently multi-label nature of unsafe videos, and they rely on static training objectives that do not support controllable precision-recall trade-offs, though the desired operating point may vary across moderation pipelines and unsafe categories. To address these gaps, we propose Adaptive Tversky Policy Optimization (ATPO), a reinforcement learning framework for Multi-label Video Safety Detection (Multi-VSD). ATPO introduces the Adaptive Tversky Reward (ATR), which dynamically adjusts false-positive and false-negative penalties during training to enable controllable precision-recall trade-offs. Experiments on SafeWatch-Bench and XD-Violence show that ATPO substantially improves multi-label performance, increasing the Jaccard Index from 40.66 to 75.44 on SafeWatch-Bench-Real. Moreover, ATR enables reliable steering of the precision-recall operating point, supporting deployment scenarios with heterogeneous policy requirements. Code and checkpoints are provided at https://bruceyg.github.io/ATPO-project-page/ .

AI.tldr: They propose a reinforcement-learning based method (ATPO) that uses an adaptive Tversky-based reward to improve and control multi-label video safety detection performance for harmful content in videos.
AI.motivation: Video-based social media exposes users to a lot of potentially harmful content, so platforms need good automated safety detection. Existing systems mostly treat safety as a simple binary problem (safe vs unsafe), even though a single video can contain multiple distinct unsafe aspects (multi-label). Also, current training objectives are static and do not allow tuning the precision-recall trade-off, even though different applications and unsafe categories may require different operating points (e.g., high recall vs high precision).
AI.method: They introduce Adaptive Tversky Policy Optimization (ATPO), a reinforcement learning framework designed for multi-label video safety detection. ATPO uses Vision-Language Models for video understanding and introduces an Adaptive Tversky Reward (ATR) that dynamically adjusts the penalties for false positives and false negatives during training. This reward adapts over time, allowing explicit control over where the model sits on the precision-recall spectrum across different unsafe categories and deployment requirements.
AI.result: Experiments on the SafeWatch-Bench and XD-Violence benchmarks show that ATPO significantly improves multi-label detection performance. On SafeWatch-Bench-Real, the Jaccard Index increases from 40.66 to 75.44, which indicates much better overlap between predicted and true unsafe labels. Additionally, ATR successfully enables reliable control of the precision-recall operating point according to desired policy requirements.
AI.conclusion: ATPO is an effective reinforcement learning framework for multi-label video safety detection that overcomes two main limitations of prior work: it explicitly models the multi-label nature of unsafe videos and introduces a controllable, adaptive training objective via the Adaptive Tversky Reward. This leads to large gains in detection quality and allows practitioners to tailor precision-recall trade-offs for different real-world moderation policies. The authors release code and checkpoints to support further research and deployment.

title: Rethinking Probability-Based Reinforcement Learning From Posterior Concentration
summary: Verifier-free reinforcement learning with probability-based rewards offers a promising way to train LLMs on general reasoning tasks where external verifiers are unavailable. Yet the reliability of these rewards, especially in long-horizon reasoning, remains underexplored. This work identifies a length-dependent failure mode of probability rewards, which we call the Posterior Concentration Phenomenon (PCP). We show that the probability of a reference answer conditioned on a reasoning trace often collapses to a low-variance interval as the trace becomes lengthy. This phenomenon results in nearly indistinguishable rewards, which, under GRPO-based settings, makes probability-based policy optimization unstable and inefficient. Motivated by this, we propose Reinforcement Learning with Concentration-aware Posterior Rewards (RLCPR), a verifier-free RL framework to explicitly account for PCP for better optimization stability and token efficiency. It has two components: uncertainty-aware data sampling, which reduces concentration-prone rollouts before generation, and concentration-aware regularization, which penalizes unnecessarily long traces when posterior rewards collapse. Extensive experiments show that, alongside higher token efficiency, RLCPR outperforms the state-of-the-art verifier-free RL baseline by up to 4.0% on six of seven benchmarks, including general-domain and mathematical reasoning challenges.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a length-dependent failure mode of probability-based rewards in verifier-free RL for LLM reasoning and proposes RLCPR, which explicitly accounts for this issue to improve stability, token efficiency, and performance on reasoning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Verifier-free RL with probability-based rewards is appealing for training LLMs on general reasoning tasks where external verifiers are not available, but existing work has not adequately examined the reliability of these rewards, especially for long reasoning chains. The authors observed that probability-based rewards can become unreliable and unstable for long-horizon reasoning, motivating a systematic study and a more robust RL framework.
AI.method: The authors first analyze probability-based rewards and identify the Posterior Concentration Phenomenon (PCP), in which the conditional probability of a reference answer given a reasoning trace collapses to a narrow, low-variance interval as the trace length grows, leading to nearly indistinguishable rewards. They then introduce RLCPR, a verifier-free RL framework that explicitly models and mitigates PCP via two mechanisms: (1) uncertainty-aware data sampling that reduces the use of rollouts prone to concentration before generation, and (2) concentration-aware regularization that penalizes unnecessarily long reasoning traces when posterior rewards show collapse. These components are integrated in a GRPO-based policy optimization setup for training LLMs.
AI.result: Across six of seven reasoning benchmarks encompassing general-domain and mathematical reasoning, RLCPR achieves up to a 4.0% performance improvement over the state-of-the-art verifier-free RL baseline, while also improving token efficiency. The method yields more stable and effective policy optimization compared with standard probability-based reward approaches.
AI.conclusion: Probability-based rewards in verifier-free RL for LLM reasoning can suffer from the Posterior Concentration Phenomenon, especially with long reasoning traces, which undermines optimization stability and efficiency. By explicitly accounting for PCP through uncertainty-aware sampling and concentration-aware regularization, RLCPR stabilizes training, uses tokens more efficiently, and improves performance on a range of reasoning benchmarks. This suggests that handling length-dependent reward concentration is critical for scalable verifier-free RL in LLM reasoning.

title: Old Ideas, Novel Problems: The Instability of LLM-Based Novelty Evaluation
summary:
Automated ideation systems are often evaluated on the novelty of the ideas they produce, and that judgment is increasingly delegated to large language models. Such judges are typically built ad hoc and validated, if at all, on human-authored papers rather than on the generated ideas they are meant to score. So, how do novelty judges perform?
  Not well. We present a systematic controlled study of novelty evaluation design choices. We first build an evaluation set automatically, mining OpenReview for passages where reviewers explicitly affirm or dispute a paper's originality and keeping only submissions with unanimous agreement at the extremes of their research area; we pair these with ideas from a vanilla LLM generator. Across six judges, we find that small prompt design choices have large consequences; e.g., simply telling the judge that reviewers found one idea novel and the other not can change its verdict on more than half of the identical idea pairs it is shown, shifting pairwise accuracy by over 50 points and occasionally pushing it below chance. The same change helps one judge and hurts another. Retrieval and larger reasoning budgets help little, and two purpose-built novelty evaluators are outperformed by our cheapest prompted baseline. These results raise questions about reported novelty gains of automated ideation systems, and call for robust novelty evaluation methods.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that current LLM-based ‘novelty judges’ for evaluating idea originality are highly unstable and unreliable, with small prompt changes drastically altering their decisions, calling into question many reported novelty gains in automated ideation systems.
AI.motivation: Automated ideation systems are increasingly evaluated on the novelty of generated ideas, and this evaluation is often delegated to LLM-based judges. However, these judges are usually built in an ad hoc manner and, when validated at all, are tested on human-authored research papers rather than on the kind of generated ideas they are supposed to score. This mismatch and lack of systematic validation raises concerns about how well such LLM judges actually measure novelty, and whether conclusions drawn from them about ideation system improvements are trustworthy.
AI.method: The authors construct an automatic evaluation set by mining OpenReview for review passages where reviewers clearly affirm or dispute a paper’s originality, selecting submissions with unanimous reviewer agreement on originality at the extremes within each research area. They then pair these human-reviewed papers with ideas produced by a standard (‘vanilla’) LLM generator. Using this dataset, they systematically vary design choices for six different LLM novelty judges, including prompt wording, presence or absence of reviewer information, retrieval and reasoning configurations, and compare the judges’ decisions against the ground-truth originality labels implied by reviewer consensus.
AI.result: Across six different LLM-based novelty judges, small changes in prompt design lead to very large differences in behavior. For example, merely informing the judge that reviewers considered one idea novel and the other not can flip its verdict on more than half of otherwise identical idea pairs and can shift pairwise accuracy by over 50 percentage points, sometimes even below random guessing. The same prompt change helps some judges but harms others. Adding retrieval and more extensive reasoning (larger reasoning budgets) yields little improvement. Moreover, two specialized novelty-evaluation models perform worse than a simple, inexpensive prompted baseline judge.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM-based novelty judges are fragile, inconsistent, and often underperform simple baselines, with their outputs highly sensitive to minor design choices. This instability undermines the reliability of reported novelty improvements in automated ideation systems that rely on such judges. The paper concludes that the community needs much more robust, systematically validated methods for evaluating novelty, especially for machine-generated ideas.

title: NextMe-800: Anticipating Personal Behavior from Months of Egocentric Video
comment: 24 pages, 7 figures. Dataset and benchmark: https://huggingface.co/datasets/mmm8383/NextMe-800 ; project page: https://kkkkawayi.github.io/nextme-800/
summary: We often plan ambitiously yet act habitually and wonder, in retrospect, whether we would have planned differently had we known what we would actually do. Hindsight offers a valuable perspective on past decisions, although we often wish we could have simulated hindsight at the moment of choosing. If a system could generate plausible trajectories from one's personal history, such previews might help people formulate more realistic plans and make better informed decisions. We introduce NextMe-800, an approximately 800-hour first-person dataset from one volunteer over 126 days with 1 Hz images, gaze, and audio, captioned at five hierarchical abstraction levels from atomic actions to major activities. We formulate personalized action anticipation as open-vocabulary K-step sequence prediction and construct NextAct, a 1,500-point benchmark combining NextMe-800 with the multi-person EgoLife dataset. Using an embedding-based soft edit distance as the metric, we evaluate how well different models can anticipate personal behavior across abstraction levels and prediction horizons. NextMe-800 and NextAct provide a months-long resource and evaluation framework for studying how far ahead personal behavior can be anticipated from egocentric observation.

AI.tldr: The paper presents NextMe-800, a long-term, single-person egocentric dataset and the NextAct benchmark to study how well and how far into the future personal actions can be anticipated from first-person data.
AI.motivation: People often fail to follow through on ambitious plans and only in hindsight realize their actual behavior patterns; there is a desire for systems that can simulate such hindsight at decision time by predicting plausible future behavior from rich personal history.
AI.method: They collected about 800 hours of first-person data from one volunteer over 126 days at 1 Hz, including images, gaze, and audio, then annotated it at five hierarchical abstraction levels from atomic actions to major activities. They define personalized action anticipation as an open-vocabulary K-step sequence prediction task and build the NextAct benchmark by combining this dataset with EgoLife. They introduce an embedding-based soft edit distance metric to evaluate models on predicting future action sequences across different levels and time horizons.
AI.result: The authors conduct experiments with various models on NextAct, measuring how accurately they can anticipate personal behavior at multiple abstraction levels and over varying prediction horizons using the proposed soft edit distance metric. The results characterize current models’ strengths and limitations in long-horizon, personalized action anticipation, though specific numbers are not given in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: NextMe-800 and the NextAct benchmark offer a new, months-long egocentric resource and evaluation protocol that enable systematic study of how far ahead one can anticipate an individual’s behavior, supporting research on realistic planning aids that simulate hindsight at decision time.

title: Typological Alignment of Stack-Based Language Models on Mildly Context-Sensitive Artificial Languages
summary: Some properties of languages, e.g., subject-object-verb (SOV) word order, are more prevalent than others among the thousands of attested natural languages (NLs). Such typological commonality is often attributed to learning biases. Computational simulations, recently with language models (LMs), have facilitated the exploration of this theory. In this paper, we extend existing analyses of the relationship between LMs' learning biases and typological commonality on both data and model sides, focusing on: (i) cross-serial dependencies, the upper limit of attested syntactic complexity, and (ii) stack-based LMs (SLMs), potentially facilitating learning of hierarchical patterns. We first evaluate generalization of SLMs on cross-serial dependencies across diverse artificial languages and confirm that they struggle with such constructions. However, SLMs with limited working memory generalize better suggesting a possible basis for such inductive bias and thus the typological commonality of some word order configurations.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how stack-based language models (SLMs) learn complex syntactic patterns—specifically cross-serial dependencies—and what this reveals about why some word orders are more common across natural languages.
AI.motivation: Certain grammatical properties, such as SOV word order, are statistically more frequent across natural languages. Linguists often hypothesize that such typological commonalities arise from cognitive or learning biases. With the advent of computational modeling and modern language models, it is now possible to simulate and test how different architectures learn various syntactic patterns. However, we still lack a clear understanding of (a) how learning biases of specific model classes relate to the distribution of syntactic patterns in real languages, and (b) whether models specifically designed to capture hierarchical structure (like stack-based LMs) can handle the most complex attested syntactic dependencies. The paper aims to fill this gap, using cross-serial dependencies as a stress-test for syntactic complexity and probing whether model limitations can explain typological preferences for certain word orders.
AI.method: The authors construct a range of artificial languages that instantiate cross-serial dependencies, which are considered among the most complex syntactic patterns attested in natural languages. They then train stack-based language models (SLMs), which have explicit stack-like memory designed to capture hierarchical structure, on these artificial languages. By varying the working memory capacity of the SLMs, they can systematically assess how memory limits affect the models’ ability to generalize beyond the training data. Performance is evaluated in terms of generalization accuracy on unseen sentences exhibiting cross-serial dependencies in different word-order configurations.
AI.result: Overall, the SLMs have difficulty generalizing cross-serial dependencies, indicating that even stack-augmented architectures struggle with this upper bound of attested syntactic complexity. However, a key finding is that SLMs with more constrained working memory actually generalize better on these constructions than those with larger memory capacity. This counterintuitive result suggests that limiting memory can induce a stronger inductive bias toward particular generalization patterns. Moreover, these biases align with the relative typological frequency of some word-order patterns: the word orders that are more easily learned and generalized by limited-memory SLMs correspond to those more commonly found across natural languages.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that architectural constraints, particularly limited working memory in stack-based language models, can give rise to inductive biases that mirror typological commonalities in natural languages. In other words, constraints that make certain complex syntactic dependencies hard to learn—and others easier—may help explain why some word orders are far more prevalent than others. The findings support the broader view that language universals can emerge from learning biases shaped by cognitive (or model) limitations, and they demonstrate that stack-based LMs provide a useful framework for probing these connections between computational learnability and linguistic typology.

title: Auditing Routing Entropy as an Uncertainty Signal in Attention-Residual Transformers
summary: Dynamic architectures leave a per-example routing trace beside each prediction, and diffuse routing is easy to read as a sign that the prediction is unreliable. We audit that reading for routing entropy in Attention-Residual (AR) variants of Swin-Tiny and DeiT-Small, trained from scratch on CIFAR-10/100 with a soft-binned calibration auxiliary loss, asking whether the trace carries information about correctness beyond what the model's own confidence already reveals. Three checks probe this increment: does a routing signal appear at fixed confidence, does it replicate across training seeds, and can a held-out predictor exploit it against output-only and shuffled-trace controls? A sensitivity audit then injects effects of known size and measures the fraction of each that the probes recover. No test in the fixed 30-test binned family survives multiplicity correction, and neither the nominal hit nor a borderline result recurs in its sibling seeds. Across 24 paired runs a scalar routing probe yields no pooled improvement in routing-stratified calibration, and an entropy-profile probe predicts correctness better than the same probe given shuffled profiles yet worse than a confidence-only predictor in both binary log-loss and Brier score: a gain over shuffled traces does not become a gain over the output. Conditioning on the complete logit vector leaves the corresponding comparison unresolved. The audit bounds how far these non-detections can be read: at an injected effect of 0.010 nats the profile probe recovers 24-59% of the oracle gain, and a reference-preserving correction probe recovers 8% and 23% in the two CIFAR-100 settings, below the threshold we fixed for applying it to real labels. The results establish control-dependent gains and incomplete estimator recovery, not the absence of conditional routing information.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether routing traces in dynamic architectures provide reliability information beyond model confidence, and finds no robust, practically useful gains under their tests, while carefully bounding what this non-detection means.
AI.motivation: Dynamic neural networks produce per-example routing traces (e.g., attention or path choices). Practitioners often interpret diffuse routing (high entropy) as a sign that a prediction is unreliable. The authors want to rigorously test whether such routing signals actually contain additional information about correctness beyond the model’s own confidence, especially in calibrated settings, and to quantify how strong any undetected effects could be.
AI.method: They use Attention-Residual variants of Swin-Tiny and DeiT-Small, trained from scratch on CIFAR-10/100, with an auxiliary calibration loss. They define routing entropy and related routing-derived signals, then conduct three main checks for incremental information beyond confidence: (1) examining routing signals at fixed confidence levels, (2) checking replication of any effects across different random seeds, and (3) training held-out predictors that use routing traces, comparing against predictors that only see the output or see shuffled traces as controls. They further perform a sensitivity audit by injecting synthetic effects of known size into the routing signals and measuring how much of this effect their probes can recover, thus calibrating the power of their tests. They evaluate using routing-stratified calibration metrics, binary log-loss, and Brier score, with a fixed family of 30 binned tests and corrections for multiple comparisons.
AI.result: No test in their 30-test binned family remains significant after correcting for multiple comparisons, and nominal or borderline findings do not replicate across seeds. Across 24 paired runs, a simple scalar routing probe does not improve routing-stratified calibration when pooled. An entropy-profile-based probe predicts correctness better than the same probe on shuffled routing profiles, but still worse than a predictor that uses only model confidence, in terms of binary log-loss and Brier score. When conditioning on the full logit vector, whether routing helps remains statistically unresolved. The sensitivity audit shows that at an injected 0.010-nat effect, the profile probe recovers only 24–59% of the oracle gain, and a reference-preserving correction probe recovers just 8% and 23% in two CIFAR-100 cases, below their pre-set threshold for deploying such corrections on real data.
AI.conclusion: Under the tested settings, routing traces provide at best very limited and fragile additional information about prediction correctness beyond what is already encoded in model confidence and logits. The apparent gains depend strongly on the chosen controls and tests, and their probes incompletely recover even injected effects, meaning that the non-detections cannot be taken as proof of no conditional routing information. Instead, the paper establishes that any practically exploitable incremental information in routing traces is small relative to confidence-based signals under their configurations, and that careful control design and power analysis are crucial when auditing such interpretability signals.

title: LLM2Jev: LLMs Are Already Jev-Style Decision Models -- When and How to Fine-Tune Them
summary: Jev-style decision models return categorical probability distributions over predefined options without generating free-form text, enabling software systems to act on their outputs directly. In this work, we investigate the extent to which general-purpose LLMs already possess this capability out of the box, and when fine-tuning is actually necessary. We present LLM2Jev, an architecture-preserving framework that extracts calibrated decisions directly from next-token probabilities over bracketed numeric identifiers. LLM2Jev provides both a training-free inference recipe and a fine-tuning objective that optimizes candidate selection via a tree-factorized listwise loss while anchoring auxiliary predictions to the base model using KL divergence penalties. Evaluating on Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3-0.6B, we find that modern LLMs are inherently effective decision models: without training, the 4B model matches community Jev-style models built on the same backbone, outperforms letter-logit readouts, supports arbitrary option counts, and natively handles multimodal decisions over images. Fine-tuning provides targeted rather than universal benefits -- substantially improving weaker models and specific tasks (such as many-option intent routing), but offering diminishing returns for strong backbones. Crucially, our KL anchors prevent behavioral degradation in conversational text generation, with LoRA delivering the strongest performance on capable models.
