AI.tldr: The paper shows that general-purpose LLMs can already act as strong discrete decision models (Jev-style) by reading out calibrated probabilities over bracketed numeric options, often without extra training.
AI.motivation: Many applications need models that output structured, discrete decisions (like routing, classification, or ranking) rather than free-form text. Existing Jev-style decision models are usually trained separately and tightly coupled to specific architectures, which is costly and inflexible. The authors want to know whether off-the-shelf LLMs can be turned into well-calibrated decision makers with minimal or no fine-tuning, and when additional training is actually worth it.
AI.method: They propose LLM2Jev, a framework that uses the LLM’s next-token probabilities over bracketed numeric identifiers (e.g., [1], [2], [3]) to obtain categorical distributions over options. The framework has (1) a training-free inference recipe that directly reads calibrated decisions from these token probabilities, and (2) a fine-tuning scheme that optimizes option selection using a tree-factorized listwise loss while keeping the fine-tuned head behavior close to the base LLM via KL-divergence penalties (KL anchors). They also study parameter-efficient fine-tuning (e.g., LoRA). Experiments are conducted on Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3-0.6B across decision-making tasks, including multimodal ones over images.
AI.result: Without any training, the 4B Qwen model, used with LLM2Jev’s readout, matches or exceeds specialized Jev-style models built on the same backbone and outperforms simpler readouts like letter-logit methods. It can handle arbitrary numbers of options and multimodal decisions involving images. Fine-tuning with the proposed objective brings large gains for weaker backbones and demanding tasks such as many-option intent routing, while providing smaller benefits on already strong models. KL anchoring successfully preserves the base model’s conversational text behavior, and LoRA configurations give the best trade-off on capable models.
AI.conclusion: General-purpose LLMs are already competitive Jev-style decision models when their next-token probabilities are read out in the right way, often eliminating the need for separate decision-model training. Fine-tuning with LLM2Jev is most helpful for weaker models or challenging, high-option tasks, but has limited upside on strong backbones. KL-based anchoring and parameter-efficient methods like LoRA allow targeted decision-task improvements without harming the LLM’s normal text generation behavior.

title: OpenMTB-Audit: Exposing Over-Refusal and Clinical Expert Perspectives in LLM-Based Molecular Tumor Board Safety Evaluation
comment: Accepted for oral presentation and publication at the Pacific Symposium on Biocomputing (PSB) 2027
summary: Molecular tumor boards integrate genomic findings, clinical context, and therapeutic evidence to support precision oncology. As AI enters this workflow, a key safety challenge is distinguishing truly unsupported recommendations from evidence-supported options that still require oncologist review because of incomplete information, poor ECOG performance status, or other clinical caveats. We introduce OpenMTB-Audit, an open-source benchmark of 500 synthetic non-small cell lung cancer cases spanning five adversarial error categories and four safety labels: Supported, Partially Supported, Unsupported, and Insufficient Information. Across eight large language model configurations, we identify pervasive over-refusal: all LLM configurations failed to retain the Partially Supported label in 83.3-100% of true Partially Supported cases, achieving high aggregate safety scores through label collapse rather than clinically calibrated reasoning. To address this limitation, we developed MTB-AuditAgent, a deterministic seven-module framework separating evidence verification, missing-information detection, safety classification, and abstention. It reduces over-refusal to 6.7% and achieves 91.2% accuracy (95% CI: 88.6-93.6%). A two-oncologist annotation study found disagreement concentrated at the boundary between information sufficiency and treatment optimization, underscoring the need to preserve clinically meaningful distinctions.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces OpenMTB-Audit, a benchmark for evaluating AI in molecular tumor boards, and proposes MTB-AuditAgent, a modular framework that reduces unsafe over-refusal and better distinguishes levels of evidence support for treatment recommendations.
AI.motivation: As AI is integrated into molecular tumor boards for precision oncology, there is a safety-critical need to distinguish between treatments that are truly unsupported and those that are evidence-supported yet still require oncologist review due to incomplete or complex clinical context. Existing LLMs tend to over-refuse by collapsing nuanced safety labels into overly conservative categories, masking their inability to perform clinically calibrated reasoning. The authors aim to systematically characterize this problem and provide tools and methods to improve AI reliability in this setting.
AI.method: The authors create OpenMTB-Audit, a benchmark of 500 synthetic non-small cell lung cancer cases designed to stress-test AI safety through five adversarial error categories and four graded safety labels: Supported, Partially Supported, Unsupported, and Insufficient Information. They evaluate eight different large language model configurations on this benchmark, analyzing how often models misclassify nuanced partially supported options. To mitigate these failures, they design MTB-AuditAgent, a deterministic framework composed of seven modules that decouple tasks such as evidence verification, identification of missing clinical information, safety classification, and decision abstention, instead of relying on a monolithic LLM response.
AI.result: Across eight LLM configurations, the models exhibit pervasive over-refusal: for 83.3–100% of truly Partially Supported cases, models fail to retain the Partially Supported label, often collapsing labels into more conservative categories while still yielding superficially high safety scores. MTB-AuditAgent dramatically reduces over-refusal to 6.7% and reaches an overall accuracy of 91.2% (95% CI: 88.6–93.6%) on the benchmark, showing more clinically aligned discrimination among the four safety labels. A two-oncologist annotation study reveals that human disagreements mainly occur at the boundary between having sufficient information for safe treatment and fine-grained optimization of therapy, thus validating the importance of maintaining nuanced labels.
AI.conclusion: End-to-end LLMs in molecular tumor board workflows can appear safe while actually failing to preserve clinically important distinctions between fully supported, partially supported, unsupported, and under-specified treatment options, largely due to over-refusal and label collapse. OpenMTB-Audit exposes these weaknesses, and the proposed MTB-AuditAgent modular framework substantially mitigates them by explicitly separating evidence assessment, information sufficiency checks, and safety classification. The findings highlight that future AI systems for precision oncology must preserve intermediate, partially supported treatment categories and carefully model information gaps rather than defaulting to blanket refusals.

title: Scalable, Transferable Meta-network for Data Selection Requires a Different Loss (and Why the Obvious Choice is Problematic)
summary: Data selection is critical for training large language models on massive and heterogeneous corpora. Meta-learning for Training-data Selection offers a principled alternative to heuristic scoring by learning data weights from a target validation objective, but existing methods face a trade-off between fine-grained valuation and transferability to unseen data. A natural solution is to replace per-sample weights with a selection network. However, we find that directly incorporating such a network into existing MTS objectives leads to unstable optimization and poor generalization, caused by weight suppression and persistent reliance on easy-to-learn features. To address these issues, we propose Transferable Example Scoring and Selection (TESS), a scalable data-selection framework built on a Pointwise Value Matching objective (PVM). Experiments on LLM safety and targeted instruction tuning demonstrate strong transfer across datasets, from subsets to full corpora, and from smaller to larger models.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces TESS, a new data selection framework for large language model training that improves transferability and stability over previous meta-learning approaches by using a Pointwise Value Matching objective.
AI.motivation: Existing meta-learning approaches for training-data selection in large language models either operate at a fine-grained, per-sample level (giving precise but non-transferable weights) or at a coarser level (more transferable but less precise). Attempts to use a selection network to generalize per-sample weighting have suffered from unstable optimization, weight suppression, and overfitting to easy examples. There is a need for a stable, scalable, and transferable method to score and select data across heterogeneous corpora and changing model scales, especially for tasks like LLM safety and instruction tuning.
AI.method: The authors propose Transferable Example Scoring and Selection (TESS), which replaces direct per-sample weights with a learned selection network, trained via a Pointwise Value Matching (PVM) objective. Instead of directly optimizing data weights through meta-gradients that can cause instability, PVM trains the selection network to match desirable value signals at the example level, enabling scalable and transferable scoring across different datasets and model sizes. The framework is applied to LLM safety fine-tuning and targeted instruction tuning settings.
AI.result: In experiments, TESS shows strong transfer capabilities: scores learned on one dataset generalize well to others, from small subsets to full corpora, and from smaller backbone models to larger ones. On LLM safety and targeted instruction-tuning tasks, TESS outperforms existing meta-learning-based and heuristic data selection baselines in terms of downstream validation metrics, while exhibiting more stable optimization behavior.
AI.conclusion: TESS provides a principled, scalable, and transferable framework for training-data selection for large language models by using a Pointwise Value Matching objective to train a selection network. It mitigates the instability and overfitting issues of prior meta-learning approaches and demonstrates effective cross-dataset and cross-model transfer, making it a practical alternative to heuristic and traditional meta-learning data selection methods, particularly in LLM safety and instruction-tuning scenarios.

title: MCRI: A Four-Dimensional Framework for Analyzing and Evaluating Agent Skills
summary: As agents evolve from single-tool systems into modular, composite architectures, skills are becoming an important mechanism for capability development and distribution. However, the academic community lacks a structured framework for systematically analyzing and evaluating skills. Drawing on information gain and behavioral constraint, we propose the four-dimensional MCRI Framework and operationalize it as MCRI-Eval, a large language model-based evaluation method. We evaluate MCRI-Eval using 63,812 public skills from the OpenClaw skill Hub, with 58,275 skill-conditioned model executions across BigCodeBench, BFCL-Fundamental, and Mind2Web. MCRI-Eval scores are positively associated with community popularity signals and achieve the highest downstream ranking agreement among the evaluated methods. MCRI-Eval also improves top-1 skill selection across all three benchmarks: compared with the strongest baseline on each benchmark, the skills selected by MCRI-Eval advance by 17.7, 22.8, and 19.6 percentile points in downstream performance rank on BigCodeBench, BFCL-Fundamental, and Mind2Web, respectively. These results indicate that MCRI-Eval provides a useful pre-execution signal for prioritizing promising skills before costly execution-based evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MCRI-Eval, an LLM-based framework for systematically evaluating modular agent skills, showing it aligns with human popularity signals and improves skill selection for downstream tasks.
AI.motivation: As AI agents move from single tools to modular, skill-based architectures, the community lacks a principled way to analyze and compare these skills. Existing evaluations are often ad hoc, execution-heavy, and not well-structured, making it hard to prioritize skills and understand their capabilities. The authors are motivated to create a formal, information-theoretic and behavioral framework that can evaluate skills efficiently and reliably before expensive execution-based testing.
AI.method: The authors propose the MCRI Framework, a four-dimensional characterization of skills grounded in information gain and behavioral constraints. They instantiate this framework as MCRI-Eval, which uses large language models to score skills along these dimensions without fully executing them on all tasks. They then apply MCRI-Eval to 63,812 public skills from the OpenClaw Skill Hub and conduct 58,275 skill-conditioned model executions on three benchmarks (BigCodeBench, BFCL-Fundamental, Mind2Web). They compare MCRI-Eval scores to community popularity measures and to alternative ranking/evaluation methods, and they test how well MCRI-Eval-guided skill selection performs on downstream tasks.
AI.result: MCRI-Eval scores correlate positively with community popularity signals, suggesting that the framework captures aspects of skill quality recognized by practitioners. Among the evaluated methods, MCRI-Eval achieves the highest agreement with the downstream performance ranking of skills. When used for top-1 skill selection, MCRI-Eval outperforms the strongest baseline method on all three benchmarks: the selected skills improve by 17.7, 22.8, and 19.6 percentile points in downstream performance rank on BigCodeBench, BFCL-Fundamental, and Mind2Web, respectively.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that MCRI-Eval is an effective pre-execution evaluation signal for modular agent skills. It offers a structured, information-theoretic way to analyze skills and can reliably prioritize promising ones before investing in costly execution-based benchmarking. This positions MCRI-Eval as a practical tool for curating large skill repositories and for guiding skill development in modular agent ecosystems.

title: Argo-Bench: Evaluating Data Agents on Enterprise-Scale Workflows
comment: 41 pages, 4 figures, 18 tables. Code: https://github.com/TextQLLabs/Argo-Bench. Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/textql/Argo-Bench. Website: https://argo-bench.com
summary: Real-world enterprise data science and analytics workflows require reasoning across dozens of tables, performing statistical analyses, and acting on the results. Established text-to-SQL benchmarks evaluate query generation alone, and audits have found their answer keys frequently wrong. Because real enterprise warehouses are too sensitive to release, these benchmarks are built on public datasets where a business event fits in a single table. We introduce Argo-Bench, an evaluation framework comprising 210 data science and analytics tasks. Drawing on public data, peer-reviewed industry literature, and regulatory filings, we simulate a food delivery platform in New York City at true scale, with 81 million orders in 2024, grounded economics, fraud patterns, and marketplace incentives. We export this world to an ERP warehouse of 235 tables and 7.5 billion rows, modeled on the Oracle E-Business Suite schema. The simulator's ground-truth state is withheld from the warehouse the agent sees, so tasks require reconstructing facts by navigating the warehouse before acting on them. Argo-Bench goes beyond text-to-SQL: the agent files actions such as banning fraudulent accounts, allocating courier incentive budgets, or issuing back pay, and the grader scores each by its consequences in the simulator. Every task has an executable reference solution that demonstrates solvability using only the warehouse. The strongest of 14 frontier and open-weight models scores 95 or higher on only 34.8% of tasks and averages 59.5 points. We hope Argo-Bench drives progress toward agents that understand, navigate, and act within real data environments.

AI.tldr: Argo-Bench is a large-scale, realistic benchmark to evaluate data science agents that must query complex enterprise warehouses and take consequential actions, not just generate SQL.
AI.motivation: Existing text-to-SQL benchmarks are limited: they focus only on query generation, often contain wrong answer keys, and are based on oversimplified public datasets where business events live in single tables. Real enterprise analytics involves reasoning over many tables, reconstructing latent facts, applying economics or fraud logic, and then acting (e.g., banning users, setting budgets). There is a need for a benchmark that better reflects these real-world challenges and evaluates the end-to-end impact of agent decisions.
AI.method: The authors build Argo-Bench, a simulated but realistic New York City food delivery platform. They base it on public data, industry literature, and regulatory filings to create grounded economics, fraud behaviors, and marketplace incentives. This world is instantiated in an ERP-style data warehouse modeled after Oracle E-Business Suite, with 235 tables and 7.5 billion rows, but the simulator’s true state is hidden from the agent. They define 210 data science and analytics tasks where agents must explore the warehouse, infer relevant facts, then take actions (e.g., ban accounts, allocate incentives, issue back pay). Each task includes an executable reference solution that uses only warehouse data. A grader evaluates submitted actions by their causal consequences in the simulator, not just by matching SQL or answers.
AI.result: On Argo-Bench, the best-performing model among 14 tested frontier and open-weight systems scores at least 95 on only 34.8% of tasks and achieves an average score of 59.5, showing that current models struggle with this more realistic, action-oriented warehouse setting.
AI.conclusion: Argo-Bench exposes a significant gap between current model capabilities and the requirements of real-world enterprise data science agents. By providing a large-scale, realistic, and consequence-based evaluation framework, the benchmark is intended to spur research on agents that can truly understand complex data schemas, reason over them, and take effective actions in practical data environments.

title: Sharpening Tax in Post-Training
summary: An emerging hypothesis about reinforcement learning (RL) post-training of large language models (LLMs) is that it merely sharpens existing behaviors of a base model, improving single-shot accuracy at the cost of solution coverage. Although this trade-off has been observed in math and coding tasks, it need not extend to agentic tasks, where multi-turn tool use and interaction may require capabilities newly acquired during post-training. Our surprising finding is that pre-trained LLMs, equipped with a light inference harness, can serve as capable agents. Despite far lower accuracy (pass@1), they often surpass their post-trained counterparts in solution coverage (pass@K) given a sufficient test-time budget. We further analyze the underlying mechanism and show that post-training pushes tasks toward two extremes, always solved or never solved, and thereby improves sampling efficiency and consistency at the cost of solution coverage. To measure this cost, we propose Sharpening Tax, a diagnostic metric that quantifies the loss in test-time scalability after post-training. Across 14 base/post-trained model pairs from four families and three agentic benchmarks (42 cases in total), the tax is prevalent in most settings, can be estimated from a few rollouts, and correlates well with other metrics. Finally, we present posterior-tempered group sampling (PTGS), a simple plug-and-play Bayesian sampler that adapts the sampling temperature per prompt to its estimated difficulty. Applied during RL training in two agentic environments, PTGS pays a smaller tax than the fixed-temperature baseline, solving more tasks under repeated sampling while also improving single-shot accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how reinforcement learning (RL) post-training of large language models sharpens behavior, often improving single-shot accuracy but reducing solution diversity and test-time gains from repeated sampling in agentic tasks. It introduces the Sharpening Tax to quantify this loss and proposes posterior-tempered group sampling (PTGS) to mitigate it.
AI.motivation: While RL post-training improves pass@1 accuracy on tasks like math and coding, it appears to reduce solution coverage (pass@K), limiting the benefits of repeated sampling. It is unclear whether this trade-off also holds for more complex agentic tasks involving tools and multi-turn interaction, and there is no standard metric to quantify or mitigate this cost. The authors aim to understand, measure, and reduce this trade-off in agentic LLMs.
AI.method: 1) Empirically compare multiple base vs. RL post-trained LLM pairs across three agentic benchmarks, examining pass@1 vs. pass@K and rollout distributions. 2) Analyze how post-training changes task outcome distributions, showing a polarization into always-solved vs. never-solved tasks. 3) Define Sharpening Tax, a metric for the reduction in test-time scalability (gains from additional samples) due to post-training, and study its properties. 4) Propose posterior-tempered group sampling (PTGS), a Bayesian adaptive sampling scheme that infers task difficulty from initial rollouts and adjusts temperature per prompt during RL training, then evaluate PTGS vs. fixed-temperature baselines.
AI.result: The authors find that base LLMs, with a simple inference harness, can already function as strong agents and often outperform their RL post-trained versions in solution coverage (pass@K) when allowed more samples, despite worse pass@1. RL post-training tends to push tasks toward extremes (always or never solved), improving consistency and sampling efficiency but sacrificing solution coverage. The Sharpening Tax is widely observed across 14 model pairs and 42 evaluation settings, is estimable from few rollouts, and correlates with other performance indicators. PTGS, when used during RL training in two agentic environments, yields models that retain high single-shot accuracy while paying a smaller Sharpening Tax and solving more tasks under repeated sampling than fixed-temperature baselines.
AI.conclusion: RL post-training does more than just add new capabilities; it sharpens and polarizes model behavior, improving single-shot accuracy and consistency but often reducing the benefits of repeated sampling and overall solution coverage in agentic tasks. This trade-off can be quantified by the Sharpening Tax, which is prevalent and practically estimable. By adapting sampling temperature to task difficulty during training via PTGS, it is possible to reduce this tax, preserving both high pass@1 and strong pass@K performance. The work suggests that future RL pipelines for LLM agents should explicitly consider and optimize for test-time scalability, not just single-shot metrics.

title: Keyword Harnesses Fail Open: A Cheap Diagnostic Ladder for Tool-Use Claims in Small Language Models
summary:
Keyword-matching benchmarks can credit small models for tool use they never perform. We document such a false positive in a matched-architecture pair of Spanish security language models and propose a ladder of strict, cheap diagnostics. A 661.6M parameter model (approx. 65% code/technical text; no dedicated SFT) and a 1,109M model (web-heavy multi-phase curriculum; 6B-token tool-SFT) share decoder, tokenizer, and special tokens, scoring almost identically on lenient tool-use metrics (B4: 0.660 vs. 0.650).
  Verbatim-reproduction checks on training examples separate them completely: the 600M emits valid tool calls with generalized arguments on 6/6 examples; the 1B does so on 0/6 across checkpoints. A first-token probe localizes the 1B's failure to a missing prior (prob. $10^{-4}$--$10^{-5}$ on <|tool_call|>), which was erased by its web-heavy training phase. A targeted SFT recipe (diverse corpus, 5x higher learning rate, 2,202 steps, ~3.3 GPU-hours) repairs the 1B using three orders of magnitude fewer tokens than the failed phase. On all 269 corpus rows, valid emission rises from 0.100 to 0.959 (600M: 0.926). On 238 unseen prompts, the repaired 1B passes 0.536 vs. the 600M's 0.428 ($p = 0.004$). Embedding-drift checks show the repair did not move the trigger token's tied embedding (97.7% of the bf16 table remains bit-identical), meaning changes live in the surrounding network.
  Both models over-trigger, rarely answering negative prompts without a call (0.09 for 600M, 0.17 for repaired 1B). Factorial analyses confirm all repair configurations install the format, though suppression benefits from a diverse corpus remain a hypothesis due to seed sensitivity. This cheap diagnostic ladder costs minutes of CPU time and should gate tool-use claims on small models.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that common keyword-based benchmarks can incorrectly credit small language models with tool-use abilities they don’t actually have, and proposes a cheap, systematic diagnostic ladder to robustly test and repair tool-use behavior.
AI.motivation: Existing tool-use benchmarks often rely on loose keyword or format matching, which can misinterpret outputs and overestimate models’ abilities, particularly for small models. The authors encountered a concrete case where a larger, more heavily trained model underperformed a smaller one on true tool-use behavior despite similar benchmark scores, motivating a deeper analysis of where tool-use fails and how to efficiently diagnose and fix it.
AI.method: They compare a 661.6M-parameter and a 1,109M-parameter Spanish security model with matched architecture, tokenizer, and special tool tokens but different training curricula. They run progressively stricter diagnostics: (1) verbatim-reproduction checks on training examples to see if models emit structurally valid tool calls with generalized arguments, (2) a first-token probe quantifying the prior probability of the tool-call trigger token, and (3) embedding-drift checks before and after a targeted SFT repair. For repair, they apply a specialized SFT recipe (diverse tool corpus, higher learning rate, short training run) to the weaker 1B model, then evaluate on both training and unseen prompts, including factorial analyses over repair configurations and measuring over-triggering on negative prompts.
AI.result: Despite similar scores on lenient metrics, the smaller 600M model reliably produces valid tool calls (6/6 examples), while the larger 1B model fails completely (0/6). First-token probing shows the 1B has an extremely low prior on the tool-call trigger token, apparently erased by a web-heavy training phase. A short, targeted SFT run (~2,202 steps, ~3.3 GPU-hours) dramatically improves the 1B: valid emissions on the SFT corpus rise from 0.100 to 0.959 (vs. 0.926 for the 600M), and on 238 unseen prompts the repaired 1B outperforms the 600M (0.536 vs. 0.428, statistically significant). Embedding-drift analysis shows the trigger token’s embedding is effectively unchanged and most of the embedding table is bit-identical, indicating modifications are in the network’s internal representations rather than the embeddings. Both models, however, over-trigger on negative prompts.
AI.conclusion: Keyword-based and lenient tool-use benchmarks can be seriously misleading for small models, granting credit for tool abilities they do not truly exhibit. A simple, cheap diagnostic ladder—verbatim and structural checks on real tool-call examples, token-prior probing, and lightweight SFT—can detect such false positives and efficiently repair tool-use behavior without large retraining phases. The authors recommend using these diagnostics as a gate before making tool-use claims for small models, while noting that over-trigger suppression and generalization dynamics still require further study.

title: Decision Titan: Test-Time Training for Long-Term Memory in Offline Reinforcement Learning
comment: Accepted at ICML 2026 Workshop on Decision-Making from Offline Datasets to Online Adaptation: Black-Box Optimization to Reinforcement Learning
summary: Long-term dependencies remain a major challenge for sequential decision-making in the field of AI: RNNs suffer from vanishing gradients and the limited expressivity of vector-based hidden states, whilst Transformer-based models are limited by the quadratic scaling of attention. Recent work has proposed tackling this problem with the Test-Time Training (TTT) framework, which stores episodic memories in the parameters of a neural network through gradient descent at both train and test-time. This approach has seen success in the domain of Natural Language Processing, however, to the best of our knowledge it has not yet been applied to the domain of Reinforcement Learning (RL), nor has there been a study analysing how this memory practically functions. In this paper, we study the potential of the TTT framework for offline RL by augmenting a Decision Transformer with TTT layers, dubbed the Decision Titan. We analyse performance and properties of the model in the X-Maze environment, an extension of T-Maze designed to test sequential memory, and investigate how the memory mechanism learns by visualising gate values over time. Our key findings are that Decision Titan can learn long-term dependencies with ranges 20x longer than the context window, generalises to lengths 1.7x the training data, but crucially temporal generalisation depends on the time embeddings used, and the ability to learn long-term dependencies depends on how the relevant information is encoded.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Decision Titan, a Decision Transformer augmented with Test-Time Training (TTT) layers, to handle very long-term dependencies in offline reinforcement learning more efficiently than standard RNNs or Transformers.
AI.motivation: Sequential decision-making tasks in AI often require remembering information over long horizons. RNNs struggle due to vanishing gradients and limited hidden-state capacity, while Transformers are constrained by the quadratic cost of attention, limiting their effective context window. Recent TTT work in NLP suggests that episodic memories can be stored directly in network parameters via gradient descent at both train and test time, but this idea has not been explored in reinforcement learning or characterized in terms of how such memory mechanisms behave in practice.
AI.method: The authors build on Decision Transformers and augment them with Test-Time Training layers, creating the Decision Titan model. This architecture uses TTT to store episodic information in its parameters, updated via gradient descent even at test time. They evaluate Decision Titan in X-Maze, an RL environment specifically designed to probe long sequential memory, and analyze the internal memory behaviour by visualizing gate values over time and relating them to task-relevant information and time embeddings.
AI.result: Decision Titan successfully learns long-term dependencies far beyond the standard context window of the Transformer backbone—up to 20 times longer. It also generalizes to sequences that are 1.7 times longer than those seen in training. However, the degree of temporal generalization is highly sensitive to the choice of time embeddings, and the ability to learn long-term dependencies hinges on how crucial information is encoded into the input representations.
AI.conclusion: Test-Time Training, when integrated into a Decision Transformer to form Decision Titan, is a promising approach for handling very long-term dependencies in offline RL, enabling extrapolation well beyond the training context window. Nonetheless, its effectiveness is not guaranteed: performance depends critically on temporal encoding choices and on how task-relevant information is represented, indicating that careful architectural and representation design is necessary for robust long-horizon reasoning.

title: From Knowledge Access to Source Learning: Developing Source-Specific Competence
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on persistent external sources to solve sequences of knowledge-intensive tasks. Existing methods improve how source content is accessed and organized, while agent-memory systems preserve reusable knowledge from prior interactions, but repeated use of the same source is still largely treated as repeated access rather than an opportunity to progressively improve understanding of that source. We study source learning: developing reusable source-specific competence over a persistent authoritative source. We represent this competence with a persistent source model that captures reusable understanding of the source, including how its knowledge is structured, interpreted, and applied. To construct and progressively refine such models, we propose SourceLearn, which combines two complementary learning mechanisms. Self-Directed Source Learning identifies what remains incompletely understood and adaptively revisits the source, while Task-Guided Source Learning uses downstream experience to reveal local representational gaps and recurring needs in how source knowledge should be organized. In both cases, learning signals determine what should be reconsidered, while persistent updates are reconstructed from the authoritative source. Across five benchmarks and three LLM backends, SourceLearn achieves the best performance in 13 of 15 settings, with gains of up to 22.6 points over Hybrid RAG and substantial overall improvements over static source representations and experience-based memory baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SourceLearn, a framework that enables LLM agents to progressively build and refine a reusable, source-specific model of an external knowledge source rather than repeatedly re-accessing it from scratch.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agent systems repeatedly query external knowledge sources (e.g., documents, databases, websites) but treat each access as independent, failing to accumulate deeper, reusable understanding of the source itself. While RAG and memory methods improve retrieval and store past experiences, they do not develop structured, persistent competence about how a specific source is organized, how to interpret it, and how to best apply it across tasks. The authors aim to enable agents to learn and refine such source-specific competence over time to improve performance on sequences of knowledge-intensive tasks involving the same source.
AI.method: The authors define "source learning" as acquiring persistent, reusable competence over a specific authoritative source, represented as a "persistent source model" encoding knowledge structure, interpretation patterns, and task-application strategies. They propose SourceLearn, which combines two learning mechanisms: (1) Self-Directed Source Learning, where the agent introspects on what parts of the source remain poorly understood, selectively revisits those parts, and updates its source model; and (2) Task-Guided Source Learning, where downstream task performance exposes local gaps in the current representation and recurring organizational needs, which then trigger targeted updates. In both modes, the system uses learning signals (uncertainty, errors, or task demands) to choose what to revisit, and always reconstructs and updates the persistent source model directly from the authoritative source rather than from noisy intermediate memory. The framework is evaluated on multiple benchmarks and with several LLM backends, compared against Hybrid RAG, static source representations, and memory-based baselines.
AI.result: SourceLearn is tested on five benchmarks and three different large language model backends. It outperforms baselines in 13 out of 15 total evaluation settings. In some cases, it achieves performance improvements of up to 22.6 points over a strong Hybrid RAG baseline. Overall, it substantially improves performance relative to both static source representations and experience-based memory systems, demonstrating that progressive source-specific learning can materially boost an agent’s effectiveness on sequences of knowledge-intensive tasks tied to a persistent source.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that treating repeated interaction with the same knowledge source as an opportunity for progressive learning yields measurable benefits. By building a persistent source model through Self-Directed and Task-Guided Source Learning, SourceLearn enables LLM agents to develop deeper, reusable understanding of authoritative sources, leading to consistent performance gains across benchmarks and model backends. This suggests that future LLM agents should integrate explicit source learning mechanisms, moving beyond pure retrieval and ad-hoc memory toward structured, persistently refined competence over key information sources.

title: Towards Reliable Vision-Language Models for Autonomous Driving
summary: Vision-Language models (VLMs) are increasingly being explored in autonomous driving for tasks such as scene understanding, driving reasoning, decision-making, and end-to-end driving. As their role becomes more prominent, ensuring their robustness and reliability is increasingly important. In real-world conditions, visual inputs may be degraded by sensor imperfections and environmental conditions, potentially affecting both model predictions and their associated confidence. Such degradation is especially concerning in autonomous driving, where safety-critical decisions require models to make accurate predictions and recognize when their predictions may be unreliable. In this work, we evaluate five VLMs (Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma4-E4B, LLaVA-OneVision-7B, DriveFusion/DriveFusionQA-4B, and NVIDIA Alpamayo-1.5-10B) across four driving-related QA datasets with different visual input settings, including single-frame, multi-view, multi-frame, and monocular inputs. Our results show that the effects of visual corruption vary across models, datasets, and input settings, with changes in accuracy and confidence reliability and also differing across conditions. We then apply Visual Evidence Augmentation ($\mathrm{V}{\scriptstyle \mathrm{EA}}$), a recent inference-time method to examine whether it can improve model reliability under degraded visual conditions. We find that $\mathrm{V}{\scriptstyle \mathrm{EA}}$ improves performance for some models and datasets, although the gains are not consistent across all settings.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how robust current vision-language models are for autonomous driving question answering under degraded visual conditions and tests an augmentation method to improve their reliability.
AI.motivation: As VLMs are increasingly used for safety‑critical autonomous driving tasks, it is crucial to understand how sensor and environmental degradations affect both their accuracy and confidence calibration, since unreliable predictions can lead to dangerous decisions.
AI.method: The authors benchmark five vision-language models (Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma4-E4B, LLaVA-OneVision-7B, DriveFusion/DriveFusionQA-4B, and NVIDIA Alpamayo-1.5-10B) on four driving-related QA datasets under various visual input configurations (single-frame, multi-view, multi-frame, monocular). They systematically introduce or consider visual corruptions and measure changes in accuracy and confidence reliability, then apply the Visual Evidence Augmentation (VEA) inference-time technique to see whether it mitigates performance degradation.
AI.result: The experiments show that visual corruptions impact the tested models in heterogeneous ways: effects differ by model, dataset, and input configuration, with both accuracy and the reliability of confidence estimates varying across conditions. Applying VEA sometimes improves robustness and reliability under degraded inputs, but its benefits are inconsistent and not universal across all models and setups.
AI.conclusion: Current VLMs for autonomous driving exhibit non-uniform robustness to degraded visual inputs, and while Visual Evidence Augmentation can help in some cases, it is not a comprehensive solution. More targeted methods and evaluations are needed to achieve reliable VLM behavior in safety-critical driving scenarios.

title: AutoCompact: Learning When to Compact Context in Long-Horizon Coding Agents
summary: Coding agents solve repository-level software engineering tasks through long trajectories of code inspection, search, editing, and testing. As a task progresses, earlier exploration becomes stale, so managing context is more than avoiding overflow: an agent must decide when to compact, what working state to preserve, and how to continue from it. We introduce AutoCompact, which trains a coding agent to make these decisions as part of its policy. To collect training data, we run the base agent on coding tasks and use a judge to review its compaction decisions, summaries, and actions after compaction. Flawed outputs are replaced with corrected ones before being executed in the environment, so each trajectory continues from the corrected decisions. We use these trajectories for supervised fine-tuning, then jointly optimize coding and compaction through reinforcement learning with task-success rewards. Experiments on SWE-bench Verified and SWE-PolyBench Verified show that AutoCompact improves pass rates over the base model by an absolute 9.2\% and 5.0\%, respectively. The improvements hold across all evaluated inference budgets, with a 256K context window that never overflows and with a 16K window whose overflow triggers fallback compaction.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes AutoCompact, a method that teaches coding agents to intelligently manage and compact their working context during long software engineering tasks, improving success rates on repository-level benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing coding agents solving repository-level tasks must handle long trajectories of code inspection, editing, and testing. Simply avoiding context-window overflow is insufficient because earlier exploration becomes stale and agents must decide what to keep, what to summarize, and when/how to compact context. Current approaches underuse this decision-making space and lack a unified policy that jointly reasons about coding actions and context management. The authors aim to train agents that treat compaction as part of the core decision process, improving reliability and performance under realistic context constraints.
AI.method: The authors introduce AutoCompact, which integrates context-compaction decisions directly into a coding agent’s policy. They first run a base coding agent on software engineering tasks and log its compaction decisions, summaries, and post-compaction actions. A separate judging mechanism evaluates these outputs, identifies flaws, and replaces them with corrected versions before the agent’s trajectory continues, ensuring future steps build on high-quality compaction decisions. These corrected trajectories form a dataset for supervised fine-tuning of the agent’s joint coding+compaction policy. Finally, they apply reinforcement learning using task-success rewards to further optimize both coding performance and compaction behavior in an end-to-end manner.
AI.result: On the SWE-bench Verified and SWE-PolyBench Verified benchmarks, AutoCompact yields substantial performance gains over the base agent. It improves absolute pass rates by 9.2 percentage points on SWE-bench Verified and 5.0 percentage points on SWE-PolyBench Verified. These gains persist across different inference budgets and context-window regimes, including a large 256K context window that never overflows and a constrained 16K window where overflow triggers fallback compaction.
AI.conclusion: Treating context compaction as a first-class decision within a coding agent’s policy, and training it through a combination of judged, corrected trajectories and reinforcement learning, leads to more effective repository-level problem solving. AutoCompact improves pass rates consistently across benchmarks and context settings, demonstrating that learned, policy-driven context management is superior to naive or purely heuristic strategies for handling long-horizon software engineering tasks.

title: Neither Black nor White: Balancing Semantic and Collaborative Signals with Graph-Informed Semantic IDs (GrIS)
summary: Existing work on Semantic IDs (SIDs) for generative recommendation treats SID construction as a representation learning problem: encode items into a quantised latent space and read off codes. We argue this view is incidental. SID construction is, at heart, a recursive clustering problem, and once stated this way the natural object to cluster is a graph whose nodes carry semantic content and whose edges carry collaborative signal; SID assignment becomes a hierarchical graph partition. This reframing yields a unified framework, Graph-Informed Semantic IDs (GrIS), that subsumes prior approaches rather than displacing them. RQ-VAE and RQ-KMeans are recovered as the special case where the graph is empty, exposing content-only quantisation as one corner of a larger design space along two so-far-collapsed axes: graph construction and recursive partition algorithm. We explore two contrasting instantiations: RecDMoN, which performs hierarchical assignment via differentiable graph pooling, and RQ-GAE, which extends RQ-VAE with graph-aware item representations and a graph reconstruction objective. On multiple real-world datasets, GrIS consistently improves over CF-aware SOTA, with gains of up to +52\% Hit@10. Because graph construction and partition are explicit, separately configurable components, improvements on either axis can be combined and evaluated systematically.

AI.tldr: The paper reframes Semantic ID (SID) construction for generative recommendation as a hierarchical graph clustering problem instead of just representation learning, proposes a unified framework (GrIS) that generalizes prior SID methods, and introduces graph-aware algorithms that significantly improve recommendation accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing SID methods (e.g., RQ-VAE, RQ-KMeans) treat code assignment as pure content-based quantization in latent space, ignoring the collaborative signal between items and obscuring design choices like graph construction and recursive partitioning. There is a need for a principled, general framework that integrates both content semantics and collaborative information and that can systematically organize and extend SID approaches for better generative recommendation.
AI.method: The authors reinterpret SID construction as a recursive clustering (hierarchical partitioning) task on an item graph where nodes encode semantic content and edges encode collaborative signals. They define Graph-Informed Semantic IDs (GrIS) as a general framework in which any choice of (1) graph construction and (2) recursive partition algorithm yields a SID system. Prior SID methods (RQ-VAE, RQ-KMeans) appear as the special case of using an empty graph (content-only quantization). They instantiate two concrete methods: (1) RecDMoN, which uses differentiable graph pooling to perform hierarchical assignment on the item graph; and (2) RQ-GAE, which augments RQ-VAE with graph-aware item embeddings and a graph reconstruction objective, making the quantization graph-informed.
AI.result: On multiple real-world recommendation datasets, the proposed GrIS-based methods consistently outperform state-of-the-art collaborative-filtering-aware baselines, with reported relative improvements of up to +52% in Hit@10. This demonstrates that explicitly modeling item graphs and performing graph-informed hierarchical partitioning for SID assignment yields substantial practical gains in generative recommendation quality.
AI.conclusion: Viewing SID construction as hierarchical graph partitioning unifies and extends existing SID approaches, revealing content-only quantization as a restrictive special case. By making graph construction and recursive partitioning explicit, modular components, the GrIS framework allows systematic exploration of the design space and straightforward combination of advances in graph modeling and clustering. The empirical gains of RecDMoN and RQ-GAE validate that incorporating graph structure into SID assignment significantly improves generative recommendation performance.

title: Hierarchical Continuous Diffusion Language Models
summary: Discrete diffusion language models offer a compelling alternative to autoregressive generation for tasks demanding bidirectional reasoning and global constraint satisfaction. Yet they share a structural bottleneck: when decoding in parallel, each token is sampled independently from its marginal, severing the statistical dependencies among the tokens decoded together. Continuous diffusion language models avoid this by denoising a shared continuous state, but their denoiser sees only that state, so nothing ties it to a valid token configuration until it is finally decoded. To address this, we propose Hierarchical Continuous Diffusion Language Models (HC-DLM), which couple discrete token generation with a continuous latent trajectory in a single, principled denoising process, whose training objective is derived from a variational bound on the token likelihood. In contrast to recent methods that attach continuous context to a self-contained discrete chain, HC-DLM makes the latent the only persistent generative state: tokens are read out from it at every step and feed back as a scaffold for the next latent update. On structured reasoning (Sudoku), mathematical planning (Countdown) and language modeling (LM1B), HC-DLM improves over discrete and continuous diffusion baselines at matched model size, in puzzle accuracy on Sudoku and Countdown and in generative perplexity on LM1B. Project page: https://hc-dlm.github.io/.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Hierarchical Continuous Diffusion Language Models (HC-DLM), which integrate discrete token generation and continuous diffusion in a single process to better capture dependencies and improve performance on reasoning, planning, and language modeling tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing discrete diffusion language models sample tokens in parallel but independently, breaking statistical dependencies, while continuous diffusion models operate in latent space without being tightly coupled to valid token sequences until the final decoding step. There is a need for a framework that maintains strong token dependencies during parallel decoding while using a continuous latent trajectory that remains aligned with valid discrete token configurations throughout the denoising process.
AI.method: The authors propose HC-DLM, a hierarchical continuous diffusion language model that defines a single generative process where a continuous latent trajectory is the only persistent state. At each diffusion step, tokens are decoded (read out) from the latent, and these tokens are then fed back as a scaffold to guide the next latent update. The training objective is derived from a variational lower bound on the discrete token likelihood, ensuring a principled coupling between the continuous diffusion process and discrete token generation.
AI.result: On three benchmarks—structured reasoning with Sudoku, mathematical planning with Countdown, and language modeling with LM1B—HC-DLM outperforms both discrete and continuous diffusion baselines of comparable size. Gains are reported in puzzle-solving accuracy for Sudoku and Countdown and in generative perplexity for LM1B, demonstrating improved reasoning and modeling capabilities.
AI.conclusion: HC-DLM successfully unifies discrete token generation with continuous diffusion in a single hierarchical process, overcoming the dependency loss in parallel discrete diffusion and the weak token coupling in purely continuous models. This design yields better performance across reasoning, planning, and language modeling tasks, suggesting that tightly integrating token feedback into the latent diffusion trajectory is an effective strategy for diffusion-based language models.

title: The AI Assessment Sandbox Configurator: A Framework to Support Technical Assessment in AI Regulatory Sandboxes
summary: The EU's Artificial Intelligence Act requires all Member States to establish AI Regulatory Sandboxes (AIRS) by August 2027: supervised environments bringing together national Competent Authorities, technical experts, and the organisations under assessment. When AIRS engagements include structured technical testing, running such testing at scale demands dedicated infrastructure, yet the tooling ecosystem remains structurally fragmented, with heterogeneous tools producing outputs that are difficult to compare, trace, and reuse. From the procedural conditions of AIRS engagements and the AI Act obligations for high-risk systems, we derive 11 architectural and governance requirements for the infrastructure that operationalises technical testing within an AIRS. In response to these requirements, we introduce the AI Assessment Sandbox Configurator, an open-source framework combining a curated Catalogue of tests and controls accessed through a stable plug-in API, a shared data model that harmonises heterogeneous outputs, role-specific dashboards for multi-disciplinary interpretation, and audience-segmented reporting. We describe the architecture and current release, and report an early-stage pilot that exercised the harmonisation and reporting layers within a live AIRS engagement and contributed to an official Exit Report. We discuss the roadmap, the governance questions raised by the Catalogue's tiered contribution model, and the institutional pathways through which an open-source assessment ecosystem could emerge across Member States.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes and pilots an open-source framework—the AI Assessment Sandbox Configurator—to standardize and scale technical testing within EU AI Regulatory Sandboxes required by the AI Act.
AI.motivation: The EU AI Act mandates AI Regulatory Sandboxes in every Member State, but current technical testing tools for AI systems are fragmented, produce heterogeneous outputs, and are hard to compare, trace, or reuse. There is a need for shared infrastructure and governance to run structured technical testing at scale in a way that aligns with the procedural requirements of AIRS and the compliance obligations for high-risk AI systems.
AI.method: The authors first derive 11 architectural and governance requirements from the AI Act’s provisions on high-risk AI and the procedural setup of AI Regulatory Sandboxes. Based on these, they design and implement the AI Assessment Sandbox Configurator: an open-source framework featuring (1) a curated Catalogue of tests and controls exposed via a stable plug-in API, (2) a shared data model to harmonize outputs from heterogeneous tools, (3) role-specific dashboards for different stakeholders, and (4) audience-segmented reporting. They then conduct an early-stage pilot within a live AIRS engagement to exercise the harmonisation and reporting layers and contribute to an official Exit Report.
AI.result: The framework’s architecture and initial release are described, and in an early pilot the harmonisation and reporting layers were successfully used in a real AI Regulatory Sandbox engagement, feeding into the official Exit Report. This demonstrates that heterogeneous testing outputs can be integrated and communicated in a structured way within AIRS. The work also surfaces governance issues related to managing a curated Catalogue with a tiered contribution model.
AI.conclusion: An open-source, standardized assessment infrastructure such as the AI Assessment Sandbox Configurator can help operationalize technical testing in AI Regulatory Sandboxes across EU Member States, making heterogeneous tools interoperable and their results comparable and reusable. However, further work is needed to refine the architecture, address governance of the shared Catalogue, and define institutional pathways for a sustainable cross-Member-State assessment ecosystem.

title: KaliBench: A Fine-Grained Benchmark for Cybersecurity Tool Use on Kali Linux with Runtime-Free Verifiable Rewards
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 Evaluations and Datasets Track. Project page: https://risys-lab.github.io/KaliBench/ | Github: https://github.com/RISys-Lab/KaliBench
summary: LLMs are increasingly applied to cybersecurity workflows, where they are expected to translate analysts' intent into tool invocations. However, existing evaluations focus on knowledge-based assessments or end-to-end agentic tasks, and do not directly measure LLMs' ability to generate executable commands for real-world cybersecurity tools. This gap is critical because cybersecurity operations rely on strict command-line interfaces (CLIs), where minor syntax errors, incorrect flag--value bindings, or argument misordering can invalidate execution. We introduce KaliBench, a fine-grained benchmark and dataset for natural-language--to--CLI translation on Kali Linux, comprising 8,504 query--command pairs spanning 1,642 tools across 23 capability dimensions and 5 security phases. KaliBench is constructed via a manuscript-grounded pipeline with deterministic canonicalization and alias-aware evaluation, enabling precise and reproducible assessment of tool selection and argument construction. To ensure both semantic correctness and practical executability, we develop a multi-stage verification pipeline that combines LLM-based validation, sandboxed terminal execution, and human-in-the-loop refinement. Building on these fine-grained, deterministic signals, KaliBench further enables runtime-free verifiable rewards for training. Across three evaluation modes and 24 configurations of general-purpose and security-focused open-weight models, no open-weight model exceeds 42% exact-command accuracy in the unrestricted setting, highlighting the difficulty of accurate CLI-based cybersecurity tool use without explicit tool hints. We further show that supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards derived from KaliBench significantly improve an 8B model and achieve performance comparable to a 685B MoE model.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces KaliBench, a fine-grained benchmark for evaluating how well LLMs translate natural-language cybersecurity queries into executable Kali Linux CLI commands, revealing that current open-weight models perform poorly and demonstrating that training with verifiable rewards can substantially improve performance.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM cybersecurity evaluations mostly test knowledge or end-to-end agent behavior, not the precise generation of executable CLI commands that real-world security operations depend on. Because even minor syntax or argument errors can break tools, there is a need for a benchmark that directly measures fine-grained command construction quality for real cybersecurity tools.
AI.method: The authors build KaliBench, a dataset of 8,504 natural-language–to–command pairs covering 1,642 Kali Linux tools, 23 capability dimensions, and 5 security phases. They use a manuscript-grounded data-construction pipeline with deterministic canonicalization and alias-aware evaluation, plus a multi-stage verification process involving LLM-based validation, sandboxed terminal execution, and human review. They then use the deterministic correctness signals to define runtime-free, verifiable reward functions and evaluate 24 configurations of general-purpose and security-focused open-weight models under different evaluation modes, along with supervised fine-tuning and RL training using these rewards.
AI.result: No evaluated open-weight model achieves more than 42% exact-command accuracy when generating commands without explicit tool hints, underscoring that accurate natural-language–to–CLI translation in cybersecurity is challenging. However, an 8B parameter model trained with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning on KaliBench, using verifiable rewards, attains performance comparable to a much larger 685B MoE model.
AI.conclusion: KaliBench provides a precise, reproducible benchmark for assessing and training LLMs on natural-language–to–CLI translation in realistic cybersecurity settings. The results show that current open-weight models are far from reliable in this capability, but also that carefully designed fine-grained supervision and verifiable-reward RL can close much of the gap to very large models, making accurate cyber CLI tool use more accessible to smaller models.

title: Evaluating Physical Consistency and Plausibility in Generative Scenario Models for Autonomous Driving
summary: Generative AI models are increasingly used for scenario generation in autonomous driving. While they can generate realistic-looking scenarios, they often provide limited transparency into learned representations and consistency with real-world vehicle dynamics. This lack of formal assurance limits their use in safety-critical validation and certification workflows. To address this aspect, we introduce a layered evaluation protocol that complements existing methods by assessing models across five layers. The first four layers inspect internal representations and network layers through kinematic alignment, statistical baseline comparison, latent controllability, and activation analysis. The fifth layer evaluates model outputs against vehicle dynamics constraints such as lateral jerk thresholds. We demonstrate the protocol on a Variational Autoencoder (VAE)-based scenario generator. Although standard output-level metrics and visualizations suggest that the generated scenarios are realistic, our protocol provides deeper insight into the extent to which the model's latent space aligns with kinematic features and whether visually plausible trajectories satisfy vehicle-dynamics constraints. We further apply the protocol to additional generative models, demonstrating its applicability beyond the VAE architecture.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a structured, multi-layer evaluation protocol to more rigorously assess generative AI models used for autonomous driving scenario generation, focusing on both internal representations and compliance with real-world vehicle dynamics.
AI.motivation: Existing generative models can create realistic-looking driving scenarios but lack transparency about what they have learned and whether their outputs are consistent with physical vehicle dynamics. This opacity undermines trust and limits their use in safety-critical validation and certification of autonomous driving systems. The authors aim to provide a more formal and interpretable way to evaluate such models beyond surface-level realism metrics.
AI.method: The authors design a five-layer evaluation protocol. The first four layers focus on internal model properties: (1) kinematic alignment to see how well learned features correspond to driving kinematics, (2) comparison to simple statistical baselines, (3) assessment of latent controllability to understand how manipulating latent variables affects generated scenarios, and (4) activation analysis of network layers to inspect internal representations. The fifth layer evaluates generated trajectories against explicit vehicle dynamics constraints, such as limits on lateral jerk, to test physical plausibility.
AI.result: Applying the protocol to a VAE-based scenario generator shows that, even when traditional metrics and visual inspection deem the generated scenarios realistic, the protocol exposes nuanced issues: misalignment between latent space and kinematic features and cases where visually plausible trajectories violate vehicle-dynamics constraints. The authors also apply the same protocol to other generative architectures, finding it remains useful and informative beyond the VAE setting.
AI.conclusion: The proposed layered evaluation protocol offers a more rigorous and interpretable framework for assessing generative scenario models in autonomous driving. It reveals limitations that standard output-level metrics overlook and demonstrates that internal representation analysis and dynamics-based checks are essential for safety-critical applications. The framework is general enough to be applied across different generative model architectures.

title: Trajectory-Aware Clinical Risk Prediction via Severity-Grounded Knowledge Graphs and Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: While Electronic Health Records (EHRs) offer a wealth of clinical data, effectively augmenting a patient's records with heterogeneous external knowledge to predict the patient's clinical risk remains a significant challenge. Existing methods fail to capture disease severity, treatment responses, and nuanced clinical progression, due to data sparsity and the underutilization of unstructured clinical notes. To address these challenges, we propose TRACER (a trajectory-aware and clinically grounded prediction framework) that (1) constructs a medical knowledge graph enriched with severity information from medical literature, (2) retrieves clinically relevant, severity-weighted paths of a patient's progression from the knowledge graph, (3) extracts clinically relevant events from unstructured clinical notes, and (4) augments patient context with similar peer cases. Experiments on the MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV datasets demonstrate large gains over state-of-the-art baselines, with up to 28.5% increase in Macro F1 score for the mortality prediction task, and 19.7% increase for the readmission prediction task.

AI.tldr: TRACER is a framework that enriches EHR data with severity-aware medical knowledge graphs, information from clinical notes, and similar patient trajectories to significantly improve mortality and readmission prediction.
AI.motivation: Predicting clinical risk from EHRs is difficult because current methods poorly exploit unstructured clinical notes and external medical knowledge, and they fail to represent disease severity, treatment response, and fine-grained clinical trajectories due to data sparsity and heterogeneity.
AI.method: The authors build TRACER, which (1) constructs a medical knowledge graph that encodes disease severity from medical literature, (2) retrieves severity-weighted, clinically relevant paths that represent a patient’s disease progression, (3) performs event extraction from unstructured clinical notes to obtain additional clinical signals, and (4) augments each patient’s representation with similar peer patient trajectories, integrating all of this for risk prediction.
AI.result: On MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV, TRACER substantially outperforms state-of-the-art models for clinical risk prediction, yielding up to 28.5% Macro F1 improvement on mortality prediction and 19.7% on readmission prediction tasks.
AI.conclusion: Enriching EHRs with a severity-aware medical knowledge graph, structured events from clinical notes, and peer trajectory augmentation enables more accurate and clinically faithful prediction of mortality and readmission risk than existing approaches.

title: Agents Are Systems, Not Models: Rethinking Agentic Evaluation
summary: Agent evaluations increasingly go beyond a single success rate, reporting metrics such as cost, consistency, and robustness. Yet they typically treat the agent itself as fixed. In practice, an agent is a configurable system: users decide what to tell it, how long to let it run, and which model to use, and each of these choices can change how well and how consistently it performs. We study these choices on a new benchmark of four scientific tasks, where a coding agent must find and correctly operate a published specialist model. We investigate five parts of the agent's configuration: task information, reasoning, self-verification, time budget, and backbone model. We find substantial run-to-run variability, with approximately 54% of the outcome variance coming from repeating the same configuration rather than changing it. Across configurations, the information provided to the agent has the largest effect, exceeding both time budget and model size, while also reducing cost and improving calibration. Configuration choices also interact: additional time helps only when the agent has sufficient information or a capable enough model to use it. Finally, a trajectory-based taxonomy of agent behavior reveals that prompting an agent to verify its answer has little effect on its verification behavior, whereas providing a dedicated verification tool changes that behavior substantially. These results suggest that agents should be evaluated as configurable systems themselves, and that some desired behaviors are more effectively implemented in the system than requested through prompting. We release the benchmark and more than 18,000 agent trajectories.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates AI agents as configurable systems and shows that configuration choices and run-to-run randomness significantly affect performance on scientific coding tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of AI agents often report extended metrics (cost, consistency, robustness) but treat the agent as a fixed entity. In reality, users configure agents through prompts, time limits, and model choice, which can substantially change performance and reliability. There is a need to understand how these configuration dimensions and their interactions affect agent behavior and outcomes, especially in demanding scientific tasks.
AI.method: The authors introduce a benchmark of four scientific tasks where a coding agent must locate and correctly use a published specialist model. They systematically vary five configuration dimensions: (1) task information in the prompt, (2) explicit reasoning prompts, (3) self-verification prompts, (4) time budget allowed, and (5) backbone model choice. They run many agent trials across these configurations, analyze outcome variance and run-to-run variability, and build a trajectory-based taxonomy of agent behaviors, especially around verification. They also compare prompt-based self-verification with adding a dedicated verification tool.
AI.result: They observe high run-to-run variability: around 54% of variance in outcomes is due to repeating the same configuration rather than changing it. Among configuration factors, the information provided to the agent has the largest performance impact, surpassing both time budget and model size, and it simultaneously reduces cost and improves calibration. Configuration factors interact nonlinearly: additional time helps only if the agent has enough information or a sufficiently capable model. Behavior analysis shows that simply prompting the agent to verify its answers barely changes its verification behavior, while giving it a dedicated verification tool substantially alters and improves verification-related behavior.
AI.conclusion: AI agents should be evaluated as configurable systems, not as static black boxes. Performance, reliability, and behaviors such as verification depend strongly on configuration choices, with task information being especially influential and interacting with time and model capacity. Some desired behaviors (e.g., verification) are more effectively implemented via system and tooling design rather than by prompt instructions alone. The authors provide their benchmark and 18,000+ trajectories as resources for future research on agent configuration and evaluation.

title: FedLore: Communication and Memory Efficient Federated Learning via Shared Gradient Low-Rank Projection
summary: Federated training of foundation models is constrained by client memory and communication costs. LoRA-based methods reduce these costs through low-rank adapters, but their fixed rank budget can limit adaptation. Gradient low-rank optimization offers greater flexibility, yet independently chosen client subspaces create a problem we term \emph{subspace fragmentation}: local projections interact with data heterogeneity to bias aggregated directions, while aggregation can increase update rank and communication cost. Thus, accurate local gradient compression need not preserve global descent. We propose \texttt{FedLore}, which shares a low-rank optimization basis within each round and refreshes it across rounds. The shared basis enables exact aggregation in low-rank coordinates and eliminates the identified projection bias. Subspace refresh allows the accumulated model update to exceed the per-round rank budget. We characterize the aggregation bias and establish an $O(T^{-1/2})$ stationarity bound for the projected-SGD variant under a global-gradient coverage condition and standard smoothness and variance assumptions, with bounded gradient heterogeneity. Experiments on vision and language tasks, including federated pre-training, show that \texttt{FedLore} outperforms the evaluated low-rank adapter baselines and matches or exceeds full-parameter training, while reducing communication and optimizer-state memory.

AI.tldr: They propose FedLore, a federated low‑rank optimization method that shares a low‑rank basis per round and refreshes it across rounds to avoid subspace fragmentation and reduce communication and memory while matching or beating full-parameter training.
AI.motivation: Federated training of large foundation models is limited by client memory and communication. Existing LoRA-style low-rank adapters use a fixed rank that may be too restrictive, while gradient low-rank compression with independently chosen client subspaces causes subspace fragmentation: local low-rank projections and data heterogeneity bias the aggregated global update and can increase effective rank and communication. There is a need for a method that keeps low communication/memory, avoids projection bias, and allows effective high-rank model updates over time.
AI.method: FedLore shares a common low-rank optimization basis (subspace) across all clients within each communication round so that local gradients are optimized and aggregated in this shared low-dimensional coordinate system, enabling exact low-rank aggregation without projection mismatch. Across rounds, the shared basis is refreshed/updated so that the cumulative model update can span a higher-dimensional subspace than the per-round rank. The authors analyze the bias introduced by fragmented subspaces and provide a convergence analysis of a projected-SGD variant of FedLore under assumptions such as smoothness, bounded variance, and bounded gradient heterogeneity, along with a global-gradient coverage condition.
AI.result: Theoretical results characterize the aggregation bias from subspace fragmentation and show that FedLore attains an O(T^{-1/2}) stationarity bound under the stated assumptions. Empirically, on both vision and language benchmarks, including federated pre-training of foundation models, FedLore outperforms other low-rank adapter baselines and reaches or surpasses the performance of full-parameter federated training, while significantly reducing communication cost and optimizer-state memory per client.
AI.conclusion: Sharing a low-rank basis across clients within rounds and refreshing this basis across rounds overcomes the subspace fragmentation problem in low-rank federated optimization. FedLore can match or exceed full-parameter federated training accuracy while keeping communication and memory costs low, and it comes with convergence guarantees under standard assumptions, making it a practical and theoretically grounded approach for federated training of foundation models.

title: Measuring the Stability Assumption Behind Action Chunking
summary: Action chunking improves the performance of policies learned by behavioural cloning, and several mechanisms have been proposed to explain why, including temporal consistency, horizon reduction, representation learning, and reduced error compounding. We instead study what happens to an action error once it enters the system. At each state, we inject a small action error and measure how fast it grows or shrinks under two execution regimes: open-loop, where the rest of the chunk is replayed without replanning, and closed-loop, where the policy replans after the perturbation. The fitted rate labels each state as contracting, expanding, or unresolved. Across twelve manipulation tasks from three benchmark suites, we find that confidently stable states are rare, while error amplification is common among states whose propagation rate can be resolved. We further find that the measured propagation rate depends strongly on the fitting horizon: amplification is typically front-loaded, so short windows can overestimate longer-horizon propagation. Finally, we train predictors on these labels and find that a state's open-loop regime can be recovered from camera frames and proprioception alone, while its closed-loop propagation is only partially recoverable because it also depends on how the policy acts after the perturbation. These results suggest that error-compounding arguments alone do not provide a complete account of action chunking: neither passive open-loop dynamics nor policy replanning consistently contracts an injected error, and replanning rarely turns open-loop amplification into confident contraction. This suggests that closed-loop reactivity should be trained explicitly, using perturbation- and tree-coverage-oriented training to expose policies to deviations they must recover from, rather than expected to emerge reliably from standard imitation learning.

AI.tldr: Study measures how small action errors propagate in chunked policies under open- and closed-loop execution, showing error amplification is common and not reliably fixed by replanning.
AI.motivation: Behavioural cloning with action chunking performs better, usually explained via reduced horizon, temporal consistency, or less error compounding, but it is unclear what actually happens to small action errors once they enter the system and how chunking interacts with system dynamics and policy replanning.
AI.method: Inject controlled small action perturbations at different states in manipulation tasks, then execute either open-loop (replay the rest of the chunk without replanning) or closed-loop (policy replans after perturbation). Fit an error growth/decay rate over varying horizons to label states as contracting, expanding, or unresolved, and train predictors from vision+proprioception to infer these regimes.
AI.result: Across 12 manipulation tasks, confidently contracting (stable) states are rare, while error amplification is common among states whose propagation regime is resolvable. Amplification is mostly front-loaded so short fitting windows exaggerate long-horizon growth. Predictors can recover open-loop regimes fairly well from sensory inputs, but closed-loop propagation is only partially predictable because it depends on the policy’s future actions.
AI.conclusion: Error-compounding alone does not fully explain the benefits of action chunking.
