Neither open-loop dynamics nor policy replanning reliably contract injected errors, and replanning seldom converts open-loop amplification into strong contraction. Effective closed-loop reactivity must be trained explicitly via perturbation- and tree-coverage-oriented training to expose policies to deviations, rather than assuming robustness will emerge from standard imitation learning.

title: CoEvolve: Construct-to-Edit Visual Grounding with Bidirectional State Refinement
summary: Visual grounding localizes an object described by language with a bounding box. Most multimodal grounding models compress target identification, spatial reasoning, and boundary estimation into one terminal prediction. Free-form rationales make reasoning linguistically explicit but do not necessarily expose measurable, editable spatial states. Intermediate localization errors are therefore difficult to diagnose and correct, allowing incorrect region choices and imprecise boundaries to persist in the final box. We introduce CoEvolve, a construct-to-edit framework that separates grounding into explicit state construction and state editing. Region-Evolution Reinforcement (RER) organizes grounding analysis into a progressive semantic--spatial trajectory, with each reasoning step committing to an explicit candidate region. Bidirectional Denoising Refiner (BDR) treats the reasoning text as fixed semantic context and refines the trajectory's coordinate fields through bidirectional same-position reconstruction. Geometry- and behavior-level objectives provide target geometry and edit-preference signals for consolidating reliable candidates, preserving accurate inputs, or correcting toward annotations. Evaluations cover natural-image and remote-sensing grounding. With a 9B backbone, CoEvolve rivals models up to 241B parameters in grounding accuracy. Under controlled corruption, a single BDR pass improves mean box overlap by over 27 percentage points, demonstrating strong recovery from substantial localization errors. State-source comparisons further support the complementarity of explicit state construction and source-matched editing. The project is at https://sundongwei.github.io/CoEvolve_Project/.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CoEvolve, a framework for visual grounding that explicitly constructs and then edits localization states, significantly improving bounding-box accuracy and robustness over much larger models.
AI.motivation: Existing visual grounding models entangle reasoning about what the target is, where it is, and how to set precise box boundaries in a single final prediction. Even methods with textual rationales do not expose explicit, editable spatial states, making it hard to diagnose and correct intermediate localization errors, such as picking the wrong region or setting imprecise boundaries. The authors aim to create a grounding process that is decomposed, interpretable at the spatial level, and correctable, so that errors can be detected and refined before the final box output.
AI.method: The authors introduce CoEvolve, a construct-to-edit framework that decomposes visual grounding into two explicit stages: state construction and state editing. First, Region-Evolution Reinforcement (RER) creates a progressive semantic–spatial trajectory in which each reasoning step outputs an explicit candidate region (bounding box), organizing the grounding process as a sequence of interpretable region hypotheses. Second, Bidirectional Denoising Refiner (BDR) takes the reasoning text as fixed semantic context and refines the coordinate fields of those candidate regions via bidirectional same-position reconstruction, effectively denoising and adjusting boxes. They incorporate geometry-level objectives to align predictions with the true target geometry and behavior-level objectives to guide how edits should prefer consolidating reliable candidates, preserving correct inputs, and correcting toward annotations. The framework is evaluated on both natural-image and remote-sensing grounding benchmarks using a 9B-parameter backbone.
AI.result: CoEvolve achieves grounding accuracy comparable to or better than models up to 241B parameters, despite using a substantially smaller 9B backbone, indicating strong parameter efficiency. In controlled corruption experiments where bounding boxes are deliberately degraded, a single pass of the BDR module improves mean box overlap by more than 27 percentage points, showing strong robustness and recovery from significant localization errors. Additional analyses comparing different state sources (constructed vs. edited) demonstrate that explicit state construction and source-matched editing provide complementary benefits.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly decoupling visual grounding into a construct-to-edit process improves both performance and interpretability. By organizing reasoning as a region-evolution trajectory (RER) and then refining spatial states with a bidirectional denoising refiner (BDR), CoEvolve can diagnose and correct intermediate localization errors and achieve competitive results relative to much larger models. The framework’s strong recovery under corruption and the complementary roles of construction and editing suggest that making spatial reasoning states explicit and editable is a powerful paradigm for future grounding systems.

title: vFedProtoQNAS: Prototype-Guided Personalized Quantum Neural Architecture Search for Virtual Federated Learning
summary: Quantum federated learning (QFL) has emerged as a promising approach for collaboratively training compact quantum neural networks (QNNs) over distributed private data on resource-constrained devices. However, differences in device capabilities make a single shared QNN architecture unsuitable for all clients. While personalized quantum neural architecture search (QNAS) allows each client to select a device-specific QNN, averaging parameters across structurally different QNN architectures mixes semantically inconsistent circuit operations. To address this, prototype-guided personalized QNAS for virtual FL (vFedProtoQNAS) is proposed, where model parameters are never aggregated across clients and federated collaboration is achieved through class-wise prototype sharing. Each client independently searches and trains a client-specific QNN, computes class-wise local prototypes from latent representations, and refines them using global prototypes from the server as federated semantic anchors. Experiments demonstrate that vFedProtoQNAS improves accuracy by 3.70\% over FedAvg and enhances class-consistent representation alignment.

AI.tldr: They propose a prototype-guided quantum federated learning framework that avoids aggregating incompatible quantum model parameters by sharing class-wise prototypes instead, improving accuracy and representation alignment.
AI.motivation: In quantum federated learning, clients have different quantum hardware constraints, so a single shared quantum neural network architecture is not suitable for all. Personalized quantum neural architecture search lets clients choose their own architectures, but standard federated averaging breaks down because parameters across different quantum circuits are semantically inconsistent. A new method is needed that supports heterogeneous quantum model architectures while still enabling collaborative learning without sharing raw data.
AI.method: They introduce vFedProtoQNAS, a prototype-guided personalized quantum neural architecture search framework for virtual federated learning. Each client locally searches and trains its own compact, device-specific QNN architecture. Instead of aggregating model parameters, each client computes class-wise prototypes in the latent representation space. These local prototypes are sent to a server, which forms global class-wise prototypes and returns them to clients. Clients then refine their local models by aligning their latent representations with the received global prototypes, using them as semantic anchors, while keeping model parameters and architectures private and unaggregated.
AI.result: Experiments show that vFedProtoQNAS achieves a 3.70% higher accuracy than the standard FedAvg-based quantum FL baseline and yields better alignment of class-consistent representations across clients, indicating more coherent shared semantic structure despite heterogeneous models.
AI.conclusion: Prototype-based collaboration can effectively replace parameter aggregation in heterogeneous quantum federated learning, enabling personalized quantum architectures tailored to each device while still benefiting from federated knowledge sharing. vFedProtoQNAS improves performance and representation consistency, demonstrating a promising direction for scalable, privacy-preserving quantum FL on diverse, resource-constrained quantum hardware.

title: TopK-Guided: Adaptive, Budget-Aware Activation Sparsity for Efficient LLM Inference
summary: Activation sparsity speeds up large language model (LLM) inference by setting unimportant activations to zero so that the corresponding computations can be skipped. Existing training-free methods, however, make different trade-offs: threshold-based methods such as TEAL adapt the sparsity level to each token but do not tightly control the realised sparsity, while TopK-based methods such as WINA enforce a fixed sparsity level but use the same sparsity budget for every token. Both also apply the same budget across transformer blocks, despite large differences in block sensitivity. We introduce TopK-Guided, a training-free method that addresses both limitations by combining bounded token-level sparsity adaptation with sensitivity-aware block-level budget allocation. Across Llama-2 and Llama-3 models, TopK-Guided consistently improves perplexity and downstream accuracy over TEAL and WINA while preserving essentially the same sparsitydependent projection compute as WINA, with the largest gains at high sparsity. Ablations show that both components provide complementary improvements.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes TopK-Guided, a training-free activation sparsity method for LLMs that adaptively assigns sparsity per token and per transformer block, achieving better accuracy at the same compute compared to prior training-free methods like TEAL and WINA.
AI.motivation: Existing training-free activation sparsity methods for LLMs either adapt sparsity per token without tight control over realized sparsity (threshold-based like TEAL) or enforce fixed sparsity with no token adaptivity (TopK-based like WINA). Moreover, they allocate the same sparsity budget across all transformer blocks, ignoring differing block sensitivities. This leads to suboptimal trade-offs between compute savings and model quality. The paper aims to design a method that retains strict control over total sparsity while adapting to token difficulty and block sensitivity to improve perplexity and downstream accuracy at a given compute cost.
AI.method: The authors introduce TopK-Guided, a training-free activation sparsity approach. It combines: (1) a TopK-style mechanism that enforces upper-bounded sparsity while allowing token-level variation in how many activations are kept; and (2) a block-level budget allocation scheme that is sensitivity-aware, assigning different sparsity budgets to different transformer blocks depending on their importance. The method is integrated into LLM inference to zero out less important activations in projection layers, thus skipping their associated computations, while keeping overall sparsity close to a desired target.
AI.result: On Llama-2 and Llama-3 models, TopK-Guided achieves lower perplexity and higher downstream task accuracy compared to prior training-free sparsity methods TEAL and WINA, while using essentially the same amount of sparsity-dependent projection computation as WINA. The improvements are especially pronounced at high sparsity levels. Ablation studies show that both components—token-level bounded TopK adaptation and sensitivity-aware block budgeting—each provide benefits and work together to obtain the best performance.
AI.conclusion: TopK-Guided effectively improves the quality–compute trade-off for activation-sparse LLM inference without any retraining. By combining bounded token-level sparsity adaptation with sensitivity-aware block-level budget allocation, it maintains strict control of compute costs while achieving better perplexity and downstream accuracy than state-of-the-art training-free baselines, particularly at aggressive sparsity settings. Both main design elements are necessary and complementary.

title: VideoEvolve: Evolving Agent Harnesses for Video Temporal Grounding
summary: Video temporal grounding aims to localize events in videos from natural-language queries. For agents built around frozen video-language models, the harness determines how queries guide temporal predictions and how those predictions are refined. Manually refining these harnesses requires diagnosing grounding failures and coordinating changes to both agent workflows and instructions. We introduce VideoEvolve, a framework that automatically evolves agent harnesses for video temporal grounding. VideoEvolve uses a Cloze-Structured Harness Representation that preserves stage interfaces while leaving agent workflows and instructions open to evolution. Branch-Guided Harness Evolution preserves promising code branches for continued refinement, using execution feedback to guide local edits and validation to determine which improvements are carried forward. Experiments demonstrate improved grounding performance across multiple benchmarks. Component analyses identify instruction refinement as a consistent source of gains, while the benefits of evolved code vary across evaluation settings. Together, these results support automated harness evolution as an effective approach to improving video temporal grounding. Code is available at https://github.com/bingjunluo/VideoEvolve .

AI.tldr: The paper proposes VideoEvolve, a framework that automatically evolves the agent harness (workflows + instructions) used with frozen video-language models to improve video temporal grounding performance.
AI.motivation: Existing video temporal grounding systems that use frozen video-language models rely heavily on manually designed and tuned agent harnesses (workflows, prompts, control logic). Improving these harnesses is labor-intensive, requires expert diagnosis of grounding failures, and demands careful coordination between workflow changes and instruction/prompt updates. There is a need for an automated way to refine these harnesses to boost grounding accuracy without retraining large models or performing extensive manual engineering.
AI.method: The authors introduce VideoEvolve, which represents the agent harness with a Cloze-Structured Harness Representation that maintains fixed interfaces between stages while allowing the internal workflows and natural-language instructions to be flexibly modified. They then apply Branch-Guided Harness Evolution: starting from an initial harness, the system proposes local edits to workflows and instructions, executes these variants on data to collect feedback, and keeps promising branches for further refinement. Validation performance decides which evolved harnesses are retained and propagated to the next evolution steps. This creates an automated search process over harness code and instructions guided by execution outcomes.
AI.result: Across multiple video temporal grounding benchmarks, VideoEvolve yields better grounding performance compared to the initial manually designed harnesses. Ablation and component analyses show that improvements consistently stem from refined natural-language instructions, while the gains from code/workflow evolution are more dependent on the particular evaluation conditions and are less uniformly beneficial.
AI.conclusion: Automated evolution of agent harnesses—especially their instructions—offers an effective, model-agnostic path to improving video temporal grounding when using frozen video-language models. The proposed VideoEvolve framework, with its cloze-structured representation and branch-guided evolution process, can systematically refine workflows and prompts to achieve higher grounding accuracy without manual tuning or model retraining.

title: RealCompanion: Benchmarking Human Understanding from Reasoning over Longitudinal Real-World Conversations
summary: A companion that talks with a person for months should come to understand them. It should remember what they said, infer who they are, and know when the past bears on the message in front of it. Testing this requires a real person's record, and such records are private, so benchmarks generate the person and the questions and settle in advance what matters. We release \bench, ten real relationships with an AI companion: 27,218 messages over up to 120 days, released as the conversation and four files derived from it, a profile, a persona, a chat ground truth and a question set, each citing the messages it rests on. Every chat label carries the reasoning trace that produced it, checked stage by stage against the conversation. Three findings follow. First, the past is rarely needed and far away. Pooled measures mislead: a recency window finds the required message for 95.9\% of probes and 2.2\% of those that need memory, and at the natural rate 96\% of the gain from supplying recorded evidence comes from messages that need none. Second, no detector we tried can tell when memory is needed on real messages, authored questions over the same histories leak the cue, and labeling the same messages as memories raises their use by ten to fourteen points. Third, three agent systems reconstruct the persona with the same F1 at a 31-fold difference in cost.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a real-world benchmark, \bench, built from long-term human–AI companion conversations, to study how well AI systems can remember, infer, and use personal information over time.
AI.motivation: Existing memory benchmarks for conversational AI usually rely on synthetic or pre-scripted personas and questions, which fail to capture the complexity and privacy constraints of real, months-long human–AI relationships. The authors want to understand what kind of past information truly matters in realistic companion settings, how often it is needed, whether models can detect when to use memory, and how costly it is to reconstruct user persona information.
AI.method: The authors collect 27,218 messages from ten real human–AI companion relationships over up to 120 days. From each dialogue, they derive four structured artifacts: (1) a profile of the user, (2) a more detailed persona, (3) a set of ground-truth memory labels for chat messages, and (4) a question set probing what the model should know, each explicitly linked back to supporting messages. Every label is accompanied by a step-by-step reasoning trace verified against the conversation. They then run analyses and memory-agent systems to: (a) measure how far back relevant past messages tend to be, (b) evaluate automatic detectors for when memory is needed, and (c) compare three multi-agent systems on persona reconstruction quality versus cost.
AI.result: (1) Relevant past information, when needed, is typically found within a relatively short recency window; this window recovers the key supporting message for 95.9% of probes and 2.2% of probes that explicitly require memory, and in natural deployment settings, 96% of the performance gains from adding evidence come from messages that actually do not require memory. (2) Existing detectors cannot reliably identify when memory is needed on real user messages; human-authored questions over the same histories reveal cues that make the task artificially easier, and merely labeling messages as memories substantially increases how often they are used (by about 10–14 percentage points). (3) Three different agent-based systems achieve similar F1 scores on persona reconstruction, but differ by a factor of 31× in computational cost.
AI.conclusion: Realistic, long-term human–AI companion data reveals that (a) most conversational turns do not need long-range memory and when memory is needed it is usually recent, (b) detecting memory-neededness in-the-wild is much harder than benchmarks with written questions suggest, and (c) systems can reach comparable persona reconstruction quality with very different cost profiles. The \bench dataset provides a grounded benchmark, with traceable labels and reasoning, for developing and evaluating memory mechanisms in conversational agents.

title: Q-Learning for Reachability in MEC-Free MDPs
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) for reachability specifications is fundamental to sequential decision-making. Prior work establishes asymptotic convergence to optimal policies, but only through model-based methods that must explicitly estimate the transition probabilities of the underlying Markov Decision Process (MDP). We present Quasar, the first model-free algorithm with asymptotic guarantees for reachability on the fragment of MDPs free of non-terminal maximal end components (MECs), a building block to which every MDP reduces by the standard MEC quotient. Our algorithm follows the classical Q-learning approach, using temporal-difference updates to converge to an optimal policy without ever learning the transition probabilities. The resulting learner reduces the memory footprint from the O(|S|^2|A|) that model-based methods require to O(|S||A|). On the standardized Quantitative Verification Benchmark Set, our algorithm converges to the optimal policy with orders of magnitude fewer samples than the previous model-based state-of-the-art. Together these results are a concrete step toward the practical deployment of reachability learning and, with it, of specification-guided RL.

AI.tldr: Paper introduces Quasar, a model-free RL algorithm with asymptotic guarantees for reachability in a certain class of MDPs, achieving optimal policies with less memory and fewer samples than model-based methods.
AI.motivation: Existing RL methods for reachability specifications either require explicit model learning (transition probabilities) or only provide asymptotic guarantees in a model-based setting, which is memory-heavy and often sample-inefficient. The authors want a model-free, theoretically guaranteed, and practical algorithm for reachability tasks, which are central in specification-guided RL and verification.
AI.method: They propose Quasar, a model-free Q-learning-style algorithm tailored to MDPs without non-terminal maximal end components (MECs). It uses temporal-difference updates to estimate reachability values directly from interaction, without estimating transition probabilities. The algorithm works on the MEC-quotient fragment of general MDPs and requires storing only state-action value estimates, reducing memory from O(|S|^2|A|) to O(|S||A|).
AI.result: Quasar is proven to asymptotically converge to an optimal policy for reachability on MDPs without non-terminal MECs. Empirically, on the Quantitative Verification Benchmark Set, it reaches the optimal policy using orders of magnitude fewer samples than the best existing model-based methods, while using significantly less memory.
AI.conclusion: Quasar provides the first model-free RL algorithm with asymptotic optimality guarantees for reachability objectives on a key fragment of MDPs, drastically reducing memory and improving sample efficiency compared to model-based approaches. This advances the feasibility of specification-guided RL and points toward scalable, practical deployment of reachability-based learning in verification-oriented applications.

title: Not All Experience Belongs in the Weights: Component Routing for Self-Improving GUI Agents
summary: Self-improving GUI agents keep the trajectories they produce and return them to the agent, by fine-tuning or by retrieval into the prompt, and studies that compare the two destinations disagree. We attribute this to the unit of experience: a trajectory bundles items with different properties, so a conclusion about the bundle depends on its mix. To address this, (i) we introduce component routing, which splits the experience into locators, procedures, state facts and lessons and sends each component to the context or to the weights, compared on the same items across three backbone families, two environments and three seeds. One pool has two destinations: locators and lessons win in the weights, procedures and state facts in the context. (ii) We fit a rule in two properties measured before any training, recurrence and state-conditionality; it recovers the destination of a held-out backbone family in 24 of 24 cells, two interventions move a component toward the boundary, and routing by the rule beats every whole-trajectory baseline and, by +3.5 points on average, the better single destination of each backbone. (iii) We identify how training and producer-consumer differences change the value of the two destinations: note readout decreases after the same component is written into the weights, most for the items that recur most, context gains increase with the information gap, and weights gains decrease with the policy gap. Code and data will be released.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how self-improving GUI agents should store and reuse their past trajectories, decomposing trajectories into components and deciding for each whether to store it in model weights or in context, finding that different types of information benefit from different destinations and proposing a predictive routing rule.
AI.motivation: Existing work on self-improving GUI agents reuses past trajectories either by fine-tuning model weights or by retrieving trajectories into the prompt context, but prior comparisons disagree on which is better. The authors observe that a trajectory mixes heterogeneous information (e.g., where to click vs. abstract lessons), so any aggregate comparison can be confounded by the composition of that mix. They aim to disentangle these factors and systematically decide which parts of the experience should go into weights versus context.
AI.method: The authors propose 'component routing': instead of treating a full trajectory as a single unit, they decompose it into four components—locators (where to act in the GUI), procedures (action sequences), state facts (observed environment facts), and lessons (higher-level insights). For each component, they experimentally compare two destinations: (1) writing it into model weights via fine-tuning, or (2) storing it for retrieval in the prompt context. They evaluate across three backbone model families, two environments, and three random seeds, and analyze performance in a controlled 'two-destination' setting. They also define two pre-training properties of components—recurrence and state-conditionality—and fit a simple rule that predicts the optimal destination based on these properties. They validate the rule on a held-out backbone family, test causal interventions that shift components toward the decision boundary, and compare routing-by-rule against baselines that send whole trajectories or all components to a single destination. Finally, they study producer-consumer dynamics, measuring how training and usage change the relative value of weights vs. context for a component, including effects of information gap and policy gap.
AI.result: Empirically, they find that when the same pool of items can be routed either to weights or context, locators and lessons yield better performance when encoded in weights, whereas procedures and state facts perform better when stored in the context. A rule derived from pre-training measurements of recurrence and state-conditionality perfectly predicts the optimal destination for a held-out backbone across 24 test cells. Interventions that alter these properties move components toward the predicted routing boundary. Routing by this rule outperforms all whole-trajectory baselines and also beats, by an average of 3.5 points, the best single-destination choice per backbone. Additional analysis reveals that the marginal usefulness of context decreases after the same information is written into the weights, particularly for highly recurring items; that context-based gains grow with the information gap between producer and consumer; and that weight-based gains shrink as the policy gap widens.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that experience from self-improving GUI agents should not be stored monolithically at the trajectory level. Different information types are better suited to different destinations: some should be baked into model weights while others should remain in retrievable context. A simple rule based on recurrence and state-conditionality can automatically route components effectively, generalizing across model families and outperforming both naive and strong baselines. Understanding producer-consumer dynamics further clarifies when each destination is more valuable. This suggests future self-improving systems should treat trajectories as structured experience and use principled routing to maximize learning efficiency and performance.

title: LineupRL: Verifiable Reinforcement Learning for Time Series Captioning via Caption-to-Series Identification
summary: Time series captioning is a fundamental step in time series understanding and can also serve as the bridge between signal and natural language. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) relies on a larger model's captions and cannot exceed their quality. Reinforcement learning (RL) can, but its rewards were designed for other modalities and other tasks, and they transfer poorly to open-ended generation in the time series domain. We address this by proposing LineupRL, a reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) pipeline whose reward is caption-to-series identification. The reward model is a frozen large language model (LLM) verifier that reads the generated caption and the candidate time series as raw values, never the chart, and must pick the described time series from multiple distractors. Matching is a far lighter demand on the verifier than writing questions or judging a caption, so an off-the-shelf LLM can supply the reward. Across two captioning benchmarks, and on forecasting and reconstruction where the predictor sees only the caption, LineupRL outperforms SFT and RL baselines on every metric. The 3B vision language model (VLM) trained by LineupRL also outperforms, at 1/24 of the parameters, the 72B VLM whose captions the SFT baseline is distilled from. Our case study shows that LineupRL resists reward hacking, and that the captioner it trains both traces the trend and names the values at key points.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces LineupRL, a reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards framework for time series captioning, using an LLM-based caption-to-series identification reward to train a compact VLM that surpasses both SFT and RL baselines and even the larger teacher model.
AI.motivation: Existing time series captioning methods either rely on supervised fine-tuning from larger models and thus cannot exceed teacher quality, or employ RL with rewards designed for other modalities (e.g., images, text) that transfer poorly to open-ended caption generation for time series. There is a need for a reward mechanism that is both aligned with the time series domain and robust, enabling smaller models to surpass their teachers without requiring expensive human annotation or complex, brittle reward engineering.
AI.method: The authors propose LineupRL, an RL-with-verifiable-rewards (RLVR) pipeline where the reward is defined as a caption-to-series identification task. A frozen off-the-shelf LLM serves as a verifier: it is given the generated caption and several candidate time series (represented as raw numerical values rather than charts) and must choose which series the caption describes. The RL agent (a 3B-parameter vision-language model) is trained to produce captions that maximize the verifier’s identification accuracy. Because the verifier only has to perform matching rather than generate content or nuanced judgments, its use as a reward model is simpler and more robust. The authors compare LineupRL against SFT (distillation from a 72B VLM) and other RL baselines on captioning, forecasting, and reconstruction tasks, where in the latter two the downstream model observes only the caption as input.
AI.result: On two time series captioning benchmarks, LineupRL consistently outperforms supervised fine-tuning and alternative RL baselines across all reported metrics. In downstream forecasting and reconstruction tasks where the predictor receives only the caption, LineupRL-trained captions yield better performance than captions from competing methods. Moreover, the 3B VLM trained via LineupRL surpasses the 72B teacher VLM whose captions are used for the SFT baseline, demonstrating that the RLVR approach can train a smaller model to exceed its teacher. The authors’ case study further indicates that LineupRL reduces reward hacking and produces captions that accurately describe both overall trends and specific values at important time points.
AI.conclusion: LineupRL demonstrates that reinforcement learning with a verifiable, caption-to-series identification reward can effectively train time series captioning models that are both more accurate and more robust than those obtained through standard SFT or conventional RL rewards. By leveraging an off-the-shelf frozen LLM as a simple verifier operating on raw series values, the method avoids complex reward engineering and enables a compact 3B VLM to outperform a much larger 72B teacher. The approach appears resistant to common RL pathologies such as reward hacking and produces captions useful not only for human interpretation but also as inputs for downstream forecasting and reconstruction tasks, suggesting a promising direction for aligning generative models with time series understanding via verifiable rewards.

title: AI-assisted mitotic counting improves reproducibility and efficiency across multiple tumour types
summary: Mitotic counting is an important component of tumour grading, diagnosis and prognostic assessment across several tumour types, but manual assessment is time-consuming and subject to inter-pathologist variability. To help address these challenges, we developed MitPro, an AI tool designed to improve consistency and efficiency by directing pathologists towards regions with the highest predicted mitotic activity and highlighting mitotic figures for review, while retaining pathologist control over region selection and the final count. We evaluated its effect on the reproducibility and efficiency of mitotic counting in a retrospective, non-interventional, paired reader study comprising 385 whole-slide images from 3 centres in 3 countries and 7 tumour types using 3 different scanners. 13 pathologists participated, with each slide assessed independently by 3 pathologists without AI assistance and again with AI assistance after a minimum 2 week washout period. Across all slides, AI-assisted counting increased the intraclass correlation coefficient from 0.589 to 0.949. Mean pathologist-level median assessment time decreased from 286.4 to 127.8 seconds, corresponding to an average saving of 151.8 seconds per assessment. Improvements in agreement and efficiency were also observed in supporting analyses using HALO AP and Sectra image management systems and in 2 additional tumour types outside the main study population. AI-assisted assessment was associated with a subtle shift towards higher mitotic counts and scores, consistent with identification of more active mitotic hotspots and fewer missed mitotic figures. The frequency of score change between unassisted and AI-assisted assessment was comparable with inter-pathologist variation during routine counting. These findings support the use of MitPro as an assistive tool for more consistent and efficient mitotic assessment in routine practice.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates MitPro, an AI tool that guides pathologists to mitotic hotspots and highlights mitoses, showing it substantially improves consistency and speed of mitotic counting while keeping the pathologist in control.
AI.motivation: Manual mitotic counting is essential for tumour grading and prognosis but is slow, labor-intensive, and suffers from considerable inter-pathologist variability. There is a need for tools that improve reproducibility and efficiency without removing the pathologist from the decision loop or restricting them to rigid, fully automated counts.
AI.method: The authors developed MitPro, an assistive AI system that predicts regions of highest mitotic activity on whole-slide images and highlights candidate mitotic figures. They conducted a retrospective, non-interventional, paired reader study with 385 whole-slide images from 3 centres, 3 scanners, 7 tumour types, and 13 pathologists. Each slide was assessed twice by 3 pathologists: once without AI and once with AI (after at least a 2-week washout). They compared interobserver agreement via intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) and measured assessment time. Additional analyses were run on HALO AP and Sectra platforms and in 2 extra tumour types.
AI.result: With AI assistance, the intraclass correlation coefficient for mitotic counts increased from 0.589 to 0.949, indicating a large improvement in reproducibility. The mean pathologist-level median assessment time decreased from 286.4 to 127.8 seconds, saving about 152 seconds per case. Similar gains were observed across different image management systems and in additional tumour types. AI assistance caused a small shift toward higher counts and scores, suggesting better detection of mitotic hotspots and fewer missed figures. The frequency of score changes with AI was similar to normal inter-pathologist variability.
AI.conclusion: MitPro, as an assistive AI that directs pathologists to mitotic hotspots and highlights mitoses, markedly improves both consistency and efficiency of mitotic counting across multiple centres, scanners, and tumour types while leaving final judgments to the pathologist. The tool appears suitable for integration into routine diagnostic workflows to standardize and speed up mitotic assessment without fundamentally changing clinical grading behavior.

title: Continuous Process-Level Evaluation for Evolving Enterprise AI Agent Skills
comment: Accepted to Workshop on Continual Learning for Enterprise AI Agents (CLEA), NeurIPS 2026
summary: Enterprise AI agent skills evolve as tool APIs, models, and specifications change, yet final-output evaluation can miss process-level behavioral drift. We present a continuous evaluation framework combining outcome-level and process-level checks, applied to Revenue and Productivity variants of a Business Value Determination skill in an enterprise Value Aware Resiliency system. The framework independently computes per-run ground truth, materializes reusable template tests, and evaluates tool selection, arguments, execution order, and database integrity through programmatic checks and a narrowly scoped LLM judge. We evaluate 240 trials across two skills, two specification variants, two agent harnesses, and three models. Of 175 trials passing all applicable final numerical checks, 162 (92.6 percent; Wilson 95 percent CI: 87.7-95.6 percent) contained another evaluator-detected deviation. Under a broader seven-check final-state definition, 151 of 164 passing runs (92.1 percent; 95 percent CI: 86.9-95.3 percent) still violated a trajectory check. Dependency attribution reduced a mean of 6.34 failed checks per run to 2.65 roots. Specification sensitivity varied by model and harness, with exploratory bootstrap interaction intervals excluding zero for all three Revenue comparisons and one of three Productivity comparisons. Runtime-resolved templates provided reusable regression coverage across the evaluated configurations; longitudinal validation under actual API evolution remains future work.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a continuous evaluation framework that tracks not only final answers but also process-level behavior of enterprise AI agents, revealing substantial hidden deviations despite numerically correct outputs.
AI.motivation: Enterprise AI agents operate in evolving environments where tools, models, and specifications continuously change. Traditional evaluation that focuses only on final outputs fails to capture behavioral drift in the agent’s internal decision process, such as tool selection, call ordering, and argument construction. This can compromise reliability, safety, and data integrity even when the final numbers look correct. The authors aim to build an evaluation approach that can detect such hidden process-level deviations and remain robust as systems, APIs, and models evolve.
AI.method: They design a continuous evaluation framework that combines outcome-level checks (e.g., final numerical results) with process-level checks on the agent’s tool-usage trajectory. The framework: (1) computes run-specific ground truth independently, (2) uses runtime-resolved templates to generate reusable tests, and (3) programmatically evaluates tool selection, tool arguments, execution ordering, and database integrity. A narrowly scoped LLM judge is used where rule-based checks are insufficient. They apply this to two AI agent skills (Revenue and Productivity variants of a Business Value Determination skill) within a Value Aware Resiliency system, testing 240 trials across multiple dimensions: two skills, two specification variants, two agent harnesses, and three models. Statistical analysis includes Wilson confidence intervals and bootstrap-based interaction intervals to study specification sensitivity.
AI.result: Among 240 trials, 175 passed all applicable numerical outcome checks, yet 162 of those (92.6%, Wilson 95% CI: 87.7–95.6%) still exhibited at least one process-level deviation. When expanding the definition of a "correct" final state to include seven checks, 164 runs passed, but 151 (92.1%, 95% CI: 86.9–95.3%) still failed some trajectory-based check. Dependency attribution techniques reduced an average of 6.34 failed checks per run to 2.65 root causes, simplifying debugging. Specification sensitivity differed by model and harness; bootstrap interaction intervals excluded zero for all three Revenue comparisons and for one of three Productivity comparisons, indicating meaningful interactions between specs, models, and harnesses. Templates resolved at runtime successfully provided reusable regression coverage across the tested configurations.
AI.conclusion: Outcome-only evaluation is inadequate for enterprise AI agents because a large majority of apparently correct runs harbor process-level deviations in tool usage and data handling. The proposed continuous evaluation framework, which adds trajectory and dependency-aware checks on top of final-state validation, surfaces these issues and helps attribute failures to a smaller set of roots. The approach appears robust across multiple models, harnesses, and specification variants, and template-based tests support regression coverage as systems change. However, the paper notes that extended longitudinal validation under real-world API evolution is still needed, leaving long-term stability and generalizability as future work.

title: Code Owns the Simulation, Jev Owns the Evaluation
comment: 10 pages main text, 20 pages total with appendix; 6 figures, 7 tables. Preprint
summary: Judgment models such as \jev{} return, in a single call and without reasoning text, a probability for each described option. This makes them attractive as an agent's action-selection layer, but it is unclear which decisions they can be trusted with. We test \jev{} on reflection tests, one-shot matrix games, the text game ALFWorld and robot control, and find a sharp boundary. \jev{} succeeds when the right option can be judged from what the input describes, which we call \emph{evaluation}. Specifically, it solves 99\% of the counterintuitive Cognitive Reflection Test questions. However, it fails when the right option depends on \emph{simulation} (i.e., predicting something not in the input), such as the opponent's action or the subgoal that must come first. In games, \jev{} plays suboptimally as if its rational opponent acted at random, because the opponent's action is not given. In ALFWorld, \jev{} favors commands that mention an object or place named in the task description. For example, given the task ``put a clean knife in the drawer'', \jev{} carries an unwashed knife straight to the drawer instead of first washing it at the sink. Surprisingly, many of these failures are not due to a lack of knowledge. Asked separately what the opponent will do, \jev{} usually answers correctly, and it responds well given the opponent's action. It fails when one call must both perform the simulation and evaluate based on it. This suggests letting code make the prediction or simulation. When code supplies it, such as a lookahead in ALFWorld and physics simulation in robot control, \jev{} becomes an expert controller through its general evaluation ability.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates judgment-only language models that output option probabilities without chain-of-thought, finding they are strong evaluators but weak simulators, and shows they excel when paired with external simulation code.
AI.motivation: To understand when probability-only judgment models can be trusted as decision modules in agents, and to characterize the boundary between tasks they solve well vs. those they systematically fail, especially without explicit reasoning traces.
AI.method: The authors empirically test a judgment model (\jev{}) on diverse tasks: cognitive reflection questions, one-shot matrix games, the ALFWorld text environment, and robot control. They categorize tasks into those solvable by direct evaluation of the described options vs. those requiring internal simulation of unobserved events (e.g., opponent moves or action sequences). They probe failure modes and run ablations where relevant predictions are supplied externally by code (e.g., game lookahead, physics simulation).
AI.result: \jev{} achieves near-perfect accuracy (99%) on counterintuitive Cognitive Reflection Test items and performs well whenever the correct choice can be inferred from the input description alone. It fails sharply on tasks where success depends on simulating hidden dynamics or future states in the same call, such as predicting opponents' actions in games or necessary subgoals in ALFWorld. The model behaves as if opponents were random and often prefers actions mentioning task keywords over correct multi-step plans. Yet, when queried separately, it can usually predict opponents and respond optimally given those predictions. When external code provides simulations (lookahead in ALFWorld, physics in robotics) and the model only evaluates outcomes, performance becomes expert-level.
AI.conclusion: Judgment-only models are highly capable evaluators but unreliable simulators when both prediction and evaluation must occur in a single call. Their strengths emerge when embedded in tool-using agents where external code handles simulation or prediction and the model focuses on comparative evaluation. Agent architectures should therefore separate simulation from evaluation and use judgment models primarily as scoring or selection oracles over simulated outcomes, rather than as sole decision-makers that internally foresee consequences.

title: On the Divergence of Accuracy and Mechanism Consistency in Time Series World Models
summary: A time series world model (TSWM) predicts a controlled system's state from its observed history and planned actions and exogenous inputs. Current approaches build forecasters with actions as covariates, trained and evaluated on prediction error under the executed plan. Yet world models compare unexecuted plans, but their responses to changed plans remain untested. We ask which design choices matter and whether accurate forecasters respond to changed plans as real systems do. We address both with a formalization and benchmark. The formalization separates state, actions and exogenous inputs, distinguishes continuous, mode and event actions, and introduces mechanism consistency, a metric built on declared action-state relations with known directions, such as a vasopressor raising blood pressure: it checks whether shifting an action moves the forecast in the declared direction. The benchmark consolidates eight public datasets with real actions from engineered infrastructure and clinical care, varying prediction space, plan fusion and plan encoding across seven backbones and five seeds. First, a frozen latent prediction space lowers MAE by 9.9% over observation space and gated output fusion lowers it by 12.7% over input concatenation on average, with both improving all eight datasets; temporal plan encoding changes average MAE by at most 2.2%. Second, prediction error and mechanism consistency diverge: the lowest-error configuration is at or below chance in consistency on four of five datasets with declared mechanisms, and no design choice avoids this. Finally, directional supervision, a loss penalizing the wrong-signed part of the response to a shifted action, significantly raises consistency on penalized mechanisms with no change in MAE. Together they give TSWMs a recipe: a frozen latent space and output-side fusion for accuracy, and a training objective for mechanism consistency.

AI.tldr: They design and benchmark time-series world models that not only forecast accurately but also react to action changes in the correct causal direction, introducing a new consistency metric and training loss to align models with known mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Existing time series forecasters for controlled systems treat actions as covariates and are judged purely by prediction error under observed (executed) plans. However, world models are used to compare and evaluate unexecuted plans, so what matters is whether the model changes its predictions in the right way when the plan changes. It is unknown which architectural choices support this and whether low prediction error ensures correct directional response to actions. The authors aim to formalize this setting and provide benchmarks and tools to measure and improve the alignment of model behavior with known action-state mechanisms.
AI.method: They formalize time series world models by explicitly separating system state, actions, and exogenous inputs, and by distinguishing different action types (continuous, mode, event). They define mechanism consistency: given declared qualitative mechanisms with known directional effects (e.g., a vasopressor increasing blood pressure), they test whether increasing an action moves the model’s prediction in the declared direction. They build a benchmark from eight real-world datasets with actual actions (from engineered systems and clinical settings). They systematically vary: (1) prediction space (observation space vs. a frozen latent prediction space), (2) plan fusion strategy (input concatenation vs. output-side gated fusion), and (3) temporal plan encoding, across seven backbone architectures and multiple random seeds. Finally, they introduce directional supervision, a loss term that penalizes only the part of the model’s response to an action that has the wrong sign relative to the declared mechanism, encouraging mechanism-consistent responses without directly optimizing prediction error.
AI.result: Empirically, using a frozen latent prediction space reduces mean absolute error (MAE) by 9.9% compared with predicting directly in observation space, and gated output fusion of plans reduces MAE by 12.7% compared with simple input concatenation; both improvements are consistent across all eight datasets. Temporal plan encoding choices have minimal effect (≤2.2% change in average MAE). Crucially, prediction accuracy and mechanism consistency are not aligned: for four of five datasets with declared mechanisms, the configuration with the lowest prediction error achieves mechanism consistency at or below chance level, and no architectural choice reliably avoids this issue. Adding directional supervision substantially increases mechanism consistency for the mechanisms it penalizes, without affecting MAE.
AI.conclusion: Architectural and training design choices for TSWMs have distinct impacts on predictive accuracy and on whether models react correctly to changes in actions. Using a frozen latent prediction space and gated output fusion improves forecasting accuracy robustly across datasets, but standard training objectives do not ensure that models respect known directional mechanisms between actions and states. Prediction error alone is therefore an insufficient criterion for evaluating world models. Incorporating directional supervision provides a practical way to enforce mechanism consistency without sacrificing accuracy, offering a concrete recipe for building more reliable time series world models that are suitable for comparing and planning alternative control actions.

title: Temporal-Difference Learning for Dragonchess
comment: Springer Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence
summary: Our research investigates how two adaptive AI methods, evolutionary transfer learning and TD(lambda), perform in the three-dimensional chess environment Dragonchess. The game challenges players with its unique board structure and computational load, making it an ideal setting to study how adaptive methods can update evaluation heuristics in novel environments. In this work we re-implement the Dragonchess engine, changing it from a PyGame engine to C++. This enables faster gameplay, allowing us to run 10,000 games with confidence intervals and significance tests, rather than a single small tournament. Both adaptive methods outperform all other agents in the round-robin tournament. Our results showed that there is no significant difference in the performance between the evolved and learned evaluations. This research establishes the efficacy of adaptive methods in structurally complex, novel game domains.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates two adaptive AI methods—evolutionary transfer learning and TD(lambda)—in the complex 3D chess variant Dragonchess, finding that both significantly outperform non-adaptive agents and perform similarly to each other.
AI.motivation: To understand whether adaptive evaluation methods can cope with and excel in a structurally complex, novel game environment like Dragonchess, where traditional fixed heuristics may struggle due to the unusual 3D board and high computational complexity.
AI.method: The authors re-implemented an existing Dragonchess engine from PyGame to C++ for higher performance, enabling large-scale experimentation. They then implemented two adaptive AI techniques—evolutionary transfer learning and TD(lambda)—to update evaluation heuristics. A large round-robin tournament of 10,000 games was run, and results were analyzed with confidence intervals and statistical significance tests to compare the adaptive methods against other agents and against each other.
AI.result: Both evolutionary transfer learning and TD(lambda)-based agents outperformed all non-adaptive agents in the round-robin tournament. Statistical analysis revealed no significant performance difference between the two adaptive methods themselves.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive evaluation methods, whether evolved or learned via TD(lambda), are effective in a complex, novel game domain such as Dragonchess. The lack of significant difference between the two approaches suggests that multiple adaptive paradigms can achieve similar performance in structurally challenging environments, reinforcing the value of adaptivity over fixed heuristics.

title: AVSD-Scenes: A Dataset for Audio-Visual Description of Urban Scenes
summary: Natural language descriptions can provide rich semantic representations of audio-visual urban scenes, yet datasets that jointly describe both auditory and visual information remain limited. In this paper, we introduce AVSD-Scenes, a paired audio-visual scene description dataset for urban environments. The dataset contains 12,291 audio-visual scene descriptions generated from the TAU Urban Audio-Visual Scenes dataset. To construct the dataset, we first generate audio- and visual-based descriptions using Qwen2-Audio-7B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B, respectively. These modality-specific descriptions are then combined using large language models, namely Qwen3-14B, Mistral-Small-3.2-24B-Instruct-2506, and Gemma-3-27B-it, to produce multimodal descriptions that capture complementary information from both modalities. We benchmark AVSD-Scenes using semantic alignment, cross-modal retrieval, scene classification, LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, and human subjective assessment. Results show that multimodal descriptions improve semantic alignment and cross-modal retrieval performance compared with modality-specific descriptions while preserving strong scene-discriminative information. The generated descriptions achieve up to 94.5% accuracy in urban scene classification, while combining audio, visual, and description embeddings further improves accuracy to 95.4%. Furthermore, the descriptions remain highly scene-discriminative even when scene labels are removed from the prompting instructions, indicating that they capture semantic information derived from the audio-visual content rather than merely reflecting label information.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces AVSD-Scenes, a dataset of multimodal natural language descriptions for urban audio-visual scenes, built from TAU Urban Audio-Visual Scenes and evaluated on multiple tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing urban scene datasets rarely provide joint natural language descriptions that fuse both audio and visual information, limiting research on semantic understanding, retrieval, and reasoning over realistic multimodal environments. The authors aim to fill this gap by creating a dataset of rich text descriptions aligned with paired audio-video data.
AI.method: They start from the TAU Urban Audio-Visual Scenes dataset and automatically generate separate audio-only and video-only descriptions using Qwen2-Audio-7B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B. Then, larger LLMs (Qwen3-14B, Mistral-Small-3.2-24B-Instruct-2506, Gemma-3-27B-it) are used to fuse these modality-specific descriptions into unified multimodal descriptions that capture complementary information. They then benchmark the dataset on semantic alignment, cross-modal retrieval, scene classification, LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, and human studies.
AI.result: The fused multimodal descriptions outperform audio-only or visual-only descriptions in semantic alignment and cross-modal retrieval tasks. Scene classification using only the generated descriptions reaches up to 94.5% accuracy, and combining audio, visual, and text embeddings further improves accuracy to 95.4%. Even when explicit scene labels are removed from prompts, the descriptions remain highly scene-discriminative, indicating that they encode semantics grounded in the underlying audio-visual content rather than copying labels.
AI.conclusion: AVSD-Scenes is an effective automatically constructed dataset that provides rich, scene-discriminative multimodal descriptions for urban audio-visual data. The multimodal fusion approach yields descriptions that enhance alignment and retrieval tasks and remain robustly grounded in the audio-visual content, offering a valuable resource for multimodal understanding and downstream applications in urban scenes.

title: Mapping the RAG Landscape: A Four Axis Taxonomy of Efficiency, Defense, Interactivity, and Reasoning
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable fluency across many tasks but remain limited by their static, parameter bound knowledge and their susceptibility to hallucinating information. Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) addresses these issues by incorporating external retrieval into the generation process, grounding model outputs in verifiable and up to date sources. While prior surveys primarily focus on core RAG architectures and standard pipelines, recent research explores broader challenges and capabilities that extend beyond these foundational designs. This survey provides a consolidated and structured examination of contemporary RAG developments, organizing the field into a four axis taxonomy: improving retrieval efficiency, strengthening robustness and security, supporting user driven and interactive workflows, and enabling multi step or complex reasoning. We formalize key components of the RAG framework and review methods spanning dense and sparse retrieval, fusion strategies, embedding optimizations, and reinforcement learning based retrieval policies, highlighting how these advances influence practical deployment and system design. We also synthesize evaluation practices, domain specific applications, and architectural variants such as Naive, Advanced, and Modular RAG. Finally, we outline persistent challenges related to retrieval quality, reliability, domain adaptation, scalability, and explainability, and identify opportunities for building RAG systems that are more reliable, adaptable, and transparent.

AI.tldr: Survey of recent advances in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), presenting a taxonomy of methods and challenges for making RAG systems more efficient, robust, interactive, and capable of complex reasoning.
AI.motivation: LLMs are powerful but limited by static, parametric knowledge and prone to hallucinations. RAG mitigates this by grounding generation in external, up-to-date sources, but the space of methods, challenges, and new capabilities has grown beyond classic RAG pipelines. There is a need to systematically organize and synthesize these developments to guide research and practical system design.
AI.method: The paper conducts a structured literature survey of contemporary RAG work. It formalizes a generic RAG framework and proposes a four-axis taxonomy: (1) improving retrieval efficiency, (2) strengthening robustness and security, (3) supporting user-driven and interactive workflows, and (4) enabling multi-step or complex reasoning. It reviews techniques including dense and sparse retrieval, fusion strategies, embedding optimization, and RL-based retrieval policies, and compares architectural variants such as Naive, Advanced, and Modular RAG, along with evaluation practices and domain-specific applications.
AI.result: The survey organizes diverse RAG research into a coherent taxonomy, mapping existing methods and systems to the four axes and to specific RAG components. It clarifies how retrieval choices, fusion mechanisms, and learning strategies affect deployment trade-offs (efficiency, reliability, adaptability). It compiles current evaluation methodologies and highlights domain-specific patterns and architectural variants, providing a structured reference for practitioners and researchers.
AI.conclusion: RAG has evolved from basic retrieval+generation pipelines into a rich design space involving efficiency, robustness/security, interactivity, and complex reasoning. Despite progress, key challenges persist in retrieval quality, reliability, domain adaptation, scalability, and explainability. Addressing these will be central to building RAG systems that are more reliable, adaptable, and transparent, and the proposed taxonomy and synthesis aim to guide future research and practical system design.

title: Counterfactual Auditing of Bias in Open-Source Large Language Models for Clinical Triage
summary: Emergency department (ED) triage is a high-stakes prioritization task in which demographic, socioeconomic, and system-context information may improperly influence acuity assignment. Although open-source large language models (LLMs) are increasingly considered for local and privacy-preserving clinical decision support, it remains unclear how counterfactual bias varies across model families, sizes, medical-domain models, and domain-adapted models. We present a comparative counterfactual audit of ten open-source LLMs for pediatric Emergency Severity Index (ESI) prediction. Starting from real and handbook-style clinical vignettes, we construct paired counterfactual variants that change only one injected demographic, socioeconomic, healthcare-access, behavioral, social, or system-context variable while holding the clinical presentation fixed. Models include Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, a QLoRA fine-tuned Qwen2.5-7B, MedGemma variants, MedLLaMA2-7B, GPT-OSS-20B, and GPT-OSS-120B. We measure any counterfactual shift, undertriage, overtriage, shifts greater than one ESI level, mean shift, and mean absolute shift. Counterfactual sensitivity varied substantially and did not consistently decrease with larger model size or medical-domain pretraining. The fine-tuned Qwen2.5-7B showed the lowest overall sensitivity, with a 5.27% any-shift rate and mean absolute shift of 0.0534, versus 16.02% and 0.1706 for the base model. Several larger or medical-domain models showed more significant shifts. Stratified and correlation analyses further revealed clinically important directionality and shared failure patterns hidden by aggregate rates. These findings support counterfactual auditing as a lightweight, clinically interpretable framework for comparing fairness risks in open-source LLMs before clinical deployment.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how much different open-source LLMs change their emergency department triage decisions when only non-clinical context (e.g., demographics, socioeconomic factors) is altered, revealing substantial, model-dependent counterfactual bias and highlighting counterfactual auditing as a practical fairness assessment tool before clinical deployment.
AI.motivation: ED triage decisions are critical and should be based on clinical acuity, but may be inappropriately influenced by demographic, social, or system-context information. As open-source LLMs are increasingly considered for privacy-preserving clinical decision support, there is a need to systematically understand and compare how sensitive these models are to non-clinical attributes that should not affect medical urgency, across different model families, sizes, and domain adaptations.
AI.method: The authors perform a comparative counterfactual audit of ten open-source LLMs on pediatric Emergency Severity Index (ESI) prediction. Starting from real and handbook-style clinical vignettes, they generate counterfactual pairs by modifying a single non-clinical attribute (demographic, socioeconomic, healthcare access, behavioral, social, or system-context variable) while keeping the actual clinical presentation constant. For each model, they compute multiple metrics capturing counterfactual sensitivity: any change in ESI, undertriage, overtriage, changes greater than one level, mean shift, and mean absolute shift. They compare base, larger, medical-domain-pretrained, and domain-adapted (fine-tuned) variants, including Qwen2.5, MedGemma, MedLLaMA2, and GPT-OSS models. They also perform stratified and correlation analyses to uncover directional and patterned biases not visible in aggregate statistics.
AI.result: Counterfactual sensitivity to non-clinical factors varies markedly across models. Contrary to a common assumption, larger model size or medical-domain pretraining do not reliably reduce such sensitivity; in fact, some larger or medical-specific models exhibit stronger counterfactual shifts. A QLoRA fine-tuned Qwen2.5-7B model shows the lowest overall sensitivity, reducing any-shift rate from 16.02% in the base model to 5.27%, and mean absolute shift from 0.1706 to 0.0534 in ESI levels. Stratified and correlation analyses reveal clinically meaningful directional effects and shared failure modes (e.g., consistent over- or undertriage for certain contextual changes) that are obscured when looking only at overall shift rates.
AI.conclusion: Different open-source LLMs exhibit heterogeneous and sometimes substantial counterfactual sensitivity to non-clinical context in ED triage predictions, and improvements in size or medical-domain pretraining do not guarantee fairer behavior. Lightweight domain adaptation (e.g., QLoRA fine-tuning) can materially reduce such sensitivity but does not eliminate it. Counterfactual auditing using paired vignettes is a feasible, interpretable approach for stress-testing and comparing fairness risks of LLM-based clinical decision support tools and should be incorporated into model evaluation pipelines prior to any clinical deployment.

title: Can AI Oversight Be Zero Knowledge?
summary:
AI systems increasingly produce outputs from confidential data, such as a fitness-for-duty assessment from medical records or the predicted properties of a drug candidate from its secret structure. It is important to verify that such outputs are correct without revealing the underlying data. A recent line of work studies verification of AI outputs via interactive proofs and debate for oracle-aided computation, where correctness may depend on an oracle such as human judgment, a physical experiment, or the web. These works focus on verification by a verifier that runs much faster than the computation. However, such efficient verification is impossible for general oracle-aided computation, and these works therefore rely on additional assumptions. We focus instead on privacy: allowing the verifier to run in time polynomial in the computation, we ask whether interactive arguments for oracle-aided computation can be zero knowledge, so that the verifier learns nothing about the confidential data beyond the correctness of the output.
  We prove that, in general, they cannot. In the random oracle model, there are no zero-knowledge proofs for all oracle-aided computations, even if both the prover and the verifier are allowed to run much longer than the computation itself. The impossibility extends to debate, a canonical model for scalable oversight.
  On the positive side, we show that if the oracle attaches a cryptographic signature to each of its answers, then every oracle-aided computation can be verified in zero knowledge with an efficient prover and verifier, assuming only collision-resistant hash functions. Beyond privacy, this also gives an alternative approach to scalable oversight that relies neither on an honest opponent, as in debate, nor on the robustness of the computation, as in prior single-prover protocols.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether we can verify AI outputs that depend on confidential, oracle-derived data in a way that reveals nothing about that data. It proves broad impossibility results for zero-knowledge verification of general oracle-aided computations in the random oracle model, but also presents a positive construction if oracle answers are signed, using only collision-resistant hashes.
AI.motivation: AI systems often operate on confidential inputs (e.g., medical records, proprietary molecule structures) yet their outputs may need to be checked by external parties. Existing interactive-proof and debate-based verification schemes focus on efficiency (verifier much faster than the underlying computation) and make strong extra assumptions, and they typically ignore privacy of the underlying data. The authors want to understand when it is cryptographically possible to have verification protocols that are both sound and privacy-preserving (zero knowledge) for computations that rely on external oracles like humans, experiments, or the web.
AI.method: The authors work in a formal model of oracle-aided computation and interactive arguments. They analyze zero-knowledge properties in the random oracle model and prove impossibility results: that no zero-knowledge proof/argument system can exist for all such computations, even with unbounded prover and verifier time. They extend this to debate protocols (multi-agent oversight). On the constructive side, they modify the oracle model by requiring that each oracle response be accompanied by a cryptographic signature. Under this assumption and using standard tools like collision-resistant hash functions, they design generic zero-knowledge verification protocols for any oracle-aided computation with polynomial-time prover and verifier.
AI.result: 1) Impossibility: In the random oracle model, there is no zero-knowledge proof/argument system that can verify correctness for every oracle-aided computation without leaking information, even if computational resources are large. This impossibility covers both single-prover settings and debate-based scalable oversight. 2) Possibility with signed oracles: If every oracle answer comes with a cryptographic signature, then there exists a zero-knowledge interactive argument system for all oracle-aided computations, with efficient prover and verifier, assuming only collision-resistant hash functions. This protocol ensures the verifier learns nothing beyond the correctness of the claimed output. 3) Conceptual result: This yields a new approach to scalable oversight of AI systems that does not depend on an honest debating agent or robustness assumptions about the model’s computation.
AI.conclusion: Zero-knowledge verification of general oracle-aided computations is fundamentally impossible under standard random-oracle-style assumptions if the oracle is completely unstructured. However, modest structure—specifically, signed oracle responses—restores the possibility of efficient, fully private verification based on minimal cryptographic assumptions. This reframes how scalable oversight protocols for AI should be designed: rather than relying on debate or robustness alone, they can leverage cryptographically authenticated oracle information to achieve both correctness and privacy guarantees.

title: Mingbird: A Local-First Agent Harness Enabling Small Open Models to Complete Real Tasks
comment: 44 pages, 9 figures. Code, benchmark protocol, scoring code, and all 288 per-cell results: https://github.com/Mingbird/Mingbird-agent
summary: Small open-weight models (2-9B) run on ordinary laptops, but under cloud-scale agent harnesses they rarely complete real tasks: tool prefill overflows the context, self-correction diverges, tool demonstrations loop, and tasks are silently abandoned. We present evidence, from a controlled single-machine comparison and one third-party benchmark, that a substantial share of these failures is attributable to the harness rather than the model. We introduce Mingbird, a local-first agent harness for Windows and Ollama whose ten mechanisms compensate point-by-point for small-model failure forms, three of them representative: a byte-level net-zero prefill budget, a finish gate that re-reads the task before accepting completion, and signature-level loop detection. On LRAB, a controlled comparison holding machine, models, budgets, and scoring fixed (4 harnesses $\times$ 4 open models (2B-35B) $\times$ 18 real tasks, deterministic artifact scoring), Mingbird reaches 0.886 overall against 0.631 (goose), 0.479 (opencode), and 0.405 (agent-mini), with all 288 cells published; on $τ^2$-bench (278 tasks, three arms, one protocol) it totals 0.856 against 0.791 and 0.737; and a frontier-model probe on the same 18 tasks spans 0.997 to 0.478 across harnesses, with well-formed scaffolds staying within 0.072 of each other. A leave-one-mechanism-out ablation is reported as directional only: same-night replications of the same arm move its mean by up to 0.069, the size of every nominal single-trial delta, and the one batch-matched comparison (full mechanism stack versus text re-read alone) gives the executable completion guards a paired +0.10 across three replications. The evidence carries stated limits: a self-built benchmark, a single machine, and single-trial scoring.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Mingbird, an agent harness designed to make small open-weight language models (2–9B) reliably complete real-world tasks on local machines by addressing harness-induced failure modes.
AI.motivation: Although small open-weight models can run on consumer hardware, they often fail to complete practical tasks when used under existing cloud-scale agent harnesses. These failures—such as context overflow, divergent self-correction, looping tools, and silently abandoned tasks—appear to stem largely from the harness design rather than model capability. The authors aim to isolate and quantify this effect and to design a harness that systematically mitigates these failure patterns so small models become practically useful on local setups.
AI.method: The authors design Mingbird, a local-first agent harness for Windows and Ollama, implementing ten mechanisms targeted at known small-model failure modes. Key mechanisms include: (1) a byte-level net-zero prefill budget to prevent context overflow while still providing necessary tool prefill; (2) a finish gate that forces the agent to re-read and verify the task before declaring completion; and (3) signature-level loop detection to stop repeated tool invocation patterns. They evaluate Mingbird on two benchmarks. First, LRAB: a controlled, single-machine benchmark varying 4 harnesses × 4 open models (2B–35B) × 18 real tasks, with constant compute budgets and deterministic artifact scoring, yielding 288 experimental cells. Second, τ^2-bench: 278 tasks under a fixed three-arm protocol. They also run a frontier-model probe on the same 18 tasks across harnesses. Finally, they conduct a leave-one-mechanism-out ablation, acknowledging limitations due to run-to-run variance.
AI.result: On LRAB, Mingbird achieves an overall score of 0.886, substantially outperforming other harnesses: goose (0.631), opencode (0.479), and agent-mini (0.405), under identical conditions. On τ^2-bench, Mingbird reaches 0.856 vs. 0.791 and 0.737 for the comparison harnesses. In the frontier-model probe, scores range from 0.997 to 0.478 across harnesses, but when using well-formed scaffolds, results stay within 0.072 of each other, suggesting the harness dominates small-model performance while large models are less sensitive. The ablation study is inconclusive beyond directional hints: same-night replications vary by up to 0.069 (similar to single-trial deltas), but a batch-matched comparison shows that adding the full mechanism stack on top of text re-read alone yields an average +0.10 gain in executable completion rate over three replications.
AI.conclusion: The study argues that many observed failures of small open-weight models in agentic settings are attributable to harness design, not inherent model weakness. Mingbird’s targeted mechanisms significantly improve task completion rates on local hardware, narrowing the performance gap with stronger models when the harness is well designed. However, the evidence is limited by reliance on a self-constructed benchmark, a single machine, and primarily single-trial scoring, so broader generalization requires further study.

title: A Comparative Explainability Framework for DeBERTa-v3 in Zero-Shot Medical Abstract Classification
summary: A comparative explainability framework is presented to audit DeBERTa-v3 under zero-shot classification of medical abstracts. The work addresses the disagreement problem in Explainable Artificial Intelligence, where different attribution methods produce divergent explanations for the same input and prediction.
